Sports.title: Rio Ferdinand claps back at fans mocking him for celebrating Man United's late equaliser against Aston Villa which left them in the relegation zone
Sports.content:
Rio Ferdinand claps back at fans mocking him for celebrating Man United's late equaliser against Aston Villa which left them in the relegation zone

Rio Ferdinand has hit back at football fans who criticised his reaction on social media to Manchester United's 4-4 draw with Aston Villa.

Former United defender Ferdinand drew criticism when he shared a photo of himself celebrating after the Red Devils' dramatic comeback on Sunday afternoon.

Michael Carrick's side had looked down and out at 4-2 in stoppage time, but late strikes from Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu meant they earned a point from the game.

They did, though, remain in the relegation zone – however Ferdinand shared two snaps to his X account following full-time.

The first showed the 48-year-old with his head in his hands, and the second saw him celebrating. He captioned the post: 'From this to THIS!!! Carrick time!!!!!!!!!! Birthday weekend just got (a) tad better in the last 6 minutes…'

Fans though flooded the replies with criticism, questioning why he was 'celebrating a draw' and calling him an 'embarrassment'. Ferdinand, though, has now taken the opportunity to respond.

Rio Ferdinand has hit back at fans who criticised his response to Manchester United's draw with Aston Villa

'Let me just address something,' Ferdinand began on Rio Ferdinand Presents. 'On socials I put a picture up and little comment underneath of me going like that (celebrates).

'That's not me celebrating a point against Aston Villa, by the way, it's me celebrating a moment in a football match. It's what football does to you. It can take over your body, take over your emotions in a moment. That moment isn't the big picture.

'So all of these people saying his standards have dropped and he's celebrating a draw... I'm not celebrating a draw against Villa, I'm celebrating the moment and the fact we actually came back and showed a bit of character.

'It's always about that moment that when you calm down and you go, look where we are in the league, that's terrible, looks how things unfolded in the game, that needs work. But, in the moment, as a football fan, you are allowed to get carried away with it.

'That's what football does. If you don't know that or don't understand it or feel it, you're not a football person, so get out.'

Ferdinand hasn't shied away from criticising his former team-mate Carrick amid United's poor run of form that has left them in 18th in the Premier League table.

United came back from behind to draw 4-4 with Villa having looked down and out in the game

His assessment of Sunday's showing was more tame, with the ex-centre back describing the effort as full of both character and chaos.

He added: 'It's like we need a punch on the nose, or two or three, to start playing. But then, the flip side of it, it's character and ability plays a part in that.

'In the end, we could have won it. But they are giving us fans grey hairs. It's crazy football.'

As thrilling as Man United's fight-back may have been to some fans, manager Carrick was still forced to answer difficult questions at full-time.

Sky Sports' Patrick Davison asked the former captain what he 'expected to happen over the next few weeks' - suggesting a question mark still lingering over his tenure despite comebacks against Roma and Villa.

Carrick's response was understandably thorny, with the manager underlining that he 'probably' would not be walking away from the role.

With United chiefs Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox in the stands, Davison pushed further asking: 'What do you expect to happen? Clearly there's going to be conversation?'

This prompted Carrick to quizzically state: 'Is there?' as the pair engaged in a back-and-forth on the subject.

Eventually Carrick replied: 'You know the situation, we haven't won enough games. But I expect to move forward with things we've been working on, showing a lot of the good from today tighten up a few mistakes and win some football matches.'

United's start of one win in 10 games is still their worst since Alex Ferguson replaced Ron Atkinson 40 years ago this week.

Sports.title: Why England have called up Liam Patterson-White to Test squad to face South Africa, why it's NOT the end of dropped Shoaib Bashir's international career and the players feeling the heat in top-order logjam
Sports.content:
England have picked uncapped Nottinghamshire left-armer Liam Patterson-White as their sole specialist spinner in their 15-man Test squad to take on world No1 side South Africa in their own back yard next month. Shoaib Bashir has been dropped for the 28-year-old, who led all County Championship Division One spinners last season with 42 wickets. Elsewhere in the squad, Jacob Bethell is back after missing the end of the summer through injury, while opener Emilio Gay retains his place despite failing to properly convince in his first six Tests against New Zealand and Pakistan, averaging just 24. Joe Root's side face the world champions in three Tests either side of the new year, having not lost a series in South Africa since 2000, and with Stephen Fleming taking the reins for the first time since replacing Brendon McCullum as red-ball head coach. Here, Daily Mail Sport analyses what it all means... A spin surprise The choice of the uncapped Patterson-White over Bashir, a bowler England have invested in for two-and-a-half years, is telling on several levels. Liam Patterson-White was the leading spinner in this year's County Championship Division One, taking 42 wickets for Nottinghamshire

Your browser does not support iframes.

First, the selectors are sticking to their pledge of picking players based on strong county form – only seven bowlers in the top flight took more than his 42 wickets, none of them spinners. As with Graeme Swann before him, a move to Nottinghamshire has proved a tough school. Trent Bridge tends to be dominated by swing and seam, but it has taught Patterson-White how to hold an end in first innings and bowl in a more attacking fashion deeper into four-day matches. His economy rate of 2.41 last season suggests he will offer control. It is also a nod to his superior batting. With three first-class hundreds to his name and a first-class average of 24.09, compared to Bashir’s 7.57, his selection would stiffen the lower order as well as offer some variation in Root’s attack. Spin tends to play a minimal part in Tests in South Africa and even when teams have opted to include a frontline spinner, they don’t always impact the game with the ball, making their potential contributions with the bat all the more valuable. An example of this came in the Cape Town Test between South Africa and India three years ago when Ravindra Jadeja did not bowl a single ball in the tourists’ seven-wicket win. Mainly because the Indian seamers took full advantage of the helpful conditions at the start of the match. At the same venue last month, however, the value of fielding a balanced attack was shown when the contest against Australia went much deeper. Veteran off-spinner Simon Harmer took full advantage of the wearing surface on day five, bagging half a dozen wickets to finish with match figures of 58.1-2-120-10. Keshav Maharaj sent down 53 overs at the same ground in South Africa’s win over Pakistan in 2024-25. Johannesburg’s Wanderers, where England’s series starts, is a venue in which pace bowling dominates. The last time England played there, winning to seal a 3-1 victory in 2019-20, part-time spinners Root and Joe Denly combined for 10 overs across the match. With Dan Lawrence able to offer serviceable off-spin as a top-six batter, Patterson-White is unlikely to see a Test debut until the Boxing Day Test in Centurion – which, like the Wanderers, encourages extra bounce at altitude – at the earliest. It is likeliest that he is made to wait until the final Test in Cape Town in the new year. Shoaib Bashir has not made the progress that England expected of him when Ben Stokes and Brendon McCullum were wooed by his high release point on YouTube clips three years ago So what happens to Bashir? Derbyshire’s Bashir has not made the progress that England expected of him when Ben Stokes and McCullum were wooed by his high release point on YouTube clips three years ago. It was an attribute they hoped would be useful on bouncier surfaces in Australia, and by association South Africa. Yet he was overlooked for five Tests as an Ashes squad member last winter and has not even made the cut this time, despite having his central contract renewed on October 1. That award suggested he remained England’s No1 spinner, particularly given that Jack Leach has dropped off the radar. But Patterson-White, who only holds a development contract with the ECB, has been favoured for his more rounded ability. One thing on Bashir’s side is time. It should not be forgotten that he is still only 23, and that he is England’s youngest spinner to 50 Test wickets. Swann did not make his Test debut until the age of 29. And he will still be in South Africa, on the England Lions tour ahead of the three-Test series, working with newly-appointed spin coach Richard Dawson, meaning he could be called up if needed. Work there might be as much about getting Bashir ready for February’s tour to Bangladesh, where England will need multiple spinners, and national selector Marcus North insisted the hierarchy ‘still have a very positive outlook’ on him. The return of Carse Brydon Carse has remained on the sidelines, and the subject of an ongoing probe by the Cricket Regulator, since a late-night incident in Derby while on Durham duty in August. However, he takes his place alongside Bashir in the Lions squad, with his former Durham director of cricket North explaining he was now ready to return to action. Brydon Carse is back in the England Lions squad after taking a period out following his nightclub incident in Derby in August ‘In the past few months, under investigation, there has been a time where he has stood back and there has been a time of reflection. It has been a challenging time for Brydon,' said North. 'We have had times when we haven’t felt that the demands of playing international cricket, and what he was dealing with, was necessarily right for Brydon, or for us.' Although he is outside of England’s 15-strong Test party for now, that could change in the next few weeks, with Fleming, in his first assignment as coach, set to draft in one or two extra bodies from the Lions. The likelihood is that one will be South African-raised Carse, with fellow fast bowler Josh Tongue missing the first Test in Johannesburg to witness the birth of his second child. Tongue, currently nursing a big toe injury that has seen him return from the white-ball tour of Australia prematurely, is one of two players with personal circumstances affecting their ability to be in South Africa this December. Sam Curran informed Rob Key, England’s director of cricket, that he was unavailable for selection for the tour because he is getting married. Shuffling of the deck chairs The return of Bethell from a chondral defect in his right knee has given England a selection dilemma ahead of the first Test in Johannesburg on December 17. Bethell appeared to have made the No3 position his own with a classy Ashes hundred in Sydney earlier this year, but injury opened the door to Jordan Cox against Pakistan at the end of the summer. The return of Jacob Bethell from a chondral defect in his right knee has given England a selection dilemma ahead of the first Test in Johannesburg on December 17 With Lawrence’s all-round qualities at No6 also a consideration, England’s selectors will use the build-up to assess their top-order options, with Gay under pressure to retain his opening berth amid heavy competition for places. England’s players will arrive in South Africa in dribs and drabs in the back end of November, with the final trio of Harry Brook, Bethell and Cox flying directly from Australia on November 29, immediately after the fourth Twenty20 in Sydney. Will Jacks will captain a much weakened England team in the fifth and final match of the series Down Under, in a move that shows Test cricket is being prioritised ahead of the heavyweight clash against the Proteas and with a home Ashes series now just seven months away.

Sports.title: Is this America's next golf superstar? Teenage sensation becomes youngest PGA Tour winner in nearly 100 years
Sports.content:
American teenage golf sensation Blades Brown has become the youngest PGA Tour winner in 95 years.

The 19-year-old beat Ben James on the second playoff hole in the World Wide Technology Championship on Sunday afternoon to clinch his maiden title.

'It hasn't set in just yet, I guess, the magnitude of being a PGA Tour winner,' Brown said.

'I just go back to 5-year-old Blades that was watching the TV and watching Tiger Woods and all those great players win major championships, and to think that I'm now in a similar spot with having won a PGA Tour event is mind-blowing.'

Brown is the youngest winner since Charles Kocsis won the Michigan Open in 1931 when he was 18, a tournament that was considered a regional event in the early years of the PGA.

James lost a four-shot lead going into the final round at El Cardonal at Diamante and then showed his moxie by smoking a 285-yard shot into 20 feet on the par-5 18th and making eagle to salvage a 70 and force the playoff.

American golf sensation Blades Brown has become the youngest PGA Tour winner in 95 years

The 19-year-old won the World Wide Technology Championship on Sunday afternoon

But he missed an 8-foot putt on the second playoff hole, and Brown made his 3-footer.

'Had a feeling that it was going to go in,' James said of his clutch eagle, the only putt he made all day longer than 15 feet. 'Hadn't really made anything all day. Just had a really good line on it and it was a good putt. Played the best I could.'

For a sleepy FedEx Cup Fall event on the southern tip of Baja California, this was pure theater between two players from the next generation.

James was the No. 1 player in the PGA Tour University ranking last season. Brown turned pro at 17 and earned his PGA Tour card this year by being among the top 20 in Korn Ferry Tour points.

He made up a seven-shot deficit in the final round and then was tested even more by going through two bags of golf balls on the range waiting to see if the two-shot lead he had over James would hold. Then it was back to the par-5 18th for the playoff.

On the first extra hole, their approach shots were side-by-side, separated by about three feet, and both narrowly missed eagle chances. They returned to the 18th tee and their drives were next to each other. Both came up just short of the green.

James nearly holed his pitch and saw it run out 8 feet. Brown, who had a similar pitch in regulation that he hit to 6 feet for a closing birdie, this time came up three feet short. James's birdie putt grazed the right edge, and Brown poured in the winner.

'I'm so obsessed with this game. It tests you in so many ways,' Brown said. 'I love golf, all the stuff that goes into it and I can't wait for what's next.'

Brown poses with the World Wide Technology Championship Trophy and his caddie, Brett Swedberg

With eight players separated by two shots on the back nine, Brown ran off three straight birdies to share the lead and then left the mistakes to everyone else. He hit a superb pitch for birdie on the final hole to post at 23-under 265.

That put him one shot ahead of Michael Kim, who played with the Tennessee teen and made birdie from 12 feet for 64 right before Brown made his putt.

Brown now has a two-year exemption, which puts him in the elite Championship Series when the PGA Tour's new model begins in 2028. The victory also assures Brown of his first major next year at the PGA Championship.

It was another setback for James, who in 13 starts since turning pro has five finishes in the top five, and two runner-up finishes.

Denny McCarthy, winless in nine years in 240 starts on the PGA Tour, made a 30-foot birdie putt on the 13th hole to take the lead. But he hit a pedestrian pitch to the par-5 14th and had to settle for par. With a wedge in hand from the 15th fairway, he came up some 40 feet short and three-putted for a bogey.

McCarthy's tee shot on the 17th was right of the 18th tee box, he put his next shot off a dirt path into a hazard and made double bogey. He shot 69.

Sports.title: BEN YOUNGS: The lightbulb has switched on for Steve Borthwick - this is how his rampant England tore Australia apart, from 'missing piece' George Furbank to a ferocious pack and electric Jack van Poortvliet
Sports.content:
BEN YOUNGS: The lightbulb has switched on for Steve Borthwick - this is how his rampant England tore Australia apart, from 'missing piece' George Furbank to a ferocious pack and electric Jack van Poortvliet

England’s rampant performance against Australia felt like a lightbulb moment for Steve Borthwick. Finally, the strategy married up with the team selection, and George Furbank looked like the missing piece of the jigsaw.

I played alongside Furbank when he made his England debut in 2020. He was thrown in at the deep end for a Six Nations game in France, a baptism of fire. He lost the ball when he had a two-on-one with Jonny May and it took him a while to get over it.

But he always looked like someone who could be a game changing full-back for England and he showcased that on Sunday. Furbank is a tough, niggly player. He’s got a bit of Mike Brown about him, which people maybe don’t appreciate.

What’s more important, however, is his silky playmaking. England look a totally different team when Furbank is there as a second distributor. He’s capable of playing fly-half, too, as he showed when we started together at No9 and 10 against Tonga. He organises and makes the right passes. He’s got time on the ball.

The best teams look at the rugby pitch like a map. When you're attacking, you’ve got structures and shapes. England split their eight forwards into a 1-3-3-1 pod system. That means they have two pods of three in the middle of the field, with Ollie Chessum and Ben Curry standing out towards the touchlines in the 15-metre channels. The pods of three forwards provide arrowheads and your playmakers work off the back of them.

What you don't want to do is get stuck in between the 15-metre lines. Then it becomes a nightmare because all those structures and shapes go out the window. You end up with both pods really close together in the middle of field. Everything becomes congested and predictable.

George Furbank looked like the missing piece of the jigsaw for England on Sunday against Australia, with his silky playmaking skills offering Steve Borthwick's side so much in attack

I played with Furbank when he was first breaking into the England team - he is a tough, niggly player with a bit of Mike Brown in him

Moving the ball to the wide channels provides the team with reference points to work from. The pictures on that map become so much clearer and that’s where Furbank was so valuable.

Furbank’s connection with No10 Fin Smith is so important. They got the ball to the edge and into the hands of electric winger Manny Feyi-Waboso throughout the first half.

Furbank's organisation around those three-man forward pods was vital. They were able to hit a pod from a touchline, play the ball out the back to Smith, then launch the next layer of attack, with the outside backs flooding around.

Jack van Poortvliet’s try just after half-time (below) was a good example of Furbank’s value. Henry Pollock charged up the left wing and centres Henry Slade and Seb Atkinson went into that breakdown. England played one more phase, found their shape, and then got the ball to Smith.

Smith had three running options and played the ball to Furbank. Who then appeared on Furbank's shoulder? Slade and Atkinson, who were on the left-hand side only four or five seconds before.

If Furbank wasn't there as a second playmaker, then Slade and Atkinson wouldn't have had time to get there. He bought them a couple of extra seconds. Without that second playmaker, all Smith could have done is crash it up through the forwards.

You can’t underestimate the leadership Furbank brings. He was Northampton captain. Furbank, Smith and Slade will be the three key drivers in that back line. The rest of those guys are very much doers, who you just want to be freed up to play.

England have missed Furbank, who has had such cruel luck with injury. That’s tough for Freddie Steward because he probably walks into most international teams. It’s crucial now that Furbank stays fit because he’s such a valuable asset.

Henry Slade and Seb Atkinson (circled) hit a ruck on the left wing in the 42nd minute

By the time the next phase is complete, the two centres (circled) are back on their feet and immediately looking to give England an overlap on the other flank

Fin Smith uses one pod of three as a dummy, passing instead to Furbank - who already has the two centres on his shoulder (circled)

The numerical advantage allows England to fly down the right through Tommy Freeman, who then whipped a pass back into the middle for Jack van Poortvliet (pictured) to score

How ferocious pack put Aussies back in their box

Ollie Chessum, Maro Itoje and Alex Coles made life a nightmare for Australia scrum-half Ryan Lonergan. The charge down pressure they brought on his box-kicks was relentless.

You may not get a charge-down from 20 attempts but that should never stop you from doing it. If you don’t get the ball, the pressure at least makes the scrum-half hook the ball out and you’ve got a lineout 15 metres upfield.

Whenever I used to practise my kicking, Chessum would always come down. We would lay down a tackle pad to create some space, I would have the ball at the other end and Chessum would try to get at my right foot.

We would discuss what the opposition nine likes to do. Are they a kick long team? Are they a kick short team? If they’re a kick long team, then your drop of the ball is lower which gives you a better chance of charging it down.

The best chance of getting someone is when they’re a right-footer kicking over their left shoulder and England targeted that. Their speed and reach to get there was first class.

People moan about caterpillar rucks but scrum-halves need them as protection because you’ve got 6ft 6in blokes who can charge down all day long.

England managed to shorten Australia’s caterpillar rucks really effectively. They were counter rucking and pulling bodies off the feet. Ben Curry was a menace.

By doing that, another body has to join or the caterpillar becomes shorter, which then opens up the opportunity to then charge down. England exploited that really well.

The likes of Ollie Chessum (right) made it a miserable afternoon for Australia scrum-half Ryan Lonergan (left)

No9 shirt now Jack's to lose

It was a great statement from Van Poortvliet in the No9 jersey. It was the best game he’s had in an England shirt. He was decisive, brought speed of ball and tempo, carried well and his kicking game was on point.

I loved the maturity he showed when he threw an interception pass for Australia’s first try. He just parked it and moved on to the next thing. As a nine, you make more decisions than anyone else on the pitch. Every ruck is a decision. Do you go left and right? Which player do you pass to? Do you kick? You need a clear head.

There's been a lot of chopping and changing at scrum-half. I think the fact Alex Mitchell is out injured freed up Van Poortvliet. He wasn’t thinking, 'I need to come up with an X factor moment' or 'if I make a mistake, I'm coming off'. That’s what it’s like in a team that’s low on confidence.

It’s Van Poortvliet’s shirt to lose now. If he plays like that for the next three weekends, then he’s in the hot seat for the World Cup.

Hip drop rule is a flop

I don't want to see people hurting their knees or ankles – no one does – but Angus Bell’s yellow card for a ‘hip drop tackle’ on Feyi-Waboso baffled me.

What is going on? It’s a new law, and I cannot work out what you're supposed to do. Is Bell supposed to just let go of him? If he lets go then Feyi-Waboso will run past and score a try and Bell’s team-mates would say, 'Er, mate, what the hell are you doing?'

If an attacker has got in behind you, I don’t see how you stop them without dropping your hip. You have to let them score or concede a yellow. I think it needs addressing after the autumn. For me, Bell did not do a lot wrong.

I don't want to see people hurting their knees or ankles – no one does – but Angus Bell’s yellow card for a ‘hip drop tackle’ on Manny Feyi-Waboso baffled me. What is Bell supposed to do?

The two fliers I'd pick to replace injured duo

Feyi-Waboso’s injury is a big blow. When he’s fit, he’s England’s most valuable player. He’s box office and he can score out of nothing.

I would fast-track Noah Caluori as his replacement for the Japan game. Caluori’s got the highest ceiling. If the attack goes wrong against Japan, England can fall back on their scrum and maul. They have the size and power to maul Japan until the cows come home!

So, it’s almost the perfect game for Noah. Tommy Freeman and Manny are England’s top two wingers so use this opportunity to develop depth. You don’t get many chances to do that.

With Atkinson also out, I can’t see why you wouldn’t give Max Ojomoh a go at No 12. He was man of the match against Argentina and he hasn't had a look-in since. If England are looking to move the ball and play, Ojomoh is the guy to do that.

Pollock's grin was damning for toothless Aussies

Henry Pollock did a brilliant job on the wing. He’s an incredible athlete. Do I think he starts on the wing? No. If England go with a 6-2 bench, is he the best person to cover the wing for 30 minutes? Absolutely.

Henry Pollock was laughing after the game about how easy it was and that’s a damning indictment of Australia

I'd bring in Noah Caluori (left) and Max Ojomoh (right) to take on Japan after the injuries to Feyi-Waboso and Atkinson

First call-up for Max Hicks with Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Tom Curry out injured England have called up New Zealand-born flanker Max Hicks for the first time after Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Tom Curry were ruled out of the November Tests. Wing Feyi-Waboso suffered an ankle injury in the 45-22 hammering of Australia. Flanker Curry was not available to face the Wallabies due to a hip issue. Both players have now departed the England squad. Centre Seb Atkinson (hip), full-back George Furbank (groin) and forward Ollie Chessum (shoulder) also have knocks and won’t face Eddie Jones’ Japan on Saturday, though it is hoped they will be fit for New Zealand a week later. Hicks, 27, is a Kiwi product who only signed with PREM Rugby side Newcastle Red Bulls from French side Perpignan this summer. He’s the headline inclusion in the squad for Japan after appearing for England’s A team in their win over an Argentina XV in Bath last Friday. Hicks’ call is a reward for his PREM Rugby form with Newcastle. He offers an athletic back-row presence, with good ball handling and line-out jumping ability. Backs Noah Caluori, Max Ojomoh, Tobias Elliot and Harlequins flanker Jack Kenningham join Hicks in receiving an England summons from head coach Steve Borthwick. One of Ojomoh or Northampton’s Fraser Dingwall are the most likely replacement for Atkinson in the No 12 jersey with Caluori an option to fill Feyi-Waboso’s boots out wide. At scrum-half Archie McParland is back and replaces Harry Randall. ‘At 12, I think it’s more likely I’ll be looking at Max (Ojomoh) or Fraser as options,’ Borthwick admitted. ‘I describe Fraser as a glue player. He makes everybody a little bit better around him. ‘He’s really skilful. Max’s point of difference is his attacking distribution and ability to see space.’ Ojomoh was player of the match on his second cap against Argentina last autumn, but hasn’t appeared for England’s senior side since. Like Hicks, he also impressed for England A. Feyi-Waboso was the victim of a ‘hip-drop’ tackle from Australian prop Angus Bell after producing an impressive start. He initially played on, before being substituted at half time. Back-row Henry Pollock came on in his place and scored two tries playing in an unfamiliar wing position. Atkinson limped off in the second period against Australia. The blows to Chessum and Furbank are noteworthy, given both are first-choice starters when fit. The pair both played 80 minutes in the seven-try dismantling of the Wallabies. Japan were beaten 28-21 by Wales in their autumn opener. Feyi-Waboso and Curry join Alex Mitchell, Guy Pepper, Sam Underhill and Benhard Janse van Rensburg in now sitting out the rest of the Nations Championship series. ‘There are a number of possibilities and having that depth of competition, it feels a little bit more like it did 12 months ago,’ Borthwick said. Borthwick added it would be unlikely he’d consider starting Northampton tyro Pollock on the wing and that he was likely to be needed in the forwards this weekend. ‘It's not that I'm refraining from playing him on the wing. I think he might be needed in the back-row,’ Borthwick said of Pollock. ‘Japan pose a different challenge. If a game gets loose, Japan are very, very dangerous. Japan have guile. They have different types of plays.’ England 36-man squad for Japan: Forwards: Fin Baxter (Harlequins), Arthur Clark (Gloucester Rugby), Alex Coles (Northampton Saints), Luke Cowan-Dickie (Sale Sharks), Ben Curry (Sale Sharks), Theo Dan (Saracens), Ben Earl (Saracens), Greg Fisilau (Exeter Chiefs), Jamie George (Saracens), Ellis Genge (Bristol Bears), Joe Heyes (Leicester Tigers), Max Hicks (Newcastle Red Bulls), Maro Itoje (Saracens), Emmanuel Iyogun (Northampton Saints), Jack Kenningham (Harlequins), George Martin (Saracens), Asher Opoku-Fordjour (Sale Sharks), Tom Pearson (Northampton Saints), Henry Pollock (Northampton Saints), Will Stuart (Bath Rugby) Backs: Noah Caluori (Saracens), Fraser Dingwall (Northampton Saints), Tobias Elliott (Saracens), George Ford (Sale Sharks), Tommy Freeman (Northampton Saints), Will Joseph (Gloucester Rugby), Joe Marchant (Sale Sharks), Cadan Murley (Harlequins), Archie McParland (Northampton Saints) Max Ojomoh (Bath Rugby), Henry Slade (Exeter Chiefs), Fin Smith (Northampton Saints), Marcus Smith (Harlequins), Ben Spencer (Bath Rugby), Freddie Steward (Leicester Tigers), Jack van Poortvliet (Leicester Tigers) By Alex Bywater

He was laughing after the game about how easy it was and that’s a damning indictment of Australia. If England were playing against New Zealand, France or South Africa, they would ruthlessly try to target him off strike moves and contestable kicks.

Australia did none of that. They gave him an armchair ride. That's rugby IQ 101. Where’s your nous? Where’s your match understanding? They could have Mark Nawaqanitawase and Joseph Suaalii as all-star wingers at the World Cup but if that was their standard of half-backs, then they are going nowhere.

For all of England’s brilliance, I still can't get over how poor Australia were. They were toothless. The All Blacks will provide the real litmus test.

I was really encouraged by England’s performance and they are going to get more and more cohesive as the series progresses.

Sports.title: Why Chelsea aren't European contenders, Tottenham aren't 'back'... and Brighton and Bournemouth are in a title race: What you should believe and what's just a mirage after 10 Premier League games - and the proof behind it
Sports.content:
We are ten games into the Premier League season and another international break provides the ideal opportunity to take stock on what has been a bewildering start to another campaign. Michael Carrick heads off for a couple of weeks with Manchester United still in the bottom three. Brighton perch second in the Premier League behind Arsenal, who are threatening to run away with it. Tottenham are only a point outside the top half, which is enough on its own to make you squint and rub your eyes. That can’t be right. We are more than a quarter of the way through now, enough time for patterns to emerge and directions of travel to settle but also not long enough for us to be entirely sure who’s still benefitting from an early hot streak or suffering from unfair misfortune. Who is where they belong? What can we believe? Daily Mail Sport digs into the numbers to figure out what’s real and what is fake about this Premier League season so far... REAL: Defences CAN win you titles, just ask Arsenal Sir Alex Ferguson was wrong, of course, when he declared that ‘attack wins you games, defence wins you titles’. Over the 31 completed 20-team Premier League seasons, fewer than half of them were won by the team that conceded the fewest goals. More than two thirds of them, however, were won by the side that scored the most. Sometimes, as was often the case during the Pep Guardiola era, teams can be the best at both. Of the 15 times since 1995-96 that the best defence triumphed, they were also the most prolific attack on nine occasions. Arsenal's goals, xG, shots and shots on target are all at their lowest per game since Mikel Arteta’s first season in charge. But thanks to their defence, they are five points clear at the top

Your browser does not support iframes.

Arsenal, however, are certainly not that. Their title win last season was only the sixth time in the previous 30 years that the best defence alone was crowned champions. They are doing it again this season, five points clear and proving that the best defence can still win you a title on its own. And it’s a good job, too, because while their defence is as rock-solid as ever, their attack is getting worse. Last season, the Gunners ranked second for goals but fourth for expected goals (xG) and shots. This term, they are sixth for goals, fifth for xG and 10th for shots. Their goals, xG, shots and shots on target are all at their lowest per game since Arteta’s first season in charge. Their win over Hull was their fourth 1-0 victory of the campaign. Not that Arteta will care. His defence means they still have the best xG difference in the division and it’s going to win him another league title. FAKE: Forest are relegation fodder That euphoric 3-1 victory over Manchester City was coming. There had been a fair amount of noise building around Oliver Glasner’s start to life on the Trent as Nottingham Forest went into the weekend second from bottom in the Premier League. One defeat in nine. Was it Glasner’s new system taking time to bed in like it did at Crystal Palace? How quickly would ‘Mr Marinakis’ lose his patience this time around and fire another head coach? This time last year, Forest were already on to their third manager of the season. Patience, for once, will reap its rewards. Forest didn’t deserve to be 19th. They have the fifth-best expected goal difference in the division. When you dig into the numbers, Forest have the best defence of any team not named Arsenal. Fewest shots faced, second-fewest shots on target faced after the Gunners, second lowest xG conceded after, yep, Arsenal. They have made the fewest errors leading to shots all season with just two. Bournemouth are next on five. Their problem is they, somehow, have not been able to score. Only Sunderland – another side doing worse than their expected numbers would suggest – have underperformed their xG in front of goal more than Forest. I was at Crystal Palace for Glasner’s return to Selhurst Park and, quite simply, Forest should have been 4-0 up by half-time. They have the lowest shot conversion rate of any side in the league at just 5.5 per cent. That’s unsustainably low. Only one team since 2014-15 has maintained one as low as that across an entire season and that was Huddersfield in 2018-19, when they finished bottom with 16 points. Forest are nowhere near that bad. Their need for a striker has long been obvious and if Liam Delap’s brace against City can spark some confidence and form, they might have the striker they need to start climbing up the table and, who knows, into European contention. Nottingham Forest will hope Liam Delap's brilliant brace against Manchester City is the start of them getting past their woes in front of goal

Your browser does not support iframes.

FAKE: Spurs are back! Listen to Jamie O’Hara on talkSPORT after a run of three wins on the trot, and he might have you believing that Spurs are back. They are not back. Along with another defeat, this time to Leeds, to bring Spurs hurtling to earth, their numbers simply are not good enough – and certainly not in attack – to be deemed as such. They may have attempted the fifth-most shots in the division but in doing so have still put up the fourth-worst xG, as their xG per shot is the worst in the division. In short: they shoot a lot but hardly ever from anywhere dangerous. That 40 per cent of their goals have come from outside the box, the highest in the league, is unsustainable. They just don’t create enough. Left back Andy Robertson has created the most chances for Spurs this season with 14. Twenty-seven players have created more than him so far, with 15 other clubs boasting at least one star higher than Tottenham’s top man. Sunderland have two above him and Arsenal, Brighton and Manchester United have three. Tottenham have the worst xG per shot in the league - meaning they rarely get into good positions to score REAL: Brighton (and maybe Bournemouth) are in a title race We have got used to seeing these modest but exceptionally run clubs punching above their weight in the Premier League but even the most appreciative of us could not have expected to see at least one of them in a title race. If, by title race, we mean the team that might get closest to Arsenal. Looking at the underlying numbers, it could even be both of them. When you look at the expected goal difference of all clubs in the division – those you should have scored from the quality of the chances you create, against those you should have conceded from the quality of the ones you allow your opponents to create – Bournemouth and Brighton sit behind only Arsenal and Man City. Brighton are the division’s top scorers by a distance, five more than anyone else, but even though they are outperforming their expected numbers (their players can’t keep scoring one in every 10 shots they take from outside the box – looking at you, Diego Gomez) the Seagulls are still putting up the second biggest xG behind City. Of the 11 players to create more than 20 chances so far, Brighton are the only side to have two names in there in Pascal Gross and Maxim De Cuyper. They also, of course, beat Arsenal and City without conceding to either team. They do need to get tighter at the back if they wish to stay near the top, mind. Brighton should have conceded about seven more goals than they have done. No side has overperformed their defensive data quite so much. Bournemouth are the ones who should be doing better, which sounds mad for a team that’s just won eight games on the bounce in less than a month in all competitions. The Cherries sit seventh but have the third-best xG, and the third-best xG conceded. That, no matter how you look at it, is a recipe for prolonged success. Brighton's Diego Gomez can't continue scoring every shot he has from long range... can he? Bournemouth are the ones who should be doing better, which sounds mad for a team that’s just won eight games on the bounce in less than a month FAKE: Chelsea are European contenders Speaking of overperforming, few teams are doing quite so well to hide their abundant flaws as Chelsea. Xabi Alonso’s side sit fifth in the Premier League and the Spaniard can be thankful to the football gods for it. They should not be fifth. Chelsea sit in the bottom half for both xG for and against. Their expected goal difference puts them in 14th, below Fulham, Manchester United and Sunderland. Only Brighton have scored more goals than they should have done based on their chances but, unlike the Seagulls, Chelsea’s baseline is far more mediocre. Opta’s expected points table has them 12th. They are also one of only two sides in the division this season not to have had a single goal scored by a substitute. Chelsea's expected goal difference puts them in 14th, below Fulham, Manchester United and Sunderland REAL: Newcastle are in trouble When you lose a manager as influential as Eddie Howe, it’s always going to be a tricky transition. When you sell Sandro Tonali, Bruno Guimaraes and Anthony Gordon and struggle to replace them adequately, it’s going to be harder still. Still, Newcastle should be doing better. They should not be creating better chances than only Hull and Coventry. Their expected goal difference is only better than Coventry, Ipswich and Palace. Opta’s expected table has them just outside the relegation zone. Only three teams have faced more shots, only three have attempted more shots on target, only five have played fewer passes into the box. Daily Mail Sport revealed last week that Newcastle’s players are ‘confused’ by new manager Matthias Jaissle’s instructions, playing style and strategy. Jaissle accused his team after the defeat to Everton of not following his instructions or executing the tactics they had worked on in training. They have to find a way of getting it to click after the international break otherwise they will be fighting out most of their season closer to that dotted line. FAKE? United are for the drop It can often be fun for supporters of other clubs around the country to revel in the pain and misery that Manchester United appear intent on inflicting on their own supporters. Even the carnage and chaos of coming from two goals down against Aston Villa and the shot of joy that can bring was still only enough to leave United 18th in the table. Do they deserve to be there? With just one win all season, the fewest in the league, you would think so. United have, perhaps, not quite been that bad – but they certainly don’t help themselves. Everyone talks about them having tons of shots, which they do. They have had the most in the division by a distance, which always keeps the xG totting up, but so many of them come from miles away. United, too often, take the scattergun approach. Manchester United have been suffering from bad luck at the back - but will it correct itself in time to save them from a relegation battle? Their xG per shot is the lowest in the division, meaning their shots aren’t from dangerous positions, and their conversion rate is one of the worst, too. When 45 per cent of your attempts on goal come from outside the box, that’s likely to happen. That makes their midtable expected goal difference slightly misleading. Their main problem is at the back – and that is where they are being consistently punished. It is the opposite story to their attack. United have faced among the fewest shots in the division but among the most on target. Their xG per shot faced is the highest in the league, and their opponents enjoy a higher conversion rate than against any other team. That, though, is unlikely to remain sustainable. They are unlikely to keep getting punished quite so harshly. That should be enough to drag them clear – but only just.

Sports.title: OLIVER HOLT: Man United fans' anti-Glazer walkout flopped because owners don't care - but it's not impossible to oust them. Here's what they should do instead
Sports.content:
OLIVER HOLT: Man United fans' anti-Glazer walkout flopped because owners don't care - but it's not impossible to oust them. Here's what they should do instead

Oliver Holt Chief Sports Writer

The only chance I ever got at holding one of the Glazer family to account in person for what they were doing to Manchester United came in Tampa, Florida, in 2009, a few days before the Super Bowl between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Arizona Cardinals. As interrogations go, mine was rather feeble.

I was there for the game but I noticed that, as part of the week’s build-up to it, Bryan Glazer was speaking at an NFL Kids Day. The event was held outdoors, in the grounds of the Raymond James Stadium and it was open to the media so I went along and listened to Bryan speak.

As he left, I wandered over to speak to him. Everything was relaxed until I introduced myself as an English sports journalist and asked him about his family’s stewardship of United. Glazer’s smile stiffened and then it disappeared.

He didn’t say a single word. He did not break his stride. He glanced meaningfully at a security guy, who was part of his entourage, and the security guy stepped across me and blocked my path. Glazer kept walking, climbed on to a golf buggy and was driven away.

Seventeen years down the line and few have got more out of the Glazers than that stiffened smile – although Avram Glazer did tell an audience of financiers at Deutsche Bank’s inaugural Sports Investment Conference in London recently that sports teams at United’s level are not dependent on success on the pitch for commercial power. He would say that.

That went down well among United supporters, obviously, and as United languish in the Premier League’s bottom three, one point off the foot of the table, anger against the Glazer ownership, which has cost the club more than £1billion in debt interest payments and shareholder dividends, is rising to a crescendo again.

Matheus Cunha (left) and Bruno Fernandes come to terms with another disappointing Manchester United performance after the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa at Old Trafford on Sunday

The United fans made clear what they think of their owners at Old Trafford

Anger against the Glazers has been fuelled by disenchantment with Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the minority owner, whose involvement in the football operation has deepened and widened the disillusionment of the fanbase with the people who are fiddling while United burns in decline. It is 40 years since United were in the relegation zone after more than nine games.

‘We Don’t Want A New Stadium, We Want New Owners,’ a banner in the Stretford End read. The idea of getting rid of the Glazers and Ratcliffe has become a panacea for United supporters. It is seen as the key to the club’s recovery, the key to everything, but the struggle to dislodge them faces huge obstacles.

The protests are redoubling. Old Trafford was awash with green and gold, the colours of tradition and disaffection at the club, for the chaotic draw against Aston Villa on Sunday afternoon and the stadium echoed to deafening chants calling for the Glazers to get out of United. Battalions of green and gold balloons took to the air before kick-off.

The problem is that the Glazers do not care. They run the club by remote control from Florida. They are detached. They always have been. I have watched protest marches before and seen supporters gathering at the start, outside the Tollgate pub a mile or so from the ground, in impressive numbers. They have achieved little.

It is not impossible for fans to oust or defy owners. The power of supporters was at its most inspiring when it faced down the plans of Manchester City, Chelsea, Spurs, United, Arsenal and Liverpool to join a breakaway European Super League in 2021.

In Germany, some years ago, when plans were revealed to stage Monday night games, there was widespread outrage at the idea of supporters having to travel to games after work. Dissent and disobedience followed.

Tennis balls were thrown on to pitches during games, a chorus of vuvuzelas filled the air, remote-controlled cars sped on to the playing surface. Monday night games were dropped.

Liverpool removed co-owners Tom Hicks and George Gillett in October 2010 through a combination of an independent board, a High Court legal battle, and pressure from the Royal Bank of Scotland, all underpinned by huge supporter demonstrations and campaigns against the US owners.

I once confronted Bryan Glazer over his family’s stewardship of United. His smile stiffened and then disappeared

Supporters have had enough - but how far are they willing to go to drive the Glazers out?

And on a smaller, but no less heroic, scale, Blackpool supporters staged a four-year boycott of their team’s matches, starting in 2015, that saw the average attendance at Bloomfield Road drop from 10,000 to 2,500 and was critical in the removal from the club of the much-loathed owners, the Oyston Family.

That Blackpool protest movement is the subject of a soon-to-be-aired documentary on Sky called Don’t F*** With Fans. One of the main lessons that the programme preaches is the need for unity in a fanbase if the protests are to have any chance of succeeding.

Achieving that unity has already been made harder at clubs like United because of the way the loyal supporter base is being diluted by the war on traditional season-ticket holders and the move towards attracting more day-trippers and tourists, who will spend more for the price of admission and more at the club superstore.

Some fans’ groups called for a mass walkout in the 21st minute of the United-Villa game, to mark 21 years of the Glazer ownership, but only a handful of home fans observed it. The popular YouTuber SaeedTV was one of them.

‘I did my bit,’ he posted on X as he stood outside the stadium almost alone. ‘Unfortunately fans don’t care enough. Glazers OUT INEOS OUT.’

Part of the problem the call for boycotts faces is that tourists don’t do protest. They have paid too much for their seat to walk out midway through the first half.

Many of the calls for a mass walkout also come from fans on social media, who are not match-going supporters. Fans who do go to the games are, understandably, reluctant to walk out when they have paid for their seats. They also know that if they were to give up their season tickets, the club would be delighted.

Some match-going fans started a tongue-in-cheek campaign aimed at armchair fans who have been trying to preach to them how best to get the Glazers out. ‘Turn off your television sets after 21 minutes,’ was the gist of it.

But the fact remains that unity is strength. It is the only chance supporters have of moving the dial at a club as big as United. History says a form of co-ordinated, well-orchestrated, mass-participation peaceful disobedience is the only way.

Unity is strength. It is the only chance supporters have of moving the dial at a club as big as United

Some fans’ groups called for a mass walkout in the 21st minute of the United-Villa game, to mark 21 years of the Glazer ownership, but only a handful of home fans observed it

It has to be something that affects the spectacle and, more specifically, the optics for television viewers. And it has to be something that affects them consistently.

Many Premier League clubs don’t care about match-going fans anymore but if the television product is affected, if the broadcasters become concerned, if sponsors start to think that they might actually be damaged by association with the disaffection at Manchester United, then maybe at least a little pressure would be brought to bear on an ownership group.

The odds are stacked more and more heavily against supporters who wish to effect change. But the opposition to the European Super League showed it could be done. The Blackpool fan boycott showed it could be done. Liverpool supporters’ demonstrations against Hicks and Gillett showed it could be done.

It is a question of whether the will exists. Of whether the unity exists. And of whether there are simply too many of the new breed of fan who would rather take selfies and queue for merchandise than turn the club back into an institution that cares more for trophies than revenue.

Sports.title: Arsenal star Declan Rice reveals why he really cut back on social media
Sports.content:
Arsenal star Declan Rice reveals why he really cut back on social media

Arsenal and England midfielder Declan Rice has spoken out about cutting back on social media after admitting abuse on online platforms had previously got to him

View 2 Images Declan Rice has cut back on his social media use (Image: Fanny-Latour Lambert / British GQ)

Declan Rice has revealed he has reduced his use of social media because it is bad for his mental health.

‌



‌



The Arsenal midfielder quit X three years ago after he was targeted for online abuse and negative comments could dramatically affect his mood. Rice still has an Instagram account but his long-term partner Lauren Fryer has also been targeted and she deleted all previous posts from her account in 2024.

‌



Rice said: “I've not been back on the app since. You could be having a great morning. You read one thing, and it just ruins your whole day.

‌



“I feel like that's one of my strongest points... the ability to block out noise and not deal with that kind of stuff.

Sports.title: Grand National hero Ballabriggs who triumphed at Aintree for Red Rum stable has died
Sports.content:
Grand National hero Ballabriggs who triumphed at Aintree for Red Rum stable has died

Ballabriggs, who triumphed at Aintree in 2011 for Donald McCain Jr, has passed away, aged 25, at his late owner’s stud on the Isle Of Man

View 2 Images Grand National winner parade with Ballabriggs, his trainer Donald McCain and owner Trevor Hemmings (left) (Image: Getty)

Grand National hero Ballabriggs, who delivered a fifth success in the big race for the Red Rum stable has died, aged 25.

‌



‌



Ballabriggs was trained by Donald McCain Jr, whose father Donald ‘Ginger’ McCain won the big race four times, on three occasions with the legendary Red Rum.

‌



Owned by the late billionaire and Preston North End owner Trevor Hemmings, a Grand National fanatic, he was to inevitably develop into a successful staying chaser. In 2011 he became Hemmings’s second winner of the race when he defeated Oscar Time and Don’t Push It under jockey Jason Maguire, A year earlier he had become a Cheltenham Festival winner when landing the Fulke Walwyn Kim Muir Chase.

‌



He made two more appearances in the Grand National, finishing sixth in 2012, but was retired after he was pulled up in the 2013 edition. He had won seven of his 28 starts, earning £624,000 in prize-money.

He was to spend the rest of his life at Hemmings’s stud on the Isle Of Man, remaining there after Hemmings’s death in 2021.

‌



McCain Jr broke the news on his social media account on Monday. He said: “I’m really sad to report that our Grand National-winning hero Ballabriggs has passed away at the age of 25.

View 2 Images Jason Maguire roars home on Ballabriggs

‌



“We're all eternally grateful for the amazing days and memories he gave us, and for allowing me to achieve a lifetime ambition of winning the Grand National in 2011.

In another post on his website, he added: “After the most fantastic career, he got to enjoy a long and wonderfully happy retirement at Mr Hemmings’ Ballaseyr Stud on the Isle of Man, where he will be laid to rest.”

Article continues below

He added: “Everyone at Bankhouse will be eternally grateful for the amazing days and memories he gave us and for allowing me to achieve a lifetime ambition of winning the Grand National in 2011, which will never be forgotten.

“Thank-you Briggsy!”

Sports.title: Michael Carrick future LIVE: Man Utd 'appointment plan' as Mauricio Pochettino leads race
Sports.content:
Head Coach Michael Carrick of Manchester United walks off after the Premier League 2026/27 match between Manchester United and Aston Villa FC at Old Trafford

Manchester United go into the international break in the Premier League relegation zone after a 4-4 draw against Aston Villa

Manchester United boss Michael Carrick has swerved the gallows for now after his side fought back to draw 4-4 against Aston Villa. But with the international break arriving, if he is going to be relieved of his duties, now would be the time to do it.

United are still wallowing in the relegation places, sitting 18th. Although they trailed by two goals on two separate occasions at Old Trafford against Unai Emery's Villa, a late Patrick Dorgu equaliser rescued a much-needed point on Sunday.

But unrest is still rife and with 10 matches played in the top flight, only eight points have been collected. United are next in action against Liverpool on November 22, 13 days away.

Although it appears Carrick's post is safe for the time being, the international break could give the club the perfect opportunity to bring in a new regime and reports suggest five names are on the shortlist - with USMNT manager Mauricio Pochettino now emerging as a surprise fifth option.

Eddie Howe, Julian Nagelsmann, Antonio Conte and Stuttgart boss Sebastian Hoeness have also been mentioned as possible targets.

So stick around as Mirror Football brings you the latest on the ever-changing situation at the Theatre of Dreams.

Sports.title: DAVID YATES: Government taskforce is 'more Dad's Army than the A-Team'
Sports.content:
My eyes roll every time I hear the words ‘government taskforce’. Behind the imagery of flak jackets and kevlar helmets there is all too often lots of talk but little meaningful action. And, if the results of a study published this week are any guide, the Illegal Gambling Taskforce, set up by the Department of Culture, Media and Sport in January, is currently more Dad’s Army than The A-Team.

Data released from the International Federation of Horseracing Authorities’ Council on Anti-Illegal Betting and Related Crime makes for chastening reading.

The survey monitored the traffic of over 300 betting websites used in Britain, of which 74 are legal and 227 operate on the black market, between 2021 and 2026.

Value Scope: The horse who can give former champion trainer Paul Nicholls a big lift READ MORE :

In the second half of 2021, for every 100 visits to licensed sites, there was just one to an illegal operator. But the corresponding figure rose to an alarming 26.6 in 2025 and, from January to July this year, is 19.4 - that’s one visit to the black market for every five to the regulated sector.

‌



By the end of 2026, it’s estimated there will have been 18.9million unique visits to illegal websites - that’s 10 times more than in 2022. British Horseracing Authority chief executive Brant Dunshea noted: “While the taskforce’s creation was welcomed as a positive development, progress so far has been limited.”

That’s putting it mildly. Nobody needs reminding that the black market means no protection for problem gamblers, no revenue via taxation for the exchequer and no money coming back into racing.

So it’s time for the ‘taskforce’ to ratchet up its offensive on the shark-infested waters. This is a conflict we can’t afford to lose.

View 3 Images Billy Loughnane: signed by Godolphin (Image: Richard Sellers/PA Wire)

‌



Loughnane signed up

Little surprise to see Billy Loughnane’s meteoric rise through the jockeys’ ranks rewarded this week with a job as retained rider to Godolphin.

Sheikh Mohammed no doubt felt he had to make a move for the 20-year-old - and fast. Days earlier, Loughnane had shone aboard Libertango at the Breeders’ Cup, while William Buick endured a nightmare on Notable Speech at Keeneland.

Godolphin stopped short of announcing a pecking order between the pair, but the bookies reckon the new signing will be top dog.

Loughnane is 1-2 to ride more Godolphin winners in Britain in 2027, with Buick 6-4 - and I don’t think that’s too far wide of the mark.

‌



View 3 Images Ethan Brown celebrates on Point Of Law (Image: Getty Images)

Bittersweet victory

Bittersweet - how else to describe the victory for Point Of Law in the Melbourne Cup on Tuesday?

The King and Queen are listed as the Frankel colt’s breeders and Point Of Law, then trained by John and Thady Gosden, carried the royal silks to victory in a Newbury maiden and Newmarket’s Bahrain Trophy this year.

It was after the latter success that Point Of Law was sold privately Down Under for a fee rumoured to be as high as £3million.

‌



Having netted ‘the race that stops a nation’ at Flemington, Point Of Law’s owners could aim for the Gold Cup, the signature race of Royal Ascot, in June.

Ouch!

Sports.title: Man Utd respond after fans accuse them of 'censorship' over removal of protest banners
Sports.content:
Man Utd respond after fans accuse them of 'censorship' over removal of protest banners

Manchester United fans once again voiced their displeasure over the club's ownership during Sunday's epic 4-4 draw against Aston Villa

View 2 Images This banner was confiscated by stewards at Old Trafford (Image: Offside via Getty Images)

Manchester United stewards removed two banners from the Stretford End protesting against the club's ownership during Sunday's 4-4 draw against Aston Villa.

‌



‌



United fans once again made their voices heard as they voiced their displeasure at the running of the club by the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

‌



A banner reading 'We don't want a new stadium, we want new owners' was unfurled prior to kick-off and shown once again before the end of the first half.

‌



Another reading 'Jim can't fix this' was also confiscated by stewards. This banner has been used in numerous protests since first being shown against Burnley at Turf Moor last season.

It is understood the 'new stadium' banner was taken down due to concerns it was blocking the view of some supporters. The second banner was removed due to its play on words from TV show 'Jim'll fix it', which was hosted by Jimmy Savile, one of the UK's most notorious sexual predators.

United fan group The 1958 posted a video on X of fans remonstrating with stewards. They added: "Once again censorship from our club and owners on fans voicing their anger at the destruction of our club in the ground today.

"Banners confiscated by stewards and lads ejected from the ground. This isn't about results, this isn't about performances. This is about generational decay of terrace culture, loyalty and our club's dignity."

On the pitch, United staged a dramatic comeback to salvage a point at the death, but there is still uncertainty surrounding the future of boss Michael Carrick.

Villa were 2-0 up in just four minutes thanks to strikes by Alysson and Nicolas Jackson, but Bruno Fernandes and Youri Tielemans hit back before the break.

The visitors restored their two-goal advantage inside eight second-half minutes with John McGinn and Leroy Goretzka on target. But stoppage-time strikes from Joshua Zirkzee and Partick Dorgu earned United an unlikely point.

Carrick insists he still expects to be given the opportunity to lead United after the international break and rejected the notion that the club are in a relegation scrap.

"You know the situation, we haven’t won enough games," he said. "But I expect to move forward with things we’ve been working on, showing a lot of the good from today tighten up a few mistakes and win some football matches.

Sports.title: Jockey, 22, fighting for her life after being airlifted to hospital following fall
Sports.content:
Jockey, 22, fighting for her life after being airlifted to hospital following fall

The jockey is in critical condition after taking a nasty fall on Sunday and being airlifted to a local hospital with suspected head injuries

View 2 Images Izzy Neale is fighting for her life (Image: Getty)

Australian apprentice jockey Izzy Neale was airlifted to hospital and is in critical condition after falling at Warren on Sunday afternoon. The 22-year-old was on board Marnoo in the Cotton Cup but was unseated and seriously injured.

‌



‌



Neale was riding for trainer Kiran Hazelton at the regional New South Wales course in a 1600m race, but both she and fellow jockey Diego Montes de Oca, who was riding Shadow Dane, came off their respective mounts with around 400m to go. Racing was called off for the day with one race remaining on the card.

‌



The horse, Marnoo, was euthanised after suffering a "near foreleg injury," according to Racing NSW Stewards. A helicopter took Neale to Dubbo Hospital after she lost consciousness on track as a result of the fall.

‌



Montes de Oca followed in an ambulance and has since been discharged after escaping with soft tissue damage in his left foot. Neale is fighting for her life after suffering reported serious head injuries.

Robbie Williams wows crowds after King's former horse wins Melbourne Cup READ MORE :

Jockey Brendan Powell taken to hospital from Plumpton after "horrible" fall at first fence READ MORE :

Monday's planned race meet at Scone has been postponed to Wednesday. Racing NSW issued the following statement: "Following consultation with jockeys and trainers engaged to participate at today's race meeting at Scone, a decision has been made to postpone the meeting.

View 2 Images The 22-year-old was airlifted to hospital (Image: Getty)

‌



Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

"The decision follows the serious race fall involving apprentice jockey Izzy Neale at Warren yesterday. Izzy remains in Dubbo Hospital in a critical condition, with her family by her side.

‌



"The thoughts and heartfelt support of Racing NSW and the entire racing community are with Izzy, her family, friends and colleagues during this extremely difficult time."

An investigation into the incident has been opened.

‌



Born in Merriwa, Neale transitioned from the academy ranks in 2024 and began riding, winning at Condobolin on her very first professional race ride.

She has netted 88 wins to date from 699 starts. On Saturday, the 22-year-old was riding at Rosehill as part of Five Diamonds Day. Neale told Sky Racing that she was about to finalise the purchase of her first house this week.

‌



Support has flooded in from the Australian racing community, with ex-jockey Melinda Turner saying: "Praying for a miracle. A terrible day for our industry."

The Australian Jockeys' Association stated: "Sending all our love and support to Izzy and Diego after a dreadful fall at Warren. Will update conditions ASAP."
