World.title: Sakaja defends Sh43.7b drop in Nairobi County's pending bills before Senate
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja tells Senate that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors. [File, Standard]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has told the Senate that pending bills in the city have been reduced from Sh118.79 billion to Sh75.07 billion through verification and payment.

Sakaja revealed that internal verification established that the Sh43.73 billion reduction was not achieved solely through payments but also involved legal assessments, court-ordered adjustments and the verification of disputed claims.

The governor, who appeared before the Senate County Public Accounts Committee at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi on Monday, said addressing the inherited debt required establishment of a verification committee to scrutinise the entire outstanding amount and establish the validity of the claims.

“The reduction of Nairobi County pending bills by Sh 43.73 billion was not achieved entirely through cash payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court-ordered reductions and disputed claims,” said Sakaja.

He told the Senate Committee chaired by Homa Bay Senator Moses Kajwang that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors and that he had constituted a committee to undertake an internal verification of the entire amount before payments were done.

Sakaja explained that the verification established that the reduction was not solely through payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court decisions and disputed claims.

“I would like to inform Senators that my administration has provided a detailed schedule accounting for the Sh43.73 billion pending bills reduction through adjustments and reconciliations,” he said.

The governor said that of this amount Sh1.63 billion related to legal assessments, while Sh19.14 billion represented government-guaranteed loans whose servicing had been suspended due to a lack of supporting documentation and loan schedules.

Sakaja told Senators that Sh19.2 billion related to LAPFUND interest and penalties which the County said had been reduced following a court consent that brought the claim down to approximately Sh8.2 billion.

He said that they had provided a signed indemnity form, in accordance with County Treasury rules governing misplaced payment documents, alongside a financial memo confirming that the works had been undertaken and payment made.

“The audit further raised concerns over Sh16.04 million in receivables from non-exchange transactions, which lacked sufficient supporting documentation,” said Sakaja.

The governor told senators that beyond the verification of pending bills his administration had also strengthened the county’s legal department to reduce expenditure on external legal services and protect public resources.

Sakaja noted that through the reforms, Nairobi saved approximately Sh8.48 billion in legal costs over two financial years by expanding its in-house legal capacity, handling more litigation internally and negotiating reductions in legal fees claimed by private advocates.

According to the County Assembly’s Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, of the 174 court cases concluded during the period under review, 84 were handled by the County’s in-house legal team, with 47 determined in Nairobi’s favour, representing a 56 per cent success rate.

Kajwang, commended the County for reducing its pending bills but asked the Governor to provide additional documentation supporting the payments and processes undertaken to account for the Sh43.73 billion reductions.

“The Senate County Public Accounts Committee requires further clarification on the verification exercise and the adjustments made to the outstanding debt,” said Kajwang.

World.title: Gachagua dismisses opposition divisions as 'polygamous family' rivalry
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County on November 8, 2026. [Peterson Githaiga, Standard]

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has dismissed claims of divisions within the Opposition, describing the disagreements among its leaders as normal sibling rivalry in a polygamous family, while insisting that the coalition remains united behind plans to field a single presidential candidate in the 2027 General Election.

Gachagua said the Opposition leaders were committed to working together to challenge President William Ruto, despite their differing opinions on the timing of selecting a joint presidential flagbearer and occasional disagreements among their political camps.

Speaking during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County, the former Deputy President likened the political differences to children from the same father competing for attention but eventually uniting whenever an external threat emerges.

“The Opposition is united to a man, and we have agreed that we will have a single presidential candidate. Everybody is committed, and we talk on a daily basis. The only challenge is normal petty problems,” he said.

He added that the disagreements should not be interpreted as a breakdown of the coalition, maintaining that such differences were healthy and expected in a broad political alliance.

“Ile shida kidogo ni ya boma, watoto wengi wa baba mmoja. Watoto huko ndani, oh, baba anakupenda kuliko mimi. Mbona ulinunua kiatu kabla mimi? Si hiyo ni kawaida kwa polygamous family?” he posed.

Gachagua said the bigger threat to Opposition unity was not necessarily disagreements among its principals but the conduct of their supporters, social media influencers and political bloggers, whom he accused of fuelling unnecessary tensions through insults and online confrontations.

He cautioned Opposition leaders against allowing overzealous supporters to dictate their political relationships, warning that unchecked political attacks could eventually weaken the coalition and undermine its common objective.

“If there is anything to separate us, it is our supporters and social media bloggers. Wanawakisha moto hakuna, watu wangu na wa Matiang'i wanatukanana na sisi tunakula breakfast pamoja,” he said.

He further claimed that some political influencers associated with his DCP party had been recruited and allegedly paid by individuals opposed to him to attack his leadership and the party.

Gachagua urged coalition principals to exercise restraint and avoid reacting to every provocation from supporters, insisting that political leaders must remain focused on the bigger picture.

“I want to ask leaders in the Opposition, be careful. Don't listen to overzealous supporters and influencers; they will lead you astray. Remain focused,” he warned.

On the question of selecting a joint presidential candidate, Gachagua revealed that differences remained over the appropriate timing, with Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka proposing that the flagbearer be identified before December, while Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna favoured February and Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua suggested May.

Gachagua, however, argued that selecting a candidate too early could expose the individual to political pressure and possible frustration from the government.

He proposed April next year as a more suitable time, maintaining that the coalition was united on the principle of having one candidate even if its leaders differed on the timing.

The DCP leader also dismissed arguments that academic qualifications, experience or political credentials should determine who becomes the coalition's presidential candidate, insisting that electoral numbers and the support of ordinary Kenyans would ultimately decide.

“As others say they have experience and an agenda in the Opposition, the deciding factor is the numbers. I'm with the people. You say you have capacity, but the person to decide is the voter,” he said.

He added: “Akili nyingi ni nzuri, but bila kura unaweza kaa nayo nyumbani.”

World.title: Mudavadi urges Western Kenya to unite, says region cannot remain on sidelines
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Prime CS Musalia Mudavadi. [File, Standard]

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi has urged Western Kenya to unite ahead of the 2027 General Election, saying the region must strengthen its political representation to have a greater say in national decision-making.

Speaking during a UDA delegates' meeting in Shitoto village, Mumias East, Kakamega County, he said Western Kenya could not afford to remain on the sidelines while decisions affecting the country were being made.

"2027 is the moment we must change the narrative. We must make sure that we are at the table where decisions are made. We cannot afford to remain spectators when the future of our country and our region is being determined," he said.

Mudavadi said parliamentary influence depended on numbers, arguing that electing more MPs would give the region a stronger voice in key parliamentary committees, including the Budget Committee.

"Parliament exercises authority in its own right. We want more MPs so that we can have a say in the Budget Committee and other important committees. These positions are secured through numbers, and numbers matter when decisions affecting the country are being made," he said.

Turning to the opposition, Mudavadi described its leaders as divided and challenged them to present clear manifestos outlining what they would offer Kenyans.

He said the divisions within the opposition would work in President William Ruto's favour as he seeks re-election in 2027, expressing confidence that he would win in the first round.

"We want Ruto to win without a petition. We want to thrash them in the first round," he said.

World.title: Family identifies two security officers involved in Abshir Abdi abduction
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

LSK president Charles Kanjama leads members in a protest over the disappearance of lawyer Abshir Abdi. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

The family of Nairobi lawyer Abshir Ahmedsadak Abdi has identified two security officers alleged to have taken part in their kin's abduction, even as his colleagues threatened mass protests to push for his release.

The Law Society of Kenya (LSK) said the two names have been forwarded to the police to aid in investigations and demanded that the office of the Inspector General of Police, Douglas Kanja, speed up the probe into the abduction.

"One is named Siad and the other is Hussein, and we want them released for investigation, arrest, prosecution, conviction, sentencing and imprisonment," said LSK.

The revelation came during a demonstration led by (LSK outside the office of the Deputy Inspector General of Police and other towns yesterday .

Abshir was forcibly taken on November 1 along Muchai Road, his vehicle was pursued and intercepted by armed individuals in two vehicles before he was seized.

While state security agencies have denied holding him in custody, court filings and colleagues suggest his abduction may be connected to his professional work representing clients in high-profile cases involving senior police officers.

Furthermore, the LSK presented additional names of security personnel linked to the incident, demanding immediate legal action against Chief Inspector Vitalis Kibet, Inspector Kennedy Kimani Karanja, Siad Mohammed, Abdurahman of the Anti-Terrorism Police Unit (ATPU), and KDF officer Ali Hussein.

The leadership voiced their frustration over the state's inaction and the alarming pattern of extrajudicial actions targeting officers of the court. Representatives insisted that lawyers must be allowed to execute their duties without fear of intimidation, torture, or abduction.

"We demand that the officers involved be handed over, arrested, prosecuted, and convicted. We will stand in the courts, in the streets, and in the boardrooms until abductions come to an end," they said in a statement.

The LSK has issued a stern ultimatum to the police command, including the president, DIG Gilbert Masengeli, Inspector General Douglas Kanja, and senior commanders. If Abshir is not released safely and the identified suspects are not formally charged in court by Monday, the LSK warned it will initiate private prosecutions itself.

Furthermore, the society threatened to bring activities to a complete shutdown and demand the immediate resignation of Kanja, Masingeli and Minister for Security Kipchumba Murkomen, carrying their demonstrations to Parliament and State House if necessary.

As court proceedings continue under a habeas corpus application at the Milimani High Court, the legal fraternity remains resolute: the protest at Jogoo House is merely the beginning of an unyielding campaign for justice and the rule of law.

In Nakuru, lawyers protested within the Law Courts, calling for his production.

“It is shocking that one of our colleagues was picked and today we do not know where he is. Unless we voice our concern, there will be complete lawlessness in the country,” said LSK member Ekaterina Handa. “Our lives matter and silencing lawyers is silencing justice. we will not relent until we get justice.”

Rift Valley LSK Chair Wangari Mwangi said it was shocking that the alleged abduction was captured on CCTV.

She rubbished the narrative that the missing lawyer was involved in a crime syndicate, maintaining that he should have been arrested and charged in court. [Additional reporting by Daniel Chege]

World.title: Goon financiers should be cursed and sent to hell, Chief Justice Koome says
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Chief Justice Martha Koome said goonism falls under serious organised crimes that goes against the Rome Statute and humanity. [Phares Mutembei, Standard]

Chief Justice Martha Koome now says those mobilising and financing goons should be cursed and thrown to hell.

Koome on Thursday said goonism falls under organised serious crimes that go against the Rome Statute and humanity.

She spoke at Kieganguru, Maara constituency, where she presided over the opening of the Maara law courts.

While calling on police to focus more on arresting the mobilisers and financiers, Koome said a time has come for the country to plead with God to protect the country and rescue the youth who are being misused and misled into organised gangs and goonism.

“Nobody gives birth to a child to be called a goon. Those organisers will go to hell, we curse them,” Koome said, adding, “If they will not go to hell they will meet God's justice. These are our children, and we reclaim them in the name of our Lord Jesus.”

According to her, the last time she checked, people are charged at the International Criminal Court with Organised crime.

She maintained that the best solution to the current goonism that wreaked havoc, especially in political meetings, is to arrest the organisers.

Koome said the courts cannot hold arrested goons without bail, yet the constitution grants them the right to bail or bond.

“When we arrest small people with petty crimes of causing disorder, the law allows us to release them on bail and bond, but when you bring the organisers, we will charge them under the Serious Crimes Act,” she said.

Koome said currently, the judiciary has gazetted a serious crimes division at the High Court to support Magistrates handling the cases.

“Let us look at the root cause of goonism across the country and rehabilitate those involved by getting them gainful employment,” she said.

Her sentiments, however, differ from those of Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen, who on Wednesday told the National Assembly that the judiciary was the weakest link in the fight against the menace.

Tharaka Nithi Governor Muthomi Njuki, in his remarks, supported Koome’s view of arresting the planners.

Njuki, who doubles up as the Council of Governors Chairperson, said politicians have had their time and organising goons against their opponents should not be condoned.

Using the analogy of a dog, Njuki said ‘every barking dog has an owner ’, and it is time serious action was taken against such characters at whatever level they are.

The county boss said CoG will work closely with county security teams to arrest the fast-rising menace and report all cases.

Security agencies have been under scrutiny regarding goons, with calls for their arrest and prosecution.

Earlier on, Koome and DCI boss Mohammed Amin differed on how to handle the goons during a National Council for Administrative Justice meeting as with the DCI boss also accusing the Judiciary of laxity and granting minor bail to arrested goons.

But Koome maintained the issue must be addressed lest it becomes a thorn in the flesh ahead of the 2027 elections.

World.title: IEBC warns UDA SG Hassan Omar over remarks on deceased voters
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

UDA Secretary General Hassan Omar meets Village Elders and Mabalozi wa Nyumba Kumi from Jomvu Sub-County’ on September 10, 2026. [Nehemiah Okwemba, Standard]

The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has issued a stern warning to Senator Hassan Omar after finding him in breach of the Electoral Code of Conduct over remarks he made at a political rally in Mombasa, cautioning that any repeat offence could attract tougher sanctions.

In a determination released on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, the Electoral Code of Conduct Enforcement Committee (ECCEC) found Omar guilty of breaching paragraphs 6(k)(i) and 6(l) of the Electoral Code of Conduct.

The committee consequently issued the senator with a formal and strict warning and severe caution, directing him to comply with the electoral regulations for the remainder of the applicable election period.

Omar was further instructed to refrain from language or conduct that could reasonably be understood as encouraging or normalising electoral malpractice or undermining public confidence in the integrity of the ballot.

The decision follows investigations into remarks the senator allegedly made during a public rally in Mombasa on September 11, 2026, which raised concerns over the possibility of encouraging electoral malpractice.

According to the commission, Omar was summoned to appear before the committee on October 21, 2026, to respond to the allegations. He honoured the summons and appeared in person, accompanied by his lawyer, where he was given an opportunity to explain his remarks and present his defence.

In reaching its determination, the committee considered the context in which the statements were made, Omar's explanation that his words were intended figuratively to encourage voter registration and participation, his subsequent clarification and the absence of evidence linking the remarks to an actual electoral incident.

However, the committee maintained that the language used could not be excused by the explanation offered.

It observed that the impugned words, considered in their original Kiswahili form and ordinary meaning, invoked the use of biometric identification details belonging to a deceased person to facilitate voting in that individual's name.

The committee consequently found the remarks inconsistent with the obligation under paragraph 6(l) of the Electoral Code to reassure voters about the integrity of the ballot.

The warning places Omar on clear notice that any recurrence of similar conduct could attract more severe sanctions under the Electoral Code of Conduct and applicable laws.

“The determination places Hon. Hassan Omar on clear and unequivocal notice that the warning issued by the Committee is intended to mark a firm boundary against any recurrence of similar conduct,” IEBC stated.

The commission further emphasised that political leaders and other electoral stakeholders have a constitutional right to campaign, criticise, debate, persuade and participate in political discourse.

However, it cautioned that political expression must be exercised responsibly, warning that statements perceived as advocating, encouraging or normalising electoral malpractice could undermine public confidence in the electoral process.

“As Kenya prepares for the 2027 General Election, the Commission calls upon all political leaders, candidates, political parties, supporters and other electoral stakeholders to exercise responsibility, restraint and vigilance in their public utterances and conduct,” the commission said.

The determination comes as political activities gradually intensify ahead of the 2027 General Election, with the electoral body seeking to strengthen compliance with regulations governing political campaigns and public conduct.

IEBC maintained that enforcement of the Electoral Code should not be interpreted as an attempt to suppress legitimate political competition or freedom of expression.

Instead, it said the measures were intended to safeguard democratic participation and ensure that every Kenyan could exercise their right to vote without intimidation, manipulation or interference.

The commission reiterated its commitment to protecting the sanctity of the ballot, assuring Kenyans that every vote must be protected and counted in accordance with the law.

It warned that it would continue enforcing electoral regulations firmly, fairly and without fear or favour, as preparations for the 2027 elections gather momentum.

World.title: Death rumours made me stronger, says ODM leader Oburu
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Speakers Moses Wetang’ula and Amason Kingi when they paid a visit to ODM leader Oburu Oginga at his Nairobi residence on November 4, 2026. [Speaker’s Press Unit]

ODM leader and Siaya Senator Oburu Oginga has said rumours about his death while he was admitted to hospital only strengthened his determination to overcome his illness.

Dr Oburu who is recovering after being discharged from hospital, assured his supporters that he was making remarkable improvement and would return to active politics soon.

Speaking at his Nairobi residence on Wednesday when Speakers Moses Wetang’ula and Amason Kingi paid him a visit, the ODM leader said the rumours only strengthened his resolve to come out of the hospital bed.

“Those who wrote me off while I was in hospital by declaring me dead only made me stronger and more determined to fight my sickness. Here I am, recovering and growing stronger by the day,” he said.

He said that his recovery was a testimony to God's protection, saying those who had spread the false reports had been put to shame.

Oburu admitted that the illness had slowed down him down but he was looking forward to returning to the political arena.

“The sickness slowed my political activities. Very soon, I will be back roaring in the best way I know how,” he said.

The senator thanked the National Assembly Speaker Wetang’ula, his Senate counterpart Kingi and other legislators for taking time to visit him following his discharge from hospital.

He said the visit had lifted his spirit and revealed that he missed participating in parliamentary debates and engaging in national political affairs.

“I have no words to explain my feelings after the Speakers of both Houses and fellow legislators created time to come and check on me,” he said.

“I miss being on the floor of the House debating and roaring in the political arena. I urge my supporters to pray for me and be patient because soon I will be back,” he added.

Despite his recent health challenges, Oburu kept his visitors entertained with his trademark humour while expressing confidence that he would soon resume his political duties.

The two Speakers condemned the spread of false information on social media, particularly rumours that the senator had died while undergoing treatment.

Wetang’ula said they were encouraged by the senator's recovery and wished him a full and speedy return to good health.

He, however, cautioned Oburu against rushing back into politics before fully recovering, urging him to give his health priority.

“Prioritise your health and avoid rushing back into political engagements before making a full recovery,” he said.

The National Assembly Speaker also praised the senator for his courage and determination in facing his health challenges.

Kingi said the Senate missed Dr Oburu's contribution to debates, parliamentary proceedings and national politics.

“As the Senate, we miss your contributions to proceedings and debates as well as your guidance in national politics. We pray that you get better and resume your political duties as soon as possible,” he said.

Those who accompanied the two Speakers included Senate Chief Whip David Wakoli, Senate Minority Leader Stewart Madzayo, Senators William Kisang and Daniel Maanzo.

Others were National Assembly Minority Whip Millie Odhiambo, Parliamentary Commissioner Mishi Mboko and MP Eve Obara.

World.title: Kenyans stranded after Saudi Arabia blocks entry over Ebola concerns
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenyan jobseekers arrive at JKIA on November 2, 2026, after being denied entry into Saudi Arabia over Ebola-related restrictions. [Stafford Ondego, Standard]

More than 300 Kenyans who travelled to Saudi Arabia in search of employment have been forced to return home after authorities blocked their entry over Ebola-related restrictions, leaving them stranded at the airport for two days.

The group, which departed Kenya on October 30, had travelled to the Gulf country on valid work visas but was denied entry upon arrival and subsequently repatriated, arriving back in the country on Monday.

The return follows a warning by Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale on Saturday, October 31, over restrictions imposed by Saudi Arabia on travellers from countries flagged over Ebola concerns.

Speaking to the media at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) on Monday, the affected workers recounted their ordeal, accusing authorities at the airport of subjecting them to harsh conditions as they waited to be repatriated.

“We were treated so harshly as though we had leprosy. We only took one meal per day and slept on the cold floors at the airport in Saudi Arabia,” said Kanyi Njau, one of the affected workers, claiming that some have even lost their luggage.

Beyond the difficult experience at the airport, the workers said their biggest concern was the financial loss incurred while preparing for the promised jobs.

Some said they had sold land, household belongings and other property, while others borrowed money to pay recruitment agents, process visas and secure travel documents in preparation for their departure.

Njau said the abrupt disruption had shattered the hopes of many who had invested heavily in securing employment abroad.

“Some of us sold things in our houses, even land. Some even took loans from shylocks just so that we could travel over there for the jobs, but now we are back with no hope,” she said.

Kenyan jobseekers arrive at JKIA on November 2, 2026, after being denied entry into Saudi Arabia over Ebola-related restrictions. [Stafford Ondego, Standard]

The workers are now appealing to the Kenyan Government to intervene and resolve the standoff with Saudi authorities before their visas expire, allowing them to return and take up the jobs they had secured.

Meanwhile, recruitment agencies have called on the Government to urgently clarify the restrictions, warning that uncertainty over a 21-day provision could disrupt the country's labour mobility programme.

Monika Mwema, the Secretary General of the Association of Skilled Migrant Agencies of Kenya (ASMAK), said recruiters had been caught off guard, with some workers already repatriated while others had confirmed tickets and were scheduled to travel.

“We are caught off guard. We have people who are coming back because they could not be allowed to enter Saudi Arabia, while others have confirmed tickets and are even supposed to leave tonight and tomorrow,” she said.

Mwema said the association was seeking clarification on what the 21-day provision meant for workers holding stamped Saudi work visas, including whether they would be required to undergo quarantine in Kenya or in a third country before being allowed into the Kingdom.

“Does it mean we have to quarantine our people here for the 21 days, then they are allowed to enter the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia? Or does it mean that we need to seek an alternative quarantine area where there is no case of Ebola?” she asked.

Kenyan jobseekers arrive at JKIA on November 2, 2026, after being denied entry into Saudi Arabia over Ebola-related restrictions. [Stafford Ondego, Standard]

She said recruiters were also concerned about the 90-day period within which migrant workers are required to travel after their visas are stamped, warning that delays could result in significant losses for agencies and prospective employees.

Mwema added that some workers had already undergone training and completed examinations in preparation for their deployment, while recruitment partners in Saudi Arabia were demanding to know when the workers would arrive.

“The losses are just too many. We have people who have already gone to school for training; others have done their examinations and are waiting to go. Our partners are calling us, asking when these people are coming, but we are all in the dark,” she said.

ASMAK is now seeking urgent engagement with the Kenyan Government and Saudi authorities to establish a clear way forward.

Mwema said the association was ready to engage the Government, including through a meeting with President William Ruto, to discuss the future of labour mobility between the two countries.

Saudi Arabia remains Kenya's biggest market for labour mobility, with recruiters warning that continued uncertainty could affect workers awaiting deployment and agencies with visas already processed.

World.title: Egypt needs 10,000 Magdi Yacoubs and double the healthcare budget, Sisi says
World.content:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said that his greatest dream is for Egypt to have 10,000 doctors with the same stature and caliber as world-renowned surgeon Magdi Yacoub.

Sisi’s remarks came during the opening session of the Third Medical Conference of the Armed Forces College of Medicine, which was held at al-Safwa International Conference Center at the Strategic Command headquarters in the New Capital.

He stated that preparing new generations of scientists and specialists requires drawing upon successful Egyptian role models and studying the factors that contributed to their excellence.

The President elaborated on his grand dream of developing the education and health sectors, stressing they are the primary drivers of progress in any nation.

“If we want Egypt to regain its position, priority must be given to health and education,” he stressed.

President Sisi pointed out that the state exerted tremendous efforts in 2013 and 2014 in both sectors; however, the challenges were so immense that those efforts were not sufficiently felt.

He explained that the scale of spending from 2014 to 2026 has been substantial.

Sisi asserted that the state prioritizes not merely the number of facilities and graduates, but also merit and quality, adding that this focus drove the state to establish twinning agreements with world-class universities and hospitals to leverage their expertise and rapidly elevate Egyptian capabilities and skills.

The president stressed that signing the cooperation protocol between the Armed Forces College of Medicine and the Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland represents one of the steps taken by the state, not just the Armed Forces, to guarantee merit.

Sisi reaffirmed the state’s focus on human development across all fields and sectors.

Armed Forces College of Medicine

Regarding the Armed Forces College of Medicine, Sisi noted that a large number of civilians applied to join this year.

Therefore, a plan was developed to expand upon this initiative by establishing six new faculties at Kayan University in the fields of Medicine, Dentistry, Physical Therapy, Pharmacy, Engineering, and Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence.

He said these disciplines represent the most advanced fields, adding that the state is actively seeking to forge twinning agreements between these faculties and their prestigious foreign counterparts.

The president noted that Kayan University will have a capacity of approximately 25,000 students.

The president emphasized that for the state to deliver high-quality healthcare as envisioned, it would require a budget at least double or triple the current healthcare allocation.

Sisi noted that providing healthcare to citizens, or to anyone seeking refuge in Egypt, is a matter that carries not only economic dimensions, but also moral, humanitarian, and religious ones.

Tahya Misr Fund

Sisi ordered the “Tahya Misr Fund” to cover the tuition costs for outstanding gifted students to attend Kayan University, provided they maintain their academic excellence.

President Sisi stated that Kayan University will be inaugurated in February 2027. Sisi called upon parents and students to take full advantage of the carefully tailored programs offered by these faculties.

The president noted his pleasure regarding the upcoming inauguration of Kayan University, as well as another new university along Ain Sokhna Road in March 2027, whose name has yet to be determined.

Both the president and the Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research noted that work is underway to develop eight universities into world-leading institutions across all aspects, including facilities, academic standards, and digitalization, confirming that the state will make significant strides if major progress is achieved in the health and education sectors.

President Sisi concluded by underscoring the importance of continuous communication between officials and citizens to highlight state efforts across all sectors, reassuring the public that Egypt is on the right track toward achieving its target goals.

The President emphasized that the progress of nations spans decades, requiring a clear action plan, diligent follow-up, robust political will, stability, and continuity.

World.title: Trump says ‘great dislike of Israel’ contributed to Republican midterm losses
World.content:
Jerusalem —

President Donald Trump said a “great dislike for Israel” was one of the reasons the Republicans lost in the midterm elections, along with the Iran war and the subsequent rise in gasoline prices.

“I think if I was on the ballot, it would’ve been a much different situation because you saw the level of popularity and love,” Trump said in an interview with CBS’ “60 Minutes” that aired Sunday. “But there’s something beyond that. They didn’t like the war. They didn’t like the fact that gasoline went up, ‘cause I had it down at a low, and there’s a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel.”

Trump’s comments underscore a sea change in US politics where Israel once had bipartisan support, as well as strong backing from Republican and Democratic presidents. But the extent of US military and financial support for Israel emerged as a frequent political liability during the midterm elections.

Michigan’s Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed may have been the most prominent critic of Israel during the elections, but he was far from the only one. Even Vice President JD Vance suggested Republicans would have to rethink their once-stalwart support of Israel moving forward.

Trump said he agrees with Vance’s position that the war with Iran is among the reasons for the Republican loss. But he said he doesn’t regret his decision to launch the war. “You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon. I think, historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not. But you know, I have to go with what’s right for our country. If they had a nuclear weapon during my term, I would be excoriated far worse than what’s happened.”

The president also said that other countries, including Israel, would have to share the costs of the war.

US Navy sailors load ammunition onto an F/A-18F Super Hornet on the flight deck of the Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln in support of the Operation Epic Fury attack on Iran February 28. US Navy/Reuters

“Those countries that we’ve protected are going to pay us back any and all costs that we’ve had for the war ‘cause without us, they wouldn’t exist. Without us, Israel would not exist,” Trump said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has long presented himself as the leader best able to manage the relationship with the United States and particularly Trump. But in just a matter of days, Trump has signaled major changes may be coming.

“Democrats and Republicans are competing to see who can distance themselves from us more,” wrote Israeli journalist Amir Tibon on X. “And if we don’t act quickly, the new Congress will start holding up arms sales.” Tibon called for a new government that can begin “repairing the damage Netanyahu is leaving behind.”

On the day of the US elections, Trump said he would end $4 billion in annual aid to Israel this year, potentially cutting off one of the key elements of Israel’s security strategy. Days later, Netanyahu said the aid would shift to a “partnership,” but didn’t say whether Trump had given him a heads-up about the surprise announcement.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog made an oblique reference to the shift in American and international perceptions of the country on Sunday, as he tasked Netanyahu’s rival, Gadi Eizenkot, with forming the next government.

“The challenges facing the State of Israel are immense. Some demand urgent and immediate attention,” he said. “Iran does not pause for a moment in its schemes and threats. We must work to build a diplomatic horizon in the region and for the day after the war.”

World.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits affair as company launches investigation into foreign spy claims
World.content:
Nvidia chief Jensen Huang has admitted to having an extramarital affair as his company announced it will investigate reports he was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

The separate statements come amid growing concern over Huang’s close relationship with an executive from Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed, Alice Huang. Several US outlets have reported that American officials suspect Alice Huang, no relation, has fed intelligence to China and helped smuggle advanced artificial intelligence chips into the country.

The controversy could undermine faith in the world’s second-largest company and a poster child for the AI boom, at a time when the US and China are racing to surpass the other in technological supremacy.

In a note to Nvidia staff, Huang said that he was “unfaithful” and hurt his wife and children. He did not name the other person in the affair.

“I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it,” Huang, 63, said, adding that he supports Nvidia’s investigation. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security.”

Meanwhile, the company said in a Sunday press release that a committee of independent directors and outside counsel will oversee its investigation.

“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the statement said. But, the board “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.”

In a note, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at merchant bank Yorkville & Ives Co., called the news “a black eye moment for Jensen” that will increase scrutiny of chip sales to China, which Huang has previously lobbied for.

The investigation will also cast a shadow over Nvidia’s share price, Ives added, as investors question whether Huang will remain at the helm of the company he helped found.

“Today’s news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption,” a spokesperson for Nvidia told CNN.

Jacob Ward, a tech journalist and CNN contributor said corporate boards historically tend to oust chief executives caught having extramarital affairs within days.

For Nvidia, which holds an outsized role in AI development, global growth and the US stock market, any existential questions about its future will have even greater economic and geopolitical implications. Another unusual factor is that the company has no clear successor for Huang, he added.

“It is a core of the American economy, if not the world economy right now. And this guy who is famously a very, very central commander of all of this stuff, suddenly being caught in this way and especially being caught perhaps being dishonest about it, it’s an incredibly big deal,” Ward said.

The China connection

Huang’s connections to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, which buys chips from Nvidia, have come under intense scrutiny as a potential channel for US semiconductors to reach Chinese buyers, despite export controls on advanced technologies.

The Financial Times previously reported that US intelligence believed that the two were in a romantic relationship.

Nvidia said in a past statement that Jensen Huang’s meetings were “not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

It added that any concerns about illegal chip diversion were “debunked last year.”

Huang joked in a previous interview that he wooed his wife Lori Huang, whom he met in college when he was 17 and she was 19, by offering to help with her homework and vowing to become a CEO by age 30. The couple married in 1985 and have two children.

In 1993 he co-founded Nvidia, which has seen its market capitalization swell to more than $4 trillion as the rise of AI has turbocharged demand for the computer chips it designs.

He has since become the face of the company and a prominent figure in the booming business of AI. Huang joined President Donald Trump with a host of other high-profile CEOs in Beijing earlier this year to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

“Nvidia and Jensen are deeply intertwined. Many people will say Nvidia without Jensen won’t be the same,” George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, wrote in a Monday note. “I don’t think it will serve the best interests of Nvidia shareholders and industry partners either if Jensen suddenly quits tomorrow.”

The US government cleared 10 Chinese firms to buy Nvidia’s second-most powerful AI chips, Reuters reported earlier this year, though its unclear how many chips have actually been sold following the approval.

On Sunday, Trump told reporters that he has not spoken to Huang since Nvidia announced the investigation, but said that he was a “fine person” and praised his contribution to the country.

When asked if he wished he had taken action when briefed on the intelligence about alleged spying last year, Trump said, “No I don’t think so. I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”

On Thursday, Republican chairmen of three influential House panels — the committees on Foreign Affairs, the Chinese Communist Party and Intelligence — said in a news release that they sent a letter to Huang requesting his appearance before their committees to answer questions about his relationship with Megaspeed and the company’s security protocols against foreign espionage.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.”

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that the allegation that Alice Huang was gathering information for Beijing was “purely groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.”

State-run tabloid The Global Times accused US media outlets of making up stories that could derail a detente between the two nations.

On Chinese social media, Huang’s admission of infidelity became one of the top trending topics with more than 40 million views on the X-like platform Weibo. However, the allegation that Alice Huang was working as a Chinese spy was largely absent from tightly-controlled online discussions.

This story has been updated with additional content.

World.title: As fresh talks near, Putin appears set on wrecking Ukraine’s economy, leaving Kyiv facing the toughest winter yet
World.content:
As Russia struggles to advance on the ground in eastern Ukraine, it is pouring more resources into the war in the skies.

Russian missiles and drones are hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure harder and earlier in the year than in previous years, analysts say, and the Kremlin has broadened its targets to further damage the Ukrainian economy.

An independent United Nations investigations panel last week concluded that Russia committed war crimes and crimes against humanity by intentionally attacking civilian infrastructure, particularly with attacks on vital energy systems during the severe winter of 2025-2026.

This winter, experts say attacks are expected to be worse. With the US set to mediate in fresh peace talks next week, Russian President Vladimir Putin is only escalating his attacks on Ukraine.

The Russian air campaign is now “clearly aimed at destroying the Ukrainian economy,” said John Lough, head of international partnerships at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, a London-based think tank. Lough also told CNN that he believes many of Kyiv’s allies in Europe haven’t grasped “just how serious this situation is that is developing in Ukraine,” nor how much of a financial burden it could place on European partners.

“Putin has concluded that he can’t win in Donbas by committing more men to battle and trying to push forward, because the Ukrainians have actually had a relatively successful summer,” Lough said.

“(Putin) has concluded the only way to break that is to actually break the economy, and they are doing that in a systematic way.”

Cristian Vlas, an Eastern Europe researcher at ACLED, a global conflict monitor, said, “We’ll see a terrible humanitarian situation this winter and much earlier than last year.”

Civilian deaths in Ukraine are at their highest since the first months of the war, with Russian strikes killing more than 2,700 Ukrainian civilians so far in 2026, according to data compiled by ACLED.

The number of Russian strikes launched on Ukraine has increased steadily in 2026. In January 2026, there were 3,650 Russian strikes on Ukraine. For October, that figure increased to 5,532.

Ukraine’s attacks inside Russia have also increased, with 2,302 strikes carried out in October. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense said it hit at least seven enterprises involved in weapons production, three military airfields and key radar and military communications facilities last month. This summer, Ukraine also launched attacks on the warehouses of Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries.

US President Donald Trump has also suggested that Ukraine may have to cede some of its territory to achieve peace. “They’re gonna end up with a little bit different shape, Ukraine,” he told “60 Minutes” in an interview that aired Sunday, just days before US negotiators are set to lead trilateral meetings in Abu Dhabi this week.

Ukraine’s territorial integrity is protected under its constitution, making a formal concession of territory illegal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

Russia targets industry, grain exports

Russian attacks on Ukraine’s Black Sea exports, Danube River ports, industrial warehouses, railway infrastructure and steel industry are now frequent events.

Some of that infrastructure has both civilian and military purposes, but experts said that recent attacks have brazenly targeted civilians alone.

At least 55 Ukrainians were killed Monday when Russia bombed a school building used as a shelter and aid center in Zaporizhzhia, one of the deadliest incidents of a conflict in its fifth year. The site was attacked again with a drone on Sunday, as emergency rescuers were searching for people trapped under the rubble, Ukrainian authorities said.

Moscow consistently denies targeting civilians.

Police officers and rescuers carry the body of a resident killed in a Russian airstrike inside the compound of a local school that was used as a humanitarian aid hub in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, on November 3, 2026. Stringer/Reuters

Meanwhile, major Ukrainian steel plants in Kryvyi Rih and Zaporizhzhia were hit in ballistic missile strikes between August and October, forcing them to shut down. The city of Kryvyi Rih has raised the alarm about “serious socio-economic consequences” and loss of income for thousands of families due to the steel plant closure.

“Those are hits to Ukraine’s tax base, not just you know ‘industry’ in a very abstract manner,” Vlas said. “It hits at the people’s salaries.”

Combined with Russian strikes on other major sectors like agriculture and grain exports, Vlas noted that it appears to be an effort by Moscow to create multiple economic firestorms across Ukraine’s economy at the same time.

“They’re targeting things like malls, storages, warehouses – so, that disrupts the flow of goods, the sale of goods, and so on,” said Kateryna Stepanenko, the Russia Team Lead at the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington think tank that closely monitors the conflict.

And while Russia once mostly attacked at night, Stepanenko said that it has been increasingly conducting daytime strikes, which are partially aimed at upending day-to-day business activities in Ukraine.

“What that does is that it activates an air alert under which many Ukrainian government buildings or businesses cannot legally operate, and so that disrupts business,” she told CNN.

Strikes on energy infrastructure also disrupt economic activity, given that power and water outages severely impact businesses.

Russian forces have also started to hit energy infrastructure in areas of Ukraine that were not previously targeted, such as the western city of Rivne, said Stepanenko, which creates new challenges for Ukraine’s threadbare air defenses.

The impacts of energy strikes are mounting. Many of Ukraine’s power stations are damaged beyond repair.

“We just have to keep in mind the cumulative effect of this war, and the very great fatigue on the Ukrainian side,” Lough said. “With the fabric of the economy strained in this way, it’s really a very dangerous moment.”

Ukraine’s capital Kyiv seen during a power blackout in October after critical civil infrastructure was hit by Russian missile and drone attacks. Gleb Garanich/Reuters

Overnight into Sunday, Russia attacked the power grid in the Dnipropetrovsk region leaving more than 600,000 people without electricity, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. He also said there are widespread power outages in other regions, including Kharkiv and Zhytomyr.

Local authorities in Kyiv said that roughly 40 percent of buildings didn’t have heating as of Saturday. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha gave yet another stark warning this weekend, as the first snowfall of the year arrived in Ukraine.

“Moscow is deliberately seeking to leave millions of Ukrainians without electricity, heating, and water as winter approaches,” Sybiha said. “Russia is trying to achieve through cold and darkness what it cannot achieve on the battlefield.”

Civilians paying the price

The higher civilian casualties come as Russia has expanded its use of jet-powered Shahed drones and loitering munitions – weapons that are difficult for Ukrainian forces to shoot down. Ukraine is working to improve its interception capabilities for both, but at the moment, experts said, the Russian weapons have an edge.

Ukraine is also dealing with a persistent shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors, which are one of the few defensive weapons that can take down a Russian ballistic missile.

As a result, “the civilian fatalities and casualties have been increasing almost since April, almost constantly. But the surge in fatalities in October – early October – is just staggering,” ACLED’s Vlas told CNN.

Civilians are also paying a high price.

A new report from the International Rescue Committee (IRC) found that in southern and eastern regions of Ukraine, financial distress is pushing civilians to abandon their homes or take grave risks to keep making money. For example, in some regions, IRC found that farmers were risking their lives to work on land contaminated with mines, just so they could retain some source of income.

A farmer, Oleksandr Havryliuk, stands by an anti-personnel mine found in a farm field in the Izium district of Ukriane’s Kharkiv region. Viacheslav Madiievskyi/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing/Getty Imagese

Among hundreds of households surveyed in the region of Mykolaiv, 91 percent said they were in urgent need of financial assistance. In Dnipropetrovsk, 42 percent cited financial assistance as an urgent need.

“The lack of financial resources is not just (about) paying the bills. It really creates the pressure to make the life-changing decisions,” said Olga Kashuba, IRC’s deputy director of field management in Ukraine.

And for many civilians in eastern Ukraine, the conflict began disrupting their lives and livelihoods in 2014, she noted, meaning they have suffered more than a decade of economic pressure.

Based in Kyiv, Kashuba herself has witnessed the growing economic anxieties and the loss of neighbors’ incomes. Her local farmers’ market closed down after it was destroyed in a Russian strike. A nearby warehouse was hit in another recent attack, damaging the inventory of multiple small booksellers, she told CNN.

“When the grocery shops are burned, when the warehouses are burned… yes, it affects the goods,” Kashuba said. “But also, this is the source of income for a number of people – for thousands of people.”

CNN’s Becky Pinnington, Kosta Gak and Victoria Butenko contributed to this report.

World.title: Joe Biden says cancer will limit him from promoting his upcoming memoir
World.content:
Former President Joe Biden announced Sunday that he “won’t be able to do as many conversations” about his upcoming presidential memoir due to his fight with prostate cancer.

“Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down. What that means is, unfortunately, I won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped. However, I’m hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves,” he wrote on social media.

The Atlantic published Monday the first excerpt from Biden’s book, which is titled “Promise Me, America” and slated for release on November 17. In it, Biden mainly criticized some of the earliest actions in President Donald Trump’s second term and expressed confidence that US democracy can withstand the era of his successor.

But the former president also offered some surprising observations about his post-election meeting with Trump at the White House. He said Trump’s tone toward him “bordered on fawning,” that Trump told him they’d be “good friends” if not for politics and that Trump praised his job creating record as “extraordinary.”

“I didn’t really understand why he was buttering me up, so I cut off his compliments to move on to the business at hand,” Biden wrote, pivoting to the foreign policy issues he wanted to raise with Trump.

Biden, who turns 84 on November 20, is the oldest living former president. He revealed his cancer diagnosis in May 2025, less than four months after he left the White House.

His office said in a statement then that he appeared to have a “more aggressive” form of cancer but that it “appears to be hormone-sensitive which allows for effective management.”

The former president’s son, Hunter Biden, told the BBC in August that his father’s cancer had “metastasized into his bones and further.”

“It’s really sad to watch,” Hunter Biden said. “The only thing that I’d say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good.”

“I hope you’ll read it,” Biden wrote on social media about his memoir. “It covers my years as President. The challenges we faced, the decisions I made, and why I made them. It’s about who we are as a nation. What we stand for. And America’s role in the world.”

This story has been updated with additional information.

World.title: Red Sea ports handle 10,000 tons of general, miscellaneous cargo
World.content:
The Red Sea Ports Authority said its ports handled a total of 10,000 tons of general and miscellaneous cargo, 500 trucks and 120 cars on Sunday, November 8, 2026.

Port traffic included the arrival and departure of 10 vessels, while a total of 965 passengers arrived at or departed from the ports, the authority said.

In a statement, the authority’s media center said imports involved seven vessels carrying 5,000 tons of cargo, along with 302 trucks and 114 cars.

Exports comprised six vessels carrying 5,000 tons of cargo, 198 trucks and six cars.

The statement stated that Safaga Port received the vessels POSEIDON EXPRESS and Amal, while the vessel ZHONG WANG, carrying 42,000 tons of phosphate, and the vessel PAN LILI departed the port.

Meanwhile, Nuweiba Port handled 4,900 tons of cargo and 211 trucks through round trips involving the arrival and departure of three vessels: Al-Hussein, Sina and Ayla.

World.title: Egypt, India discuss boosting strategic partnership in innovative financing, startups
World.content:
Minister of Planning and Economic Development Ahmed Rostom discussed on Sunday, November 8, 2026, with Indian Ambassador to Cairo Suresh K. Reddy ways to strengthen the strategic partnership and expand cooperation in innovative financing and support for startups.

The meeting came as part of Egypt’s efforts to strengthen international partnerships and deepen economic and investment cooperation with India in support of national and regional development agendas.

During the meeting, Rostom praised India’s leading experience in digital infrastructure, fostering innovation and creating an enabling environment for startup growth. He stressed the importance of benefiting from India’s experience, as well as the innovative financing mechanisms and solutions developed by the Indian side.

He said entrepreneurship is a key driver of sustainable economic development, contributing to job creation, promoting innovation and encouraging the establishment of startups, thereby boosting productivity and enhancing the competitiveness of the national economy.

In this regard, he said the government, through its ministerial group for entrepreneurship, is working on an ambitious executive plan to develop the sector, encourage the emergence of new unicorn companies, launch initiatives targeting students and researchers, and provide financing to support the sector’s growth.

Rostom added that the Egyptian government is committed to pursuing economic reform to consolidate economic stability, create a favorable environment for domestic and foreign investment and enable Indian companies to capitalize on Egypt’s competitive advantages, including its strategic geographic location and investment incentives across various sectors.

For his part, the Indian ambassador highlighted his country’s experience, noting that India is home to more than 240,000 startups. He said the Egyptian market serves as a regional hub for companies seeking to expand into African and European markets.

Reddy stressed the importance of including financial technology (FinTech) companies and digital solutions providers, such as the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), in upcoming investment delegations to Cairo to strengthen opportunities for partnerships between the two countries.

He announced that arrangements were underway for a high-level investment delegation comprising more than 150 major Indian companies to visit Egypt and explore investment opportunities firsthand.

The ambassador expressed his country’s appreciation for its partnership with Egypt, pointing out that Indian companies have investments worth nearly $5 billion in the country. These investments are spread across around 55 Indian factories, providing more than 35,000 jobs for Egyptian citizens.

He noted that exploratory visits to Egypt by numerous Indian businesspeople had generated new investment interest, reaffirming Egypt’s position as a destination for economic and regional stability.

Reddy also extended an official invitation to Rostom to visit India, stressing the importance of familiarizing the Egyptian side with India’s “Vision 2047” alongside Egypt’s “Vision 2030.”

He explained that India has an ambitious vision to become a developed economy by 2047, when it will mark the centenary of its independence.

The Ambassador also invited the Egyptian side to participate in India’s annual conference on building the startup ecosystem, organized by the National Association of Software and Service Companies (NASSCOM).

At the conclusion of the meeting, both sides stressed the need to institutionalize cooperation through the launch of a “Joint Egyptian-Indian Startup Forum,” which would serve as a permanent platform for dialogue and integration between young talent in the two countries and open new horizons for investment and mutual growth, ensuring the partnership’s sustainability and expansion into new areas.

World.title: Egypt wins gold award for top cultural tourism destination
World.content:
Egypt won the gold award in the 25th edition of the British magazine Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards in the category of “Most Desirable Cultural and Heritage Destination,” ranking first ahead of several leading transnational tourist destinations, based on readers’ votes.

The Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards are among the travel industry’s prominent honors, with winners selected through votes by the magazine’s readers, reflecting travelers’ preferences and actual experiences.

CEO of the Egyptian Tourism Authority Ahmed Youssef received the award at a ceremony held at the historic Painted Hall of the Old Royal Naval College in London’s Greenwich district, attended by around 500 senior travel and tourism industry leaders from around the world.

In his keynote speech, Prince Harry Duke of Sussex and founder of the Travalyst initiative, stressed the importance of promoting responsible and sustainable tourism practices and cooperation among stakeholders to ensure a more sustainable future for the sector.

On the occasion, Minister of Tourism Sherif Fathy welcomed the award, saying it reflected Egypt’s distinguished position on the global tourism map and its unique cultural and heritage assets, which showcase the richness of ancient Egyptian civilization and its thousands of years of history, as well as its exceptional museums and archaeological sites.

He said the award recognized Egypt’s efforts to preserve its cultural heritage by maintaining museums and archaeological sites, ensuring their sustainability for future generations, improving services and enhancing the visitor experience.

Fathy added that these efforts were part of the ministry’s strategy to highlight Egypt’s unparalleled tourism diversity and strengthen its position as an integrated destination offering distinctive experiences for visitors with varied interests, thereby boosting its competitiveness globally.

For his part, Youssef said the award reflected Egypt’s strong appeal among travelers interested in cultural and heritage tourism and its ability to offer rich experiences combining authenticity and diversity while meeting the preferences of visitors seeking meaningful cultural and historical experiences.

He added that the award further strengthened the international recognition of Egypt’s tourism sector, enhanced its presence in global markets and supported promotional efforts to attract more cultural and heritage tourists.

It could also encourage previous visitors to return and explore the country’s diverse tourism offerings.

World.title: Liberia: Record Billions at the Top, Rising Hunger at the Bottom
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia – In central Monrovia, where vendors line the sidewalks with trays of biscuits, chocolate and soap, the national budget is not measured in billions. It is measured in how many customers stop, and how much they can spend.

By Rodney D Sieh

Patrick Mamligar, who sells snacks on those streets, told FrontPageAfrica earlier this year that the finance minister’s claims about an improving economy were simply not true.



His was one voice among many in that survey of traders and shoppers. Few of them could point to anything in their own lives that matched the government’s upbeat numbers.

The finance minister has heard the complaint before. Pressed on whether Liberians were feeling relief, Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan asked whether the government was expected to hand out actual bread and butter before citizens accepted that their concerns were being addressed. The remark has followed him ever since.

The ledger and the street

On paper, Ngafuan’s second tour at the Finance Ministry has been a run of records. In September, the Liberia Revenue Authority crossed US$1 billion in domestic collections for the first time in the country’s history. On Friday, the government sent lawmakers a US$1.538 billion budget for 2027, the largest Liberia has ever proposed.

The minister points to growth of 5.1 percent last year, inflation brought under control and the absence of the budget shortfalls that dogged the previous government. In one interview, he summed up his case in a line: Liberia is “not where we want to be,” but no longer where it was.

He also argues that patience is part of the plan. Stabilizing prices, revenue and public finances, he has said, must come before any expansion that ordinary people can feel. Roads now, he insists, mean jobs and cheaper goods later.

His critics hear something else. Opposition leader Alexander Cummings has turned the debate into a slogan about eating today rather than waiting for tomorrow.

The opposition Citizens Movement for Change recently praised Ngafuan as eloquent, then questioned his credibility, citing audit gaps and unreconciled revenue records between the ministry, the LRA and the Central Bank. Last year, the General Auditing Commission flagged US$2.8 million in ministry payments without adequate supporting documents; Ngafuan called it a paperwork problem, not theft. Critics, including opposition figures, independent analysts and a former director of the ministry’s own budget department, now describe the lapses at the Finance Ministry as among the most serious failings of President Joseph Boakai’s Unity Party-led government. Some have openly called for the minister’s removal.

The sharpest challenge, however, has come not from his political rivals but from one of the government’s closest partners.

The World Bank’s paradox

On November 3, the World Bank launched the seventh edition of its Liberia Economic Update, titled Beyond Growth. Its central finding cuts straight through the government’s narrative: the economy grew, and so did extreme poverty.

By the Bank’s estimate, the share of Liberians in extreme poverty rose from 34.6 percent in 2024 to 36.1 percent in 2025 – in the same year the economy expanded 5.1 percent. Country Manager Georgia Wallen called it the paradox at the heart of the report.

The explanation lies in where the growth came from. Mining output jumped 17 percent. Agriculture, which feeds most Liberian households and makes up about a third of the economy, grew just 2.6 percent. In short, Liberia is growing fastest where few Liberians work.

The labour figures are starker.

About 78 percent of workers are in what the Bank calls vulnerable employment – street trading, small-plot farming or unpaid family work. Wage jobs make up just 20.9 percent of employment, a share that has barely moved in two decades. Reserves covered only about 1.6 months of imports at the end of 2025, leaving the country exposed if oil or food prices spike.

The Bank expects extreme poverty to ease to 33.2 percent this year, but only if farming recovers. It also anticipates a value-added tax (VAT) starting in early 2027 – a change that could push up prices at the very stalls where Liberians already feel squeezed.

None of this is Ngafuan’s doing alone. But as the minister who sets budget priorities, he owns the question the Bank is asking: why does so little of Liberia’s new money reach the farms, markets and households where most people make their living? Agriculture, the “A” in President Joseph Boakai’s ARREST Agenda, has received less than 1 percent of recent national budgets.

‘Lower inflation is not the same as lower prices’

One of the sharpest readings of the paradox comes from a man who once sat in Ngafuan’s chair. Amara Konneh, who succeeded him as finance minister under Sirleaf and now serves as a senator, told FrontPageAfrica that Liberia’s macroeconomic numbers may be improving, but too many Liberians are still not feeling it in their pockets.

Konneh points to the Central Bank of Liberia’s own August 2026 figures. Headline inflation was 4.6 percent, down from 5.6 percent a year earlier. But domestic food prices were rising at 11.1 percent, transport at 7.6 percent and imported fuel at 6.2 percent. “Lower inflation is not the same as lower prices,” he said. A bag of rice that became expensive does not get cheaper simply because prices are rising more slowly.

He noted that the World Bank attributes the rise in poverty largely to inflation and sluggish farm growth. With mining up 17 percent, agriculture up only 2.6 percent and manufacturing shrinking 2.8 percent, he argued, growth is happening in sectors where few Liberians earn a living. Some 86 percent of Liberian firms are microenterprises.

Konneh also questions why a stronger Liberian dollar has not brought prices down. He blames the cost of moving goods from the Freeport of Monrovia to rural markets – port charges, delays, storage and unofficial fees along trade routes. “Is the stronger Liberian dollar increasing the purchasing power of Liberians?” he asked. “If not, we still have work to do.”

His most pointed figure goes to the heart of how Ngafuan’s ministry spends. Citing the World Bank, Konneh said government capital spending fell from 8.5 percent of GDP in 2024 to 5.7 percent in 2025 – from about US$406 million to US$297 million – even as revenue climbed to record highs. “That should concern us,” he said.

Konneh proposes three fixes before Christmas: a single published schedule of port charges with clearance targets; regular Commerce Ministry price monitoring to make sure a stronger currency reaches shoppers; and temporary relief for small businesses hit by delays beyond their control. He framed his comments as constructive, acknowledging the government’s progress on stability. But, he said, stability “is a means to an end. It is not the end itself.”

The first time around

Ngafuan has been here before. He first entered Ellen Johnson Sirleaf’s cabinet in 2006, at 35, as head of the Bureau of the Budget. He served as finance minister from August 2008 to February 2012, then moved to the Foreign Ministry until he resigned in 2015.

That first tenure is remembered for real achievements. Liberia reached the end of the World Bank and IMF debt relief process in 2010, wiping out close to US$5 billion in external debt. A new Public Financial Management Law passed in 2009, and civil servants began receiving salaries by direct deposit.

But it was also marked by the same tension that haunts him now. Growth in those years was strong, averaging about 7 percent a year between 2004 and 2014, according to the World Bank. Yet much of it came from mining, rubber and donor-funded reconstruction, and it did little to change daily life for most families. As late as 2016, more than half of all Liberians lived in poverty, and in rural areas the figure exceeded 70 percent.

Accountability questions surfaced then too. In 2010, a General Auditing Commission review of debt-relief-era spending asked Ngafuan and other former officials to account for more than US$1 million in expenditures made without vouchers during his time at the Budget Bureau. He rejected parts of the findings as riddled with errors.

The parallels are hard to miss: headline growth that bypasses the poor, audit queries that Ngafuan dismisses as paperwork, and a minister whose technical fluency wins praise from donors but not from the market. Last year he himself traced one of today’s documentation problems back to a 2011 contract he signed to modernize the ministry’s archives – a system, he admitted, that later broke down.

The case for the minister – and the test ahead

Ngafuan’s defenders say he inherited a broken budget, and that collecting more revenue is the first step to spending it well. They note that the 2027 plan raises health spending by 22 percent, sets new pay floors for teachers, adds about 4,350 public workers and, for the first time, commits to repaying nearly US$60 million the government owes the national pension fund.

Those are real promises. But Liberians have heard promises before, and the budget’s own numbers leave room for doubt. Part of this year’s billion-dollar milestone came from a one-off US$200 million signing bonus paid by steelmaker ArcelorMittal. Health still gets less than 9 percent of the budget, and agriculture barely features in the government’s summary at all.

The coming months will show whether Ngafuan’s economy can reach the street. Three markers matter most: whether extreme poverty falls toward the World Bank’s 33.2 percent projection; whether the planned VAT protects basic goods that poor families buy; and whether teachers, nurses and pensioners actually receive the money the budget promises them, on time.

Back on the sidewalks of central Monrovia, the verdict will not come from a report or a budget speech. It will come from whether more customers stop at the trays of biscuits and soap – and whether, at the end of the day, a vendor can carry home enough to feed a family.
