World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 9, 2026
World.content:
Seven Killed, More Than 100 Injured in Egypt Train Collision

At least seven people have been killed and more than 100 injured after two passenger trains collided in Egypt's Giza province, south of Cairo. Authorities said one train struck the rear of another while travelling along the line between Cairo and the southern city of Aswan, causing one train to derail and several carriages to overturn. More than 50 ambulances were dispatched to the scene. Emergency crews and cranes worked to clear the railway line. President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi ordered an investigation and called for anyone found negligent to be held accountable. The cause of the collision has not yet been established. The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.

ANC Suffers Worst-Ever Election Result in South Africa

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

South Africa's Electoral Commission has officially declared the 2026 Local Government Elections free and fair, with national voter turnout reaching 52%, an increase from 45.9% in the 2021 elections. The African National Congress emerged as the largest party with 30.76% of the vote. The Democratic Alliance (DA) came second with 24.64%, retaining majority control of the city of Cape Town. Former president Jacob Zuma's uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MK Party) came third overall with 9.76%. The Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), led by Julius Malema, once seen as a serious challenge to the ANC, came fourth with 6.22%. However, the ANC recorded its worst-ever electoral performance, losing its outright majority in several major metropolitan areas amid growing voter dissatisfaction over municipal service delivery, unemployment, crime, and corruption. The DA retained control of Cape Town, while 127 of the country's 213 municipalities have hung councils, setting the stage for coalition negotiations. The IEC said that the elections were largely peaceful, with 90% of voters surveyed considering the process free and 91% describing it as fair.

34 Killed as Migrant Boat Sinks Off Senegal Coast

At least 34 people have been killed after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of northwestern Senegal near Kebemer, about 180 kilometres north of Dakar. The vessel was reportedly carrying people attempting to reach Spain's Canary Islands through the dangerous Atlantic migration route, which has claimed thousands of lives in recent years. Senegalese authorities initially reported that 21 bodies had been recovered and one person rescued, with search operations continuing as the death toll rose. The tragedy comes as authorities on El Hierro in Spain's Canary Islands have declared an emergency following a sharp increase in migrant arrivals. More than 3,300 people have arrived on the island in about 30 boats over the last month or so, sparking concerns about pressure on local facilities and emergency services.

Ruto Challenges Kenya's Opposition to Present Development Plans

Kenyan President William Ruto has challenged opposition leaders to present clear development plans, warning Kenyans against gambling with the country's future by electing politicians who lack concrete solutions to national challenges. Speaking during an interdenominational church service in Nyamira County, Ruto said political leaders should be judged by their policies and ability to address issues such as the high cost of living, unemployment, education, agriculture and infrastructure. He defended his administration's development record, citing investments in roads, healthcare, electricity and education, including the employment of 100,000 teachers. Ruto also announced that the government had allocated 1.2 billion Kenyan shillings to modernise tea factories in western Rift Valley, with further funding expected in the next budget. He additionally announced 11 billion shillings for 180 kilometres of tarmac roads in Nyamira, alongside plans for a new hospital and an international stadium.

UN Warns of Critical Aid Shortages as Sudan Displacement Crisis Deepens

United Nations agencies have appealed for urgent international assistance to support millions of people displaced by the ongoing war in Sudan, warning that humanitarian supplies are running dangerously low. The fighting that broke out in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has left millions in need of shelter, food and other critical assistance. The UN estimated that 15.4 million people urgently require shelter, but funding shortages mean humanitarian organisations can currently assist only about one in 10 people in need. The International Organization for Migration said its emergency warehouses are now empty, while the UN refugee agency warned that women and children make up three-quarters of the country's internally displaced population. More than 5.2 million people have returned to their areas of origin. Many cannot access their homes or basic services because of destruction and looting. Sudan's 2026 humanitarian response plan, which requires 2.9 billion dollars, has received only 47% of its funding.

Close 

Somalia's HirShabelle Capital to Be Relocated to Hiiraan

Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud said that the regional capital of HirShabelle will be allocated to the Hiiraan region in an effort to address growing political tensions and grievances among local communities, particularly the Hawadle clan. Speaking at the inauguration of HirShabelle's new leadership, the president said residents of Hiiraan had been granted the right to host the regional capital but would need to identify a suitable city where government officials could live and work. His announcement follows growing dissatisfaction among political groups in Beledweyne over political representation, the location of the regional capital and the leadership of the HirShabelle administration, which comprises Hiiraan and Middle Shabelle regions. Mohamud urged residents and opposition groups to remain calm and avoid retaliatory actions, saying their demands had been addressed. However, the relocation process still requires a formal decision by HirShabelle's leadership in line with the regional constitution. The newly appointed Vice President, Abdifitah Hassan Afrah, is also holding talks in Beledweyne to ease tensions and encourage dialogue.

World.title: South Africa: Three Killed in Grassy Park Shooting - South African News Briefs - November 9, 2026
World.content:
press review

Three Killed in Grassy Park Shooting

Three men have been shot dead and another wounded in a suspected gang-related shooting in Grassy Park on the Cape Flats, reports SABC News. Police said that the victims, aged between 22 and 39, were sitting outside a premises in Glen Close when occupants of a white Toyota Tazz opened fire before fleeing. Police Spokesperson FC Van Wyk has said that no arrests have been made yet. He said detectives from the Anti-Gang Unit are probing the incident.

Cat Matlala Set to Testify at Madlanga Commission

The Madlanga Commission resumes its public hearings with alleged crime kingpin Vusimuzi "Cat" Matlala expected to testify about his alleged links to senior police officials and individuals involved in criminal activity, reports EWN. The inquiry is also expected to hear from Police Minister Senzo Mchunu, KwaZulu-Natal Police Commissioner Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi and Crime Intelligence head Dumisani Khumalo. The commission is expected to submit its final report to President Cyril Ramaphosa by 25 January 2027.

Senzo Meyiwa Murder Trial Resumes in Pretoria

The Senzo Meyiwa murder trial is set to resume at the High Court in Pretoria, reports SABC News. This follows the conclusion of testimony by a second defence witness for accused number three, Mthobisi Mncube. Witness Thalente Ntombela disputed key state witness Constable Sizwe Zungu's account, accusing him of lying about being with the five accused on the day Meyiwa was murdered in 2014. Ntombela testified that accused number one, Muzi Sibiya, only moved to Gauteng in 2017 and had never been there before.

World.title: Africa: Model Citizens - 23 African-Born Immigrant Win in U.S. Elections
World.content:
blog

The growing political visibility of recent African immigrants in the United States is a standing reproach to dated conceptions of belonging back home.

Members of the Democratic Party are not the only ones celebrating the party's stunning victory in last week's midterm elections. Across Africa, where the exploits of African-born Americans are closely monitored, the outcome of the elections has generated considerable excitement. The reaction in Nigeria to the success of fourteen Nigerian-Americans in various state-level elections--incidentally all on the platform of the Democratic Party--is typical. Nigerians in Diaspora Commission chairperson Abike Dabiri-Erewa went on social media to congratulate the victorious cohort, making sure to append a graphic vividly displaying their names, headshots, and respective constituencies.

In all, a record twenty-three African-born immigrants from at least ten African countries spread across thirteen U.S. states won their respective races to become lawmakers in various American federal and state legislatures, extending a run that had seemed to reach a highwater mark back in January when Ugandan-born Zohran Mamdani became New York's youngest mayor in over a century.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The feeling of pride among Africans is both justified and understandable. For many, the fact that African-born immigrants are finding their feet and flourishing across various walks of life is a welcome rebuke to racial bigots of all stripes who equate blackness with underachievement. For such Africans, there is a special gratification in seeing recent African immigrants atop the totem pole across American industry, higher education, medicine, technology, and, not to forget, sports and entertainment. Recent African immigrants from Cameroon, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa rank among the most educated and highest paid immigrant groups across the United States. The average Nigerian-born immigrant (immigration to the United States from Nigeria is heavily dominated by Yorubas and Igbos from the southern region of the country, but still) boasts more degrees than a thermometer. According to the Washington-based Migration Policy Institute, 61 percent hold at least a bachelor's degree, "compared with 31 percent of the total foreign-born population and 32 percent of the U.S.-born population."

Unsurprisingly, in the same way that they use the United States itself as a mostly favorable point of reference, Africans also use the success of recent African immigrants to the United States to call attention to yawning and recurrent gaps in everyday life across Africa on the one hand, and the delinquencies of African leadership on the other. For many, the fact that someone would have to leave Africa in order to find personal and professional fulfillment, taking all their talent and expertise with them, and the lack of urgency by African leaders in response to this ongoing hemorrhaging of human capital, is an indictment of the situation in a majority of African countries.

All things considered, the noted feeling of pride at the increased political visibility and general success of African-born Americans is tinged with not a little anguish that Africa basically continues to give away what it cannot afford to lose.

None of this is to downplay the enormous social challenges that recent African immigrants themselves continue to confront. The case of Deqa Dhalac, the first African-born female mayor who, earlier this year, announced that she would not run for reelection into the Maine (Portland) House of Representatives because, according to her, "Throughout my tenure, I have experienced persistent racism, harassment, and threats that reflect a broader national pattern targeting Black and Brown elected officials," is a reminder that, for many, the path to political visibility can be quite rocky, and that, when it comes to full acceptance, it is definitely not yet uhuru.

That said, it cannot be denied that, in the final analysis, the United States continues to offer (political) possibilities that are not available to these recent African immigrants back home in Africa. The explanation for this is as follows: The conception of citizenship that prevails, albeit imperfectly, in the United States, is modern, vis-à-vis the regnant conception across Africa, which is predominantly static. Whereas, in principle, American citizenship is open to anyone who is born in, emigrates to, and is dedicated to the foundational tenets of the United States, citizenship in many African countries is still framed and invariably weighed down by the logic of autochthony. As President Trump stated during a naturalization ceremony in January 2019, echoing a belief that has served as a beacon to successive generations of Americans, "The beauty and majesty of [American] citizenship is that it draws no distinctions of race, or class, or faith, or gender, or background. No matter where our story begins, whether we are the first generation or the tenth generation, we are all equal. We are one team and one people proudly saluting one great American flag" [PDF].

Contra the American promise, quaint and often ridiculous markers, particularly regarding ethnicity, religious affiliation, caste, and gender, continue to animate politics across many African countries. The most profound--and, from a certain perspective, the most tragic--testament to this is the situation in South Africa (for anyone who may be interested, my three-part essay on the country's struggles is available here), where the collective mentality lags behind a constitution whose liberalism ordinarily puts it on par with the Constitution of the United States. In Nigeria, the heartland of regressive nativism, social discourse continues to be dominated by demeaning and ultimately meaningless conversations about one's "state of origin." In different ways, both South Africa and Nigeria demonstrate the inflexibility of political identity in Africa.

Which should ordinarily change the level of concern if, say, your African citizenship, parsimonious as it is, secured you some benefits. Just the opposite. In the words of Cornell University political philosopher Olufemi Taiwo, "the non-responsive and non-responsible character of African governments" effectively means that "most nationals of African countries do not enjoy the most basic privileges of citizenship in their homeland: protection from the predations of their fellows and the overreaching of state functionaries; the provision of basic amenities for the citizens; a minimum standard of living that keeps them above subhuman levels with some luxuries thrown in for good measure; and the privilege of having a hand in the constitution of the government that rules them."

The role played by this denuded form of citizenship in forcing African nationals to consider the exit option has been remarked. What could do with more attention is the opportunity that the modern form of citizenship affords for self-discovery and self-fashioning for the potential immigrant. As many immigrants to the United States understand, American citizenship opens up opportunities that would be otherwise permanently foreclosed, precisely because the United States is the one country where, at the end of the day, political modernity currently finds its fullest fulfillment. I know from personal experience that immigration advocates in the United States have little appreciation of this nonmaterial dimension of immigrant quest for the American dream, reducing immigration to the impact of climate change and whatnot.

Close 

In the meantime, what this means for diasporic Africans is clear enough. As we continue to redeem the promissory note of modernity across Euro-America, it is incumbent on us to affirm and invest in ideas and policies that advance and strengthen the same across Africa. The easiest and costless way to do that is to stop treating Africa and Africans, not as moral aliens, but as a region and people subject to the same rules and expectations of dignified treatment that apply to human beings everywhere. To refrain, as many do, from criticizing human rights violations in Africa under the pretext of not wanting to patronize African leaders is to assume that Africans are not mature enough to be approached and treated as adults. It is hypocritical to demand--as we should--access to the rights and privileges of modern citizenship across Western countries, while ignoring the entrenched violation of the same rights and privileges in Africa.

And for my African compatriots: It is not enough to celebrate the fact that Africans flourish outside of Africa. All of us must commit to the imperative of making Africa itself livable for anyone who desires to make a home there.

Imagine a time in the not-too-distant future when the mayor of Abuja is a Norwegian-born Nigerian, and the mayor of Johannesburg just so happens to be a Russian-born South African, both with equal and unfettered access to the respective bounties and prohibitions of Nigerian and South African citizenship.

Imagine that.

Nathan Schoonover contributed to the research for this article.

World.title: Nigeria: U.S. Trade, Security Partnership Could Create Opportunities in Nigeria
World.content:
U.S. Air Force Gen. Dagvin Anderson, commander of U.S. Africa Command, conducts an interview with Olivia Burrows, reporter for Citizen TV Kenya, in Nairobi, Kenya, July 28, 2026.

analysis

Washington is linking commerce to security. For Nigeria, the measures are market access, non-oil exports, investment and jobs.

Nigeria's ambition to expand non-oil exports and attract investment provides a practical test of Washington's effort to connect commercial engagement, diplomacy and security across Africa.

Following the Africa Strategic Dialogue at the National Defense University in Washington on 29 October, senior US officials explained how their institutions were approaching those connections. US Africa Command commander, Dagvin Anderson, identified Nigeria among the countries where he had encountered interest in constructive American economic engagement.

US Department of State's Bureau of African Affairs Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Frank Garcia Jr. framed the approach as an economic partnership, with benefits required on both sides.



"It has to be a good deal for African partners and a good deal for the US taxpayers and industry," Mr Garcia said.

He also identified the conditions companies need to operate.

"Conflict impedes companies from building, hiring, growing," he said.

Mr Anderson approached the relationship from the security side, explaining why cooperation needed to extend beyond military activity.

"And so we can't just focus on the security piece," he said. "We have to look at how we bridge into that stability and investment."

However, the commercial relationship has its own institutional foundation and explicitly stated national priorities.

The US-Nigeria Commercial and Investment Partnership was established through a five-year memorandum signed in July 2024. Its working groups began meeting in June 2025 across agriculture, the digital economy, and infrastructure, bringing government and private-sector participants together to identify obstacles to trade and investment.

Those activities predate the latest AFRICOM dialogue. The bilateral partnership is a commercial framework, not a military programme directed by the command.

At a ministerial meeting in Lagos in January, Nigeria's Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Jumoke Oduwole, emphasised export diversification and access to the American market.

She said "a central priority for us is to accelerate non-oil export diversification and to ensure that more Nigerian businesses can access U.S. markets in a way that is competitive, sustainable, and inclusive," according to the US Mission's published account.

Her formulation supplies a Nigerian measure of success. Expanding opportunities for American companies in Nigeria and helping Nigerian businesses compete in the United States are related ambitions, but they require different results.

The partnership's working groups were tasked with identifying barriers other than tariffs and recommending solutions to policymakers. By the January ministerial, they had developed proposals intended to improve the business environment and facilitate private-sector activity.

That work provides a setting in which to assess the wider language of mutual benefit. For a Nigerian exporter, progress means more than an announcement of interest. It means being able to compete, secure customers, and deliver products into a market on commercially workable terms.

At the October discussion, Mark Mitchell, the Commerce Department's deputy assistant secretary for the Middle East and Africa, Global Markets, described commercial-support activity across technology, energy, manufacturing, critical minerals and infrastructure.

He distinguished formal Commercial Advocacy cases from the department's broader support for business engagement.

That distinction matters when assessing the scale and status of commercial opportunities. A prospective procurement, an awarded contract, an approved financing package, and an operational project represent different stages. They should not be presented interchangeably as completed investments or demonstrated local benefit.

In a written statement following the roundtable, the US Department of Commerce said, "The Department of Commerce is focused on the mutual wins of trade relationships and commercial deals that can deliver economic prosperity and security. We are working toward a long-term partnering relationship through trade."

The statement makes the intended connection explicit.

The US Department of Energy was also represented in the October discussion by William Schirano, the Energy Department's deputy assistant secretary for multilateral engagement and market development. He described energy access and technical cooperation as foundations for broader economic activity.

A public G20 energy ministers' statement issued in September provides one example of that wider agenda. It calls for financing, stronger distribution systems, and local and regional value chains for clean cooking, while recognising that countries will choose different technologies according to their circumstances. It includes liquefied petroleum gas, electricity, natural gas, and other options. The statement is a multilateral commitment, not an announcement of a Nigeria-specific project.

AFRICOM's organisational developments show how the military side is approaching economic engagement.

Recent reporting suggests that the command had established a Defense Economics Office to examine how economic, commercial, and financial activity could produce security effects. Mr Anderson identified Joshua Stinson, a colonel, as the command's lead for defense economics.

The reported remit extended beyond investment promotion. It included infrastructure and access, critical mineral supply chains, and efforts to disrupt adversaries' revenues. The office's emergence formed part of a wider setting in which the United States, China and Russia compete for influence and access across Africa.

"We're not looking to replace what Commerce does, by any means," Mr Anderson said, according to publicly available news reports.

That boundary is important. Security priorities may influence American engagement, but commercial negotiations, financing decisions, and Nigerian economic policy retain separate responsibilities.

Mr Anderson acknowledged another limit during the October exchange. Providing access to the American economy was not his direct responsibility, but he could help connect African requests with relevant institutions and convene discussions.

Close 

His military resources had been "reduced," he said, making coordination with other agencies part of his explanation of how AFRICOM could continue pursuing security objectives.

The approach, therefore, joins institutions around potentially overlapping interests without making those interests identical.

Ms Oduwole's stated priorities concern a more diversified Nigerian economy and stronger opportunities for Nigerian businesses. Washington's stated objectives include American commercial gains and security benefits from more durable relationships.

For Nigerian businesses, results would be visible in barriers removed, financing secured, contracts performed, and exports delivered. For households, the relevant consequences include employment, affordable services, and opportunities to participate in productive economic activity.

Nigeria has articulated what it wants from the commercial relationship. The task now is to assess whether the institutions pursuing partnership can translate those objectives into results--and distinguish opportunities being discussed from benefits already delivered.

Pearl Matibe is a Washington, D.C.-based correspondent and geopolitical analyst covering US-Africa relations, defence, diplomacy, and international security. She reports across print, broadcast, and digital platforms, including The Shaka Spear, examining how policy decisions affect African countries and their publics. She regularly covers the Pentagon, State Department, and White House. Follow her on X: @PearlMatibe.

World.title: Kenya: Food Crisis Hits Ethiopians Fleeing Violence Into Kenya's Moyale
World.content:
Nairobi — Thousands of Ethiopian families who fled violent clashes in their country and sought refuge in Kenya's Moyale area are facing acute food shortages, with more than seven in ten households reporting insufficient food, a new humanitarian assessment has found.

An estimated 50,000 people had crossed into Kenya by October 29, according to an assessment conducted by the Government of Kenya and the Marsabit County Government, with support from the International Organization for Migration (IOM), United Nations agencies and humanitarian organisations.

The assessment found that 71 per cent of households surveyed did not have enough to eat, while 80 per cent identified food as their most urgent need, highlighting the growing humanitarian needs among displaced families and the communities hosting them.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Families who fled are facing serious shortages of food, water and adequate shelter, while communities hosting them are already facing limited resources," said Nomagugu Ncube, IOM Kenya Chief of Mission.

"Assistance needs to reach both these displaced families and the communities that have opened their homes to them," she added.

The findings also point to worsening living conditions, with displaced families struggling to access clean drinking water, adequate shelter and healthcare.

Most of the families have been accommodated by relatives and members of host communities, placing additional pressure on households already dealing with limited resources.

Others have sought refuge in schools and temporary displacement sites, while some have been forced to sleep in the open.

Children account for more than half of the displaced population, including a significant number of children under five, raising concerns about their health and well-being amid inadequate food, water and sanitation.

The assessment further established that 44 per cent of surveyed households had insufficient access to drinking water, while more than three-quarters lacked handwashing facilities.

Conditions were particularly difficult at temporary displacement sites in Somare, Taqwa Mosque and St. Mary's Catholic, where access to water and sanitation services was severely limited.

Access to healthcare has also emerged as a major challenge, with more than half of the households reporting difficulties reaching nearby health facilities, largely because of high costs and shortages of medicines.

The assessment, conducted between October 29 and 30, covered 758 households across temporary displacement sites and host communities in Moyale.

It found that 96 per cent of the households surveyed had fled Ethiopia, mainly from the Oromia and Somali regions, while nine in ten respondents reported that their entire villages had fled, underscoring the scale of displacement.

Close 

With food, shelter, water and healthcare needs continuing to mount, IOM and humanitarian partners are calling for urgent funding to scale up assistance to displaced families and host communities.

The humanitarian agencies say the funding is needed to support food distribution, emergency shelter, clean water, sanitation and access to healthcare as pressure on resources in the border region increases.

World.title: Kenya: Water Rationing Looms in Nairobi As Ndakaini Dam Levels Decline
World.content:
Nairobi — Water rationing is set to intensify in Nairobi and neighbouring counties after declining levels at Thika/Ndakaini Dam forced a 35 per cent reduction in water production at two major treatment plants supplying the capital.

Nairobi City Water and Sewerage Company said the reduction at Ngethu and Kigoro water treatment plants took effect immediately, warning that customers should brace for extended periods without water as the utility moves to preserve the dwindling reserves.

In a notice issued on Monday, November 9, the company attributed the production cuts to below-average rainfall in the dam's catchment area, which has affected water inflows into the reservoir.

"Thika Dam, the principal source of water for Nairobi and surrounding areas, has experienced a significant decline in storage levels due to below-average rainfall within its catchment area," the company said.



It added that reduced inflows had necessitated a temporary reduction in water abstraction to preserve the available reserves and ensure sustainable supply over the coming months.

The company warned that the cuts would translate into longer water rationing periods for customers served by seven water utilities across Nairobi and neighbouring counties.

Besides Nairobi City Water, the affected providers are Githunguri Water and Sanitation Company, Kiambu Water and Sanitation Company, Karuri Water and Sanitation Company, Mavoko Water and Sewerage Company, Oloolaiser Water and Sewerage Company and Olkejuado Water and Sewerage Company.

The affected areas span Nairobi, Kiambu, Machakos and Kajiado counties, raising the prospect of increased pressure on households, businesses and institutions that depend on the utilities for daily water needs.

Nairobi Water said it would continue monitoring the dam's storage levels and prevailing weather conditions, with production volumes subject to periodic review depending on improvements in reservoir recovery and water inflows.

"Production volumes will be reviewed periodically based on reservoir recovery and water inflows," the company said.

The utility urged consumers to adopt water-saving measures, avoid unnecessary wastage and reserve available supplies for essential household and other critical needs.

It acknowledged that the reduction would disrupt normal supply but appealed to residents to cooperate as it manages the available resources.

"We recognise the inconvenience that the reduced water production may cause and sincerely appeal for the public's patience, understanding and cooperation as we work to sustainably manage the available water resources," the company said.

World.title: Somalia: Somali Opposition Accuses President of Using Force to Seize Supreme Court
World.content:
Mogadishu, Somalia — Somalia's opposition coalition, the Somali Future Council, has accused President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud of using security forces to take control of the country's Supreme Court, escalating a political confrontation over the independence of the judiciary and the president's mandate.

The council, led by former president Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed and comprising several former Somali leaders, issued a statement condemning what it described as an assault on the Federal Supreme Court and an attempt by Mohamud to seize control of the country's highest judicial institution.

The opposition group also accused security agencies of intimidating former Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed and judges who issued a ruling challenging the terms of the country's federal institutions.



"The Somali Future Council strongly condemns the assault and coup against the Federal Supreme Court," the statement said, describing the developments as an attack on judicial independence.

The council welcomed the Supreme Court's decision, identified as MS/DST/1/2026, which ruled that the mandates of the president, parliament and federal government had expired.

The court also called on political leaders to agree on an electoral framework within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, according to the ruling.

The judgment directly challenges the government's position that constitutional amendments approved by parliament in March allow Mohamud and federal lawmakers to remain in office until 2027.

The Supreme Court ruled that the amendments extending presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years could not be applied retrospectively to the current officeholders.

The council described the judgment as an opportunity to end the country's political deadlock and resolve disagreements over the electoral process through an inclusive political agreement.

It said Somalia was facing a critical political situation and urged national leaders to respect the court's decision and pursue negotiations to prevent further instability.

The dispute intensified after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed on November 4 and appointed his predecessor, Ibrahim Idle Suleiman, to replace him.

The Supreme Court subsequently declared the dismissal null and void, saying the president had failed to follow the constitutional procedures required to remove the chief justice. It also accused the presidency of attempting to interfere with a pending constitutional case.

The presidency had justified Baashe's removal by citing complaints from judges, judicial staff and legal professionals about the administration of justice and the need for judicial reforms.

In its statement, the Somali Future Council urged citizens to remain vigilant, warning of what it described as serious threats to the country's stability, population and statehood.

Close 

The opposition coalition also placed responsibility for the escalating political crisis on Mohamud, accusing him of being at the centre of the dispute.

It warned that the president would bear responsibility for any consequences arising from the situation.

The confrontation comes amid a broader dispute between the federal government and opposition leaders over constitutional amendments, electoral arrangements and the future of Somalia's political transition.

The government has maintained that the constitutional changes provide a legal basis for its electoral roadmap, which schedules parliamentary elections for April 2027 and a presidential vote in May.

Opposition leaders, including the Somali Future Council, have rejected the government's approach and called for an inclusive political agreement on elections.

The latest developments have raised concerns about judicial independence and the potential for further political instability in a country already facing security challenges from Al-Shabaab militants.

The federal government had not immediately responded to the opposition council's latest accusations.

World.title: Africa: Rethinking the Frequency of UN Climate Summits After COP31
World.content:
guest column

As world leaders and critical stakeholders converge on Türkiye for the 31st UN climate summit, a difficult but necessary question hangs over the familiar ritual. The poser is: after more than three decades, is an annual COP still the best way to advance the global climate agenda?

The two-week conference opening on November 9 in Antalya will gather presidents, diplomats, scientists and activists to bring the climate emergency into sharp focus. Nearly 100 agenda items have been tabled for negotiations, ranging from climate finance and adaptation to loss and damage and energy transition.

I watched that familiar choreography up close at COP29 in Baku in 2024 – the endless pavilions, the late-night huddles over bracketed text, the stirring speeches about urgency followed by painstaking negotiations over wording. It was a powerful reminder of both the value and the limits of these gatherings.

But beyond the elegant speeches and communiques, we must ask whether the annual frequency of the summits has become a substitute for effectiveness. The case for moving from annual to biennial summits is not a call to retreat. Far from it. It is a plea for a more strategic, cost-effective and results-driven model of climate governance.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Success should be measured not by how often governments meet as output, but by how faithfully their pledges translate into cleaner air, safer communities and more resilient economies in places like Borno, Turkana, the Mekong Delta or the Amazon Basin as outcome. That conversation on the frequency of the summit deserves space at COP31, even if outside the formal negotiating rooms, for many reasons.

First is cost, and the burden is no longer just an African story. Hosting a COP is a massive logistical undertaking: security, accommodation, transport and conference infrastructure for 40,000 to 80,000 participants. The UK spent an estimated 300 million pounds to host COP26 in Glasgow. For any host, it is a fiscal stretch.

For African economies already juggling debt distress, food insecurity and energy poverty, the bill can be prohibitive. It also explains why, despite bearing some of the harshest consequences of the climate crisis, Africa has hosted the summit only five times in 30 years – COP7 in Marrakech in 2001, COP12 in Nairobi in 2006, COP17 in Durban in 2011, COP22 in Marrakech in 2016, and COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh in 2022.

The same hosting fatigue is felt elsewhere. Small Island Developing States, which face an existential threat from rising sea level, have never hosted a COP due to scale and cost. Latin America, home to the Amazon, has hosted only three times. When the venue rotates, the Global South often has to build a temporary city from scratch.

Then there is the carbon cost, which is becoming hard to ignore. A 2026 study in Communications Sustainability estimated that air travel by Party and Observer delegates from COP1 to COP29 generated about 710,282 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent. More telling is the quantum trajectory: from 2,959 tonnes in Berlin in 1995 to 76,931 tonnes in Baku last year, an increase of roughly 2,500 percent!

Those figures do not capture the full footprint of the summits, but they reveal an uncomfortable paradox that delegates themselves whisper about in the corridors – thousands boarding long-haul flights to discuss how to reduce emissions. A biennial rhythm would halve the frequency of these mega-gatherings and create room for more virtual consultations, regional climate weeks from Africa to Asia-Pacific, and leaner forms of engagement.

There is also the question of implementation. Climate action needs time, and the most vulnerable need even more of it. The annual cycle leaves ministries in a near-permanent state of negotiation. Pledges made in November are barely converted into national budgets and sub-national projects before the next round of talks begins.

We see this at home. Recent floods in Nigeria displaced over a million people. Lake Chad has shrunk by more than 90 percent since the 1960s, deepening conflict between farmers and herders across sub-Sahara Africa. The Sahel is heating 1.5 times faster than the global average.

The pattern is global, and the costs are increasingly human. Global climate impacts now include catastrophic events such as the glacier collapse in Nepal that claimed over 1,000 lives with about 5,000 missing, and extreme heat in Europe linked to tens of thousands of excess deaths. In Pakistan, the 2022 floods caused over 30 billion dollars in damages before its recovery plan could be fully funded by the next COP.

In Brazil, deforestation rates in the Amazon fluctuate faster than annual finance pledges can track. In Vanuatu and Tuvalu, leaders travel each year to plead for survival, yet the Loss and Damage fund agreed at COP27 took another two years to become operational. These are not problems that can be solved between COPs.

A two-year interval would change the incentive. Delegates would return not with a fresh set of promises, but with evidence: how much of the long-promised climate finance actually reached adaptation in Africa, how many hectares of the Great Green Wall were planted, how many communities in Southeast Asia have embraced energy transition, and how many homes in Florida or the Philippines were retrofitted for resilience. That would shift COP from a stage for declarations to a platform for accountability.

Finally, there is credibility. When annual summits end with familiar hollow language and thin follow-through, public fatigue sets in. In Baku, participants listened to the chilling tales of young activists from Kenya and Indonesia who had travelled 48 hours by bus and plane to be there. Their frustration was palpable: "We come every year, but the floods still come every year too."

That fatigue is now visible across continents. Polls in Europe show declining trust that COP pledges will be met. In the US, cities like Phoenix and Miami are spending billions on heat and flood adaptation while federal negotiating positions shift with each election cycle. Communities losing homes in Maiduguri, harvests in Malawi or fishing grounds in Fiji are not waiting for another declaration; they are waiting for irrigation, crop insurance, early warning systems and resilient infrastructure.

Close 

Spacing the major conferences two years apart could restore a sense of occasion and scrutiny. Media coverage would be less routine, assessment by environmental rights advocacy groups would be more substantive, and the political cost of empty promises more palpable. The intervening year should not be a pause, but an accountability window.

This does not mean switching off climate diplomacy every other year. Technical negotiations must continue. The UNFCCC already has the architecture for annual synthesis reports, implementation reviews and regional climate weeks. What changes is not the continuity of work, but the frequency of the grand summit.

Yes, critics will worry that a biennial COP could sap momentum. That concern is valid, but urgency should compel better action, not simply more meetings. The UNFCCC has been indispensable in keeping climate on the global agenda. But no institution should be exempt from asking whether its operating model still fits the challenge it was built to address.

COP31 offers more than a negotiating deadline. It offers a moment to ask how we can make climate diplomacy work better for those who need it most. We all need it.

Aliu Akoshile, Editor-in-Chief of NatureNews Africa, writes via eic@naturenews.africa

World.title: SCOTUS allows Trump admin to temporarily resume border construction in Texas' Big Bend
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The U. S. Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in West Texas, granting an emergency request from the federal government to lift a lower court's hold on the project.

The justices' ruling stays a preliminary injunction issued last month by a federal district judge in El Paso, who had temporarily halted border wall construction in the region designated by U. S. Customs and Border Protection as the Big Bend Sector while litigation proceeds.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated she would have denied the stay request but did not file a written dissent.

LIBERAL JUSTICE HAMMERS SUPREME COURT FOR FAST-TRACKING EMERGENCY DOCKET CASES

The lawsuit against the project was brought by a coalition of environmental groups and local residents, who claim the Department of Homeland Security violated constitutional provisions by proceeding without congressional authorization and bypassing environmental regulations.

Spanning more than 500 miles, the Big Bend Sector covers roughly a quarter of the U. S.–Mexico border, though it accounted for just 1. 3% of all border apprehensions in 2025, Reuters reported.

MULLIN TELLS CONGRESS PRIMARY BORDER WALL WILL BE DONE BY JUNE 2027, SECONDARY WALL BY SUMMER 2028

Administration officials have argued the wall is vital to stopping cartel operations active south of the border and curbing the smuggling of large quantities of illicit drugs into the U.S.

Most of the proposed construction in the Big Bend Sector will take place on privately owned land, according to administration officials.

Big Bend National Park is slated for a 17-mile barrier, though officials noted it will not feature the 30-foot steel pedestrian fencing planned in other areas along the southern border.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

President Donald Trump has long touted border wall expansion as a signature initiative of his strategy to seal the southern border and crack down on illegal immigration.

World.title: New California law will restrict sales of some muscle-building supplements to minors
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Gavin Newsom has signed legislation banning the sale of some "muscle-building supplements" to Californians under 18 years of age.

The legislation (AB 2030), which was signed on Sept. 28, covers over-the-counter diet pills and dietary supplements for weight loss or muscle building. It will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

"Nonprescribed, medically unapproved products may cause dangerous side effects," the governor’s office said in its announcement. "Products can be mislabeled or contaminated with substances such as steroids."

WHY STACKING SUPPLEMENTS WITHOUT A BLOOD TEST FIRST CAN DO MORE HARM THAN GOOD

California’s law restricts minors’ access to supplements marketed for muscle building – specifically, those that are "labeled, marketed or otherwise represented for the purpose of achieving weight loss or building muscle."

Courts may consider whether a product contains "creatine, green tea extract, raspberry ketone, garcinia cambogia or green coffee bean extract," the legislation states.

The law does not impose an outright ban on all creatine products. Restrictions depend on how the supplements are labeled, advertised and marketed to consumers.

TAKING DAILY SUPPLEMENT MAY HELP PRESERVE MUSCLE AS YOU AGE — EVEN WITHOUT EXERCISE

The law does not apply to people under 18 who have a prescription for an over-the-counter diet pill or dietary supplement for weight loss or muscle-building.

The release cites research indicating that nearly one in 10 adolescents have used such products.

It also references studies linking over-the-counter diet pill use to a sixfold greater likelihood of an eating disorder diagnosis within three years.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The announcement does not specify whether whey protein or creatine products are included in the ban.

Sellers who do not adhere to the new law will face civil fines of up to $500 per violation.

"Nonprescribed, medically unapproved products may cause dangerous side effects."

The American Herbal Products Association, based in Maryland, released a statement opposing the law.

CLICK HERE TO 

"Lacking any scientific justification, AB 2030 casts a shadow over safe, beneficial products," said Robert Marriott, the association's vice president of regulatory and government affairs, in the statement.

The organization argues that the law's scope is unclear and notes that it does not explicitly exempt protein products.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The Center for Science in the Public Interest, based in Washington, D.C., shared public support of the new legislation.

POPULAR DRINKS LINKED TO HEART ATTACKS, CARDIAC ARREST IN YOUNG ADULTS, STUDY FINDS

"Manufacturers of these products often prey on kids and teens with deceptive claims that lack any scientific evidence," said Jensen Jose, a regulatory counsel at CSPI, which co-sponsored the legislation.

Dr. Sigrid Wolf, a pediatric sports medicine physician at Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago, recently addressed the use of creatine products among teenagers, stating that evidence of benefits is limited.

POISON CENTERS LINK GROWING BENADRYL ABUSE AMONG TEENS TO DANGEROUS SOCIAL MEDIA TRENDS

"In some cases, they might even be dangerous," wrote Wolf, who is a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics' sports medicine committee, in an article published on HealthyChildren.org, the American Academy of Pediatrics' parenting website.

"Creatine can come with negative side effects such as weight gain, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Studies show that many supplements contain harmful substances that go undetected," she added, instead recommending prioritizing nutrition, training, sleep and hydration.

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment.

World.title: Rubio's defense of Trump's Iran war draws sharp contrast with Vance's midterm blame
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the Trump administration's war against Iran on Sunday, days after Vice President JD Vance blamed the conflict for Republicans' devastating midterm losses, as the White House confronts an unresolved standoff with Tehran.

"I think the president took on something that other presidents have failed to do. Sometimes, when you do the right thing, you don't know whether it's popular or not, but it's still the right thing to do. Presidents are elected to take on the hard things, sometimes difficult things, but necessary things," Rubio said Sunday.

Vance made his argument in a post on X last week.

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote last week.

"But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there," he added.

VANCE REFUSES TO PUT A CLOCK ON IRAN CONFLICT AS KEY QUESTION KEEPS US FORCES ENGAGED

Vance cited an unnamed pollster in the X post who said voters who had abandoned the GOP wanted the administration to end the conflict, address inflation and the cost of living, put America first and change its relationship with Israel.

The vice president's argument that the war was the primary driver of Republicans' losses, however, is complicated by polling. The Fox News Voter Poll found that 89% of voters considered the cost of living a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, compared with 74% who said the same about the war in Iran. The findings suggest broader economic frustrations were also a major concern among voters, although the two issues may overlap and the polling does not establish which ultimately drove Republican defections.

Fox News Digital contacted Vance's office five times seeking clarification on whether ending the conflict would mean lifting the blockade, withdrawing American forces or securing new concessions from Tehran, but received no response.

The contrasting assessments come as Republicans begin looking ahead to 2028, with Trump naming Rubio as a possible presidential contender during an interview with CBS.

Some longtime Trump donors are reportedly expressing doubts about backing Vance in 2028, fearing his ties to the Trump administration and the GOP’s devastating midterm losses could hurt his presidential prospects, with some floating Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and other Republicans as alternatives, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Meanwhile, Trump and Vance are pursuing another diplomatic opening with Iran, with Qatar mediating talks over a possible agreement that could ease the U.S. blockade and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Trump met with Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani Monday to discuss mediation efforts and potential terms for ending the conflict with Iran.

Rubio expressed skepticism Sunday that negotiations were nearing a breakthrough, arguing that Iran's demands remained unrealistic. Vance has been personally involved in indirect talks with Iranian representatives through regional mediators in recent weeks, according to Axios.

"I’m not in a political office," Rubio told reporters Sunday when asked about the midterm results. "As you know, I just don’t comment on domestic politics."

TRUMP SAYS HE DOESN’T DISAGREE WITH VANCE THAT IRAN WAR FUELED GOP LOSSES

Trump initially projected that Operation Epic Fury, launched against Iran in February, would involve four to five weeks of combat operations. More than eight months later, the broader confrontation continues despite the end of major U.S. combat operations in April.

After a June Memorandum of Understanding with Iran failed to produce a lasting resolution, the Trump administration returned to economic and military pressure, with renewed limited strikes, continued maritime tensions and an unresolved standoff over Iranian missile capabilities and the flow of oil and natural gas through the Strait of Hormuz.

Vance played a role in the administration's negotiations with Iran, helping lead diplomatic efforts that produced the June agreement before it unraveled.

Trump even joked in June that Vance would take the blame if the Iran deal failed.

"If it works out, I'm going to take the credit. If it doesn't work out, I'm blaming JD," Trump said at the time.

The vice president has previously defended the administration's military campaign, crediting U.S. forces with significantly weakening Iran's conventional military and its ability to threaten commercial shipping.

"The VP has let it be known for a few months now that he is not in full agreement with the President on Iran. But [the] social media post is striking, if not shocking," Ludovic Hood, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute's Center for Peace and Security in the Middle East, told Fox News Digital.

Hood also questioned Vance's emphasis on the war as the primary cause of Republicans' losses, arguing that broader economic concerns played a significant role in voters' frustration.

AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR?

Trump dismissed suggestions that Vance's comments about Iran had strained their relationship on Sunday, defending Vance's remarks while suggesting he should have gone a step further in expressing support for the administration's actions.

"No, not at all," Trump said when asked whether Vance's comments had affected their relationship. "But a lot of people didn't like his comments, but not me. He was right."

Trump added that Vance "should have made one other statement," arguing that the administration's actions against Iran were worth repeating.

TRUMP'S IRAN GAMBLE DIVIDES GOP HAWKS AND 'AMERICA FIRST' CONSERVATIVES OVER WHAT VICTORY LOOKS LIKE

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth also publicly defended the Iran campaign, calling it a "courageous and historic" effort even as Vance questions its political costs. Hegseth also faces questions about his future in the administration, although the president publicly insisted he intends to keep his Pentagon chief.

Beyond the political fallout, assessments differ over whether the administration has achieved its military objectives and what risks remain for the United States.

GOP CRACKS WIDEN OVER IRAN WAR AS VULNERABLE CANDIDATES BREAK WITH TRUMP, DEMAND ITS END

Retired Army Lt. Col. Daniel L. Davis, a veteran of four combat deployments and host of the "Daniel Davis Deep Dive" show on YouTube, offered a sharply critical assessment of the campaign's results, arguing that the administration has failed to accomplish the objectives Trump outlined when the operation began.

On Feb. 28, Trump pledged to destroy Iran's missile capabilities and production facilities, eliminate its navy and prevent Tehran's regional proxies from destabilizing the Middle East.

"Eight months and 9 days later, none of those objectives have been met," Davis told Fox News Digital.

The White House has offered a starkly different assessment. In April, the administration declared that U.S. forces had achieved the military objectives of Operation Epic Fury, pointing to the destruction of Iranian military infrastructure and significant degradation of Tehran's missile and naval capabilities.

Davis said that although American strikes inflicted significant damage on Iran's conventional military, Tehran retains the ability to threaten U.S. forces and regional allies through missiles, drones and naval assets protected in underground facilities. He warned that renewed major combat operations could expose American forces and Gulf allies to further retaliation without eliminating those capabilities.

VANCE'S SCATHING IRAN WAR POSTMORTEM PUTS POTENTIAL 2028 GOP SHOWDOWN IN FOCUS: 'EVERYONE KNOWS WHY'

"First, it should be clear: shooting the same targets, with the same missiles, is not going to produce a different outcome," Davis said.

"Can't put lipstick on this pig: it would be ugly and seen as an admission of defeat," Davis said. "But that is still profoundly better for our interests than going back to combat ops that will only deepen, significantly, the cost of our failure."

Hood, however, rejected the suggestion that the United States should abandon pressure on Tehran, arguing that Iran continues to pose a serious threat to regional stability and American interests.

"Trump seems to get that Iran, as currently governed, is a singularly dangerous threat to the region's stability and ability to prosper; is, has long been, a source of international terrorism; and would be even more dangerous with nuclear weapons," Hood said.

Hood said the administration needs to more clearly explain its strategic objectives, including whether Washington is seeking significant concessions on Iran's nuclear program or a political shift in Tehran.

World.title: Jared Goff's SI Swimsuit wife had a big Miami weekend, college football gets greedy & Christmas decor time?
World.content:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

Well, it happened.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

My wife pulled the rug out from under me and ripped down all the Halloween decor around the house over the weekend. Didn't even give me warning. No heads-up. I left Friday morning and everything was pumpkins and cobwebs, and by the time I got home late in the afternoon, it may as well have been May.

What a punch to the gut. I went to Target later that day, and it was pretty much Santa's workshop in there. Christmas music blaring down every aisle. Reindeer hanging from the ceilings. Ribbons everywhere.

And just like that, fall was over — and the holiday season had begun. I held out for as long as I could, but I was ambushed. Now, we're in an undecorated house because the Christmas stuff is in the attic and, frankly, I don't have it in me to go up there quite yet.

So, we wait. Perhaps this weekend, when a cold front is supposed to be in town for a few days? An actual cold front. Our first since March!

Until then, we're in November purgatory. Sad.

NFL WEEK 9 SUNDAY TAKEAWAYS: BENGALS, 49ERS AND PACKERS LOOK SUPER, RAMS FINALLY OVER .500

Welcome to a Monday Nightcaps — the one where Jared Goff's wife, Christen Harper, had a dominant weekend in Miami and helped the Lions to a 19-9 win over my Miami Dolphins.

Most ethical tank ever, though. What a pleasure it's been to watch this season!

What else? I've got college football officially killing off conference championship weekend, Ron DeSantis (sadly, the outgoing governor of the great state of Florida) weighs in like the PATRIOT he is, and when is an acceptable time to put the Christmas decorations up?

You all know where I stand, but I'm curious to see if I'm in the majority or minority here.

OK, grab you something to deck your halls (whatever that means), and settle in for a Monday 'Cap!

Christen Harper had a big weekend in Miami

Big college football Saturday, and a big NFL Sunday yesterday. Let's spin the wheel and start the week with ...

The NFL! We'll get to college here in a bit. Crooks.

Pretty solid Sunday of football, right? Browns-Saints was a good one. Cowboys-Colts was a mess. The Pats got absolutely steamrolled, which was nice to watch as a Dolphins fan.

And my Dolphins ... continued the most ethical tank in NFL history yesterday against the Lions. I've watched a lot of tanks in my 30 years as a Fins fan, and what the fellas are doing this season is a true masterpiece.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM'S COWBOY HAT MESSAGE HAS FANS TALKING, HOLLY ROWE'S WNBA FINALS PLAN & IS TEXAS' FIELD GRAY?

The defense — truly a no-name defense — held the best offense in football to 19 points yesterday. Nineteen! Quick, name ONE person on the Miami defense.

You can't. I barely can, and I watch the games!

I was a little skeptical coming into this season about how I'd feel week in and week out rooting for a team that just stinks. I've gotta say — it's been a pleasure. Seriously.

There is absolutely no pressure on NFL Sundays anymore. None. The team is young, playing well, and losing every game because they just don't have the talent. It's a win-win. I miss watching a winning team, and I miss the feeling of winning a big game. Winning on NFL Sunday is the absolute best feeling as a sports fan.

But boy, it's been nice to be stress-free, too.

Now, let's check in with Jared Goff's SI Swimsuit wife, Christen Goff (Harper), and get this week started right:

Ron DeSantis is right, this playoff format smells fishy

"Ended the weekend with a W."

Indeed, Christen. You did. Can't argue that. Get us now, NFL, while you still can. The Dolphins are COMING.

PS: Shoutout to Jahmyr Gibbs for scoring the game's only touchdown yesterday. I had Gibbs, Ken Walker and George Pickens parlayed for all three to score the first touchdown in their respective games. Walker hit early. Gibbs finally hit in the third quarter (!!!). Pickens never played!

Not a bad little payout, which I needed because I got absolutely slaughtered by the books on Saturday.

Speaking of college football ... it's official, folks. The playoff will expand to 24 teams next season, and conference title games will be officially eliminated.

Thoughts, Mr. Governor?

Christmas, Jefferson-Pilot (!!!) & Sophie backs the blue!

"A short-sighted move that might bolster profits in the near term but will further erode what has traditionally made college football special," DeSantis posted in response to Monday's official announcement.

Thoughts? First impressions?

I've said from the beginning that I don't love any of it. Now, I do love more playoff games on actual campuses. That's the biggest issue I have with the current format. Neutral site games are for the birds when it comes to college football. Every single game should be on a college campus. I'll die on that hill.

But the elimination of Championship Weekend hurts. I hate it. The first Friday and Saturday of December are unofficial holidays, as far as I'm concerned. Back in the day you'd have the Pac-12 title game on Friday, and the Big 12, SEC, ACC and Big Ten on Saturday — in that order.

It was awesome. We have one more dance with it next month, and then it's gone forever.

Soak it all in, folks. You will miss it this time next year. I promise.

Speaking of missing things, let's rapid-fire this Monday class into a big Monday night of FOOTBALL.

First up? This came across my desk today, and I've watched it 50 times already:

Today is the 24-year anniversary of LSU's improbable Hail Mary against Kentucky, better known as the Bluegrass Miracle.

More importantly ... it was played on Jefferson-Pilot Sports, which is pure nostalgia for kids my age that grew up in the south.

Remember Jefferson-Pilot? Man, was it the best.

Nothing – and I mean nothing – beat going from College GameDay to whatever third-tier SEC game Jefferson-Pilot was airing at noon. Jay Cutler and Eli Manning had some EPIC showdowns on JP back in the day. It was never the best game, or the best picture quality, or the best announcers.

But buddy, it was college football at it's best. That's what they're taking from us!

OK, that's it for today. Good start to the week. I leave you with Sophie Cunningham at yesterday's NASCAR finale in Homestead, and a question:

When do YOU put up the Christmas decorations? It's been nine days since Halloween. Too early? Too late? What's the cutoff?

Let me know! Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.

Now, let's have a big week.

World.title: WWE legend shares the importance of standing for the national anthem, working with US military members
World.content:
In a world where standing for the national anthem with your hand over your heart has become a topic for debate, WWE Hall of Famer Goldberg left no doubt on where he stood on the issue.

Goldberg, whose real name is Bill Goldberg, appeared on NewsNation and told former Charlotte 49ers head football coach Bill Poggi that his respect, appreciation and admiration for those who have served in the U.S. military is the reason why he shows allegiance when "The Star-Spangled Banner" is played.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

"Well, especially in today's day and age when people like to forget history and people don't necessarily appreciate who came before them," he said. "I stand for the national anthem and I put my hand over my heart because there's so many people who have put their lives on the line for people that they don't know just as a job to protect the country. And that, in itself, is a reason to stand up and show allegiance. I cannot tell you the joy that I get out of seeing these men and women deployed and deriving some type of enjoyment and excitement to interact with someone such as myself. So why wouldn't you spread that as much as humanly possible and make it part of every day of your life to try to put a smile on somebody's face and, in this case, a veteran who again put their lives on the line for people that they don't even know to serve their country?

"So for me, if I can go out of my way to pat someone on the back and look them in the eye and say thank you and have them understand that it's truly coming from my heart with no ulterior motive whatsoever. I don't care about getting somebody taking a picture of me shaking somebody's hand and posting it and showing what a good guy I am. That's not why I do it. I do it because I can look in their eye and see how much they appreciate it."

Goldberg credited his parents, his sister and those who came before him with teaching him "how to be a human being." He said, now, taking care of his children and his family along with "taking care of our military" are some of the most important things in his life.

"And so I will service the kids and the military till the day I die," he added. "And it means everything to me. It truly does."

Goldberg played 14 games in the NFL with the Atlanta Falcons between 1992 and 1994. He also spent time in the World League of American Football. After being cut by the Carolina Panthers in 1995, he would pop up in World Championship Wrestling (WCW) by the end of 1997.

Ella Bennett, who entered foster care at age 3, was among the students recognized during Trump's visit to LSU over the weekend, where the first lady announced a $7.2 million scholarship endowment.

"The scholarship has definitely helped alleviate some financial stress, just because when applying, looking and going to college, I don't really have the financial support system that everybody else comes with," Bennett said.

"It was kind of like a breath of fresh air. I didn't really have too much of an impression going in, but I did definitely leave with a good one. She seemed genuinely interested in what I wanted to do with my life and where I wanted to go."

The permanent endowment includes a $5 million commitment from MMR Group, led by LSU alumnus James B. "Pepper" Rutland, and an additional $2.2 million raised from 75 LSU Foundation donors.

LSU Foundation President and CEO Krista Raney said the contributions had brought the scholarship fund to "more than $7.2 million and growing."

"Every young person from foster care should have the chance to build an extraordinary life. Education is the center of that plan," Trump said.

Bennett told Fox News the ceremony, where the first lady appeared flanked by LSU cheerleaders and the school's mascot, Mike the Tiger, was "very high energy."

"It felt great to put awareness out there for more foster kids and everything — just to see how big this program is really going to go," said Bennett.

World.title: Supreme Court paves way for Trump to build a section of his border wall in the Big Bend area of Texas
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday allowed President Donald Trump to move forward with construction of his border wall in the remote Big Bend region of southwest Texas.

Construction there had been challenged by an environmental group and locals who say it would damage the environment and historic sites.

The justices blocked an injunction imposed by a federal judge in Texas that had blocked construction while litigation continues.

In a five-page unsigned decision, the court said that the federal judge who ruled on the issue had no authority to do so, adding that the Trump administration was “extremely likely to prevail” on that point.

The government, the court added, has “compelling interests” when a challenged policy involves border security.

Of the nine justices, only liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.

The segment of the border adjacent to the Rio Grande is sparsely populated, with the Trump administration saying that 89,000 people have been detained trying to enter the United States there in recent years.

Demonstrators rally against the construction of a section of the U.S.-Mexico border wall at Santa Elena Canyon in Big Bend National Park, Texas, on Aug. 12. Kaylee Greenlee / Bloomberg via Getty

The section in question, which the government says would involve 341 miles of construction, includes Big Bend National Park. The legal dispute focuses on three waivers issued by then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in February and her successor Markwayne Mullin in May and July that allowed the government to evade environmental and conservation laws.

In a court filing, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said Congress in 1996 gave the government “broad authority” to build border infrastructure without getting tied up in red tape.

The move was challenged by the Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental group; Friends of the Ruidosa Church, a nonprofit group dedicated to restoring a historic church in the area; and Danny Miller, a river guide who owns property in the area.

Lawyers for the challengers said that if construction goes ahead, it would “result in the permanent alteration of an irreplaceable landscape” and “threaten unique historic and cultural resources.”

Contrary to the government’s assertions, the Big Bend area has “the lowest apprehension rates” for migrants anywhere along the border, they added.

Government data shows that Big Bend has the section of the southern border with the lowest number of encounters between federal agents and migrants.

The plaintiffs say that the 1996 law only allows for limited waivers for border construction projects in areas where illegal crossings are pervasive.

U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone on Oct. 2 invalidated Noem’s waivers, saying the secretary lacked such sweeping powers.

Cardone declined to put her ruling on hold, prompting the administration to turn to the Supreme Court.

Trump’s pledge to build a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border has been one of his signature policies ever since his first presidential campaign in 2016. It is part of his hard-line immigration policy that focuses on border security and mass deportations.

Officials have warned that if other parts of the wall are built but the Big Bend area remains open, it would be exploited by those seeking to enter the country illegally.

Boosted by construction funding from the Republican-controlled Congress, the administration seeks to fulfill Trump’s plan by completing a 2,000-mile installation including steel panels, vehicle barriers and new surveillance technology.

World.title: The ‘slam dunk’ that wasn’t: Promising cholesterol drug fails to prevent heart attacks or stroke
World.content:
An experimental drug that held great promise in driving down a dangerous form of cholesterol didn’t show any measurable impact on heart attack or stroke in a clinical trial. The failure of the Novartis drug pelacarsen to help people who have high levels of lipoprotein(a) stunned researchers, who called it a massive blow to preventive cardiology.

Results of the clinical trial of pelacarsen, an injection, presented Saturday at a meeting of the American Heart Association, found there were zero decreases in stroke, heart attack, cardiovascular deaths or the number of procedures to open blocked arteries or restore blood flow to the heart.

“I really thought that this was going to be a slam dunk,” said Dr. Amanda Doran, an assistant professor of medicine in the division of cardiovascular medicine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Vanderbilt was one of nearly 800 sites involved in the clinical trial, called Horizon. “We were pretty invested, so it obviously hurts.”

Pelacarsen targets a stealthy and particularly lethal form of cholesterol called lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a). Much like low-density lipoprotein — LDL, or the “bad” cholesterol — Lp(a) causes plaque to build up in arteries. But it also helps form blood clots, and unlike LDL, it is entirely genetic.

About 1 in 5 Americans have high Lp(a), according to the American Heart Association. Most don’t realize they’re at risk.

Because people are born with those high levels, diet and exercise have no effect. That’s why heart experts have been so keen to find a drug that would handle the problem.

The Horizon trial included 8,322 people with high Lp(a) levels and who’d already had a heart attack, stroke or other heart problem within 10 years of starting the trial.

The drug did reduce Lp(a) significantly, by 78%, compared with a placebo drug that cut levels by 13%.

But that huge reduction ultimately meant nothing in terms of cardiovascular health.

Dr. Steven Nissen, the chief academic officer of the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at the Cleveland Clinic, led the trial. He said the dismal results took him by “extreme surprise.”

“Everybody, me included, believed that lowering levels of lipoprotein(a) substantially would reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events,” he said. “There is simply no evidence here that people that got more reduction did better.”

The findings, also published Saturday in the New England Journal of Medicine, confounded Nissen and other cardiologists who’ve long known that controlling other markers of heart health — LDL and blood pressure, for example — provides clear benefits.

“I have not seen a more shockingly neutral trial in a while,” said Dr. Karol Watson, co-director of the UCLA Program in Preventive Cardiology and a professor at UCLA’s David Geffen School of Medicine. Watson was not involved with the research.

There are several theories as to why the drug didn’t work as anticipated. It’s possible, Watson said, that the therapy was given too late in life to make a difference. The average age of Horizon’s study participants was 60, and they were followed for an average of five years.

“Remember that Lp(a) is a genetic disorder, so from the time a baby’s conceived, their Lp(a) is high. If we just swooped in in the last five years, maybe that’s too late,” Watson said.

Study participants were also treated aggressively in other ways to drive down their LDL cholesterol and get blood pressure readings into a healthy range. Participants may have also been taking aspirin because of a history of heart attack or stroke, which could have lessened Lp(a)’s clotting risk.

“How much of the Lp(a)-associated risk was remaining? We just don’t know,” Watson said.

Does Lp(a) still matter as a marker of heart health?

Doctors have only recently begun screening for it. Earlier this year, the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association released guidelines that every adult should have their Lp(a) levels measured. It’s a blood test that’s done once because levels are fixed and don’t change over time.

Experts stress that Lp(a) remains an important and valuable indicator of heart disease risk, even though the Horizon study failed to show any health benefit to driving down Lp(a) levels.

“None of that invalidates Lp(a) as a robust marker of cardiovascular disease risk,” said Dr. John Wilkins, a cardiologist at Northwestern Medicine and a professor in the division of cardiology at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine. Wilkins was also one of the authors of the Lp(a) guidelines.

“It’s still worth testing for Lp(a) because it can help identify individuals with a higher probability of an event, and we do have other interventions that can help reduce their risk,” Wilkins said. “It’s just that at present, at least with this particular drug in this particular group of patients, we did not see benefit. That doesn’t mean that we might not find something or some way to lower Lp(a) that reduces risk. We just need more science to figure that out.”

UCLA’s Watson and Vanderbilt’s Doran agreed. “We have really good data to show that Lp(a) levels are predictive of disease,” Doran said. “People who have high Lp(a) need to be aware of that in order to pursue aggressive prevention strategies.”

What’s next in treating Lp(a)?

No further study of pelacarsen is planned, Nissen said, but similar drugs are in the pipeline: Eli Lilly’s lepodisiran, Amgen’s olpasiran and Silence Therapeutics’ zerlasiran.

All are injections that work by blocking the liver’s ability to produce Lp(a), but use different approaches. Pelacarsen is what’s known as an antisense oligonucleotide. The others use a technology called small interfering RNA, or siRNA, and may have fewer side effects, such as injection site reactions, Nissen said, than pelacarsen.

Like pelacarsen, all reduce Lp(a). Clinical trials to show whether they have any real-world heart health effects are ongoing.

Eli Lilly is also studying an oral drug called muvalaplin, and CRISPR gene-editing technology designed to permanently switch off the gene that produces Lp(a) is in early development.

“I’m still so hopeful,” Doran said. “We’re going to get it in the end.”
