World.title: Cruise ship employee is rescued after going overboard near Southern California
World.content:
The Coast Guard is investigating what sent a cruise ship employee overboard near the coast of Southern California over the weekend.

In a statement, the Coast Guard said it received a notification from a “good Samaritan who recovered a conscious individual from the water approximately 10 miles northeast of Avalon Harbor” on Friday.

Newport Beach Lifeguards responded to the call and rescued a man who they said was an employee of the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship, according to the Coast Guard.

The cruise ship employee was in stable condition but was taken to a hospital in Santa Ana for medical evaluation and care, the Coast Guard said.

The Coast Guard referred questions about the details of the rescue operation to Newport Beach Lifeguards, which did not respond to a request for comment on Monday.

On Sunday, Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS Los Angeles that rescuers found the man “pretty much in the middle of the ocean.” He believed the cruise ship employee may have gone overboard nine hours before he was found.

The Ovation of the Seas is a 14-deck cruise ship operated by Royal Caribbean. In service since 2026, it can accommodate more than 4,000 passengers and a crew of 1,550.

According to Royal Caribbean’s sailing schedule, the Ovation of the Seas was scheduled to return to Los Angeles on Friday following a four-night cruise with stops at Catalina Island and Ensenada, Mexico.

Two spokespeople for Royal Caribbean did not respond to requests for comment on Monday.

World.title: Supreme Court allows border wall construction in Big Bend region
World.content:
Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume building a border wall and other infrastructure through a remote area of West Texas while litigation over the project moves forward.

In an unsigned decision, the high court agreed to lift a district court's injunction that temporarily stopped construction of the wall and related infrastructure in the Big Bend sector, which covers more than 500 miles of the southern border and includes Big Bend National Park.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson said she would have denied the Justice Department's request for emergency relief.

In its five-page decision, the Supreme Court said in part that the lower court's order delays construction of the border barrier and roads in the Big Bend region and "impedes the Government from advancing its 'compelling interests' in border security and integrity."

The challengers to the wall project "claim that construction in the Big Bend Sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area," the court said. "But Congress's enactment of [immigration law] — which permits the Secretary to waive the requirements of environmental-protection and other conservation laws — reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert."

The Center for Biological Diversity, one of the plaintiffs that sued to stop wall construction, lambasted the Supreme Court's decision.

"The Trump administration and its contractors are hellbent on destroying one of America's greatest national parks, and the Supreme Court just gave them the green light," Laiken Jordahl, the group's national public lands advocate, said in a statement. "This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal. They're signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us."

The Trump administration had asked the Supreme Court last month to step into the legal fight over the border wall in the Big Bend region and argued that the halt ordered by U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone frustrated its ability to combat illegal border crossings in the area.

Stopping construction of the wall and roads along that portion of the U.S.-Mexico border would have serious consequences, Solicitor General D. John Sauer warned, including "disruption of the government's ability to secure a quarter of the southern border against cartel incursions, drug trafficking, and illegal entry; creation of a massive vulnerability in border protection that risks funneling illegal entry and trafficking into the unsecured Big Bend Sector; and irreversible delays, costs, and operational harms from halting already-begun construction."

But an environmental nonprofit, a professional riverboat guide and a religious organization, which filed a lawsuit challenging the project, argued that allowing the Trump administration to resume construction of roads and the wall would permanently alter an "irreplaceable landscape" that includes Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, and nearly 200 miles of the Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River corridor.

"Once habitat is destroyed, vegetation cleared, historic resources damaged, livelihoods and private property destroyed, and wilderness landscapes fragmented by roads, barriers, and associated infrastructure, no final judgment can restore the status quo," lawyers for the plaintiffs wrote in a Supreme Court filing.

President Trump has promised to build a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border for more than a decade and has made the 30-foot barrier a cornerstone of his plan to tackle illegal immigration.

To speed up construction of the wall and other barriers along the southern border in Texas, the secretary of Homeland Security — first Kristi Noem and then Markwayne Mullin — issued a total of three waivers for project areas in the Big Bend region beginning in February.

The federal government would typically have to ensure compliance with federal environmental protection and historical preservation laws before moving forward with construction. But the Department of Homeland Security invoked a 1996 federal immigration law that gives the secretary the authority to waive all legal requirements deemed necessary to ensure "expeditious" construction of barriers and roads near the southern border.

In response to the move, the plaintiffs filed their lawsuit to stop the Trump administration from building new 30-foot bollard walls and other infrastructure in the Big Bend region. The waivers issued by DHS, they said, would "authorize massive projects that would cleave through the Chihuahuan Desert, sever public and wildlife access to iconic sections of the Rio Grande, and mark one of the final—and most consequential — steps towards completing 'the Wall.'"

Separate from the litigation, the president's planned wall garnered pushback from Republican and Democratic lawmakers, cattle ranchers and local law enforcement in Texas when photos and videos shared to social media in August showed bulldozers arriving at Big Bend National Park.

In response to the backlash, Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott announced that construction inside the park would be paused until the end of September. Scott has said that the proposed 30-foot border wall will not cut through Big Bend National Park, but other infrastructure would, including more than 200 miles of patrol roads and roughly 17 miles of a vehicle-barrier system, according to CBP.

Construction of a 47-mile-long stretch of wall in Hudspeth County, which is part of the Big Bend region, began in September, according to immigration agencies.

But last month, Cardone, the district judge, granted a preliminary injunction that barred the Trump administration from building border barriers or related infrastructure, or engaging in "any construction or ground disturbing activities" in the Big Bend sector.

Cardone found that the secretary of Homeland Security exceeded his authority when issuing the waivers that allowed construction of the wall to proceed.

The Trump administration and the challengers to the project were at odds over whether the Big Bend sector is an area of "high illegal entry" requiring additional border barriers.

The government has argued that immigration officers apprehended more than 89,000 people trying to cross into the U.S. illegally in that area between 2021 and 2025.

But the plaintiffs said that Big Bend ranks last for apprehensions compared to the other six sectors along the southern border. While the area covers more than 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border, annual apprehensions in the Big Bend Sector ranged between 0.3% and 2.2% of total border-wide apprehensions, according to court filings.

World.title: Nvidia stock slumps amid board investigation into CEO Jensen Huang
World.content:
Nvidia's stock price slid on Monday amid questions about CEO Jensen Huang's future at the chipmaker, following the board of directors' investigation into allegations that China targeted him in an intelligence operation.

The investigation is raising concerns about Huang's role at the company, which he co-founded and helped build into the world's second-most valuable company, with a $4.5 trillion valuation. Nvidia is barred from selling its high-end chips, specifically designed to power artificial intelligence models, to China due to competitive concerns.

Nvidia shares sank 4.7%, or $8.68, to $177.96 in late afternoon trading, shrinking the chipmaker's market valuation by about $211 billion.

The allegations center around reports that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency. On Sunday, Nvidia's board said it is starting an "independent investigation" into the allegations, sparking questions about the CEO's future with the company.

"This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons," Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said in a research note. "The key question investors will be asking is: Will Jensen remain CEO of Nvidia?"

Ives added, "There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation, and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally."

In a statement to CBS News, an Nvidia spokesperson said that "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." The company didn't respond to a question about whether Huang had violated any of its corporate policies.

The company's board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised. John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, told CBS News on Sunday, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."

The Chinese government dismissed allegations that it targeted Nvidia's chief executive, who co-founded the company in 1993, as part of an espionage operation. "The so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear," Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said in a statement.

Who is Alice Huang?

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a former executive at a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed International, whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.

Many offices in Singapore were closed on Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment.

Succession challenges

Replacing Jensen Huang, 63, would prove challenging because he is viewed as integral to the company's success, tech analysts said on Monday. Huang also serves as the public face of Nvidia, appearing at industry events and media interviews in his trademark black leather jacket.

Huang is the company's fifth-largest shareholder, with about 3.4% of its shares, according to financial data provider FactSet.

"There is no known succession plan, and there is no leader in the company who would be the clear next step if he had to step down. In many ways, Jensen is Nvidia's Steve Jobs," said Daniel Newman, CEO of tech consulting firm Futurum, in an email.

He added, "That does not mean they cannot find a Tim Cook in the future, but it would be a massive changing of the guard, and the company has not been set up for that."

Another blow for the AI trade

The scandal puts more pressure on Nvidia shares, which have already been bruised by mounting investor concerns about the valuations of companies driving AI growth. Prior to Monday's early decline, Nvidia's shares had tumbled almost 20% over the last month amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks.

The board investigation into Huang could loom over Nvidia and raise the risk that U.S. regulators could impose additional restrictions on the company's chip exports, according to Adam Crisafulli, an analyst at Vital Knowledge.

"The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised," said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy.

In recent years, Jensen Huang has lobbied federal authorities to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China, winning approval from President Trump to sell its H200 chips this year. Those chips are not Nvidia's most advanced models, but they are still considered important products for Nvidia.

Previously, Huang also lobbied Mr. Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia's less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China.

"The real potential fallout from the Jensen Huang scandal will be the U.S. government imposing dramatically more draconian restrictions on sales of sophisticated chips to China (the issue isn't the H200 but instead the fact that a large amount of higher-end Nvidia products are still making it into the hands of Chinese buyers)," Crisafulli said in a research note.

World.title: Massie introduces Hegseth impeachment articles, teeing up vote
World.content:
Washington — Rep. Thomas Massie on Monday introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war against Iran without congressional authorization and abusing the powers of his office.

The impeachment effort could attract more bipartisan support, since members of both parties are frustrated with Hegseth's handling of the war with Iran and Republicans are reeling from their defeats in the midterm elections. Lawmakers returned to Capitol Hill on Monday to reconvene for the final weeks of the GOP-controlled Congress, and Massie's move will force leaders to bring the impeachment resolution up for a vote within two legislative days.

Even before the midterm elections highlighted voters' concerns about the war in Iran and its impact on the cost of living, the push to impeach Hegseth was underway in Congress. Massie, a Kentucky Republican who has broken with the administration on a number of fronts over the past year, originally introduced impeachment articles against the defense secretary in September. House GOP leaders recessed the chamber early, pushing off a vote on the issue until November.

Massie introduced updated impeachment articles on the House floor on Monday, restarting a two-day clock for GOP leaders to schedule a vote.

The Kentucky Republican accused Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanours in a 34-page impeachment resolution with eight articles. Three charges accuse him of abusing the powers of the Department of Defense by waging war against Iran without congressional authorization.

Massie also alleged that in the conflict, Hegseth ignored laws that minimize civilian casualties, citing the strike on an Iranian school earlier this year. Another impeachment article points to the Pentagon's boat strikes in the Caribbean, while one cites the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. Another centers on free speech and the Pentagon's scrutiny of Sen. Mark Kelly after he was among a group of lawmakers who released a video calling on service members to "refuse illegal orders."

Massie argued that Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law."

"Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office, and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States," Massie wrote.

Hegseth has criticized the effort by Massie, who's leaving Congress after losing his primary earlier this year.

"A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice," Hegseth said in a video posted on X last week. "You see, their policies don't work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It's all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me."

Hegseth told reporters Monday, "we're not worried about that." He said he planned to hold a news conference on the impeachment effort Tuesday morning.

Whether other Republicans support the effort remains to be seen. But some GOP members appeared more open to the prospect, and more eager to criticize the defense secretary, after the brutal losses for their party in the midterms.

Rep. James Comer, a Kentucky Republican who leads the House Oversight Committee, said on News Nation that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth."

"We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one's happy about Iran," Comer said. "I think the Republican voters are more upset about what's going on in Iran than the Democrat voters."

GOP Rep. French Hill of Arkansas indicated that he's still considering whether to support the effort, saying on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday that he wants to hear the debate on the issue "to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War."

"If you don't think he's done a good job conducting his job, that doesn't mean per se that he's committed an impeachable offense," Hill said.

Retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who has been critical of the administration on some issues, said he's "wrestling" with whether to support the impeachment resolution.

He said Hegseth's handling of a number of topics "bothers me" and "I feel like he deserves a little bit of his own treatment, but that's not the right way to handle impeachment."

"I don't think he's been a good secretary, but do you impeach a guy for that? It has to be a high crime or misdemeanor," Bacon told reporters Monday at the Capitol.

Democrats are widely expected to support the impeachment effort. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on ABC's "This Week" on Sunday that he's a "hard yes" on the impeachment effort. But with a narrow GOP majority, Republican votes will be needed.

Massie said in a post on X on Monday that he's seen some of his colleagues say "Hegseth has been effective and they agree with the war, so they'll vote not to impeach." But he said "that's not the question."

"The question is whether he committed impeachable acts," Massie said. "And the answer is yes, eight times."

Hegseth would be the third Cabinet secretary in history to be impeached. Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached in 1876 over corruption allegations. Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas was impeached by the GOP-controlled House in 2024 over the Biden administration's handling of the southern border. Belknap was acquitted by the Senate. Mayorkas had his charges dismissed.

World.title: Google faces mounting backlash for controversial AI school policy
World.content:
Google faces mounting public pressure to change a new policy that would limit U.S. students' access to the internet giant's widely used search platform unless schools also offer its artificial intelligence-based education tools.

In a letter to Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai on Monday, Sen. Edward Markey demanded that Google's corporate parent reverse the policy, which blocks search for K-12 student accounts that don't also provide access to apps such as Google Classroom.

Markey, a Massachusetts Democrat, said Google shouldn't use its dominance in the education technology market to effectively force AI on students by restricting their access to critical research tools like Google Search. Roughly 150 million students and teachers use Classroom.

"At a time when schools, parents and policymakers are working hard to implement safeguards on AI chatbots for our children, Google is recklessly forcing AI on schools and treating kids like collateral damage," Markey said in the letter. "Schools deserve the right to block student access to AI chatbots without also forfeiting access to an important educational tool."

Google maintains that its policy change gives schools more control over how they allow AI into schools. An Alphabet spokesperson also told CBS News that Google's AI features are now so tightly integrated into search that it cannot offer the latter without also enabling the AI services.

"We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach," Google vice president and general manager of education Chris Phillips wrote last week in a blog post announcing the policy change.

Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Markey's letter.

Markey said Google's decision to block search access for students who opt out of AI "places schools in an impossible position," forcing them to choose between giving students access to a potentially dangerous technology and depriving them of "a critical educational research tool."

"Although Google has a right to create and offer new educational tools, it should not use its dominant market position to force schools to adopt them," he added.

Markey is asking Alphabet if Google will commit to allowing schools to turn off AI features and chatbots in K-12 student accounts while still allowing students to access Google Search. He also requested that Google disclose any research it has conducted on the impact of its AI tools on students' mental health.

Markey has requested that Google disclose any research or testing it has conducted on the safety of its AI functions and their impact on the mental health of K-12 students.

Google's policy has drawn fire from other critics. In a statement posted on social media, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused the tech giant of "trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools."

World.title: Why shopping for car insurance is important now
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

There may be opportunities to lower what you pay for car insurance without sacrificing important coverage. Sakchai Vongsasiripat/Getty Images

Car insurance is one of those expenses that can quickly — and often quietly — become much more expensive over time. Part of the issue is that once coverage is in place, it's easy to let the policy renew year after year without giving it much thought, especially if you haven't filed a claim or had any problems with your insurer. But a lot can change between the time you first purchase a car insurance policy and the time your next renewal rolls around.

And the car insurance market has undergone some significant changes in recent years. With inflation still problematic, insurers have had to contend with issues like rising repair costs, increasingly expensive vehicle technology and shifting claims patterns, all while adjusting how they price and offer coverage. Meanwhile, drivers may have experienced changes in their own circumstances that affect what they need from an insurance policy.

Those developments make it worth reconsidering whether the car insurance coverage you've relied on for years still makes sense. There are several other reasons why shopping around for car insurance may be particularly worthwhile, too. So, why exactly is it important to compare car insurance policies right now? That's what we'll examine below.

Learn how Luva can help you save on your car insurance policy today.

Why shopping for car insurance is important now

There are a few different reasons why comparing car insurance policies could be particularly worthwhile in today's market, even if you're satisfied with your current insurer. Here's what drivers should consider:

Insurance companies can charge dramatically different rates

Not all insurers calculate premiums the same way. Each car insurance company uses its own pricing models to assess risk, and those differences can translate into substantial variations in what you're quoted for identical coverage.

For example, one car insurer might place greater weight on your driving history, while another could be more sensitive to your vehicle type, location or annual mileage. Some companies also offer discounts that others don't, which could make one insurer considerably cheaper for your circumstances.

In other words, the car insurance company offering you the lowest rate several years ago may no longer be the most affordable option. If you take time to compare quotes from at least three insurers, though, it can help you identify whether you're overpaying for your current car insurance coverage.

Compare your car insurance coverage options online now.

Your renewal rate may no longer be competitive

It's easy to assume that staying with the same car insurance company will result in better pricing, particularly if you've maintained a clean driving record. But loyalty doesn't necessarily guarantee the lowest car insurance premium.

Car insurers regularly update their pricing models based on claims experience, operating expenses and other risk factors. That means a car insurance company that offered the best rate two years ago may no longer be the most affordable option.

So, rather than automatically renewing your car insurance policy, you may want to request quotes from several competing insurers before your current coverage expires instead. Note, though, that you could still find meaningful savings elsewhere, even if your premium hasn't increased dramatically.

Your personal circumstances may have changed

Car insurance premiums aren't determined solely by broader industry trends. Changes in your personal circumstances can also affect what you pay for your policy, and some of those changes could make you eligible for lower car insurance rates.

For example, driving fewer miles, moving to a different ZIP code, improving your credit-based insurance score where permitted or changing vehicles could affect your car insurance costs. You may also qualify for additional discounts if you've completed a defensive driving course or installed certain safety features.

By shopping around and comparing car insurance policies, you have an opportunity to see how different insurers evaluate your current circumstances rather than relying on pricing based on an older application.

Discounts can vary significantly between insurers

Most car insurance companies offer discounts, but the types available and the potential savings can differ considerably. One car insurer might provide substantial savings for bundling auto and homeowners insurance, while another may offer more competitive discounts for safe driving, low annual mileage or paying your premium in full.

Some car insurance companies also offer usage-based insurance programs that monitor driving behavior and may reward safer habits with lower premiums. However, certain usage-based programs can also increase rates based on driving data, so it's important to understand the terms before enrolling.

When comparing car insurance quotes, ask each insurer to identify every discount you're eligible for. You may find that the lowest advertised rate isn't necessarily the lowest rate you'll actually qualify for.

You could find better coverage for the same price

Shopping for car insurance isn't just important for finding the cheapest available policy. It's also an important part of determining whether you're getting enough protection for the premiums you're paying.

For example, another car insurer might offer higher liability limits, better rental car reimbursement benefits or additional coverage options for roughly what you're currently spending. This matters because inadequate coverage could leave you responsible for significant expenses after an accident. But comparing policies based on both price and protection can help you avoid sacrificing important benefits simply to reduce your monthly bill.

The bottom line

Sticking with the same car insurance company year after year may be convenient, but it doesn't necessarily result in getting the best value for your money. With rates, coverage options and your own needs changing over time, a car insurance policy that made sense a few years ago may no longer be your best choice.

Taking the time to compare quotes from multiple insurers can help you make a more informed decision about your coverage and potentially uncover meaningful savings. And even if you decide to stay with your current provider, you'll have a better understanding of how your policy stacks up against the alternatives and whether you're getting the protection you need at a competitive price.

World.title: U.S. gas prices on track to fall below $4 a gallon, experts say
World.content:
Motorists could soon see U.S. gasoline prices fall below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, according to energy experts.

Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at price-tracking firm GasBuddy, told CBS News that he expects the national average for gas, which the price-tracking firm put at $4.06 a gallon on Thursday, to dip below the $4 threshold by next week. He also predicted diesel could fall below $6 a gallon by Thanksgiving.

The average price was still at $4.06 early Friday, according to GasBuddy.

Gas and diesel prices have both dropped in recent weeks. The decline was partially due to market expectations that the U.S. midterm elections would underscore public dissatisfaction with the war in Iran and increase pressure on the Trump administration to strike a deal ending the conflict, De Haan said.

"Oil prices have been falling in the run-up to the election," he said. "My read is because there was optimism that after the midterms these problems would be addressed."

Other factors pushing down gas prices

Other factors are also putting downward pressure on fuel costs. Oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has picked up, easing constraints on global oil supply, De Haan said.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell below $100 on Thursday for the first time since September, trading at $97.44 by midday. West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was trading at $90.42 a barrel.

The recent drop in gas prices is also partly due to seasonal shifts. Prices tend to dip in the fall when Americans pull back on road trips and summer travel, De Haan noted. Filling stations are already switching to winter-blend gas, which is less costly to produce than summer-blend fuel.

Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, predicts that the average U.S. gas price will sink below $4 within the next 10 days. The profit gas stations earn on each gallon of gas sold — currently around 75 cents per gallon — is also larger than usual.

"Historically, that is too outsized," he said in an email. "A more normal markup would be 40 cents a gallon, and that means that even if futures prices and physical markets hang around present levels, we should see lower pump prices for the foreseeable future."

The Trump administration has used various tools to ease gas prices. That includes expanding access to tax-free red-dyed diesel, opening the door to Russian diesel imports, and waiving what's known as the Jones Act, a federal statute that requires goods shipped between U.S. ports to be moved on ships that are U.S.-built, U.S.-flagged and U.S.-crewed.

World.title: NASA is recruiting new astronauts. Here are the qualifications.
World.content:
NASA is recruiting its next class of astronauts, inviting U.S. citizens to apply before midnight ET on Dec. 3 for the chance to "live and work" on the moon.

The space agency's application portal states there are "few vacancies" for the role, which pays $164,395 annually and requires recruits to relocate to Houston, where they'll work at the Johnson Space Center.

While the job is open to all citizens, applicants must meet certain educational criteria and possess specialized experience. In other words, not just any Tom, Dick or Harriet will qualify for the job.

The next group of astronauts is being selected as the U.S. plans to build a moon base and send crewed missions to the lunar surface. NASA's Artemis II mission recently sent a crew of four astronauts around the moon in April, setting a record for the farthest distance humans have ever traveled from our planet.

"The people we select could walk on the moon, live and work at the moon base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement. "Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork and courage."

Here are the qualifications NASA is looking for in an astronaut.

Educational background

NASA's job application portal states that applicants must fit into one of the following four educational profiles:

A master's degree in a qualifying field of engineering, biological science, physical science, computer science or mathematics.

Two academic years of qualifying doctoral coursework in one of those fields.

A qualifying medical degree, such as an MD, physician assistant or nurse practitioner.

Completion of a recognized test pilot school by July 2027.

Specialized experience

Applicants must also select a discipline they best qualify for based on their work experience, with NASA requiring three years of professional experience after completing their degree program or pilot training.

Pilots: Must meet one of three thresholds: 750 hours as lead pilot of a high-performance jet; 1,500 hours in other fixed-wing aircraft, with 750 in command; or 1,000 hours in rotary-wing aircraft, with 300 in command. Initial flight training and drone hours are excluded.

Must meet one of three thresholds: 750 hours as lead pilot of a high-performance jet; 1,500 hours in other fixed-wing aircraft, with 750 in command; or 1,000 hours in rotary-wing aircraft, with 300 in command. Initial flight training and drone hours are excluded. Flight test: Requires test pilot school completion or enrollment, with completion by July 2027, as well as three years of related flight test experience.



Requires test pilot school completion or enrollment, with completion by July 2027, as well as three years of related flight test experience. Medical: At least three years of professional experience after earning a medical degree. NASA said that residencies count toward the experience.

At least three years of professional experience after earning a medical degree. NASA said that residencies count toward the experience. Biological and medical science: At least three years of related experience.



At least three years of related experience. Physical science : Three years of related work experience.

: Three years of related work experience. Engineering: Three years of related work experience.

Three years of related work experience. Operations: Three years of related work experience in "high-consequence environments that require real-time decision-making and intensive teamwork, where errors carry irreversible and physical risk to personnel, missions or vehicles," NASA said.

Other requirements

Applicants must also pass a series of clearances, including medical and psychiatric exams; vision that can be corrected to 20/20 in each eye; and a background check and drug screening.

Aspiring astronauts must be able "to perform moderate to arduous physical activities, including heavy lifting, crouching, crawling and exposure to inclement weather" and "be willing to work in dangerous, life-threatening situations and live/work in remote, isolated, small or confined spaces for prolonged periods." Applicants also have to pass a swimming test.

On top of that, applicants must "be willing to deploy to space for 12 months or longer, accepting extreme isolation, austere living conditions and separation from loved ones."

World.title: Thomas Massie files articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
World.content:
Thomas Massie files articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth

toggle caption i Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images

Rep. Thomas Massie has reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, setting up a vote in the House of Representatives in the next two days.

The Kentucky Republican's resolution accuses Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors and lists eight specific charges against him.

The allegations include:

3 charges for illegally waging war against Iran in violation of the War Powers Resolution

1 charge for ignoring laws designed to minimize civilian casualties

1 charge for overseeing "extrajudicial killings" in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean with strikes on alleged drug boats

1 charge for suppressing free speech, brought in connection to the effort to punish Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for a video telling service members they can refuse illegal orders

1 charge for the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization

1 charge for illegally waging war against Yemen in violation of the War Powers Resolution

toggle caption i Finn Gomez/Getty Images

Hegseth defended his record at the Pentagon in a video released last Thursday, dismissing Massie's effort as "sham articles of impeachment."

Sponsor Message

"Didn't work against President Trump and it won't work with me," Hegseth said.

Massie has long been a staunch critic of Hegseth. During the GOP primary, Hegseth campaigned on behalf of Ed Gallrein, who went on to defeat Massie.

He first sought to bring the impeachment resolution to the floor before the midterm elections, prompting Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to call an early recess to avoid the vote. That caused the resolution to expire, which is why Massie reintroduced the resolution Monday.

Presumptive next House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has already signaled support for an impeachment push against Hegseth.

Even Republican members who oppose impeaching Hegseth have said the Trump administration could do a better job making the case to Congress and the public about what the plan is for the Iran war going forward.

Rep. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio., indicated to NPR that impeachment would be hypocritical given that administrations going back to the Korean War have largely ignored Congress' war powers efforts.

"I think trying to scapegoat Pete Hegseth is just the status quo politics in Washington," he said. "I think it would be a mistake to impeach."

Davidson said lawmakers who want changes are better off trying to leverage the power of the purse to withhold money from the conflict.

Sponsor Message

There could likely be sufficient votes to impeach Hegseth in the House, with the support of all Democrats, Massie, and a handful of Republicans. However, it is unlikely to clear the higher Senate threshold for convicting and removing Hegseth from office — which requires two-thirds of the Senate.

World.title: Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution
World.content:
Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution

toggle caption i Manish Swarup/AP

NEW DELHI — A thick blanket of smog shrouded India's capital Monday after firecrackers lit up the skies over New Delhi during Diwali celebrations, compounding dangerously high pollution levels and intensifying the seasonal air pollution crisis that grips the city every year.

Despite restrictions on fireworks, residents in New Delhi celebrated the Hindu festival of lights with firecrackers on Sunday evening, releasing smoke and fine particulate matter into the atmosphere. The air quality index exceeded 350 in several parts of the capital on Monday morning, reaching the severe category and posing significant health risks.

Monitoring stations across the city recorded similarly alarming levels, while visibility deteriorated as a gray haze blanketed streets and high-rise buildings.

Sponsor Message

India's Supreme Court in October had sought to limit Diwali pollution by restricting conventional firecrackers and allowing only approved "green firecrackers" under specified conditions for three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday. The crackers produce fewer emissions but are not pollution-free. They still release particulate matter and other pollutants, adding to the city's already hazardous air.

Isyad, a New Delhi resident who uses one name, said the worsening smog was taking a toll on his health.

"Because of the pollution there is irritation in the throat and itching in the eyes," he said.

New Delhi and its metropolitan region, home to more than 30 million people, regularly rank among the world's most polluted areas during winter. Pollution worsens as Diwali fireworks coincide with cooler weather and smoke from crop-residue fires in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana.

After harvesting rice, farmers often burn leftover stalks to clear their fields for the next planting season. The smoke drifts toward New Delhi, adding to pollution from vehicles, industries, construction dust and other local sources.

The problem becomes particularly acute in late October and November, when cooler temperatures, low wind speeds and stagnant atmospheric conditions prevent pollutants from dispersing. The result is a thick haze that can linger over the capital and surrounding areas for days.

toggle caption i Manish Swarup/AP

Authorities in New Delhi have implemented a set of measures to curb pollution, which include limits on construction activity and restrictions on diesel generators, while courts have sough restrictions on firecrackers. But the measures have not prevented the return of severe pollution each year.

Sponsor Message

Environmentalists say long-term solutions, such as cleaner energy and stricter controls on vehicle emissions, are needed to prevent the annual crisis.

Shweta Narayan, a public health expert at the Global Climate and Health Alliance, described the government's response so far as "knee-jerk" and "temporary."

"A lot of interventions happen only because the government is pressured or pushed in a corner to do something," she said.

World.title: British comedian Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years for rape and sexual assault
World.content:
British comedian Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years for rape and sexual assault

toggle caption i Elizabeth Cook/PA/AP

Russell Brand, the raunchy, irreverent British comedian who became a celebrity darling in the early 2000s, has been sentenced to over 10 years in prison after being found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

"The total sentence is one of ten years, six months," said Judge Justice Bennathan on handing down the sentence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Monday.

Brand, 51, was a career chameleon who went from stand-up comic and MTV host to a political analyst esteemed by Britain's left, only to become a conspiracy theorist and Christian convert beloved by the U.S. right.

Sponsor Message

But critics of Brand said there was always a clear thread of misogyny running through his comedy routines, and that his mistreatment of women had been an open secret for decades.

Over the past four weeks, six women testified against the comedian in court in London, in a trial that garnered massive media attention.

A jury found Brand guilty last week on four of the seven counts against him. He was found guilty of raping a woman he'd met at one of his shows in 2009 and of sexually assaulting three women — at a bar, a radio station and a TV studio — between 2004 and 2009.

Brand denies all charges and said he never had non-consensual sex.

Before the judge handed down the sentence, four of the women who brought the case against Brand gave victim impact statements to the court. Three of the statements were read out by the prosecution, while one woman appeared in court behind a curtain to read her own.

None of the women have been publicly named and the trial was not televised.

Victim impact statements read

The prosecution read out an impact statement from the one complainant, who Brand was found guilty of anally raping at his home in 2009. In her statement she said: "It's something I carry with me every day and it often feels never-ending."

Sponsor Message

"I doubt my ability to make good decisions and no longer trust my instinct in the way I did," her statement said, adding that because of Brand's fame she didn't think she'd be believed if she reported him.

toggle caption i Matt Sayles/AP

Another complainant, who Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting at a bar in 2004 when he grabbed her breasts, said the confusion of what she "should" or "could" do had stayed with her for over 20 years.

The complainant, who spoke in person from behind a curtain in the courtroom, said she felt "physically sick" seeing Brand in the press afterwards as his fame rose.

Another of Brand's victims, who he was found guilty of sexually assaulting in 2005, said the assault had "a lasting impact on her life" and that over the years "hearing his voice on television or seeing his image has made me jump."

A fourth woman, who Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting when they worked together at a TV studio, said she was badly affected and afterwards felt her working environment was unsafe.

Brand holds rosary and prays

British media who were in the court for the sentencing said Brand, who had spent the weekend in prison, was in the suit he was convicted in on Thursday and sat holding a set of white rosary beads as the victim statements were read. Brand's wife Laura, who had supported him throughout the case, was in court, as was his father.

After the victim statements, the defense and prosecution teams had the opportunity to make their last statements.

The prosecution called for a long sentence, saying there were aggravating circumstances in the anal rape case, such as Brand removing a condom. The defence meanwhile said Brand was "a fundamentally different person" from who he was at the time of the crimes.

Sponsor Message

After considering the victim impact statements and those by the defence and prosecution, the judge handed down the sentence live on camera.

In his remarks, he said Brand had become "a sexual predator" and paused "to pay tribute to the determination and bravery" of the women who'd come forward.

He then ordered Brand to be taken down to the cells.

World.title: Congress is back after GOP's midterm defeat. And, Trump appoints new chief of staff
World.content:
Congress is back after GOP's midterm defeat. And, Trump appoints new chief of staff

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

President Trump has appointed Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. It's Trump's first major personnel change since the Republicans' defeat in the midterms. Miller, who was deputy chief of staff, has been key in shaping many of Trump's controversial policies, particularly on immigration. Voter data indicates that the Democrats gained support partly due to Trump's immigration enforcement.

toggle caption i Alex Wong/Getty Images

🎧 Miller supports unchecked executive power. By selecting him, Trump is signaling his readiness to confront an opposition Congress, NPR's Mara Liasson tells Up First. The president has also posted on social media that he offered the White House Press Secretary job to Dana White, the CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship. He later said it was a joke. As president, the public takes his words seriously, and the fact that people cannot take his statements at face value poses a challenge for the U.S., Liasson says.

The 119th Congress is reaching its final weeks before a new Democrat-controlled House and Senate step in. Lawmakers' key agenda item is keeping the federal government open, as funding runs out on Dec. 11. They will likely use a short-term continuing resolution to extend funding, because they lack the time and political will to negotiate the typical 12 appropriations bills.



Sponsor Message

🎧 Attendance could be a problem for many of the Republicans defeated in the midterms, NPR's Eric McDaniel says. With only a two-vote majority in the House, any absenteeism could jeopardize Republican plans to end their time in power on their own terms. McDaniel says Senate Republicans will likely want to confirm as many judges and Trump appointees as possible before Democrats take over in January. Once the Democrats take control, McDaniel says those confirmations won't happen without significant compromises from the White House.

Massive artificial intelligence chip maker Nvidia is launching an internal investigation after reports that its CEO was involved in a close relationship with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. The New York Times reported that a Chinese intelligence operation targeted Jensen Huang to send advanced Nvidia AI chips to China. NPR reached out to the Chinese Embassy in Washington, D.C., for comment but has not received a response. China denied the allegations on Monday in a press briefing.



🎧 Nvidia plays a crucial role in the U.S. economy as a leading company at the center of the AI revolution, NPR's John Ruwitch says. Huang has significant access to Trump, communicating frequently and even traveling to China with him. When asked about Huang and the incident, Trump said he thinks "Huang is a fine person." The U.S. restricts exports of advanced chips to China, including Nvidia's best chips. Huang has argued that allowing China to buy these chips would slow the growth of its chipmaking industry and benefit America. Despite ongoing investigations, Nvidia believes that neither national security nor its secrets are compromised. The House of Representatives has requested a closed-door briefing from Huang regarding his interactions with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.

Sponsor Message

Deep dive

Connie Hanzhang Jin/NPR

Climate change is transforming the vibrant colors of nature, from Arctic landscapes to coral reefs. The effects of these color shifts are complex, and scientists are racing to understand them. Here's how climate change is altering the colors of the world:

➡️ Every summer, climate-driven wildfires blanket Arctic ice in soot. These dark particles from oil and gas operations, commercial shipping and tourism absorb heat from the sun, accelerating melting ice and contributing to sea-level rise.

➡️ As permafrost thaws deeper into the soil, nutrients become more available, enabling larger vegetation to take hold and turning the landscape greener. A 2020 study in Nature Communications found that about 38% of sites in Alaska, Canada and western Eurasia showed greening.

➡️ Thawing permafrost can also mix soil with lake water, turning them darker. A 2021 study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America (PNAS) found green wavelengths in lakes in the boreal Arctic zone declined by 15% from 1984 to 2019, making these lakes appear darker to the naked eye. The darker a lake gets, the more heat it can store.

➡️ Some insects have changed color due to warmer climates. North American male dragonflies are losing wing color, according to a study in PNAS. This helps them stay cooler but also reduces the coloration that attracts females.

Picture show

toggle caption i Tamera Merino for NPR

The Atacama Desert in Chile has transformed into a vibrant patchwork of pinks, yellows, lilacs and purples, thanks to the El Niño super cycle. This floral bloom has been the largest and most colorful in at least 30 years. The phenomenon followed unprecedented rainfall that caused flash floods, damaging homes and forcing evacuations. The rain reached deep into the parched ground, awakening millions of dormant seeds, bulbs and tubers. Now, more than 200 species have burst into color, creating a breathtaking spectacle where every crevice is streaked with hues.

Sponsor Message

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Alastair Grant/AP

Comedian Russell Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence as a London court is set to announce his punishment today after a jury convicted him on three counts of sexual assault and one count of rape. Brand has denied all charges. The U.S. homeless population decreased by more than 6% in 2025, according to the Department of Housing and Urban Development. This marks the second consecutive year of decline. Pope Leo XIV arrived in South America on Friday for a 12-day trip across three countries. This will be his longest and most significant journey to date, as well as his first major overseas visit since undergoing lung cancer surgery.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Why a South Korean city is turning to a U.S. college to outsmart AI?
World.content:
Why a South Korean city is turning to a U.S. college to outsmart AI?

toggle caption i Anthony Kuhn/NPR

CHUNCHEON, South Korea — "Is the Frankenstein monster human?" a teacher asks students at the Toegye public elementary school in Chuncheon city, some 50 miles east of Seoul, as they discuss Mary Shelley's novel Frankenstein.

"I think we can call it a human being with no soul," ventures student Ma Yeonwoo.

The Toegye school has adopted the " Great Books" educational model used by St. John's College, whose main campus is in Annapolis, Md.

The class's discussion then shifts to whether artificial intelligence is human.

"No," Ma Yeonwoo responds, because humans created AI, and although it is intelligent, it "has no creativity."

Sponsor Message

In the "Great Books" model, teachers do not lecture, they only guide discussions. There are no majors or elective courses. Students do not seek answers from outside sources such as the internet and rely only on their readings, their own reasoning and class discussions with their peers.

That suits Ma Yeonwoo, who says he enjoys debating with his classmates.

"If only the teacher talks we can have one idea, but if we all debate together, like, we can get many ideas together," he says.

This nascent educational movement addresses several concerning trends. One is that international tests such as PISA have shown a post-COVID drop in South Korean reading skills, after decades in which South Korean and other East Asian students outperformed their American counterparts.

Another is South Korea's rapid adoption of AI in education. 51% of South Korean students say they use AI chatbots to study at least once a week, according to Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) figures. Students also face intense competition to pass college entrance exams, which piles pressure on them down to the pre-K school level and prompts many South Korean families to send their children to cram schools to gain a competitive edge, or to foreign schools to escape the system.

toggle caption i Anthony Kuhn/NPR

"We all feel that this system leaves students with no time to read and think," because they're too busy memorizing facts to pass tests," says Lee Yonghwa, a professor of English language and literature at Incheon National University, where he co-founded South Korea's first "Great Books" program in 2019.

Sponsor Message

But now, Lee laments, "Korean students are even losing their old capacity to memorize facts because they collect facts and ideas mainly from A.I."

And if they can't reason and think independently, he adds, they can't judge the quality of the results that AI generates for them.

The limitations of their educational system motivates many South Koreans to look for alternatives, from education overseas, to educational experiments at home.

"As someone who went through this system, I felt those limitations keenly," Chuncheon Mayor Yook Dong-han said in an interview at city hall. "When I became mayor, I wanted to introduce a different kind of education and a distinct educational philosophy to the city of Chuncheon."

Chuncheon draws visitors from neighboring Seoul to enjoy its mountains, lakes and rivers, and dakgalbi, a local dish of grilled or stir-fried marinated chicken.

Chuncheon's government established an academic partnership with St. John's College last year to promote the "Great Books" educational model.

There are now 120 college students and some 770 younger students taking the "Great Books" program in South Korea, and 40 teachers in training, according to Lee Yonghwa.

Although the program is still in its infancy, Yook says it represents a "small but revolutionary achievement — a breakthrough that challenges established practices," and generated interest among participating students that has exceeded his expectations.

South Korean students following the "Great Books" model read Aristotle, Shakespeare, Euclid, and Korean authors including Nobel laureate Han Kang .

toggle caption i Anthony Kuhn/NPR

In one Chuncheon high school, students read Martin Luther King Jr.'s 1963 Letter from Birmingham Jail.

They discuss King's ideas about what kind of laws are just and unjust, and which laws citizens should obey or disobey.

Lee Yonghwa says he's impressed that students connected King's letter to their own country, such as in 2024, when citizens and lawmakers defeated former President Yoon Suk Yeol's attempt to put South Korea under martial law.

Sponsor Message

That fits the purpose of the "Great Books" model, in which "each seminar table really becomes a miniature republic, where ideas clash but people cooperate," St. John's College President J. Walter Sterling wrote last year in an opinion essay .

Through civic participation and liberal education, he adds, "we quietly stitch the fabric of our democracy…before it unravels beyond repair."

NPR's Se Eun Gong contributed to this report in Chuncheon and Seoul.

World.title: Democrats won big on issues like immigration. But ICE still has the money
World.content:
Democrats won big on issues like immigration. But ICE still has the money

toggle caption i Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images

In the days leading up to the midterm elections, hundreds of people left their "I voted" stickers on a memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo , a Houston man killed by federal immigration agents earlier this year.

"The fact that people were thinking of my dad and thinking of other immigrants — that just means the world to me," said Ronaldo Salgado, Salgado Araujo's son, told NPR.

Those votes resulted in a seismic political shift in Texas: for the first time, a Latina, Democrat Gina Hinojosa , will be governor. Texans also elected the state's first Democratic U.S. senator in nearly 40 years, and the Texas House of Representatives flipped .

Sponsor Message

"Unfortunately, Texas has become like the epicenter of ICE enforcement and like gross violence against immigrants," Ronaldo Salgado said. "Well, the voters have spoken — incoming lawmakers now have a duty to listen to us."

The political fallout

Immigration policy was one of the top issues on voters' minds this election, according to exit polling . Artemio Muñiz of the Texas Federation of Hispanic Republicans, told NPR "with these anti-immigrant-type policies, I think the Hispanic community got fed up."

That seems more true than ever in the counties along the U.S.-Mexico border, which flipped Democratic after supporting Trump in 2024.

"I think the message is clear from the Texas Hispanic community that the only acceptable or effective Hispanic outreach from the Republican Party in Texas is one that includes a reasonable solution for immigration," Muñiz said, suggesting the solution should include secured borders and a legal pathway for undocumented immigrants who have been in the U.S. for decades.

toggle caption i Brandon Bell/Getty Images North America

In Texas, Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa is facing calls to end the state's partnership with ICE.

"That's something that can happen on day one," said César Espinosa, the executive director of the Houston-based advocacy organization FIEL. He said his group would also like to see Hinojosa and the Texas legislature to push for driver licenses for undocumented immigrants. Already, Houston's mayor is reducing his police department's cooperation with ICE.

Sponsor Message

Nationwide, immigration advocates say they want to see ICE defunded, or severely restricted.

"We demand that the incoming Congress hold ICE accountable", says Murad Awawdeh of the New York Immigrant Coalition.

What could the new Congress actually do?

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become the next chair of the House oversight committee, had two words of advice for Republicans on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

Garcia has promised to look into several issues, including ICE accountability.

ICE is the highest funded federal law enforcement agency in the U.S. Congress essentially gave immigration enforcement a blank check in 2025 and in 2026 they awarded ICE and Customs and Border Patrol around $240 billion.

toggle caption i Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images

It's enough funds to run the mass deportation operation for the remainder of Trump's term.

Congress could claw back that money. And lawmakers are already eyeing more stringent oversight.

"We have to rein ICE in because its illegal, out-of-control activities (have) killed individuals … assaulted individuals … have incarcerated individuals," said Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., who is likely to chair the House Homeland Security Committee. "That system has to have accountability for the men and women who work in it."

He said he'd like to legally require policies, like requiring the use of body-worn cameras for federal immigration agents and banning them from wearing face coverings.

The major hurdle is President Trump: following the midterm election results the President said he would welcome the nickname "Mr. Veto."

Another possible indication of how the administration will be seeing immigration enforcement moving forward came Friday, a few days after the midterm elections. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller was promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller's central project in government has been immigration control and mass deportations. Miller is considered the architect of the first Trump administration's child separation policy, and as NPR reported, was deeply involved in the project of turning large warehouses into immigration detention centers.

Sponsor Message

Naureen Shah at the ACLU says she thinks one of the most powerful things that could happen to change ICE behavior is Congressional oversight via subpoenas.

"ICE has to be afraid," she said. "They have to be afraid of losing their funding, they have to be afraid of being subpoenaed and asked extremely hard questions before a live audience of the American people."

The Trump Administration vows that "Deportations will continue".

The day after the Midterm elections, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin posted a three-word tweet : " Deportations will continue ."

Vice President JD Vance took to X to share his thoughts on the Republican Party's big loss. He said he believes it is due to voter's concerns over the economy, inflation and the war with Iran. He left immigration enforcement off that list.

He did, however, say he is open to changing enforcement tactics by focusing more on businesses that hire undocumented workers. But he said immigration amnesty is not the solution.

Shah of the ACLU says she believes ICE enforcement and the current state of the economy are inextricably linked. "What's really clear is that the stories of life becoming harder for everyday Americans are actually also stories about ICE's impact. People are afraid to take their kids to school, afraid to go to work. It impacts our schools, our teachers. It impacts the labor force when people aren't showing up for their jobs. So Democrats have an opportunity through their oversight device to tell a story about how to make everyday life more affordable for all Americans."

Could we see more oversight on ICE detention facilities?

toggle caption i Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images

The Trump administration has spent billions of dollars to expand ICE detention facilities — many of which have faced criticism and protest over dire conditions. There have been a record number of deaths in detention since the start of Trump's second term.

Sponsor Message

The day after mid-term election results the two major private detention center companies that contract for ICE, CoreCivic and the GEO Group , had their quarterly investor calls.

The main question asked by investors at the CoreCivic call was: how will the result of the midterms affect ICE operations?

CoreCivic President Lucibeth Mayberry optimistically, pointing out that "[ICE] have again began increasing enforcement activity. They have the secure funding to do so." But then she offered a word of advice to ICE about purchasing new detention centers: "we would urge the ICE administration to move quickly."

World.title: On wild Cumberland Island, a land swap proposal stirs controversy
World.content:
On wild Cumberland Island, a land swap proposal stirs controversy

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

CUMBERLAND ISLAND, Ga.— Wild horses, feral hogs and deer roam free on this 18-mile barrier island, one of the largest and most ecologically diverse along the Atlantic coast. The landscape includes salt marshes, maritime forests, and an expansive stretch of pristine, untouched beach only accessible to the public by ferry.

Since 1972, the National Park Service has managed Cumberland Island National Seashore, including roughly 9,800 acres of wilderness designated by an act of Congress which stated that "the seashore shall be permanently preserved in its primitive state."

But there's more on this island than federally protected wilderness. Visitors also can find Native-American relics, remnants of Spanish missions, the ruins of ante-bellum plantations, and opulent homes built by the wealthy Gilded Age industrialist Thomas Carnegie and his wife Lucy, who had 9 children.

Sponsor Message

Descendants of the Carnegies still live or vacation here on private property, and the park service has proposed a land swap with them that would allow for new construction. That possibility is creating tension between the many stakeholders who all have differing views of what it means to preserve the island they hold dear.

Park superintendent Melissa Trenchik has been defending the plan, giving media tours to an area under a grove of huge live oak trees on Cumberland's west side, which overlooks an expansive salt marsh and Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay on the horizon.

It is currently parkland, which under the proposal would be handed over to two branches of Carnegie descendants for the construction of up to eight new private homes.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

"They obviously want to be with this incredible view," Trenchik told Georgia Public Broadcasting ' s Jillian Magtoto, as they stood on the edge of a maritime forest looking out over the Cumberland Sound.

The idea, Trenchik said, is to consolidate private ownership on the west side of the island, so the park can better interpret natural and cultural resources on the Atlantic beachside of Cumberland, including sensitive coastal and wilderness areas where the government could then prohibit development. The park service received more than 12,500 public comments on the proposal.

Sponsor Message

"Right now, if we do nothing, development is possible," she said of the private land the park service seeks to acquire.

Trenchik said the eight new "modest" homes would be subject to permanent conservation limits and could not exceed 35 feet in height. Critics, however, say the 15,000-square footage allowance, including driveway and outbuildings, is anything but modest.

"We're swapping for McMansions," said Joseph Manning, an attorney with Defenders of Wildlife, a Washington D.C. based conservation group fighting the deal.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

Manning sees what's happening on Cumberland as the latest attempt by the Trump Administration to privatize public lands, pointing to other attention-grabbing headlines about a baseball park in Grand Teton, a land exchange in Yosemite , and repeated shrinkage of Bears Ears National Monument.

"Possibly the universal theme among all of these parks and refuges land exchanges that we're seeing is that they are not being done to expand public access," Manning said. "They're being done to benefit a particular special interest or just a handful of individuals or families, as is the case at Cumberland Island."

Barclay McFadden is a great-great-grandson of Thomas Carnegie, the brother of Pittsburgh steel magnate Andrew Carnegie.

"The hysteria about mansions and the Gilded Age and all that is so unfounded," McFadden said. "We love our island."

McFadden, who is involved in one of the land deals, said he's hurt by the way the debate over the land swap paints his family as modern-day robber barons without taking into account their history on the island.

"Five generations have been buried there. We have a family cemetery. It's still there. That's where I'll go," he said. "For our children and our grandchildren, it's a sacred place."

The land swap will allow them to build homes for those younger generations, McFadden said.

"We have been wonderful stewards of the island, and we have taken care of the island," he said, pointing out that his grandmother's generation had the opportunity to sell their property to developers in the 1970's. "They protected the island from turning into a golf course."

Sponsor Message

His cousin Jamie Ferguson, who is not directly involved in the current land swap proposal, said he trusts the Carnegie descendants' legacy of protecting what's special here. He jointly co-owns (with about 40 others) a Carnegie mansion here, now operated as a bed and breakfast – the Greyfield Inn.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

"It's kind of like a live oak family tree - it's really widespread," said Ferguson, the family's unofficial historian. "The common thread we have though is this place."

He said his grandmother was adamant that the land remain in the family, even when other Carnegie descendants donated property to the National Park Service.

One advantage Ferguson sees to the land swap is greater visitor access to what he calls the "most important historical monument on Cumberland," a site known simply as The Chimneys. The remnants of about two dozen brick and tabby chimneys are lined up in rows under Spanish moss draped oak trees. It's where enslaved workers lived on an old sea island cotton plantation that pre-dated the Carnegies.

Ferguson points out the National Park Service is tasked with not just preserving the island's natural history, but also its cultural history.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

"Like it or not, we're part of that cultural history," said Ferguson. "And I don't mean that in a bad way. I mean, I believe that we're a part of that cultural history, and that comes with some responsibility too."

There are a few other private homes on Cumberland that are not owned by Carnegie descendants. Naturalist Carol Rucksdeschel lives in one of them. After living on the island for more than 50 years, she's still excited each day at what she discovers.

"God look at that - that's so beautiful," she said one recent day, spotting a pair of wood storks descending into the marsh grass.

At 85, Ruckdeschel still surveys Cumberland Island every Friday morning, combing the beaches looking for stranded sea turtles and new nests. The ecologist has emerged as one of the main voices opposing the land swap, which she worries is the "first nose under the tent" towards greater development on the island.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

"This plan to me is a real affront to the American people, but it's also an insult to the Park Service," Ruckdeschel said. "It's not what they're supposed to be doing. They're supposed to be protecting this place."

Sponsor Message

She's also not happy that the park service plans to double daily visitation to Cumberland, up to 700 visitors a day.

Ruckdeschel, who is involved with the conservation group Wild Cumberland, said she's friends with Carnegie descendants and acknowledges their love for the island. Still, she said, more homes and more people will disturb what the island should be – a pure primitive wilderness where nature overtakes what humans have left behind.

"It's stepping into its climax stage, which is terribly exciting," Ruckdeschel said of the rewilded maritime forest she's witnessed take over old plantation cotton fields.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

"And that's what I would have loved to have seen the whole island do," she said. "And then people die out, places go back to nature and that's it."

World.title: He was diagnosed with cancer. Then he was told he lost his Medicaid
World.content:
He was diagnosed with cancer. Then he was told he lost his Medicaid

toggle caption i Chris Machian/KFF Health News

Eli McCreary of Omaha, Neb., said he had recently been diagnosed with kidney cancer when he got a call from a local hospital run by CHI Health. He said he was informed that he wasn't insured anymore under Medicaid — and that the hospital would cancel his appointments unless he paid out-of-pocket.

McCreary, who was 64 at the time, said he phoned a call center for help. He said he was told his benefits under Medicaid, the government health program for people with low incomes or disabilities, now required that he have a job.

"You're required to do work to stay on," McCreary said a representative told him. "And you haven't fulfilled your work requirement."

Sponsor Message

For decades, McCreary said, he has battled drug addiction. A substance use treatment program discharged him in March, and in June he was diagnosed with cancer in his right kidney, according to documents reviewed by KFF Health News. He also has diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

"I don't understand what job I can get," McCreary said. "I can't walk. I can hardly breathe. I can't move around. What job am I going to get?"

McCreary said he canceled a CT scan and other tests at the hospital, which is part of CommonSpirit Health, the nation's largest Catholic health system. He also delayed a cancer-related appointment with a physician who travels back and forth to Omaha. "I missed my window of opportunity with him for another month," he said.

Taylor Miller, a spokesperson for CHI Health, declined to answer questions about McCreary's experience. In an emailed statement, she said that "CHI Health is committed to helping patients understand their health care coverage and access to care, including available financial assistance resources."

Determined to be the first state to enforce Medicaid work requirements under President Trump's signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Nebraska launched the new rules May 1 — eight months before most states are set to do the same. With their newly elected majorities in Congress, Democrats have said they plan to repeal the changes to Medicaid in their first 100 hours in office in January. But it is unclear if they will be successful, because Trump could veto it.

Sponsor Message

Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen said in December that state officials "certainly appreciate President Trump and his whole administration for delivering this key reform." Pillen spoke alongside a videoed-in Mehmet Oz, the Trump administration official overseeing Medicare and Medicaid.

"We're excited to be able to be the first to make it happen," the Republican governor said.

Laura Strimple, a spokesperson for the governor, didn't respond to requests for comment. Jeff Powell, a spokesperson for Nebraska's Department of Health and Human Services, said its rollout "has been very successful." He pointed to state data showing 86% of affected applicants met the requirement or qualified for an exclusion and 93% of existing enrollees kept their coverage.

Health clinics and organizations advocating for poor and working-class Nebraskans say the rollout has been rife with problems — many due to poor training and inadequate staffing.

The high price of cutting benefits

About 70,000 adult Medicaid recipients in Nebraska are subject to the work requirements. They must prove they're working or participating in a similar activity for 80 hours a month, unless they qualify for an exemption. State officials and consultants advising them have said the May 1 date was challenging to meet.

toggle caption i Chris Machian/KFF Health News

To deploy the law's Medicaid coverage restrictions, Nebraska budgeted millions of dollars for government contractors, according to state documents KFF Health News obtained via a public records request. Documents from Nebraska's health department outline $8.2 million in contractor costs to enact Medicaid changes, including work requirements and more frequent checks for whether people still qualify.

Nebraska operates the information technology system that determines who in the state qualifies for Medicaid, unlike most states, which outsource the work to companies under contracts often worth hundreds of millions of dollars. But Nebraska's health department nonetheless relies on the private sector to help administer its Medicaid program.

The $8.2 million in costs span two years. They stem from two companies that Nebraska uses to increase agency staffing: Public Consulting Group, based in Boston, and Atlanta-based Covendis, which supplies information technology staffers.

Sponsor Message

One of the companies has praised Nebraska's implementation of work requirements. A post on Public Consulting Group's website quotes senior consultant Latanya Michaux.

"I really cannot brag enough about how well Nebraska handled this requirement," Michaux said, crediting the firm's "incredible relationship" with the state.

Covendis executives did not respond to requests for comment. Powell said the health department "uses contracted staff when hiring a state employee is either uneconomical or impractical because of time constraints, or when the role requires highly specialized skill sets."

Advocates who work with Medicaid enrollees in Nebraska say that participants are confused and don't know whether the rules apply to them. These advocates say enrollees also have gotten inaccurate information.
