The president said more than 23 million people in Mexico held formal sector jobs at the end of October, “the highest figure in history.” She said 161,077 formal jobs were added in October and 571,277 in the first 10 months of 2026. The number of formal jobs is up 299,180 from October 2025. 🏦 Sheinbaum credits Banxico rate cut to the economy’s “good performance”: She noted that the central bank cut its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 6.25% last Thursday. Sheinbaum said the decision reflected the strong performance of Mexico’s economy, although INEGI reported Monday that annual inflation rose to 3.75% in October from 3.45% in September.

She noted that the central bank cut its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 6.25% last Thursday. Sheinbaum said the decision reflected the strong performance of Mexico’s economy, although INEGI reported Monday that annual inflation rose to 3.75% in October from 3.45% in September. 📈 “ We’re doing well and we’re going to do better”: Sheinbaum said Mexico “is doing well on all the economic indicators,” and recalled that she had predicted an improvement in the second half of 2026 as public infrastructure projects got underway.

Sheinbaum said Mexico “is doing well on all the economic indicators,” and recalled that she had predicted an improvement in the second half of 2026 as public infrastructure projects got underway. 💵 “ Cash isn’t going to be phased out”: Sheinbaum sought to calm concerns about the new Digital Economy Law, which gives the Finance Ministry the power to designate sectors where digital payments will be the only option. She said the aim is to increase digital payments, but cash won’t disappear.

Sheinbaum sought to calm concerns about the new Digital Economy Law, which gives the Finance Ministry the power to designate sectors where digital payments will be the only option. She said the aim is to increase digital payments, but cash won’t disappear. ⛽ Cash to be eliminated at gas stations to combat fuel theft: She said exclusive use of digital payments at gas stations will help end fuel theft and illegal fuel imports by allowing complete traceability. Cash payments at toll booths will be phased out “gradually,” Sheinbaum said.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Monday morning press conference, President Sheinbaum talked up the strength of Mexico’s economy, specifically pointing to formal employment numbers and the Bank of Mexico’s decision last week to reduce its benchmark interest rate.

As detailed in the latest MND Economy Index™ article, Mexico’s economy is performing well in a range of areas including growth, exports and manufacturing output.

In Sheinbaum’s words, Mexico “is doing well on all the economic indicators,” although the country’s high informality rate and relatively low productivity growth remain concerns.

At today’s mañanera, the president also sought to allay concerns regarding a new law that seeks to limit, and in some cases prohibit, people’s use of cash. In one particularly noteworthy remark, Sheinbaum said that the government wouldn’t prohibit cash payments at stores.

Sheinbaum touts record formal employment

Sheinbaum told reporters that the number of people in formal sector jobs reached a record high in October.

“I have another piece of good news. The Mexican Social Security Institute will release the official information at around midday, but I can say in advance that we reached a peak in formal jobs this past month, the month of October,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that 23,088,353 people (23.08 million people) were in formal sector jobs at the end of October.

“It’s the highest figure in history,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that 161,077 new formal sector jobs were added in October, while the number of people in such positions increased by 571,277 in the first 10 months of 2026. Compared to October 2025, the number of people in formal sector jobs rose by 299,180.

Later in the press conference, Sheinbaum noted that she had said that Mexico’s economy would improve in the second half of 2026 due to the commencement of various public infrastructure projects.

“And, indeed, the country is doing well on all the economic indicators,” she said.

Sheinbaum acknowledges Banxico rate reduction

Sheinbaum noted that the Bank of Mexico (Banxico) cut its key interest rate after a monetary policy meeting last Thursday.

The central bank reduced its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 6.25%.

Sheinbaum pointed out that Banxico’s rate cut came after the U.S. Federal Reserve raised its key interest rate in September. The Fed’s current target range is 3.75%-4%.

Sheinbaum said that Banxico’s rate cut was due to the “good performance” of Mexico’s economy. A majority of Banxico board members voted in favor of a 25-basis-point cut despite recent increases in inflation. The national statistics agency INEGI reported on Monday that Mexico’s annual headline rate was 3.75% in October, up from 3.45% in September.

Asked whether Mexico’s economy is doing well, Sheinbaum responded with a phrase she has used on previous occasions.

“We’re doing well and we’re going to do better,” she said.

Sheinbaum: ‘Cash isn’t going to be phased out’

Sheinbaum acknowledged that the aim of the Digital Economy Law for Digital and Electronic Payments — which was approved by the Senate last month — is to reduce the use of cash in Mexico.

However, she stressed that cash isn’t going away.

“In a community in Chiapas I visited on the weekend, a lady said to me, ‘Hey, don’t take away cash,'” Sheinbaum said.

“Cash isn’t going to be phased out,” she said.

However, efforts will be made to increase digital payments, Sheinbaum said.

The Digital Economy Law, which was also approved by the Chamber of Deputies last month, gives the federal Finance Ministry the authority to determine “the strategic sectors and relevant activities in which the acceptance of digital and electronic payment methods will be the only form of payment.”

Sheinbaum has said that cash payments at gas stations and highway toll booths will be eliminated starting this year. On Monday morning, she said that the exclusive use of digital and electronic payments at gas stations will aid the fight against fuel theft and fuel smuggling.

“It will help us … put an end to fuel theft and the illegal importation of fuel and allow complete traceability of fuel from production or importation to sale,” Sheinbaum said.

“… It’s only in the case of gas stations that we want to completely eliminate the use of cash,” she said, adding that cash payments at toll booths will “gradually” be phased out.

“In the end, people will agree,” Sheinbaum said.

“There is nothing to be worried about. On the contrary, it will be very beneficial,” she said.

World.title: Sheinbaum meets with teen inventor of recycled solar water heater at National Palace
World.content:
Xóchitl Guadalupe Cruz López, a teenage girl from Chiapas who invented a solar water heater from recycled materials, visited President Claudia Sheinbaum at the National Palace on Nov. 5 to promote her invention and discuss ways to bring it to more households.

The meeting, which was livestreamed on Sheinbaum’s official TikTok account, took place after content creator Alexis Omman shared a video asking Sheinbaum to take notice of Cruz’s work.

Dubbed by Mexican media as the “niña genio” (genius girl), Cruz, 16, told Sheinbaum she began developing her project when she was in second grade, at just eight years old.

The project, called “Baño Calientito” (Warm Bath), uses recycled materials including black-painted PET bottles, hoses and glass to harness solar energy and heat water for household use.

Her intention was to provide an alternative for families in her hometown of San Cristóbal de las Casas, Chiapas, who relied on firewood to heat water or otherwise had to take cold showers. Since then, she has made modifications to improve the device’s performance.

According to Cruz, it costs less than 500 pesos (US $26) to build and can heat up to 50 liters of water. Six units have been installed in homes within their community, including her own, where their use has helped reduce fuel consumption.

During her visit to the National Palace, Cruz also participated in Sheinbaum’s Science in One Minute informational video segments, where she explained more details about her invention.

Sheinbaum’s praise joins other national and international recognition. In 2018, Cruz won the 2018 ICN Recognition for Women presented by the Institute of Nuclear Sciences at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) — making her the first female minor to receive this honor.

Later, in 2020, TIME magazine included her in its selection of seven young inventors who are proposing solutions to global problems, highlighting Warm Bath.

To support Cruz’s invention, Sheinbaum pledged that her administration would review the project’s large-scale viability and expedite its registration with the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI).

Moreover, she promised to support the academic pursuits of the young girl, who wishes to study medicine and subsequently specialize in neurosurgery.

With reports from El Informador, Crónica, El Mexicano and Infobae

World.title: From hummingbirds to howler monkeys: Hiking adventures in Chiapas
World.content:
The colonial city of San Cristóbal de las Casas sits in a mountain valley in Chiapas at an altitude of 2,200 meters (7,200 feet), surrounded by cloud forests, limestone formations and rugged hills, with a remarkable variety of landscapes within easy reach of town.

Add to this the colorful markets, excellent cafes and restaurants, centuries-old churches and colonial buildings, and the living cultures of the Tzotzil and Tzeltal Maya communities in the surrounding highlands, and you have a city that is hard to resist.

And then there are the trails. Some lead through forests, some climb hills for spectacular views, and others take you into landscapes that seem a world away from the busy streets of San Cristóbal.

I asked local guide Emiliano López, who works for an outfit called Explora Travel, to tell me about some of his favorite hikes.

“First off,” López said, “I should mention that our organization originally specialized in multi-day excursions inside the Lacandon Jungle. But then along came COVID-19 and there was no way the public was going to spend all day getting there, packed inside a van with a bunch of strangers. So we began taking people of all ages, from 5 to 80, to the gorgeous mountains just outside San Cristóbal, places you can drive to in minutes.

“There we would talk to them about the history of the place and the biology, and we would look for birds. And it turned out that people loved these hikes … and they still do!”

Huitepec: Hummingbird mountain

One of López’s favorite sites is El Cerro de Huitepec, a cloud forest atop an extinct volcano. At 2,750 meters (9,022 feet), it is one of the highest points in Chiapas. The word Huitepec means “Hummingbird Mountain” in Nahuatl, and in the forest you may be lucky enough to spot a few of the eight species of hummingbirds usually buzzing around this place. If you go there on a night hike, you might even see a flying squirrel or the curious ring-tailed cacomistle.

“Besides the hummingbirds, there are 92 other species of birds on the mountain,” López told me. “If you want to see some of them, the ideal time to leave is 7 a.m. Twenty minutes later we will be there. The trail is a loop of around 10 kilometers, and there’s an altitude gain of about 550 meters. We typically get back to San Cristóbal at noon or at the most by 2 p.m.”

According to Lopez, Huitepec is an iconic landmark in San Cristóbal. “For the Mayas, it’s a sacred mountain, and up at the highest of its three peaks there’s a ceremonial center where rituals are still carried out,” he explained. “The general public no longer has access to it, but we can still hike to the other peaks.”

Moxviquil: Where paths meet

Another fascinating outdoor site — the closest of all to San Cristóbal — is the Moxviquil Ecological Reserve and Orchid Garden, a conservation project dedicated to protecting the region’s remarkable plant life.

Its greenhouses display an impressive collection of native orchids, including rare and endangered species, along with bromeliads and other tropical plants. When you’re out hiking, most orchids are high in the branches above your head, but here they’re all at eye level where you can appreciate their beauty and scent … yes, some orchids in Chiapas are wonderfully fragrant!

But Moxviquil — which means “Meeting of Paths” — offers more than gardens. A short hiking trail climbs into the surrounding oak and pine forest, where you can discover ferns, wildflowers and other native vegetation while enjoying views of the highland landscape. If you’re lucky, you may glimpse the extraordinary red-lipped arboreal alligator lizard, which is native to Chiapas.

This walk offers a welcome escape from the city and a chance to experience the natural world of Chiapas up close.

1 of 3

Experience the jungle: Río Ixcán Camp

This campsite is deep inside the Lacandon Jungle, Mexico’s largest rainforest.

“We have set up this site for people who really want a jungle experience,” López said. “There’s no electricity, no telephone, no internet, but yes, we have water: hot water, in fact.”

Reaching the jungle site from San Cristóbal involves a 5.5-hour drive to Las Nubes Ecotourism Center (via the town of Comitán), and 90 minutes boating or kayaking down the Lacantún River.

Macaws, spider monkeys and honey bears

“The camp is on the edge of the Montes Azules Biosphere Reserve, famous for having the greatest biodiversity in all Mexico,” López said. “Here you’ll find macaws, motmots, spider monkeys and — hidden in the canopy — the nocturnal kinkajou, also known as the honey bear. And you will see gigantic ceiba (silk cotton) trees that are incredibly tall: 40 meters (131 feet) high. For the Maya, these sacred trees represent the axis connecting the sky, the human world and the underworld.”

The likelihood of seeing wildlife in the Lacandon Jungle, López told me, depends on luck and timing, “and it is diminishing day by day, due to competition from high-impact activities.”

He went on to say, “So here we are trying to practice responsible tourism. We’re supporting solid conservation projects and the involvement of the local people.”

From Camp Ixcán there’s an 8.5-kilometer trail through the Lacandon Jungle to the top of Pico Ixcán, with an altitude gain of 650 meters.

“We do this over a period of two days,” said López, “accompanied by two local guides. We camp at the base of the mountain on day one. The next day we top the mountain and return to base. During the hike, we typically see deer, tapir and birds like toucans, macaws and the very rare tinamou, a member of one of the most ancient living lineages of birds.”

Suffice to say, by the time you leave Río Ixcán, you’ll have enough stories to entertain generations of grandchildren.

John Pint has lived near Guadalajara, Jalisco, for more than 30 years and is the author of “A Guide to West Mexico’s Guachimontones and Surrounding Area” and co-author of “Outdoors in Western Mexico.” More of his writing can be found on his website.

Paraguay is trying to calm a banking crisis by changing the people who run the central bank. On Monday 9 November its Senate approved Jorge Schreiner, an economist and former securities regulator, as president of the central bank, while President Pedro Alliana told his ministers to offer their posts.

Six days after the central bank seized Ueno Bank, Paraguay has a new central bank chief. The Senate approved Jorge Luis Schreiner on Monday by 31 votes out of 33 senators present, with one abstention and one vote against, according to the Senate record.

Why Paraguay Is Changing Its Central Bank

The crisis began on Tuesday 3 November, when the central bank took control of Ueno Bank, a digital lender, for lacking enough capital. Almost three million people lost access to their deposits.

Ueno has been under central bank control since 3 November, and Peña had governed since August 2023 (a term that ran to 2028). Three days later the Senate removed Peña in an impeachment vote, and he was detained.

He held shares in Ueno’s parent group until 2025. See our report on the removal and our update on his pretrial detention.

Who Is Jorge Schreiner?

Schreiner, an economist, once led the National Securities Commission, the market regulator, and sat on the central bank’s board, its top decision-making body. Alliana proposed him for the post on Sunday 8 November.

The Supervisor Who Saw It Coming

Rivarola is the more symbolic pick. Paraguayan press reports say he wrote a supervision report that warned about risks at Ueno before its collapse, and Alliana praised him as “committed and brave”.

We have not seen the report itself.

A Cabinet on Notice

On X, the social network, Alliana said he had told his chief of staff, Rolando de Barros, to ask ministers, secretaries and top officials in posts of trust to put their jobs at his disposal. He insisted that “the functioning of all institutions will continue with absolute normality”.

On Monday he also swore in Ariel Martínez as interior minister, Juan Carlos Baruja as public works minister and de Barros as head of the Civil Cabinet.

What It Means for US Readers

Paraguay is a major soy and beef exporter, so a central bank that depositors and lenders trust matters to traders in its bonds and its currency, the guaraní (Paraguay’s national currency). The winners from Monday’s vote are savers, who now have a regulator-turned-governor and a whistle-blowing supervisor at the bank’s helm; the losers are officials tied to the old Peña circle, who face a review of their posts.

Our profile of Alliana explains the new president. His priorities, set out on Monday, are to speed up the return of savings and to ease taxes for people hurt by the collapse.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a US prediction platform, prices Pedro Alliana at 12.5% to win Paraguay’s 2028 presidential election, behind two rivals at 19.5% and 16.2% (9 November, 4:00 p.m. ET). The market has seen about US$18,000 in trades, so it is thin.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Comes Next

Three things would show whether the reset is working: the first repayments to Ueno savers, the outcome of the ministers’ offers, and the next hearing in Peña’s case. None has a published date, and Peña has not been convicted of anything.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Paraguay's new central bank president?

Jorge Luis Schreiner, an economist and former head of the National Securities Commission. The Senate approved him on 9 November 2026, 31 votes to one.

Why did Paraguay change its central bank chief?

Ueno Bank, a digital lender, was seized on 3 November and left almost three million people without access to deposits. President Peña was removed by the Senate on 6 November.

What Andy López Beltrán, the former president’s son, answered TV Azteca’s owner in a video of over 30 minutes.

When Monday, 9 November 2026, in a video posted on social media.

The questions He put a list of questions to Salinas Pliego, including how TV Azteca was bought.

Background Salinas Pliego had put questions to him before, and López Beltrán says he is the target of a defamation campaign.

Not known No reply from Salinas Pliego or TV Azteca was available; the points are López Beltrán’s claims.

Who Is Involved

Andrés Manuel López Beltrán is a member of Morena, Mexico’s governing party, and the son of Andrés Manuel López Obrador, who was president until 2024. Ricardo Salinas Pliego owns TV Azteca, one of Mexico’s two largest national broadcasters alongside Televisa, a rival network, and the wider Grupo Salinas, his business group in retail, banking and media.

Salinas Pliego had posed questions to López Beltrán before this reply. López Beltrán answers them in the video.

López Beltrán asked who set the sale price and whether the company was worth at least ten times what was paid. He also asked whether it was immoral to accept money from Raúl Salinas de Gortari, a businessman and brother of Carlos Salinas de Gortari, who was president while the company was being sold.

Salinas Pliego has publicly acknowledged receiving about US$30 million from Raúl Salinas de Gortari toward the purchase, which he calls a loan that he has repaid. López Beltrán’s questions about the sale are his own claims, not findings by a court.

Why It Matters Beyond Mexico

TV Azteca has dollar bonds, debt securities held by investors, and its debts are being fought over in courts in Mexico and New York. The company is also in a court-supervised insolvency process in Mexico, a restructuring that is not an automatic bankruptcy.

The exchange also shows how openly López Beltrán and Salinas Pliego, the owner of TV Azteca, now trade accusations. Readers in Mexico will watch for his reply, which had not appeared at publication.

What Is Not Known

Only López Beltrán’s side of the exchange was available at publication. His points are his own claims, not established facts.

What It Means for You

For readers following Mexican politics or TV Azteca’s debt, this is a public accusation from one side, not new evidence. Watch for a reply from Salinas Pliego and for any court filing in the insolvency case.

He is a member of Morena, Mexico’s governing party, and the son of former president Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

What did López Beltrán accuse Ricardo Salinas Pliego of?

He accused him of running a defamation campaign against him and put a list of questions to him about TV Azteca’s origins and debts. These are his claims, not court findings.

Has Salinas Pliego replied?

No reply from Salinas Pliego or TV Azteca to the video was available at publication. This article will be rewritten if one is made public.

World.title: Chile’s Matte Family Now Relies on Banking
World.content:
Pulp and paper used to be the engine of Chile’s Matte family business, and now a bank is pulling the load. The family controls Empresas CMPC (CMPC, a Chilean pulp, paper and packaging group) and the bank-led financial group Bicecorp.

As of 9 November 2026, the latest results show CMPC in a quarterly loss while Bicecorp earns more than five times what CMPC earned in the first half. For US investors with Chilean exposure, that changes where the family’s profit and risk now sit.

Bicecorp’s first-half profit was more than five times that of CMPC. •Exit. CMPC chief executive Francisco Ruiz-Tagle will leave in April 2027; no successor is named. •Cash. Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index, with 62.9 points (November 2026 edition).

The Matte family controls a paper giant and a bank group, and this year the bank, not the mills, is carrying the profits.

CMPC Slides From Profit Into Loss

CMPC reported a third-quarter loss of US$7.2 million on Thursday 5 November 2026. A year earlier it had earned a profit of US$33.8 million.

Over the nine months to September, profit fell 84% to US$26.3 million, including a US$11 million deferred-tax charge tied to the packaging sale. Sales still rose about 1% to US$5.665 billion.

The slide began earlier in the year. First-half profit was about US$33 million, down 74% from about US$131 million.

Even so, 2024 had been a solid year, with profit of US$491 million, up 4.4% from US$470 million. The company is still planning a large new mill abroad, as our report on CMPC’s Brazil mill permit explains.

Bicecorp Becomes the Family’s Main Earner

Bicecorp, also known as Grupo BICE, earned CLP 183,076 million (about US$189 million) in the first half of 2026, up 59.8%. That is profit attributable to its controlling shareholders, converted at CLP 967 per US$1, the market rate of 9 November 2026.

Its lending arm, Banco BICE, alone earned about CLP 151 billion (about US$156 million), up 98%. The Matte family also took control of Grupo Security, a Chilean bank and insurance group, which was merged into Bicecorp, so part of the jump reflects that merger.

Set against CMPC’s first-half profit of about US$33 million, Bicecorp earned more than five times as much. These are group profits and are not adjusted for the family’s ownership share.

The family’s power company also had a weaker half. Colbún, a Matte-controlled electricity producer, said on Wednesday 29 July 2026 that first-half profit fell 53% to US$60.9 million from US$130.6 million.

Asset Sales and a New Chief Executive

CMPC agreed in September 2026 to sell its Chilean corrugated packaging business to Smurfit Westrock, a global packaging group, for US$420 million. We covered the deal in our report on the packaging sale.

On Wednesday 21 October 2026, CMPC’s subsidiary Forestal Mininco agreed to sell about 60,000 hectares in Chile’s Maule region for US$365.5 million. The buyer is Bosques San Pedro, linked to JPMorgan Natural Capital, an investment business.

The land is about 5% of CMPC’s forest area, and closing is expected within about three months. Our report on the forest land sale has the details.

On Friday 30 October 2026, CMPC told Chile’s financial regulator, the CMF (Comisión para el Mercado Financiero), that chief executive Francisco Ruiz-Tagle will leave. He has held the job since 2018 and stays until April 2027.

The board has opened a search for a successor and has named no one. Bernardo Larraín Matte became chairman in 2025.

In Plain English CMPC makes pulp, paper and packaging, while Bicecorp is a financial group whose main arm is Banco BICE. The Matte family controls both, along with the power company Colbún. Deferred tax is tax a company expects to pay later. Forestal Mininco is CMPC’s forestry subsidiary.

Why It Matters

The mechanism is simple: when a family’s industrial core earns less, the rest of the group must carry the weight. Bicecorp earned more than five times what CMPC did in the first half.

CMPC’s planned Natureza pulp mill in Brazil’s Rio Grande do Sul state would cost several billion dollars, and the state environmental agency Fepam has granted a preliminary licence. The board has not yet taken a final investment decision.

What To Watch Next

The first checkpoint is around January 2027, when the forest land sale is expected to close. That is about three months after the agreement of Wednesday 21 October 2026.

The second checkpoint is April 2027, when chief executive Ruiz-Tagle is due to leave. The board’s search for a successor is open, so a name could come at any time before then.

What Is Not Known

Whether CMPC will need new capital from its owners is not known. The same is true of the final decision on its Brazil mill.

The successor to Ruiz-Tagle is not known, and neither is the board’s final decision on the Natureza mill. See our Chile hub for more.

For now the bank runs faster than the mills. The next filings will show whether CMPC can restore the balance.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did CMPC lose in the third quarter?

CMPC lost US$7.2 million in the third quarter of 2026. A year earlier it had earned a profit of US$33.8 million.

Who earns more, CMPC or Bicecorp?

Bicecorp earned more than five times CMPC’s first-half profit, at US$189 million against about US$33 million. These are group profits and are not adjusted for ownership share.

Is CMPC’s chief executive leaving?

Yes, Francisco Ruiz-Tagle will leave and stays until April 2027. The board has opened a search and has not named a successor.

Will CMPC build its Brazil pulp mill?

The preliminary licence is granted, but the board has not taken a final investment decision. The planned cost is several billion dollars.

Sources: Empresas CMPC results and notices to Chile’s financial regulator, the CMF (cmfchile.cl). Colbún press release of Wednesday 29 July 2026 (colbun.cl) and Bicecorp financial statements at the CMF (cmfchile.cl).

World.title: Argentina Power Firm Edenor Widens Into Fuel
World.content:
Edenor, which keeps the lights on for much of Buenos Aires, is turning into far more than a power utility. Its latest filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), dated 6 to 9 November 2026, shows debt up 67% as it moves into gas, fuel and mining.

Key Facts •Who. Edenor, a Buenos Aires power distributor listed in New York as EDN, is buying beyond electricity. Edenor agreed with state-controlled oil firm YPF to buy 70% of gas distributor Metrogas, in a US$780 million package. •Why it matters. A US-listed utility is becoming an energy group, with more debt to fund it. •Next. The Metrogas purchase still needs regulatory approval; further deals are not yet named. •Power Index. Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index, with 60.2 points (November 2026 edition).

Edenor’s latest accounts show a profitable power company that is borrowing heavily to become a broader energy group across gas, fuel and metals.

Edenor Reaches Beyond The Grid

Edenor is the electricity distributor for Buenos Aires, and its shares trade in New York under the ticker EDN. Its statements for the nine months to 30 September 2026 came as a Form 6-K, the report foreign companies file with the SEC.

Note 1 of those statements says the company is “currently acquiring and continuously evaluating other energy assets”. The list includes power, electricity transmission and hydrocarbons, meaning oil, gas and fuels.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Argentina ranks 4th of 14 with 60.2 points. Strongest pillar: future resources (68); weakest: economic relationships (23). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The same note names “complementary assets in the sale, final refining, and/or distribution (downstream) of hydrocarbons, oil, and their derivatives”. In plain terms, downstream means the business after crude oil is pumped: refining it and selling fuel.

In October 2026 the company also created Edenor Inversiones SAU, a new holding vehicle, according to Note 1. Its stated purpose is acquiring and managing stakes in other companies.

The biggest step so far is the Metrogas deal, which we covered in our earlier story on the US$780 million purchase. On 10 August 2026 YPF, Argentina’s state-controlled oil company, accepted Edenor’s offer for a 70% stake in the gas distributor.

The Obelisk on Avenida 9 de Julio in central Buenos Aires at night, with the Argentine flag.

Profit Slips While Debt Climbs

Nine-month revenue reached ARS 3,051,244 million (about US$1.97 billion), against ARS 2,824,769 million (about US$1.83 billion) a year earlier. We convert Argentine pesos (ARS) at US$1 = ARS 1,545 (the market rate of 9 November 2026), so figures in these inflation-adjusted pesos are approximate.

Operating result, the profit from running the business, rose to ARS 308,181 million (about US$199 million) from ARS 132,137 million (about US$86 million). Net income fell 12.5% to ARS 209,467 million (about US$136 million) from ARS 239,309 million (about US$155 million).

The 2025 period included a one-off gain of ARS 265,941 million (about US$172 million) from an agreement with CAMMESA, the wholesale power market operator. That gain is absent in 2026.

Borrowings stood at ARS 2,444,948 million (about US$1.58 billion at book value) on 30 September 2026. That compares with ARS 1,464,197 million (about US$948 million at today’s rate) at 31 December 2025, a rise of about 67% in inflation-adjusted pesos.

Long-term debt rose from ARS 871,072 million (about US$564 million) to ARS 1,971,137 million (about US$1.28 billion). Short-term debt fell from ARS 593,125 million (about US$384 million) to ARS 473,811 million (about US$307 million).

From Gas Pipes To Fuel And Metals

The cash-flow statement shows an advance of ARS 118,816 million (about US$77 million) paid toward the Metrogas share purchase. Closing needs approval of the change of control from ENReGE, the national gas and electricity regulator.

In fuel, Swiss commodity trader Mercuria bought the Argentine business of the fuel group Raízen, including the Dock Sud refinery in Avellaneda, near Buenos Aires, and a Shell-licensed network of about 890 service stations. The price was about US$1.42 billion including assumed debt, and the deal closed on 1 September 2026, as our report on Raízen’s sale of its Argentine fuel arm describes.

The Boletín Oficial, Argentina’s official gazette, carried a notice on 28 October 2026 renaming the operating company, formerly the Argentine unit of Raízen, as Signar Energy S.A.U. It has been reported but is not confirmed in the company’s filing that Mercuria holds 60%, Edenor 20% and businessman José Luis Manzano, who invests through Integra Capital, an Argentine investment group, 20%.

Edenor owns 40% of the capital of Polimetales del Noroeste, a copper exploration company in Catamarca province, and 15% of Integra Recursos Naturales Minerales, a lithium company. The copper holding carries about 11.8% of the votes, so it is not control.

Our Argentina hub collects the latest stories on the country’s economy and companies. It is the best place to follow how these moves develop.

In Plain English Edenor distributes electricity to homes and businesses in Buenos Aires. Metrogas does the same job for gas. Constant pesos are pesos restated to remove the effect of inflation. CAMMESA is the wholesale power market operator.

Why It Matters

The mechanism is leverage, meaning growth funded by borrowing rather than by profit. Borrowings of about US$1.58 billion are about 67% higher in inflation-adjusted pesos than at the end of 2025.

For US investors holding EDN shares, the story is a utility turning into an energy group. Our report on Edenor’s power debts covers an earlier chapter of its finances.

What To Watch Next

Two checkpoints matter: the decision of ENReGE, the gas and electricity regulator, on the Metrogas change of control, and any new deal that Edenor names. We have no confirmed date for either.

What Is Not Known

Edenor has not named the targets, amounts or timing of its next deals. It is also unclear how it will fund them with debt up 67%.

Whether ENReGE will approve the Metrogas change of control is open. The reported ownership split of Signar Energy is not confirmed in the company’s filing.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Edenor?

Edenor is the electricity distributor for Buenos Aires, with shares listed in New York as EDN. It says it is acquiring and evaluating other energy assets.

How much is the Metrogas deal worth?

The price is US$780 million for a 70% stake in gas distributor Metrogas, plus 5% of Metroenergía, a related gas trading company, which YPF accepted on 10 August 2026. Closing needs approval of the change of control from ENReGE, the national gas and electricity regulator.

How did Edenor’s profit change?

Nine-month net income fell 12.5% to about US$136 million. The 2025 period included a one-off gain of about US$172 million that is absent in 2026.

How much debt does Edenor have?

Borrowings were about US$1.58 billion on 30 September 2026. That is about 67% higher, in inflation-adjusted pesos, than the ARS 1.46 trillion (about US$948 million at today’s rate) at the end of 2025.

Sources: Edenor Form 6-K with financial statements to 30 September 2026 (US Securities and Exchange Commission filing). Edenor investor page and Argentina’s Boletín Oficial (official gazette).

COLOMBIA · OIL POLICY

Rejected Colombia’s oil workers’ union (USO) rejected selling more state shares in Ecopetrol, Colombia’s oil company, on 9 November.

Proposal The conservative Centro Democrático party’s bloc suggested the sale to plug the fiscal gap without new taxes.

Missing The draft gives no price or amount, and no stake size is given.

Defence Former president Álvaro Uribe defended the sale on 9 November, with a governance pact to protect the company.

Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.1 points (November 2026 edition).

Colombia’s oil workers’ union USO rejected a proposal to sell more state-held Ecopetrol shares to cover the government’s budget gap, in a statement published on Monday 9 November 2026. The union, whose full name is Unión Sindical Obrera, represents Colombia’s oil workers.

For US readers, the dispute puts the ownership of a Latin American oil producer into a budget fight. Investors will watch whether the idea becomes a formal amendment, and Ecopetrol reports third-quarter results on Thursday 12 November.

What the Proposal Says

The Centro Democrático party, a conservative party whose leading figure is former president Álvaro Uribe, put the idea in its congressional bloc’s first discussion draft of an alternative to the government’s Economic Rescue Law, released on Saturday 7 November 2026. The law is the plan of President Abelardo de la Espriella’s government to close the budget gap and is moving through Congress.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.1 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The draft proposes considering the sale of an additional percentage of the State’s stake in Ecopetrol to plug the fiscal hole without more tax reforms. It gives no price or percentage.

It suggests prioritising the solidarity sector (cooperatives and similar mutual groups) and institutional investors as buyers. It also proposes an independent, technical management of Ecopetrol, with the president no longer appointing its leadership.

The same draft proposes eliminating or merging more than 200 state bodies to cut spending. It also opposes a higher value-added tax (VAT) on essentials such as coffee and health insurance.

File photo. An Ecopetrol office building in Bogotá, Colombia. Photo: Felipe Restrepo Acosta, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Uribe Defends the Idea

Álvaro Uribe, who was Colombia’s president from 2002 to 2010 and leads the Centro Democrático, defended the sale on Monday 9 November 2026. He said a good management can strengthen Ecopetrol under its current structure, but a bad one risks that others bankrupt it and destroy it.

Uribe linked the idea to the country’s debt and said part of the company should be sold together with a governability pact that protects it. He recalled that a share sale also took place during his own government.

On management, he said there must be a rule that guarantees an appointment free of the president’s whim, and that this should come with a pact that also guarantees the company’s excellence. The draft is a first version, not a final decision.

Live Company Intelligence Ecopetrol SA ADR — the full investor dossier Company overview and the latest Rio Times coverage.

How the Union Answered

The USO said the proposal ignores the world’s geopolitical reality, because oil, gas and other fossil fuels still supply more than 80% of the energy consumed in the world. It argued that the country’s fiscal deficit is not solved by selling off its most strategic and profitable asset.

The union warned that the consequences of that serious mistake would show in the short term for all Colombians. It added a farm image, saying you cannot take milk and eat meat from the same cow.

The USO called Ecopetrol the backbone of the national budget. It said the company gave the Nation more than 180 trillion pesos (about US$56 billion) in four years through taxes, dividends and royalties, converted at about 3,230 pesos per US$, and this is the union’s figure.

The Union’s Energy Supply Warning

The union also says Colombia’s energy supply is in crisis, and these are its claims, not figures we have verified. It says imports cover 41% of natural gas, 43% of gasolines, 20% of diesel and 12% of the light crude oil fed to the Barrancabermeja refinery, Colombia’s largest.

The USO adds that both refineries run at full capacity, and it blames weak incentives for exploration and delayed offshore gas. It also warns of El Niño, a weather pattern that can cut hydropower and rain.

What the Union Plans Next

The USO says it will call on workers to defend the company, according to its own announcement. It gave no date and named no action.

Readers who want the company background can follow Ecopetrol’s recovery plan. Our earlier report on the gas plan and reserves covers a separate strand of the same story.

What It Means for You

A sale of state shares is so far only a suggestion in a discussion draft, even with Uribe’s backing, so US investors who follow Ecopetrol have nothing to price yet. No price or buyer has been set.

Ecopetrol reports third-quarter results on Thursday 12 November, the next company news investors can price. The union’s call to mobilise workers has no date yet.

What Is Not Known

The state’s current stake and how much would be sold are not known. Nor is it known whether the government backs the idea, since we found no position.

It is also unclear whether the draft becomes a formal amendment. What happens at the union’s mobilisation, which has no date, is not known either.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the USO union reject?

The USO rejected a proposal to sell an additional percentage of the State’s stake in Ecopetrol to cover the fiscal gap. It said so in a statement published on Monday 9 November 2026.

Who made the proposal?

The bloc of the Centro Democrático party, a conservative party whose leading figure is former president Álvaro Uribe, made it in a first discussion draft released on 7 November 2026. The draft gives no price or percentage.

How much does the union say Ecopetrol gives the state?

The union says Ecopetrol gave the Nation more than 180 trillion pesos (about US$56 billion) in four years through taxes, dividends and royalties. That is the union’s figure.

When does Ecopetrol report results?

Ecopetrol reports third-quarter results on Thursday 12 November 2026, after postponing them from Tuesday 10 November. Whether it will comment on the proposal is not known.

What did Álvaro Uribe say about selling Ecopetrol?

Uribe said that, given the country’s debt, part of Ecopetrol should be sold with a governability pact that protects it. He warned that a bad management could let others bankrupt the company.

World.title: Chile Wants Copper Miner Bonuses Paid Back
World.content:
The Chuquicamata open-pit copper mine in northern Chile, operated by state-owned Codelco. File photo, 2018. (Photo: kallerna, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

CHILE · COPPER

Key Facts Demand Daniel Mas, Chile’s economy and mining minister, said on 9 November that all Codelco bonuses must be returned.

Cause State copper miner Codelco overstated its output by more than 42,000 tonnes across 2024 and 2025.

Cost Codelco’s chair put the preliminary accounting write-down from inflated inventories at US$120 million to US$140 million.

Inquiries Prosecutors have the case, two audit firms are investigating, and eight executives were dismissed.

Unknown Mas gave no bonus amounts, repayment mechanism or list of recipients.

Power Index Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 62.9 points (November 2026 edition).

Daniel Mas, Chile’s economy and mining minister, said on Monday 9 November 2026 that every bonus paid at the state copper miner Codelco must be returned. Codelco is the world’s largest copper producer, so the demand lands on a company at the centre of the global copper trade.

Mas spoke in a radio interview, days after Codelco told its shareholders that it had overstated its copper output. For US readers, the case shows how a government handles a governance failure at the biggest producer of a major industrial metal.

What the Minister Said About the Bonuses

Mas said all the bonuses have to be returned, and he repeated the word all for emphasis. Asked what happens if some workers or executives refuse, he answered that the government will see.

He gave no amounts, mechanism or list of recipients, and said the administration is talking with the groups that received bonuses about how they will repay. In May, Codelco said it would recover about US$14.3 million in bonuses from 6,322 people, tied to its 2025 output figures.

How the Overstatement Came to Light

Codelco told its shareholders on Thursday 5 November 2026 that it had overstated output by more than 42,000 tonnes. Its chair, Bernardo Fontaine, said about 24,000 tonnes fell in 2024 and a little over 18,000 tonnes in 2025, while Codelco puts the combined figure at 42,100 tonnes.

The chair put the preliminary write-down from inflated inventories at between US$120 million and US$140 million. Eight executives were dismissed.

A group of deputies from two conservative parties, Renovación Nacional and Evópoli, asked the Council of State Defence, the state’s legal defender, on Friday 6 November to consider legal action over the inflated figures. The case has been referred to public prosecutors, and two international audit firms, KPMG and EY, are investigating.

Why Mas Says the Controls Failed

Mas said the matter could have been swept under the rug and could have kept happening. Neither internal nor external controls were enough, he said, because nobody would have noticed without an anonymous complaint.

He added that bonuses alone do not explain the problem. In his words, the company was framed by significant production pressure, and a company culture has to change.

Who Else Could Leave Codelco

Mas confirmed that eight executives were dismissed, but he said the group involved was larger than the eight. If the investigation finds people above or below them on the organisation chart involved, he said, they also have to leave.

Asked whether he rules out the board of directors, he said he is not excluding anyone and that the case must be investigated to the last consequences, whoever is responsible. He added that the board does have a responsibility, though he did not assign individual blame.

In Plain English, Who Is Who

Codelco is Chile’s state-owned copper company, and Mas is the cabinet minister who oversees the economy and mining. The Council of State Defence is the legal body that defends the state’s interests in court.

Overstated output means Codelco reported more copper than it actually produced. A tonne is 1,000 kilograms, so 42,000 tonnes is about 42 million kilograms of copper.

What It Means for Copper Watchers

The repayment demand shows Santiago treating a production error at the world’s largest copper miner as a question of accountability. The write-down stays preliminary, at US$120 million to US$140 million, and the picture may change as the inquiries advance.

Readers can follow Mas on the governance review and Codelco’s confirmation of the overstatement for the earlier steps. Our reports on the eight executives dismissed and the deputies’ request for a lawsuit cover the rest of the sequence.

What Is Not Known

Mas did not say how large the bonuses to be repaid are, who exactly must repay them or what legal mechanism would force repayment. Those details will decide how far repayment reaches.

It is not clear whether more executives will leave, and the outcome of the prosecutors’ and audit firms’ work is still open. Those findings will decide how far the dismissals and repayments reach.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Chile’s minister say about Codelco bonuses?

Daniel Mas said on 9 November 2026 that all the bonuses have to be returned. He gave no amounts, mechanism or list of recipients.

How much copper did Codelco overstate?

Codelco told shareholders on 5 November 2026 that it overstated output by more than 42,000 tonnes in 2024 and 2025. Codelco’s chair put the preliminary accounting write-down from inflated inventories at US$120 million to US$140 million.

Who is investigating the overstatement?

The case has been referred to public prosecutors, and two audit firms, KPMG and EY, are investigating. A group of deputies also asked the Council of State Defence, the state’s legal defender, to consider legal action.

Does Mas blame the board?

Mas said he is not excluding anyone and that the board has a responsibility. He did not assign individual blame.

Sources: Chile’s Ministry of Economy and Ministry of Mining, public statements of the minister, 9 November 2026; Codelco shareholder meeting and press releases, May and 5 November 2026; Chamber of Deputies request to the Council of State Defence, 6 November 2026.
