World.title: Costa Rica’s Marchamo Amnesty Is Off for 2027, So Pay by Dec. 31
World.content:
If you’re behind on your marchamo and hoping lawmakers would wipe the debt this year, don’t wait. The amnesty proposed for 2027 failed, and a new version wouldn’t help anyone until 2028. Your 2027 marchamo is due by Dec. 31. Any older years you haven’t paid still carry their interest and fines.

The original plan was simple. Bill 25.630, filed on June 22 by Liberación Nacional deputy Mangell McLean, would have forgiven every unpaid marchamo from 2026 and earlier, including interest, fines and penalties. All you had to do was pay the 2027 marchamo before Jan. 1, 2027.

To take effect in time for this year’s payments, the bill needed a fast track. On Sept. 8, lawmakers voted 29 to 20 against that, with the ruling Pueblo Soberano caucus opposed. Without the fast track, the bill went into the regular queue and can’t move quickly enough to cover your 2027 payment.

McLean has now filed a new bill, number 25.886. It moves everything forward a year. You would have to pay the 2028 marchamo before Jan. 1, 2028, and anything unpaid from 2027 and earlier would be forgiven. The new version is narrower. It covers only cars and motorcycles with a fiscal value of 13,020,000 colones (about $28,700) or less, so newer and higher-value vehicles would not qualify.

It is a proposal, not a law. It still has to clear committee and two floor votes, and it would need support from a ruling party that has so far opposed it. The debt behind the push is large. According to Finance Ministry data cited by McLean, 10.6 million unpaid marchamos piled up between 2015 and 2026. That figure counts unpaid years, not vehicles, because a single car can owe several.

McLean argues that an amnesty would turn debt the state can’t collect into immediate revenue and help families get their vehicles back on the road legally. Opponents in the ruling party argue that forgiving the debt would reward people who didn’t pay. Costa Rica has done this before. In January 2022, lawmakers forgave old marchamos for nearly a million vehicles, but only 108,785 of the 992,598 eligible vehicles took advantage. A second amnesty passed in September 2023.

Here is what to do now. Look up your total by license plate on the INS marchamo website or by calling 800-MARCHAMO (800-6272-4266). The breakdown shows each item, including any older years you still owe. Expect the mandatory SOA insurance in your marchamo to cost a little more. For a private car, it rises 5.4% to 31,881 colones (about $70). The SOA covers medical care for people injured in a crash, up to 6 million colones per person.

This is also the first year of the new digital sticker, which is meant to last up to 10 years. It carries a separate charge of about 1,200 colones. Motorcycles keep the traditional sticker for now. Before you pay, check your total for an optional add-on insurance policy. If you don’t want it, you can uncheck it and the amount will adjust.

Regular collection of the 2027 marchamo runs through Dec. 31. More than 2 million marchamos were issued for collection this cycle.

World.title: Guanacaste Town Hall Took 29 Million Colones in Cash Its Bank Refused
World.content:
A Guanacaste municipality accepted 29.3 million colones (about $64,600) in cash for a property tax bill after its bank refused to deposit the money. The municipality held the cash until judicial agents seized it, according to internal audit documents. The Municipality of Nandayure, on the Nicoya Peninsula, received the payment on March 4. A man came to the counter to pay a corporation’s property taxes on two properties, covering 2023 through the first quarter of 2026.

He paid in bundles made up mostly of 10,000- and 20,000-colón bills. He also handed over copies of his identification, a sworn statement, the company’s legal registration, a trust agreement, a loan contract and a promissory note. Municipal staff tried to deposit the cash at Banco Nacional that same day and again on March 6 at the bank’s Jicaral branch. Each time the bank turned it away and asked for a withdrawal slip or other proof of where the money came from.

On the March 6 trip, the cash went by municipal vehicle with no police escort and no transit insurance, the documents show. The money stayed under municipal control until March 10, when agents of the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) seized it. The municipality’s Internal Audit has since sent its documentation to the OIJ, which is working to establish the origin of the funds.

According to the audit findings, municipal accountant Xinia María Cambronero and cashier Lilliam Artavia warned that the cash should not be accepted without proof of its origin. Artavia told auditors she asked Mayor Teddy Zúñiga Sánchez directly what to do. She said he told her to accept the money and issue a receipt, and assured her she would not face problems. She described the situation as unprecedented at the municipality.

Cambronero said she warned the mayor the bank would likely reject the cash. She said he told staff to accept it because municipal taxes must be honored. The documents also note that the municipality had no security cameras, no permanent security staff and no protocol for handling large cash payments.

Zúñiga denied giving a specific order to the finance department or the accountant. In a written response, he described the matter as an institutional consultation for the responsible department to resolve. In other official communications, the mayor said he had asked for more documents, including a withdrawal slip, and that the cash should have stayed in the municipal safe. He argued that the municipality acts as a tax collector, not a financial institution.

Zúñiga also said he does not know the people involved and was not part of the receiving process. He said the municipality is cooperating with the investigation and has annulled the 29.3-million-colón receipt, so the tax debt is pending again. The mayor said the judicial case is against an unidentified person and that, as far as he knows, no criminal investigation targets municipal officials. He said the taxpayer may have filed a constitutional appeal but that he had not confirmed it.

The Public Prosecutor’s Office said in April that the case was being investigated against an unidentified person and did not involve municipal employees at that stage. That same month, the Comptroller General’s Office closed a separate administrative complaint over the payment because a judicial authority was already handling the matter.

The cash payment is one of two matters at the Nandayure municipality now before judicial authorities. On Nov. 4, the OIJ and prosecutors raided the town hall in an unrelated case and detained two officials. One is an inspector surnamed Venegas. The other works in the Maritime-Terrestrial Zone Department, which handles beachfront concessions.

The two are suspected of concusión, a crime in which a public official uses the position to demand an improper payment. According to the court file, the inspector allegedly used WhatsApp to ask a resident for 4 million colones (about $8,800) to speed up a land concession process. He allegedly also offered privileged information about other lots in the area.

The resident wanted to buy a lot from a third party and did not know it was a concession inside the maritime zone. The events date to June 12, and the case began with the resident’s complaint. The court file points to possible involvement by other officials, who have not been named.

The municipality confirmed the detentions and the seizure of files related to the case. It said it is cooperating with judicial authorities, recently made changes in the Maritime-Terrestrial Zone Department, and that procedures for concession holders and applicants will continue as normal.

No connection between the two cases has been reported. No one has been charged in either matter. Under Costa Rica’s maritime zone law, the strip of land within 200 meters (656 feet) of the high-tide line is public. The first 50 meters (164 feet) cannot be privately held, and local governments grant concessions on the remaining 150 meters (492 feet). That makes municipal concession offices one of the most consequential public counters along the country’s coast.

World.title: Driving South This Week? Térraba Bridge Closures Run Through November 14
World.content:
If you’re driving the Interamericana Sur through Palmar Norte this week, check the clock before you leave. The bridge over the Térraba River, between Palmar Norte and Palmar Sur in Osa, has partial closures every day from Monday, November 9 through Saturday, November 14. Tonight it closes completely.

Both lanes close from 10 p.m. tonight until 5 a.m. Tuesday, according to the Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT). If you reach the bridge during those hours, you’ll have to wait until morning to cross. Today’s partial closures run from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. before the full overnight shutdown. From Tuesday through Friday, partial closures come in two blocks each day, from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. and again from 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. On Saturday, partial closures run from 7 a.m. to noon.

Outside those hours, both lanes stay open as usual, MOPT said. This bridge is the gateway to everything south of Palmar Norte. That includes Palmar Sur and its airport, Sierpe, where boats leave for Drake Bay, the turnoff to Puerto Jiménez, Golfito, and the Paso Canoas border crossing into Panama. The Costanera Sur coastal highway joins the Interamericana Sur at Palmar Norte, so drivers coming down from Dominical and Uvita who are heading farther south cross it too.

If you have a flight out of Palmar Sur or a boat to catch in Sierpe, leave extra time during the daytime closure hours. If you’re driving to the Panama border tonight, plan to cross the bridge before 10 p.m. or after 5 a.m. MOPT hasn’t announced an alternate route, so your best option is to time your trip around the schedule.

MOPT says the work will raise the bridge’s clearance and let heavy trucks cross safely. Repairs began in late January, and a second phase is reinforcing the structure from underneath. The ministry reported the project was 70 percent complete in late October, up from 40 percent in March.

The rehabilitation costs more than $10 million and is funded through the government’s emergency infrastructure reconstruction program, known as Proeri. The bridge is one of the most important structures on the southern Interamericana. It opened on February 26, 1961, and MOPT’s historical records describe close to 161 metric tons (about 177 US tons) of reinforced steel in its frame and supports.

This week’s closures won’t be the last. MOPT said closures like these will continue into early 2027 and that it will announce new dates as the work moves forward. Check the schedule before any trip through the southern zone in the coming months.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Dry Season Starts This Week in Guanacaste and the Central Valley
World.content:
If you live in or are visiting Guanacaste or the Central Valley, the rain is about to switch off. Costa Rica’s dry season settles over the North Pacific and the Central Valley this week, and the rest of the Pacific coast follows within three weeks. That is the outlook from the National Meteorological Institute (IMN), whose four-week forecast goes from Nov. 9 to Dec. 6 and describes the dry season taking hold across the Pacific slope and the Central Valley under a pattern of below-normal rainfall.

With that said, here is the timeline. The North Pacific, which is Guanacaste and the Central Valley, home to San José, Alajuela, Heredia and Cartago, enter the dry season this week. The Central Pacific, including Quepos and Manuel Antonio, follows the week after.

The South Pacific, from Dominical and Uvita down to the Osa Peninsula, joins the week of Nov. 23 to 29. By Nov. 30, the IMN expects very dry conditions across the North Pacific, the Central Pacific and the Central Valley. Keep in mind, dry does not mean zero rain, at least not yet. For this week, the forecast still allows weekly totals of 1 to 70 millimeters (up to 2.8 inches) in the North Pacific and 5 to 80 millimeters (0.2 to 3.1 inches) in the Central Valley, mostly as isolated afternoon showers in the mountains.

The Central Pacific could also see 10 to 80 millimeters (0.4 to 3.1 inches) this week, and the South Pacific 20 to 80 millimeters (0.8 to 3.1 inches). Today is the hand-off. The low-pressure system that soaked the Pacific over the weekend is drifting west, away from the coast. Expect some early rain on the Guanacaste coast this morning, isolated afternoon showers in the mountains and stronger trade winds from the afternoon on but tonight should be dry.

The weekend left its mark first. Nosara recorded 51 millimeters (2 inches) of rain on Sunday, and parts of the eastern Central Valley reached 60 to 65 millimeters (2.4 to 2.6 inches), according to the IMN. That followed a Saturday when five regions were on yellow alert. Those afternoon winds are the real signal. Trade winds are the signature of the dry season in the Central Valley and Guanacaste as they bring cool, clear mornings and blue skies, but they also dry out pastures and forest quickly.

If you are on the Caribbean coast or in the Northern Zone, nothing changes. Those regions have no defined dry season but even so, the IMN expects rainfall there to run about 30 percent below normal from November through January. This year’s switch comes in the middle of a very strong El Niño, which the IMN expects to hold at that intensity through January. The institute has warned that temperatures could run up to 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal and may break records, in line with a December El Niño peak forecast by the World Meteorological Organization.

IMN climatologist Daniel Poleo said in October that the transition could be drier than normal, after a month the institute projected would end 40 to 60 percent short of normal rainfall in much of the country. Back in September, forecasters were already saying El Niño could end the rainy season early.

A drier-than-usual start matters most for water availability. Guanacaste enters the dry months after a year in which water rationing reached dozens of Pacific communities and authorities issued the country’s first red alert at sea. One caveat before you put the umbrella away. The hurricane season runs until Nov. 30 in both the Atlantic and the Pacific, and storms during the transition can still bring short, intense downpours. On Sunday, the US National Hurricane Center gave the weekend’s low a 20 percent chance of becoming a tropical depression within 48 hours.

Having said all that, what does this mean for you? Pack a light layer for windy Central Valley mornings, carry more water than you think you need on Pacific beaches, and keep an eye on afternoon clouds in the mountains for the rest of November. For most of Costa Rica, the change means clearer skies, cooler highland nights and long stretches of sunshine through April. It also starts the five-month stretch when every liter of water on the Pacific side counts.

World.title: Diesel Up 17% as Costa Rica Prices Rise for a Second Straight Month
World.content:
Costa Rica’s cost of living is climbing again. Consumer prices rose 0.39% in October, and the year-on-year rate reached 0.55%, the second straight month above zero after 16 months of annual declines, according to figures from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC).

That October jump compares with 0.11% in September and 0.19% in October 2025. The interannual rate also climbed from 0.34% a month earlier. Transport drove most of the increase. INEC reported that the transport division rose 1.71% in a single month and accounted for 0.30 percentage points of the overall index, with diesel up 17.39%, gasoline up 3.10%, taxi fares up 5.73% and bus fares up 2.02%.

Nelson Castillo Mendoza, coordinator of the INEC price index unit, said the main upward pressure came from fuel and public transport fares. He noted that those prices are set by the Public Services Regulatory Authority (Aresep) and moved in line with international fuel prices during the month.

The rise follows September’s warnings of higher fuel prices as oil climbed back above $100 a barrel. Regulated goods and services rose 1.99% in October, according to INEC data, while unregulated items rose just 0.16%. Energy prices as a group rose 2.75%. Entertainment also cost more. The recreation, sport and culture division rose 0.96%, which INEC attributed mainly to higher ticket prices for events. Eggs rose 4.09%.

Some grocery staples moved the other way. Onions fell 10.73%, potatoes 3.50%, ground beef 2.44% and chicken breast 1.73%, and food and non-alcoholic beverages as a whole rose only 0.09%. Of the 293 goods and services in the basket, 45% rose, 33% fell and 22% were unchanged, with 10 of 13 spending divisions moving higher.

The longer view still shows Costa Rica with unusually low inflation. Cumulative inflation from January through October was -0.01%, essentially flat, compared with a 1.77% decline over the same period of 2025. Full-year 2025 inflation was -1.23%.

That keeps Costa Rica well below the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) target of 3%, with a tolerance band of one percentage point in either direction. The October reading sits 1.45 points below the bottom of that range, and inflation has now been below target for 42 consecutive months. The last time it was inside the band was April 2023.

The BCCR expects that gap to close. In its October Monetary Policy Report, the bank projected headline inflation near 2.7% in the second half of 2027, higher than its July forecast, and tied the revision to expected higher hydrocarbon prices. It kept its monetary policy rate at 3% and said it would adjust its stance if conditions or risks change.

The central bank listed extreme weather, including El Niño, geopolitical conflict and higher oil and grain prices among the risks that could push inflation up faster. A stronger colón and weaker global growth were among the factors that could hold it down. For households, the October figures arrive alongside other pressures. Earlier this month, INEC data showed unemployment climbing to 6.5%, while the exchange rate has left dollar earners with fewer colones than in January.

Rents have also been outpacing general inflation for months. The return of rising prices ends a long stretch of falling prices in Costa Rica. Whether the shift becomes a steady climb back toward target or a short fuel-driven spike will depend largely on oil markets and on the next round of regulated price adjustments, which anyone who fills a tank, rides a bus or takes a taxi in Costa Rica will feel first.

World.title: Alcaraz Wins First Paris Masters Title Ahead of ATP Finals
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz won his first Paris Masters title Sunday, beating American Ben Shelton 7-6 (5), 7-5 to claim his fifth trophy of the season and strengthen his late-season run ahead of the ATP Finals. The 23-year-old Spaniard needed one hour and 57 minutes to finish the match, adding a ninth Masters 1000 title to his career collection. The victory also reversed the outcome of their U.S. Open quarterfinal in September, when Shelton won in five sets.

Alcaraz heads toward the season-ending tournament in Turin with consecutive titles in Vienna and Paris. His latest win was the 29th tour-level title of his career, continuing a recovery from the right wrist injury that interrupted his season. Shelton made him work for it. The American created six break-point opportunities in the opening set but could not convert any of them. Alcaraz escaped a particularly difficult service game early on, saving four break points to keep Shelton from taking control.

The first set remained on serve through 12 games. In the tiebreaker, Alcaraz held his nerve and closed out the set after 65 minutes when Shelton sent a forehand long. The American broke through in the second set, but Alcaraz recovered the break and put the pressure back on his opponent. With Shelton serving at 5-6 to force another tiebreaker, the Spaniard earned two championship points.

He converted the second, finishing an exchange at the net with a backhand winner before celebrating with his team. “It is something I have been chasing for a long time,” Alcaraz said during his on-court interview. Paris had remained a gap in a Masters 1000 record that already included victories on clay and outdoor hard courts. He has now won seven of the nine tournaments in the category, with Canada and Shanghai the only titles missing.

The result also made him the third player to win a Masters 1000 title in five consecutive seasons since the series began in 1990, joining Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic. For Alcaraz, the significance extends beyond another trophy. After returning from injury, he has won titles in Tokyo, Vienna and Paris, building a strong finish to a season disrupted by months away from competition.

His next stop is the ATP Finals, scheduled for November 15-22 in Turin, Italy. Alcaraz arrives with 19 wins from 21 matches since his return, giving him a strong recent record to carry into the season’s final ATP Tour event.

World.title: Bird Watching Helps Older Adults Stay Sharp, and in Costa Rica It Costs Almost Nothing
World.content:
In nursing homes from Connecticut to Bavaria, caregivers have found an unlikely ally against loneliness, agitation and memory loss among older adults. It does not come in a pill bottle. It perches on a feeder outside the window.

Bird watching is now being used deliberately as therapy for older people, and the results have been strong enough to draw researchers’ attention. In Costa Rica, which has more than 940 recorded bird species and a yigüirro singing in nearly every backyard, the same benefits are within reach of any family at almost no cost.

One of the best-known programs, Bird Tales, began in Connecticut in 2011, when dementia care specialist and registered nurse Randy Griffin teamed up with Audubon educator Ken Elkins. Their sessions combine photographs, feathers and plush birds that play real bird calls with feeders installed outside care home windows.

The four Connecticut nursing homes that piloted the program reported needing less medication to calm agitated residents. When the Bird Conservancy of the Rockies later brought Bird Tales to care facilities in the Denver suburbs, an activities director at one of them said residents stayed calm for hours after a session, even when they could not remember it had happened.

The strongest evidence comes from Germany. Since 2017, the Bavarian bird protection society LBV has set up feeding stations in nursing homes across the state and given staff and residents the materials and guidance to look after them.

Researchers at the Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt followed 1,684 residents with varying degrees of impairment and published their findings in the Journal of Environmental Psychology in 2023. The team, led by psychologist Elisabeth Kals, reported that regular bird watching particularly supported residents’ cognitive abilities, mobility and social wellbeing.

The LBV has since adapted the program for older people living at home, with training for relatives and volunteers. In Britain, a weekly dementia-friendly birdwatching group for people living with dementia and their carers meets at the RSPB’s Sandwell Valley nature reserve on the edge of Birmingham.

Why does it work? Birds offer something new every day that still follows a predictable rhythm. They engage sight and sound, and they give people something to talk about. Perhaps most important, they hand people a small responsibility. Specialists in elder care have long warned that care settings can breed dependency and helplessness. Filling a feeder each morning is a modest task, but it is one that belongs to the resident.

The Tico Times could find no structured program of this kind in Costa Rica’s hogares de ancianos, care homes, or in its day centers for older adults. Occasional activities show the interest is there, such as a November 2024 birding walk for older adults led by tourism students at the Costa Rica Institute of Technology’s San Carlos campus.

But families caring for an older relative at home do not need to wait for an institution. Nearly everything required is already growing in the garden or sitting in the kitchen. Start with the right spot. Choose a window, porch or balcony where your relative already spends much of the day, ideally one facing a tree, hedge or patch of garden.

Then put out fruit. A ripe banana, papaya or plantain peel set on a board, a flat stone or a fence post will draw blue-gray tanagers (viudas), kiskadees (pecho amarillos) and yigüirros within days. Skip bread, rice, salty leftovers and honey, which are poor food for birds. Replace the fruit every day so it does not spoil or attract rats.

A shallow dish or old plate of water draws just as many visitors, and watching birds bathe is often the highlight of the day. Change the water daily, because standing water breeds the mosquitoes that spread dengue every rainy season. For hummingbirds, skip the store-bought feeder and plant flowers instead. Cuttings of rabo de gato, heliconia and other tubular flowers can usually be had free from a neighbor, and they root easily in Costa Rica’s climate. Flowers need no cleaning and give hummingbirds natural nectar.

Technology helps too. The free Merlin Bird ID app from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology identifies birds from a photo, and its Sound ID feature recognizes many common species from a song picked up by a phone’s microphone. Download the Costa Rica bird pack and the field guide works offline.

For someone with poor eyesight or who is confined to bed, recordings of familiar songs can stand in for the birds themselves, much as the singing plush birds do in Bird Tales. For many Costa Ricans, the song of the yigüirro, the national bird, whose singing traditionally announces the arrival of the rains, carries a lifetime of memories.

The routine matters more than the equipment. Let your relative put out the fruit each morning, even if that only means handing a banana to a caregiver. Keep a notebook or calendar where they record the date and the birds they saw. Naming, counting and remembering are exercise for the mind. Grandchildren can send photos of the birds in their own yards. That turns a phone call into a conversation about who came to visit today rather than a review of aches and pains.

A few cautions apply. Keep feeding spots away from places where cats can hide. Never trap or cage wild birds, which Costa Rica’s Wildlife Conservation Law prohibits and which defeats the purpose entirely. For anyone living with dementia, a safe chair and the same routine each day are part of the benefit. Repetition is not a problem to be solved.

None of this replaces medical care, and families should keep working with doctors on any treatment plan. But in a country whose population is aging quickly, and where many families care for parents and grandparents at home, a banana on a fence post may be one of the most affordable tools available.

The birds are already here. All they need is an audience.

World.title: How Living in Costa Rica Changed the Way I See the World
World.content:
When speaking of the 1980s and 90s, I like to refer to it as the previous century. “In the previous century, we didn’t have high speed internet,” I might say. It lends a sort of historical ring to it, like a time and place long ago and far away. In a sense, it was a long way back. Last night, I laid in my bed and watched the last innings of the final game of the baseball World Series on my cell phone. I couldn’t have done that in the previous century. Times change, things evolve. People too– we change and evolve with the passing of the years as well.

This is relevant to me because I recently reread articles I wrote back in the 1990s about my life in Costa Rica. I was younger then, less patient, more ready to criticize and lampoon Tiquicia. I wrote a column, for two different monthlies that catered to the expat communities here. I was, to put it bluntly, a smart ass.

I cringed while reading some of my more pointed articles. At the time I was writing from the point of view of an American who was frustrated with the things we took for granted up there. Down here, the telephone company was still a monopoly. Cell phones were rare and the still in demand landline phones always had a long waiting list.

Many heavily traveled roads and streets were dirt, which meant dust in the summer and mud and potholes in the rainy season. Cops were either apathetic and poorly trained or corrupt predators, using the badge to solicit bribes. I ridiculed shopkeepers who whipped out their calculators for the simplest addition. The local customs, the local diet, all was fair game. My audience, which consisted mainly of other impatient expats like myself, ate it up.

I was in the early years of my second marriage– to a Tica– and the only time I wrote without a condescending voice was the occasional article about home and family life. Otherwise, I felt like my marriage to a local somehow gave me a free pass to be a self-appointed expert on everything that Ticolandia lacked.

A Tico friend who was fluent in English read my stuff and wasn’t overly offended, mainly because he shared my acerbic sense of humor. He suggested that I turn the tables, and write something from the point of view of a Costa Rican fed up with Gringo arrogance. So I did. I wrote from the perspective of a fictional brother-in-law.

I have numerous brothers-in-law, but none speak English well enough to write like my imaginary cuñado. I laid it on heavy, with over the top mentions of fat, aging gringos, their tongues coated blue from sucking on tablets of viagra, chasing girls young enough to be their granddaughters.

My narrator bragged about all the naive, panting young gringas he happily bedded and then dropped when the next Latino hungry candidate caught his eye. It was a 600 word middle finger in the face of the expat community. I had hoped it would be taken in jest, but I was wrong. One retired military vet angrily asked where my make believe brother-in-law lived, because he was ready to punch him out. Another reader greeted me with a frown and said that visiting tourists would read it and never want to come back. The response was so overwhelmingly negative that I found myself avoiding people on the street until the next edition of the monthly came out.

Imagine writing something and then hoping people did not read it. That month was a turning point in the way I looked at the place I had chosen to live. Just because most Ticos would not be able to read my articles did not make them any less nasty. It was a bit like making faces at a blind person.

I began to write from a more objective and empathetic viewpoint, with an eye toward getting to know the culture and the history. I mined my wife and her family for material– not for laughs but for honest appraisals of their lives and how they differed from my own. I sometimes made myself the butt of the joke and discovered it was okay to laugh at my own occasional ineptitude when it came to adapting to my surroundings.

And so it has followed all these years later. I am no longer an outsider, looking in, ready to ridicule. I am as much Tico as Gringo, on the inside now, where the viewpoint is completely different

World.title: Belize moves to integrate National Human Rights Institution into Ombudsman operational framework
World.content:
Belize moves to integrate National Human Rights Institution into Ombudsman operational framework

By Zoila Palma: Today marks the official start of a targeted three-year, nationwide initiative to integrate the National Human Rights Institution (NHRI) directly into the Office of the Ombudsman’s operational framework.

The Government of Belize noted that this project modernizes the country’s internal processes for meeting international standards and focuses on legislative reviews, improved case-management systems, and community outreach.

Backed by a €400,000 contribution from the European Union and executed through the United Nations Development Programme in Belize, the initiative establishes a strong baseline for administrative transparency, oversight, and equal protection under the law for all citizens.

World.title: International News: Haiti’s 400 Mawozo gang calls for peace talks as security forces intensify crackdown
World.content:
International News: Haiti’s 400 Mawozo gang calls for peace talks as security forces intensify crackdown

By Zoila Palma: Haiti’s powerful 400 Mawozo gang says it has reached out to the country’s National Commission for Disarmament, Demobilization, and Reintegration to pursue dialogue and peace negotiations.

In a three-page statement sent to The Associated Press on Friday, the gang called for “peace, stability and national reconciliation,” arguing that dialogue should not be viewed as surrender but as an effort to save lives.

The gang also announced plans to participate in a peaceful demonstration later this month to help lay the groundwork for national dialogue.

It called for relevant military forces to suspend operations in certain areas while negotiations are pursued, saying a pause could help protect civilians and create an opportunity for a lasting political solution. However, the commission confirmed that an individual had contacted it on behalf of the armed group and stressed that any dialogue must follow the roadmap established by the Haitian government.

The outreach comes as Haitian police and foreign forces continue operations against armed groups.

In addition, 400 Mawozo said it was concerned about social media threats directed at the home of its leader, Wilson Joseph, widely known as Lanmò Sanjou.

The gang pointed to comments attributed to El Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, who responded to a post allegedly showing Joseph’s home by writing, “Where is that house? Give us the exact address, and we’ll destroy it.”

The gang described the property as a symbol of peace within its proposed de-escalation process and called for civilian homes and property to be protected.

The gang’s appeal comes weeks after El Salvador deployed more than 2,000 troops to Haiti following an attack on Salvadoran aviation technicians.

World.title: International News: Love affair or security risk? Nvidia CEO under investigation over alleged Chinese spy links
World.content:
International News: Love affair or security risk? Nvidia CEO under investigation over alleged Chinese spy links

By Zoila Palma: The board of directors of Nvidia has launched an investigation into allegations surrounding CEO Jensen Huang and his reported relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China.

The matter has drawn attention because of Nvidia’s significant role in the global artificial intelligence industry and the ongoing technological competition between the United States and China.

Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the company as president and CEO since then, admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at technology company Megaspeed.

In a message to Nvidia employees, he apologized for his actions, acknowledging the hurt caused to his wife and children. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” he stated. He also confirmed that he was cooperating fully with the board’s investigation.

According to Yahoo tech, the circumstances surrounding how Huang met Alice Huang remain unclear, although the two were photographed together at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan, in 2024.

Around that period, Megaspeed reportedly began expanding into artificial intelligence and had promoted its membership in Nvidia’s partnership programme, which provides access to the company’s latest technology. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was gathering information for the Chinese government, an allegation that China has rejected as an attempt to smear the country.

The controversy has also raised questions about possible national security implications.

Reports indicate that U.S. officials are examining whether the relationship could have exposed confidential information about Nvidia’s technology or its agreements with the U.S. government.

Nvidia executives reportedly contacted the U.S. Commerce Department last year seeking information about an investigation into Megaspeed, which was later transferred to the Department of Justice over concerns that Nvidia products may have been illegally routed to China. Nvidia’s board, however, stated that the company does not believe its trade secrets or national security interests were compromised.

Nvidia is one of the world’s leading manufacturers of specialized computer chips, with its technology powering much of the global artificial intelligence industry.

World.title: International News: Latin American Banana growers seek higher prices as extreme weather hits production
World.content:
International News: Latin American Banana growers seek higher prices as extreme weather hits production

By Zoila Palma: Banana growers across Latin America are calling for higher prices as extreme weather linked to El Niño continues to affect production and export volumes.

High winds in Colombia, heavy rainfall in Peru and Ecuador, and anticipated drought conditions in the Dominican Republic are raising concerns about the region’s banana supply.

Research by Fairtrade found that during the previous El Niño cycle, banana productivity declined by 13 percent in the Dominican Republic, 22 percent in Ecuador, and 6 percent in Peru.

The latest weather-related challenges are adding pressure on growers already facing rising production costs, Fresh Plaza reports.

In Colombia’s Caribbean region, banana exports dropped by 32 percent to US$122 million between July and September. September shipments alone fell by 42 percent year-on-year, with export earnings declining from US$70 million to US$40 million.

Fairtrade is calling for stronger United Kingdom legislation to address purchasing practices, including low or delayed payments and contracts that shift risks onto growers.

World.title: International News: Pope Leo condemns drug violence against children during visit to Uruguay
World.content:
International News: Pope Leo condemns drug violence against children during visit to Uruguay

By Zoila Palma: Pope Leo has condemned the growing violence affecting children in Uruguay, calling for greater protection of vulnerable communities during a visit to one of the country’s most crime-affected neighborhoods.

The pontiff made the remarks on Saturday while visiting Casavalle in Montevideo, on the second day of his 12-day South American tour.

During his visit, residents shared personal accounts of gun violence, abuse and insecurity in the community, where the murder rate is reportedly four times the national average.

Pope Leo expressed concern over children being exposed to violence and unable to attend school because of fears for their safety. “There are children in Uruguay who do not go to school for fear of never returning home,” he said.

The Pope also blessed 12 newly constructed low-income houses financed by the Catholic Church and met with residents who welcomed him with cheers and applause, AFP reports.

Later, during a candlelit prayer vigil at Montevideo’s Centenario Stadium, which drew approximately 60,000 people, he encouraged young people to embrace marriage and family life. “Young people, dare to take the step of marrying and starting a family yourselves. Don’t be afraid of ‘forever’!” he told the crowd.

During another engagement at the Catholic University of Uruguay, Pope Leo warned about the potential dehumanizing effects of artificial intelligence in education, urging schools and universities to put human dignity ahead of technology.

World.title: International News: Police raid home of former Paraguayan President in Ueno Bank collapse investigation
World.content:
International News: Police raid home of former Paraguayan President in Ueno Bank collapse investigation

By Zoila Palma: Paraguayan police have raided the home of former President Santiago Peña as part of an investigation into the collapse of Ueno Bank, one of the country’s largest digital banks.

The bank’s failure has triggered a major economic and political crisis, leaving nearly three million customers unable to access their savings and sparking widespread protests, Aljazeera reports.

Peña was removed from office on Friday after Paraguay’s Senate voted unanimously to dismiss him, rejecting his attempt to resign a day earlier.

Prosecutors have charged the former president with breach of trust and administration for personal gain, offences that could each carry prison sentences of up to 10 years. He has denied wrongdoing, while his lawyer, Ricardo Preda, said he would plead not guilty and cooperate with investigators.

Investigators allege that Peña used his political influence to direct large amounts of public funds into Ueno Bank despite concerns about its financial condition.

Peña reportedly held shares in the bank’s parent company until March 2025.

Prosecutors also allege that he obtained approximately $500,000 in loans from the bank in 2024 to construct his mansion. Former Central Bank chief Carlos Carvallo has also been charged in connection with the scandal and ordered into pretrial detention.

The bank’s collapse followed a Central Bank intervention after Ueno reportedly breached minimum solvency requirements.

Authorities found that the lender had made approximately $146 million in questionable loans to companies linked to its owner.

Newly sworn-in President Pedro Alliana said on Sunday that the government had refunded 1.2 million customers, with approximately $158 million paid out so far and additional reimbursements expected.

World.title: International News: France to increase minimum wage in December as cost-of-living protests continue
World.content:
International News: France to increase minimum wage in December as cost-of-living protests continue

By Zoila Palma: Today, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced that the government will bring forward a planned increase in the national minimum wage from January to December as it seeks to ease growing public frustration over the cost of living.

The decision comes following weeks of demonstrations that have escalated into widespread unrest in several major cities, Reuters report.

Labour Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou said the minimum wage will increase by 1.6%, bringing the monthly take-home pay to €1,502, an increase of €24. The adjustment was originally scheduled for January 1 and follows a previous €35 increase in June to account for rising inflation.

However, the increase falls short of demands from major labour unions.

The demonstrations initially began over concerns about underfunded schools in September but have expanded into broader protests over living costs, public services and political stagnation. Riots in major cities on October 17 caught security forces off guard, increasing pressure on the government to respond to public concerns.

World.title: Khris Rosado fined $5,000, avoids jail time in fatal traffic accident that killed police officer Arsenio Cus
World.content:
Khris Rosado fined $5,000, avoids jail time in fatal traffic accident that killed police officer Arsenio Cus

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Businessman and Thirsty Thursday nightclub owner Khris Rosado has been fined $5,000 and spared a prison sentence for causing the death of Police Constable Arsenio Cus in a fatal traffic accident on the Philip Goldson Highway in July 2025.

Rosado was sentenced on Monday, November 9, 2026, by High Court Justice Derick Sylvester, bringing an end to months of sentencing delays following his guilty plea to causing death by careless conduct on June 16.

Justice Sylvester ordered Rosado to pay the $5,000 fine within six months or face six months in prison.

The court heard that Rosado’s insurance company had already paid financial compensation to Cus’s family. While the amount was not disclosed, Justice Sylvester determined that no additional compensation order was necessary.

In arriving at his decision, the judge considered the aggravating and mitigating circumstances, along with a Social Inquiry Report confirming that the family had received compensation. Although the court considered a custodial sentence ranging from six to nine months, Justice Sylvester ultimately determined that a non-custodial sentence was appropriate.

The judge also considered whether Rosado should be disqualified from holding a driver’s licence but concluded that the circumstances did not warrant such an order.

The sentencing follows an emotional hearing on Friday, November 6, when Cus’s sister, Paulina Cus, delivered a victim impact statement describing the devastating effect her brother’s death has had on their family.

“Our lives were shattered. His death left a void that altered our future,” she told the court.

Paulina recalled her brother’s generosity, his support for relatives during the COVID-19 pandemic, and the trauma of identifying his body following the accident. She also spoke about the birthdays, holidays and family gatherings his loved ones would never again share with him.

Cus, 38, of Silver Creek Village, was killed on July 28, 2025, while riding his motorcycle from Ladyville toward Belize City. Police investigations revealed that a vehicle entered his lane and collided with him between Miles 6 and 7 on the Philip Goldson Highway.

The officer sustained severe injuries and subsequently died from multiple blunt force traumatic injuries.

Police later located Rosado at his Ladyville residence, where investigators discovered a damaged 2009 Honda Ridgeline pickup truck. Forensic testing subsequently linked blood recovered from the vehicle to the deceased officer.

Rosado was initially charged with several offenses, including manslaughter by negligence, but the case ultimately proceeded in the High Court on a charge of causing death by careless conduct, to which he pleaded guilty.

Cus was reportedly just one week away from being promoted from Police Constable to Corporal when his life was cut short. He also left behind a young daughter.

The sentencing comes more than 15 months after the fatal collision.

Breaking Belize News previously reported on the family’s emotional victim impact statement, which highlighted the lasting grief and trauma caused by the officer’s death.

World.title: Andre Ruddock found guilty of murder
World.content:
This combo photo shows deceased Taneka Gardener (left), who was allegedly killed by Andre Ruddock (right)

KINGSTON, Jamaica—Jurors brought in a majority guilty verdict for Andre Ruddock in his murder murder trial Monday, following deliberations in the Home Circuit Court.

Ruddock is on trial for murder in relation to the October 17, 2021 killing of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner. Six of the seven jurors found him guilty of the offence.

It is alleged that Ruddock cut Gardner’s throat at the Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in St. James on instructions from his then-pastor, Kevin Smith.

There were 13 witnesses in total in the case. Twelve appeared in the witness box, and one witness was agreed by both the defence team and prosecutors which meant that statements and documents from that particular witness were admitted into evidence without him having physically appear in court.

The defence team comprises Anthony Williams and Venice Brown.

On the prosecution’s side, LaToya Bernard and Carolyn Wright represented the Crown.

World.content:
Andre Ruddock is pictured at the Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries premises in St James after police stormed the compound.

Jurors in the case of Andre Ruddock have been sent back by Judge Leighton Pusey to deliberate again following a 5-2 verdict split among the seven-member panel.

Jurors had indicated to the police at 1:25 that they were ready to deliver a verdict.

When they returned to the courtroom, it was not revealed whether the majority had voted to convict Ruddock or not, only that the verdict was not unanimous.
