World.title: Warning!
World.content:
PASCOE...find something more productive, even going into farming yourself, it will be in your best interest (Photo: JIS News)

SENIOR Superintendent of Police (SSP) Oral Pascoe is urging agricultural thieves to abandon their criminal activities and find legitimate employment, warning that the police intend to intensify their crackdown on offenders amid an increase in large-scale livestock theft across Jamaica.



His warning comes as the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Agricultural Protection Branch (APB) is reporting 1,424 arrests for agriculture-related offences islandwide so far this year, a more than 600 per cent increase from the approximately 200 arrests during the corresponding period in 2025.

“My warning to the thieves is that they need to change the profession of stealing agriculture produce for a living, because we are sharpened and we are determined to ensure that the farmer benefits from what they do,” Pascoe declared on Sunday in an interview with the Jamaica Observer.

“We have zero tolerance, and we’re going to ensure that once we identify you as a larcenist, and you prey on farmers, we’re going to put you on our monitoring list, and we’re going to target you for snap raids and other operational activities to ensure that you do not carry out those offences,” he charged.

Pascoe, head of the APB, disclosed that the increase is consistent with a seasonal trend in which the demand for meat rises ahead of the Christmas period, with some farmers losing dozens of animals in a single incident.

“Traditionally in Jamaica, in the Yuletide, meaning from about September, accelerating in October to December, there’s a spike in the demand for meat and, of course, our local goat and beef is preferred,” he explained.

He said that, while thieves would usually target one or two animals at a time, the police are now encountering cases involving significantly larger numbers.

“We have about three or four instances where they stole about 40 goats, 30 goats, [animals] in large numbers. Normally, they steal one or two during the year, but…the value of what they steal in terms of livestock is a lot larger,” he noted.

Pascoe further disclosed that the police have received approximately 230 reports of praedial larceny up to the end of September, with that figure climbing to just over 250 following an increase in incidents during October.

He identified Manchester, Clarendon, St Elizabeth, St Mary, St Catherine, and St Thomas among the parishes most affected, noting that the highlighted areas account for approximately 70 to 80 per cent of reports islandwide.

The senior officer said that some of the thefts were not necessarily being committed by individuals acting alone, but by organised criminal groups.

He pointed to incidents in Colbeck, St Catherine, where several animals were reportedly being stolen nightly, forcing the police to intensify their presence.

“They were just going on, and four, five, six animals per night — cows, herds of cattle — were being stolen, until we had to set up foot patrol in the area…and do some serious investigation,” he told the Observer.

The SSP explained that some criminals slaughter animals in remote areas, a practice commonly referred to as bush slaughter, while others attempt to pass stolen livestock off as legitimately owned animals.

“Sometimes those animals end up in another farmer’s [herd], especially if they’re untagged…and they launder them, and they use their legitimate receipt book from RADA [Rural Agricultural Development Authority] and sell them on as if they are legitimate livestock, [as if] they are the owners,” he explained.

“So that is one of the practices that we’re stamping out. We have increased patrols in the vulnerable areas, and the sensitisation with the farmers have increased significantly,” the SSP added.

Pascoe also expressed concern that some farmers are failing to report incidents of theft, making it more difficult for the police to respond effectively.

“Some farmers are not reporting the situation to us, so we can’t respond. So, once we get a report, immediately, we have an operational response, an internal mechanism, to try to recover, arrest, detain, and arrest suspects, and try to control so that it doesn’t escalate,” he said.

The senior lawman encouraged farmers to report suspicious activities and the public, generally, to remain vigilant, while maintaining that the police will continue their operations to disrupt livestock theft networks.

“So just change your lifestyle, find something more productive, even going into farming yourself. It will be in your best interest,” Pascoe warned.

World.title: Do not give up on your child
World.content:
Stacy Ann Reid and her son Stevondre Calvin

FROM shortly after her son was born, Stacy Ann Reid knew something was different about him.

While his older sister was a fast learner, Reid watched as her little boy struggled to keep pace with the milestones she had expected him to reach.

What followed was a long, emotionally draining and expensive journey of medical tests, assessments and uncertainty, which eventually confirmed that her son, Stevondre Calvin, was autistic.

Now, seven-year-old Stevondre is making his way through primary school and Reid, 41, is using her experience to encourage other parents of children on the autism spectrum not to lose hope or give up on their children.

In fact, a decision to share a glimpse of her son’s life on social media has unexpectedly turned her into a source of information and encouragement for parents across Jamaica who are struggling to find answers and support for their own children.

It started with a TikTok video two months ago, as the new school year got under way. Reid posted a video of Stevondre with the message: ‘Autism is not a death sentence.’

She did not anticipate the response. The video took off, attracting more than 50,000 views, while another video subsequently garnered more than 40,000 views. As the numbers climbed, so too did the messages from parents seeking advice.

“They started to reach out to me, asking me how I got him into school, if I had any recommendations, how I got him assessed, where I got him assessed, what he eats, and how I got him to start talking, because he was non-verbal at first, but he’s talking now,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

For Reid, the overwhelming response was an indication of just how many parents were quietly navigating similar challenges, often without knowing where to turn.

Her concerns about Stevondre began when she noticed that he was developing differently from his older sister, now 14, who attends St Hugh’s High School. Reid began taking him to paediatricians, who recommended several tests to determine what might be affecting his development. They included hearing and eye tests, as well as an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) and a brain examination.

“The tests are very expensive,” the single mom shared, but she refused to give up on her son.

“I first had him assessed at The University of the West Indies, but I was not entirely satisfied with the process, so I took him to McCam [Child Development and Resource Centre],” Reid told the Observer.

Opened in 1986 in St Andrew, McCam Child Development Centre provides educational opportunities for children from as young as three months old. It also offers a specialised programme for young children with autism, designed to strengthen their communication, social and academic skills thus preparing them for successful integration into the mainstream primary education system.

Reid shared that when she took her son to the centre she found that there was a long waiting list. Luckily, she secured an appointment in December last year, after another person dropped out of the queue.

According to Reid, the lengthy waiting period created by the demand for assessments leaves parents uncertain about their children’s needs and the next steps to take.

But getting Stevondre diagnosed was only one part of the battle. Finding a school willing and equipped to accommodate him proved equally difficult.

Reid said he was initially enrolled in a school when he was three years old, but she eventually withdrew him when he was four years old “because the school did not adequately understand his condition or how to support him. And as I said, he wasn’t speaking at the time”.

Since then, she has had to shoulder much of his learning and development at home, with help from his sister.

Because she had to balance that with her job, Reid said she relied on television programmes and electronic devices, including a tablet and phone, to help him learn.

However, Stevondre’s separation from the traditional school experience was particularly painful for Reid during September.

“It hurt when I watched other children going out to school September morning and he had to go to the daycare. I didn’t like that feeling,” Reid told the Observer.

That has now changed. Stevondre has secured a place at St Martin de Porres Primary and Infant School in Gordon Town, St Andrew, where he is in grade one and has the assistance of a shadow — a trained support person who helps him navigate the school environment and participate in classroom activities.

Reid said she is pleased with his progress so far, noting that he is colouring, tracing, singing, and making strides in communication.

Asked what was her greatest moment of joy with her son, Reid, without hesitation, replied: “When he started talking.”

What was the first thing he said?

“Stacy,” she shared, adding that he was five years old at the time.

But the journey has also included frightening moments, particularly when Stevondre was unable to communicate his discomfort or pain.

One of the most difficult experiences, she said, was when she took him for the MRI examination.

“They told me I had to put him to sleep, like I had to give him the sleeping medicine. So I had to give him… I watched my baby just drop asleep and then I had to walk with him to put him in the machine. That was one of my scariest moments,” Reid said.

Another frightening incident occurred when he fell at school and sustained a serious cut to his forehead, requiring stitches.

“I had to hold him for them to stitch the cut. That scared him too, because he couldn’t talk but I could see him looking in my eyes to say, ‘Mommy’, you know, like him in pain, but he couldn’t express himself,” she shared.

It is that difficulty communicating, she said, that makes it especially important for parents and caregivers to understand the needs of autistic children and exercise patience with them.

She is urging parents who notice developmental differences to seek professional assessments rather than allowing fear, embarrassment or uncertainty to prevent them from getting help.

“The first thing I’ll tell them is to treat the child as a normal child. We know that they are autistic, but I think once you start treating them like they are disabled, that’s when they will not thrive,” Reid argued.

She said that through the videos that have brought her son’s story to thousands of people, she hopes other parents will find the encouragement to ensure that their children’s diagnosis does not become a barrier to their development.

Her message is simple: Do not give up on your child.

World.title: Who took the crocodile?
World.content:
Authorities are yet to locate a crocodile that was found in Clarendon last week (Photo: Adobe Stock)

A week after a crocodile was removed from a residential community in Clarendon by individuals suspected to be driven by ulterior motives, its whereabouts are still shrouded in mystery.

On Sunday the Hayes police confirmed that they had received a report of the matter and are investigating, but said they could not divulge any details.

Word of the animal’s removal was passed to the Jamaica Observer on Saturday by a woman living in Hayes Phase 2, where the incident with the crocodile unfolded on Sunday, November 1, 2026.

The woman, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said she became aware of the matter when a resident of the community started a TikTok LIVE stream about 5:00 am.

“I wasn’t really in the community at the time but I joined the live when I heard there was a croc there,” she said.

“The people there were trying to ensure that the crocodile did not go into anybody’s house and to keep it away from animals,” she said. “I called RoosterJA and reported it.”

Her reference was to Rooster’s World JA, the environmental consultancy and eco-tourism enterprise founded by well-known conservation biologist Damion Whyte.

He told the Observer that he received the call about 7:00 am and immediately contacted other conservation experts, some of whom work with the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA) and Caribbean Coastal Area Management.

“What they normally do when they get the call is they make arrangements for a team to make it down there. But in this case, the NEPA people couldn’t make it, so they would call other partners,” he said.

Whyte said he joined the live and started talking to the people in the community who, he found, were growing anxious. They told him that they, too, had called NEPA.

“I don’t know who they got, but I reached out to people and they said that they were getting people to go there to move the animal because they were unable to get there at the time,” he said.

Whyte said he continued talking with the residents on the TikTok LIVE stream, reminding them that crocodiles are protected by law and encouraging them not to harm the animal. However, he said that on more than one occasion other people joined the live “talking crazy stuff” like getting the crocodile’s tail.

“I heard people saying is $70,000 for the tail and things like that,” Whyte told the Observer, adding that he kept getting messages from other people about the crocodile.

“So during the live [stream] the people in the community said the people who they called for help came,” Whyte said. That was 8:30 am.

However, the individuals who arrived in the community instructed the residents to stop videoing.

Whyte said he found that strange because when he and other conservationists go into communities to remove crocodiles they don’t prevent residents from recording their actions.

He said at exactly 8:45 am he left the livestream to take a message. The word was that the team from Caribbean Coastal Area Management did not make it to the community. On hearing that, he rejoined the livestream and asked the residents who actually were the individuals who came to help. At that point, the residents started expressing doubt about the legitimacy of the men who turned up to move the crocodile.

“And from deh so, mi nuh know what happen to the crocodile,” Whyte said, expressing regret that he was unable to get to the community to rescue the animal.

“It’s gone. It’s not the people who are supposed to move it, move it. Nobody showed identification,” he said, adding that he has since received reports that the individuals who took the crocodile have chopped its tail off.

The Hayes police said they, too, have received that information, but are unable to confirm it.

“I feel bad about it, because I was advising people not knowing that it was not legitimate people who moved it, so I feel bad as a conservationist,” he said.

When the Observer contacted NEPA on Friday the agency said it has not received a report about the removal of the animal.

In the meantime, Whyte said he was proud of the residents as they tried to protect the crocodile.

“But one of the lessons learned from this is that when we get reports like this we have to react quickly, because I feel that if I could have left Kingston I could have moved the animal. And the second point is, I had told the people that whoever come there they should ask for identification, because it was strange that the men who came told the people don’t video,” Whyte said.

World.title: Dudsymil balances finance, music
World.content:
Dudsymil

On his third body of work, Rise Again, recording artiste Dudsymil decided to make it more personal.

The 13-track album, released on October 19 via Sky Factory Music, reflects his own journey.

“Rise Again was inspired by life itself. Over the past few years I’ve experienced moments that tested my career, my relationships, my trust, my faith, and ultimately how I viewed myself. There were moments of uncertainty, disappointment, and betrayal. But through those experiences I came to understand that rising again doesn’t necessarily mean returning to the person you were before the pain. Sometimes you’re meant to emerge differently — wiser, stronger, and more aligned with your purpose,” Dudsymil told the Jamaica Observer recently.

“The album reflects that transformation. It’s not about pretending the fall never happened. It’s about acknowledging it, learning from it and finding the courage to move forward. I often say, ‘The river was deep. The frequency changed. Now we Rise Again.’ That really captures my musical and personal journey,” he shared.

Dudsymil, whose real name is Andre’ Dehaney, works in finance. Originally from Havendale in St Andrew, he moved to Toronto, Canada, more than 20 years ago, where he has been making a name for himself with his musical blend of reggae, dancehall, Afrobeat, and R&B, while creating music that encourages reflection and celebrates life’s experiences.

Prior to migrating to Canada, Dudsymil attended Lannaman’s Preparatory, Campion College, and later The University of the West Indies, Mona.

Rise Again features collaborations such as Align with Blk Orchid, Straight Road with JUNO-award-winning reggae artiste Kirk Diamond, and potent tracks such as Like the Ocean, Unwavering, Be Careful, and Only You My Love.

Dudsymil serves as executive producer of Rise Again.

He worked with a group of music professionals from Africa, Canada and Jamaica.

“It was important for me to bring together different musical influences while maintaining the authenticity of my Jamaican roots. The album moves between reggae, Afrobeat, dancehall, R&B and soul, and that diversity reflects the creative contributions of the people involved. I was also very hands-on throughout the process because I had a clear vision of the emotions and messages I wanted the music to communicate,” said Dudsymil, who also gave props to his recording and sound engineer who played an integral role in the finished product.

“We recorded most of the album together, and he handled the mixing, mastering, and post-production. His patience was remarkable. He wasn’t afraid to challenge me vocally or ask me to redo a line until we captured exactly what we were looking for. For me, production isn’t simply about creating a polished sound. It’s about making sure the listener can feel the emotion behind the music.

Rise Again is the follow-up to Dudsymil’s 2025 six-track EP titled The Frequency. Prior to that he released the 14-track Zymil (Deep Rivers) album.

He shared how he has evolved musically between projects.

“I see my three major projects as different chapters of the same journey. Zymil (Deep Rivers) was deeply introspective. It explored some of the darker emotional spaces we navigate as human beings — pain, pressure and the complexities of life — while The Frequency represented a shift in energy. I was exploring more uplifting vibrations, relationships, spirituality, and the simple pleasures of being alive. With Rise Again I feel those experiences have come together with greater clarity and maturity. I’ve become more comfortable expressing vulnerability through my music, particularly through my vocal delivery. I’ve also become more intentional about the musical arrangements, instrumentation, and overall emotional experience of each recording.”

Beyond commercial success, Dudsymil wants his music to reach as many ears as possible while connecting with them on a deeper level.

“I want someone listening to this album to recognise a part of their own journey in the music. Of course, I also want people to enjoy the music, dance, fall in love, and simply feel good. More than music, it’s a feeling. It’s a journey. It’s meds music,” said Dudsymil.

Questioned on how he has been able to balance a career in finance while creating music, Dudsymil was quick to point out, “…I’ve come to appreciate how these two worlds complement each other. Finance is a demanding profession that requires discipline, structure, critical thinking, and accountability. Music, on the other hand, allows me to explore the emotional, creative, and spiritual side of who I am. There have been moments when the pressures of my professional life have inspired some of my most meaningful music. In fact, some of the experiences behind

Rise Again came directly from challenges I encountered while navigating my career. I don’t necessarily see finance and music as competing interests. In many ways, one helps me manage the other. Finance keeps me grounded. Music gives me somewhere to put the things that numbers cannot explain.”

He shared that music is not a hobby for him.

“I’ve been involved in music for more than two decades. My early recording experiences included working with Jamaican producer Stephen ‘Di Genius’ McGregor, and over the years I’ve continued developing my craft while navigating the responsibilities of my professional career. The journey hasn’t been a straight road. There have been periods when my professional responsibilities demanded more of my attention, but music has always remained an important part of my life,” he noted.

World.title: Grange blasts Opposition conduct, calls for respect in Parliament
World.content:
GRANGE...as the mother of the house, and someone who was a political prisoner who was exiled from this country, I know how far we fell and how far we have come in our politics (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

VETERAN legislator Olivia “Babsy” Grange on Sunday fired the latest salvo in the bitter verbal joust between the Government and Opposition over last week’s bust-up in the Parliament, saying she is disturbed by the “unacceptable” conduct of some Opposition members and urged a return to respectful behaviour in the House.

“How can a serious Opposition defend the derogatory remark, expletive, and insult hurled by Member of Parliament (MP) Mikael Phillips at MP Desmond McKenzie as Mr Phillips pushed members out of the way, advanced towards Mr McKenzie, and had to be restrained by other Members who wisely considered that a physical altercation would have even more severely damaged the standing of the House in the opinion of the public?” Grange said in a statement.

“Who could have ever imagined seeing the shocking physical assault on Speaker Juliet Holness and the blocking of the aisle as she exited the chamber by MP Angela Brown Burke who also screamed at the Speaker and called her a coward? I saw this transpire and remain disturbed. This conduct by member Brown Burke is unacceptable and should be appropriately addressed. As chairman of her political party, Dr Brown Burke ought to set a better example,” Grange added.

At the end of last Tuesday’s sitting of the House of Representatives a heated exchange erupted between Phillips and McKenzie as Holness was leaving the Chamber.

Phillips had directed strong criticism at the speaker, prompting McKenzie to intervene and urge him to remain respectful. The exchange soon escalated into a verbal confrontation, drawing the attention of several parliamentarians.

In the aftermath of the fracas, McKenzie alleged that he told Phillips that he would not like it if anyone spoke to his mother in the manner in which he had spoken to Holness. He also said that in response Phillips made a derogatory comment about him and his mother.

The following day Phillips apologised for his use of an expletive during the confrontation and accused McKenzie of making an offensive remark about his deceased mother.

Since then both sides have been trading barbs with the Government also highlighting video showing the incident involving Brown Burke and the speaker.

On Sunday, Grange said both Holness and McKenzie “showed tremendous restraint in the face of unwarranted attacks”.

She pointed out that she was sitting immediately beside McKenzie “and never did he utter anything inappropriate about Mr Phillips’s mother. I would not have sanctioned him saying anything like that.”

Added Grange: “These scenes have rightly offended the nation which is looking on in disbelief as the Opposition attempts to defend what is indefensible.”

She said that over the past few years she has been moved to comment on behaviour in the country’s politics, “particularly in our Parliament where the conduct of some Opposition members has been deplorable. I’ve been urging members in my Sectoral Debate presentation and on other occasions to cool it.”

Grange said it is accepted that Parliament is a place where “robust exchanges will take place from time to time, and that is good, provided that the exchanges are constructive and do not include personal or physical attacks”.

She reminded that in her 2024/25 Sectoral Debate she had said: “There will always be differences, but we mustn’t allow them to harden into anger and disrespect. As the mother of the house, and someone who was a political prisoner who was exiled from this country, I know how far we fell and how far we have come in our politics. That is why I am concerned about some of what I hear and see in our political discourse. Today I say, let us choose to act in a spirit of goodwill and respect for one another.”

World.title: EU offers cash for Black Sea attack response
World.content:
She also announced an additional €10 million in EU cash for Romania’s search-and-rescue operations. The sums are tiny compared to the €16.7 billion Romania is getting under the EU's SAFE arms loans program.

The hub, announced last year, is a joint control center to be run by Romania and Bulgaria and is expected to be fully operational by the end of the year.

It aims to monitor maritime activity in real time and safeguard vital infrastructure such as undersea power and communication cables. It would offer both countries a unified view of the sea and sky, helping them detect threats before they strike.

Monday's announcement follows weeks of mounting violence on the Black Sea. Since early October, at least nine ships have been struck in the exclusive economic zones of NATO and EU members Romania and Bulgaria; four were sunk, and 34 sailors are dead or missing.

Other ships have been hit off Russia's shores.

Both Romania and Bulgaria raised the issue at last month's meeting of EU leaders and are pressing for more security support. However, while Romania has blamed Russia, Bulgaria has stopped short. Von der Leyen is set to visit Varna, on Bulgaria’s coast, on Tuesday.

World.title: La France accuse l’Iran d’être à l’origine des cyberattaques visant les supermarchés
World.content:
PARIS — Le ministre français des Affaires étrangères, Jean-Noël Barrot, a déclaré que l'Iran était à l'origine de la récente série de cyberattaques "sans précédent" visant les réfrigérateurs de plusieurs grandes chaînes de supermarchés du pays le mois dernier.

"Grâce à l’excellent travail des services gouvernementaux, je suis en mesure de confirmer que la responsabilité de cette attaque incombe aux Gardiens de la Révolution iranienne", a déclaré le ministre aux journalistes lundi, lors d’une réunion du G7 à Paris. "Nous allons imposer des sanctions au niveau européen à l’encontre des responsables", a-t-ajouté.

Jean-Noël Barrot a déclaré que 700 points de distribution alimentaire en France avaient été touchés par cette cyberattaque. Peu après, le parquet français a annoncé l'ouverture d'une enquête.

Bien que Jean-Noël Barrot ne fasse référence qu’aux incidents signalés en France, des supermarchés dans toute l’Europe, et même des banques de sang françaises, ont été pris pour cible par des pirates informatiques ces derniers jours. Des experts en cybersécurité avaient déjà fait part de leurs inquiétudes quant au fait que ces attaques pourraient s’inscrire dans le cadre de la guerre hybride que mène actuellement la Russie contre l’Europe, bien que le Kremlin ait nié toute implication.

World.title: Who’s who for Europe at the Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi
World.content:
The European contingent includes national security advisers from France, the U.K., Germany and Italy, in addition to senior officials from NATO as well as the European Commission and the European Council. The inclusion of EU figures as well as an Italian representative follows a push by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who warned of fragmentation in a letter to European Council President António Costa last week.

Despite their presence in Abu Dhabi, though, the European team is not expected to be inside the room during the main negotiations, according to two senior officials aware of the format. A German official told POLITICO that the format of talks would be “determined as the discussions progress.” The Kremlin has voiced opposition to Europeans directly participating in the talks, according to the same senior officials.

Here’s a quick look at the key players from Europe in Abu Dhabi.

Günter Sautter (Germany)

Sautter is German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s foreign and security policy adviser and a senior career diplomat who has become a major figure in Europe’s efforts to end Russia’s war — and secure a European seat at the negotiating table.

Besides representing Germany in the E3 format, Sautter is also coordinating the German-led “Berlin Format” — a German-led coalition to bring together Ukraine, the E3 and other European nations such as Italy, Poland or the Scandinavian countries as well as NATO, EU and others including Canada — that seeks to steer Ukraine’s peace talks and coordinate support for Kyiv.

At a press conference with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week, Merz remarked that Sautter “is now devoting a significant portion of his workforce to diplomatic efforts to end this war.”

World.title: France blames Iran for cyberattacks targeting supermarket fridges
World.content:
Though Barrot was only referring to the incidents reported in France, grocery stores across Europe and even French blood banks have been targeted by hackers in recent days. Cyber experts had previously raised concerns that the attacks may have been part of Russia’s ongoing hybrid warfare against Europe, though the Kremlin has denied any involvement.

In a statement, a spokesperson for France’s foreign affairs ministry said the French investigation found that Iran’s cyber unit, Shahid Kaveh, carried out the destructive attacks. Shahid Kaveh, which is linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, carries out offensive cyber operations.

The French investigation will focus on the unit’s head, the Paris prosecutor’s office said in a statement, adding that about 20 fires had been started because of the cyberattack.

“The attackers took remote control of the equipment via web interfaces to trigger abnormal defrost cycles of unlimited duration, while disabling the security alerts on the sensors that were supposed to activate once a certain temperature was exceeded,” it added.

“We just heard now that [the cyberattacks] were attributed to Iran,” European Council President Kaja Kallas said after Barrot’s statement, adding that the matter would be discussed at next week’s European foreign affairs council. If the attribution is confirmed, she said, “[Europe’s] response should be strong.”

The European Commission is also looking into these cyberattacks, which EU Agriculture and Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen described as a “deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain.”

Iran’s foreign affairs ministry and its embassy in Paris did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

This story has been updated.

World.title: Macrons sue far-right podcaster Candace Owens personally in Tennessee
World.content:
The latest move by the French president and his wife comes after a court in Delaware ruled it only had jurisdiction over Owens’ corporations registered in the state.

PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife, Brigitte, filed a defamation lawsuit against Candace Owens in the far-right podcaster’s home state of Tennessee.

The fresh legal move is the latest development in a sprawling legal case brought by the Macrons after the podcaster falsely claimed in multiple episodes of her podcast “Candace” that Brigitte is a transgender man.

The French presidential couple first filed a defamation lawsuit against Owens and her two media companies in July 2025 in Delaware, where her businesses are registered. But a Delaware court last month narrowed that complaint, ruling that it only had jurisdiction over Owens’ corporations in the state.

World.title: COP31 : comment Emmanuel Macron a perdu le goût du climat
World.content:
“Je ne comprends pas, franchement, pourquoi il n’y va pas, pourquoi il n’aide pas l’Union européenne à aller de l’avant”, regrette Laurence Tubiana, ancienne diplomate et architecte de l’Accord de Paris sur le climat. “C’est dommage”, poursuit-elle, relevant les “hésitations” du chef de l’Etat sur les sujets climatiques.

Officiellement absent pour des raisons d’agenda, comme l’a révélé POLITICO, Emmanuel Macron aurait pourtant aimé en être, lui qui “a pris du plaisir” à participer aux grandes messes du climat, assure ainsi la ministre de la Transition écologique Monique Barbut. “Je pense qu’il regrette [de ne pas pouvoir venir], assure-t-elle. C’est un endroit où il est plutôt très bien accueilli”.

Parmi les soutiens du président, on revendique le choix de manquer certains sommets.

“La COP n’est pas un rituel incontournable où il faut se montrer. C’est un lieu de négociation pour faire bouger les lignes”, défend quant à elle l’ex-ministre de la Transition écologique Agnès Pannier-Runacher, qui estime qu’il n’y a “pas d’espace de jeu” cette année.

Reste que parmi ceux qui le connaissent, tous ne sont pas tombés de leur chaise en apprenant la nouvelle, le président n’étant pas, de leur point de vue, un mordu de l’écologie.

Emmanuel Macron n’est pas “quelqu’un de nativement écolo, ce n’était pas dans son logiciel de base”, reconnaît ainsi sans fard un ex-conseiller de l’exécutif. “Sur la scène internationale, il y voyait une façon de se positionner, d’être un président cool, qui parle aux jeunes”, assure le même.

World.title: SPONSORED EPISODE: The science and evolution of cancer care
World.content:
Precision oncology and digitally enabled cancer care are transforming what it means to live with cancer. The number of people in Europe alive more than five years after a cancer diagnosis grew 41 percent between 2010 and 2020, to nearly 15 million. As science progresses, a growing number of advanced cancers could be managed as chronic diseases, like diabetes or hypertension.

But many patients are only able to access innovative treatments as part of a clinical trial, and Europe’s share of global commercial trials has almost halved in a decade. Access to screening and advanced diagnostics also varies widely across the bloc.

In the first of two special podcast episodes produced by POLITICO Studio, experts in oncology, clinical research and drug development explore how precision oncology works, how artificial intelligence can draw on vast pools of health data to develop new treatments and where science is heading next.

Guest speakers include: Fatima Cardoso, head of clinical trials, scientific affairs and international development in breast oncology at the Centre Antoine Lacassagne in Nice, France, and president of the Advanced Breast Cancer Global Alliance; Giuseppe Curigliano, professor of medical oncology at the University of Milan and head of the Division of Early Drug Development at the European Institute of Oncology; and Johanna Bendell, chief development officer, oncology for Pfizer.

POLITICAL 

The sponsor is Pfizer Inc., 66 Hudson Blvd E, New York, NY 10001, USA.

The political advertising is related to calls for EU policymakers to improve access to precision cancer care.

World.title: Ukraine slams French far-left presidential hopeful Mélenchon
World.content:
“The people of Donbas … have the right to decide whether they want to be Ukrainian or Russian,” he argued, referring to a region in eastern Ukraine that is the central territorial dispute of the war with Russia.

It’s not the first time Ukrainian top officials have spatted with France’s presidential front-runners in recent weeks: Last month, the war-torn country’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also directly replied to far-right candidate Marine Le Pen’s pledge to cut financial aid to Kyiv.

France’s staunch support for Ukraine could be dramatically overturned if Mélenchon or Le Pen wins next year in a high-stakes presidential election to replace Emmanuel Macron. According to polls, the two politicians could face off in the second round.

Like Le Pen, Mélenchon is often accused by political opponents of being soft on Moscow — accusations that are intensifying as the presidential campaign heats up.

After Saturday’s political rally, centrist Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot described the far-left leader as a “Kremlin spokesperson.” Mélenchon dismissed the accusations.

Muriel Domenach, a former French NATO ambassador now working on the campaign for center-left candidate Raphaël Glucksmann, also slammed France Unbowed’s recently released presidential platform that calls for leaving NATO and mentions Ukraine only briefly. France Unbowed lawmaker Bastien Lachaud replied, saying his party has always backed aid to Kyiv until a peace agreement is reached.

“We have made it clear from the outset of the conflict that, as long as these negotiations remain unresolved, aid to Ukraine must continue without reservation,” he said.

World.title: Polish president and PM join Krakow Silent March for victims of market shooting
World.content:
The march began promptly at 20:00 to the sound of the St Mary's bugle call, at the junction of the Main Market Square and Sławkowska Street, the place where the first shots were fired during Saturday's attack. The participants then walked towards St Mary's Basilica. The march ended near the Town Hall Tower.

 

Those taking part, at the invitation of the mayor of Kraków, Łukasz Gibała, included the President of Poland, Karol Nawrocki, Prime Minister Donald Tusk, the Archbishop of Kraków, Cardinal Grzegorz Ryś, the governor of the Małopolska region, Krzysztof Klęczar and the marshal of the region, Łukasz Smółka.

Even before the ceremony began, the mayor of Kraków had encouraged residents to commemorate the victims together.

"In this difficult time, let us show solidarity and show that Kraków will always be a proud city, but also hospitable and open" wrote Łukasz Gibała on social media. Prime minister Donald Tusk also encouraged people to take part in the event.

"This evening in Kraków thousands of Poles have gathered to pay tribute to the victims of the attack of 7 November. May they rest in peace" wrote Prime Minister Donald Tusk on X.

As the mayor had previously announced, no speeches were planned during the march. No addresses were scheduled after it either.

An important element of the ceremony was the commemoration of the places where the tragic events took place. Candles were lit at each of the three locations where victims of the attack were killed.

At the end of the event, the bugler played "The Sound of Silence" on the trumpet, and the Archbishop of Kraków, Cardinal Grzegorz Ryś, said a short prayer for the dead.

The March of Silence was held on the last day of national mourning, declared by President Karol Nawrocki for 8 and 9 November. The authorities of Kraków have, however, decided on a longer period of remembrance. In the city the period of mourning will last until the end of Wednesday, 11 November.

During this time the flags on public buildings will remain at half-mast or draped in black crepe. Signs of mourning have also appeared on public transport - flags with black ribbons have been placed on Kraków's buses and trams.

Residents who want to express their sympathy to the families of the victims can also write in a book of condolence.

The traditional book has been made available in the lobby of Kraków City Hall on Wszystkich Świętych Square. It can be signed until Wednesday 11 November, between 9:00 and 19:00.

The city has also opened an online condolence book which will remain available until 11 November at 19:00.

Injured police officers decorated by the president

Even before the March of Silence began, information emerged that two officers who had been seriously wounded while intervening against the attacker were to be honoured.

The head of the National Security Bureau, Bartosz Grodecki, announced on social media that President Karol Nawrocki had decided to award Senior Constable Jakub Kulik and Senior Constable Artur Morański the Officer's Cross of the Order of Polonia Restituta.

The decorations were awarded for special services in actions for public safety and order, as well as for courage and dedication in the performance of their duties.

"The heroic conduct of the officers, who at the risk of their own lives stopped the attacker, inspires admiration and deserves the highest recognition. I thank both officers for their decisive intervention and their readiness to defend others. I wish them a swift recovery" said Bartosz Grodecki, conveying the president's position.

Both injured police officers received the decorations from the President of Poland, Karol Nawrocki in person.

First words of one of the injured police officers after waking from coma

27-year-old Senior Constable Artur Morański and 24-year-old Senior Constable Jakub Kulik were the first to intervene directly against the armed attacker who opened fire in the centre of Kraków on Saturday.

During the operation they neutralised the attacker, but were themselves shot by him and taken to hospital in a critical condition. Morański and Kulik were then placed in a medically induced coma.

On Sunday doctors began the process of waking both officers. A day later further information appeared on the condition of the 27-year-old.

The mayor of Kraków, Łukasz Gibała, reported that the officer had been extubated and his condition had started to improve.

As the mayor of Muszyna, Jan Golba, said on social media, Morański first words after waking up were: Is Kuba [Jakub] alive? ("A Kuba żyje?").

Bloodbath in tourist hotspot

On Saturday a 24-year-old man, Michał Oksiński, drove a car onto the main market square in Kraków and opened fire with an automatic weapon, apparently at random.

Six people were killed and 16 were injured, including two police officers and the attacker, who died in hospital early on Monday morning.

Those killed in Krakow's mains square and tourism hotspot were four Polish citizens, a British man and an Austrian woman. Among the 15 wounded are people from Britain, Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.

In Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, in the attacker's family flat, police also found the bodies of his parents and sister, believed to have been killed hours before the attack in the centre of Krakow.

World.title: A huge explosion at a steel factory in Western Turkey has left at least 17 people dead and 13 injured
World.content:
The blast happened at midday local time, when a crane lifting a replacement boiler collapsed and fell into a furnace used during the liquid steel casting process.

 

The fire at the HABAS plant in Aliaga, Izmir province, claimed at least 17 people's lives and also injured 13 people, two of them critically, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said in a televised address following a scheduled Cabinet meeting.

"The circumstances surrounding this tragic incident, which has deeply saddened our nation, including how and why it happened, whether there was any negligence and who bears responsibility, will be established," Erdogan said on television.

According to eye witnesses, the explosion "felt like an earthquake".

Izmir mayor Cemil Tugay said on X that rescue teams were "continuing their work to remove the collapsed platform" and that those affected were factory workers.

EU president Ursula van der Leyen has expressed her condolences

HABAS is a privately owned group and one of Turkey's top steel producers. The plant was established in 1987 and can produce 4.5 million tons of steel annually, according to the company’s website.

Workers' groups said there was a long record of safety issues at HABAS.

World.title: China's robots, AI agents and Nvidia probe: Web Summit 2026 Opens in Lisbon
World.content:
Dancing robots from the company Aigibot opened the Web Summit 2026 technology conference in Lisbon on Monday, putting China's artificial intelligence technology firmly on stage.

 

"The superstars of the future are not coming from California; they're coming from China," Web Summit CEO and founder Paddy Cosgrave told an audience of up to 12,000 people.

"Chinese companies are building more of our shared future than anyone else," he added, referring to the open source technology.

The United States and China are in an artificial intelligence race to build out the technology, as Washington has tried to restrict exports of the most high-powered chips to China.

The US and China are locked in an escalating tech race, with artificial intelligence at the forefront, and Washington has sought to restrict exports of the most high-powered chips to the country.

Meanwhile, US chip giant Nvidia US tech giant Nvidia is opening a probe into its CEO, Jensen Huang, after reports that Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort” in his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Asked about the news of Huang, Cloudflare's cofounder and CEO Matthew Prince said on stage, "it's very salacious" but that in the long term it remains to be seen if he would be "a hero or villain," referring to the impact on the industry, adding that "Jensen did a lot to cement the AI ecosystem."

AI agents were also featured on the Web Summit stage. The technology is designed to take autonomous actions to assist humans and does not require a human to tell it what to do.

Manus AI, originally founded in China, showed off an impressive 30-second AI-generated video with its new 2.0 video technology that required just a 13-word prompt.

Tao Zhang, co-founder and CPO of Manus, said AI was changing how he hires his own team of engineers.

"We found the people we are looking for; it's not just a good attitude. We don't need more people; we need people who can work with AI," he said.

Web Summit expects to receive close to 70,000 attendees, including 900 speakers, and more than two thousand startups.

Cosgrave said it was the most international edition of Web Summit Lisbon with every European country present.

World.title: Argentina: Pope Leo XIV urges Milei's government to protect the most vulnerable
World.content:
On Monday Pope Leo XIV called on Argentina to protect the most vulnerable people and placed attention on those with disabilities at the heart of his message during his first full day in the country. The Pontiff visited Cottolengo Don Orione, a care centre located in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires, whose work has been affected by the austerity measures of Javier Milei's government.

 

The institution, founded in 1935 by an Italian priest, houses more than 400 people with disabilities on a 50 hectare site. Known as the "city of charity", the centre has suffered the consequences of cuts to health and social services, as well as funding difficulties for specialised care and therapy programmes.

Not a burden but a blessing

During his tour, Leo XIV hugged residents in wheelchairs, talked with them and gave them his blessing. The arrival of the Pope brought some workers and residents to tears. Addressing them, he said that their lives are a blessing and not a burden for society.

In the centre's chapel, the Holy Father defended the dignity of all people and called for the importance of solidarity to be restored in the face of the pursuit of economic success and the cult of appearances. "The progress of a nation is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs," he said.

Pope Leo XIV arrives to preside over a Mass at Monumento de los EspaÒoles in Buenos Aires Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. Photo: Andrew Medichini. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

The message carries particular weight in a context of tension between the Argentine government and organisations working in the field of disability. Last year Congress overturned Milei's veto of a law that provided for an increase in funds for this sector. However, the executive has resisted implementing it, arguing that it could put at risk the fiscal balance achieved.

Government opposition to funding care of the disabled continues

As a consequence, care centres such as Cottolengo have outstanding debts amounting to hundreds of thousands of euros. In addition, the government's adjustment measures have affected specialised therapy programmes that for decades have been fundamental for many of the approximately five million people with disabilities living in Argentina.

The papal visit also comes just a few days before the Senate is due to study a draft bill that seeks to reserve funds for disability benefits in next year's budget. Milei opposes this initiative.

Kuyen Rolon Rey, a Cottolengo volunteer, highlighted how important it is that Leo XIV chose to start his tour of Argentina precisely in this establishment. "The people here deserve this grace," he said. He also praised the fact that the Pontiff chose a place that is small in size, but big in the love it represents.

A call to business leaders and trade unions

The visit to the care centre opened a day in which Leo XIV was scheduled to meet at the Catholic University of Argentina with business representatives, trade union leaders and representatives of popular movements.

The meeting is part of the message of Catholic social teaching that the Pope is developing during his trip: putting the weakest and most vulnerable people at the centre of economic decisions. This line also revives an integral part of the legacy of Pope Francis, who was Argentine by birth.

On Sunday, during his first speech in the country and in Milei's presence, Leo XIV had already recalled one of his predecessor's recurring ideas: money must be at the service of people and not the other way round. "The economy must serve the person, not the person the economy," he said.

Those expected to take part in Monday's meeting include representatives of national manufacturers, affected by the arrival of low-priced imported products after Milei removed trade restrictions that had been in force for years.

Members of the main Argentine trade union confederation were also invited, whose representatives conveyed to the Vatican in September their concern about job losses and falling wages.

Since coming to power at the end of 2023, Milei has driven a broad austerity programme that has turned him into one of the leading figures in the international conservative backlash against the liberal establishment.

His government has defended cuts to disability programmes as part of a reform process aimed at eliminating fraud and unnecessary spending in the federal administration.

World.title: Storm Charles to hit Portugal and Spain with torrential rain and 120 km/h winds
World.content:
Portugal is still under the influence of depression Bruna, but a new storm is already heading towards the Iberian Peninsula. A new depression, named Charles, will lead to a further deterioration in the weather, with torrential rain and winds that could exceed 100 km/h.

 

According to the Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (IPMA) (source in Portuguese), depression Charles is expected to worsen the weather in Madeira from late Tuesday and on the mainland on Wednesday, with orange-level warnings.

In Spain, the Agencia Estatal de Meteorología (Aemet) also identifies Wednesday as the most severe period and Thursday as a day that will still be unstable, but less intense.

The two meteorological models, the European (ECMWF) and the American (GFS), indicate that the depression's initial track will run between the north of the Canary Islands and the Madeira archipelago. The next part of its path is still uncertain, but the available data suggest that the core of the storm could move towards the Iberian Peninsula via the Gulf of Cadiz or between Sines and Cabo Carvoeiro.

In Madeira, where Bruna caused widespread damage over the weekend, the worsening weather will be felt between the end of the day on Tuesday, the 10th, and the morning of Wednesday, the 11th. There is expected to be persistent and at times heavy rain, with accumulations of more than 100 mm in 12 hours in some areas, especially in the mountain regions.

The wind will pick up, blowing from the southwest, with gusts between 80 and 100 km/h, and could reach around 130 km/h in high ground. Sea conditions will also worsen during this period, with southwesterly waves of 3.5 to 4.5 metres on the south coast of Madeira island.

On the mainland, the deterioration in the weather associated with depression Charles is expected to be felt from late Wednesday morning. Gusts of wind of around 100 to 120 km/h are expected, and could locally be higher, IPMA says.

Rain will at times be heavy over much of the country. Along the coast, southwesterly waves of between 4 and 6 metres are also forecast south of Cabo Carvoeiro from Wednesday afternoon.

The Azores archipelago is not expected to be affected by the passage of depression Charles.

IPMA to issue orange-level warnings

IPMA has announced that orange-level warnings will be issued, without ruling out the possibility of an upgrade in some regions after the next updates of the weather forecast models. The orange warning, the second most serious on the scale, is issued by IPMA whenever there is a "meteorological situation involving a moderate to high risk".

Charles is the third named storm of the 2026/2027 season, after Adam, which remained over the Spanish Mediterranean, and the current Bruna. The new depression is a system of subtropical origin that formed at lower Atlantic latitudes, that is, in the areas where tropical cyclones occur.

Depression Bruna, which will remain almost stationary to the northwest of the Iberian Peninsula until Friday, is an independent system from Charles.

In Madeira, depression Bruna caused flooding, left ten people homeless and there is still one person missing. Between Saturday and Sunday it also forced dozens of flights to be cancelled at Funchal airport.

Civil Protection recommendations ahead of depression Charles

Because depression Charles is approaching, Civil Protection has urged the public to adopt preventive measures and avoid risky behaviour as the weather conditions worsen.

ANEPC warns in particular of the risks associated with travelling along the coastline, advising people to avoid staying in areas exposed to rough seas and to comply with all banned or restricted access areas that are properly signposted.

Another appeal is for people not to cross flooded areas, whether on foot or by car, because of the risk of people and vehicles being swept away, particularly into holes in the road surface or open manholes.

The authorities also recommend extra care when travelling or staying in wooded areas, because of the possibility of falling branches and trees, and keeping away from run-down buildings, retaining walls and embankments, where landslides may occur.

As part of prevention, they also advise the clearing of rainwater drainage systems, by removing leaves and other objects that could block the flow of water. Another measure recommended is the securing of loose structures, such as scaffolding, billboards and suspended structures, as well as objects outdoors and on balconies and windowsills, such as flowerpots, garden furniture or others.

At home, ANEPC also advises that shutters and windows be closed and reinforced, especially those facing into the wind.

On the roads, Civil Protection is calling for defensive driving, at reduced speed and with attention to the possible formation of standing water.

World.title: US drug watchdog orders new safety warnings for weight-loss drugs over potential risk of vision loss
World.content:
The US drug watchdog FDA on Monday said the weight-loss drugs had been associated with non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION), a condition that can lead to sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss.

 

The new warning requirements cover all GLP-1 receptor agonists, a class of medicines widely used to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity. They include popular treatments such as Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy, Eli Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound, as well as other medicines in the class.

The FDA's assessment included an analysis of 126 clinical trials involving over 134,000 patients. The agency also reviewed real-world data and published observational studies. While it acknowledged limitations in the available evidence, it concluded that a potential increased risk warranted additional warnings across the drug class.

The move adds to the safety scrutiny surrounding a rapidly expanding class of medicines that has become central to the treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Last year, Europe’s medicines watchdog (EMA) determined that NAION should be classified as a very rare side effect of semaglutide, the active ingredient of some weight-loss medicines, affecting up to one in 10,000 patients.

World.title: Argentina: Pope Leo XIV receives warm welcome in Claypole
World.content:
Standing in the popemobile, Pope Leo XIV waved to crowds lining the route before stepping down to greet people waiting near the entrance. Footage shows him walking past the faithful, acknowledging those who had come to see him, then pausing in the chapel before the relic of St Luigi Orione's heart.

 

At the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole, in Almirante Brown partido some 30km south of Buenos Aires, the pope unveiled a commemorative plaque and toured part of the 50-hectare site, which houses more than 400 people with disabilities in 16 homes. Welcomed by Bishop Jorge Rubén Lugones of Lomas de Zamora and the centre's director, Brother Jorge David Silanes, he told residents their lives "are not a burden for society, they are a blessing", and said a nation's progress is measured by how it welcomes people with disabilities.

The visit forms part of his 12-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. Argentina is the homeland of his predecessor, Pope Francis, and had not hosted a reigning pontiff since John Paul II in 1987. Leo XIV arrived in Buenos Aires on Sunday 8 November, welcomed by President Javier Milei at Jorge Newbery. The choice of Don Orione, founded in 1935 as a "city of charity", turned attention on care services at a moment when disability funding is politically contested.

World.title: Turkey courts Egypt to tip the scales in eastern Mediterranean power game
World.content:
This week’s joint naval exercises between Turkey and Egypt in the eastern Mediterranean are the latest move in a burgeoning partnership, as Ankara intensifies its efforts to draw Cairo closer and loosen its bonds with Turkish rivals Greece, Cyprus and Israel.

Advertising

The "Sea of Friendship 2026" naval drills, held from 4-9 November off the coast of Alexandria, follow five years of rapprochement after nearly a decade of mistrust sparked by the 2013 ouster of Mohamed Morsi, a close ally of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, by Egypt's President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.

It is the second year in a row that Turkey and Egypt have held the joint drills, after a 13-year break.

“I think it's already a sign that the two countries are getting closer,” said Africa expert Elem Tepecikoglu of Ankara’s Social Sciences University. In her view, the naval exercises are part of an evolving partnership.

“This normalisation process started five years ago in the diplomatic realm,” she explained. “And then we see cooperation in the security domain as well. So this is why I say I'm optimistic that Egypt might come closer to the Turkish side.”

The strengthening alliance between Turkey and Egypt is stirring unease in Israel, at a time when Israeli-Turkish relations are already frayed by the war in Gaza and Ankara’s support for Hamas.

“Obviously, Israel does not see this as necessarily positive, because of the heightened tensions between Israel and Turkey,” warned Turkey analyst Gallia Lindenstrauss of the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University.

She noted that Israel is growing ever more wary of Turkey’s expanding reach in the eastern Mediterranean. “There is concern that Turkey and Egypt can cooperate in ways that will squeeze Israel’s room to manoeuver, politically but also militarily.”

Lindenstrauss said she does not see this as a likely scenario, affirming that the 1979 peace agreement between Israel and Egypt is “still very much in place, despite many geopolitical turnovers”.

“But there was always a fear that the other countries surrounding it would unite and act against Israel,” the analyst added.

Lindenstrauss believes Egypt’s strong ties with Turkey’s rivals, Greece and Cyprus, allay fears of Israeli encirclement. “It is very important that this relationship keeps going ahead because it is a source of stability in the eastern Mediterranean,” she said.

Houthi war risks dragging Israel and Turkey into Horn of Africa standoff

Turkish leverage

Egypt, Greece, Cyprus and Israel are bound by a tightly knit strategic energy alliance centred on the Eastern Mediterranean Gas Forum, a regional organisation formed in 2020 that has its headquarters in Cairo.

Just last month, they stood united in condemning the Libyan parliament's ratification of a maritime deal with Turkey that encroached on Greek and Egyptian waters.

Still, Jalel Harchaoui, a regional expert at the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a London-based think tank, observes that Turkey and Egypt are forging ever-closer collaboration on issues ranging from Libya to the Sudanese civil war to the Horn of Africa. Harchaoui suggests this growing cooperation is steadily boosting Ankara’s leverage over Cairo.

“I think observers should ask, can Egypt afford to do without Turkey? And the answer is probably no, and Turkey probably is aware of it,” he said.

Even so, Harchaoui doubts Cairo is ready to pivot fully toward Ankara. “If [Egypt] switches 180 degrees, it would be a disaster for the other side. I'm talking about Greece and Cyprus and Israel. So you could also ask yourself, can Egypt afford to anger its traditional friends?”

Libya-Turkey maritime deal stokes tensions in eastern Mediterranean

Egypt's balancing act

Ankara is stepping up its diplomatic courtship of Cairo, hoping to lure Egypt away from its longstanding partners.

But Turkish ambitions stumbled when Egypt declined to join the Mecca Defence Alliance with Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August. Analyst Lindenstrauss sees this as a clear sign of the boundaries in Turkish-Egyptian ties.

“Egypt has already moved closer to Turkey than was imaginable a few years ago,” she said. “However, at the end of the day, there are limits to how much it can accept greater Turkish influence. I think Turkey pretty much reached where Egypt is willing to agree to, and it will not give Turkey concessions in the eastern Mediterranean that will endanger its relationship with Greece and Cyprus, or its peace agreement with Israel.”

Lindenstrauss believes that despite diplomatic tensions with Israel over the war in Gaza, it still remains in Egypt’s interests to maintain ties with all sides. “Because of Egypt's importance in the region, I think it can definitely go ahead with this balancing act. It gives it all the gains and the risk is relatively low compared to having Egypt choose sides,” she added.

Ankara stands ready to ramp up its campaign to win over Cairo as the battle for influence in the eastern Mediterranean intensifies. In the unfolding rivalry between between Turkey on one hand and Greece, Cyprus and Israel on the other, Egypt is emerging as the pivotal player.
