World.title: Environmental groups embrace AI, even as they warn of data center impacts
World.content:
Environmental groups worldwide are using artificial intelligence to analyze climate data, track forest fires and count endangered wildlife — embracing a technology they also warn is driving a surge in electricity demand, water use and greenhouse-gas emissions.

The contradiction is forcing these organizations to justify their AI use in carrying out missions to combat climate change or protect natural resources.

“We recognize that AI can come with environmental costs, and we need to be thoughtful about how we use it,” said Ali Swanson, AI lead at the U.S. nonprofit Conservation International. “But at a time when the climate and biodiversity crises are becoming more urgent, AI can help us move faster and make better use of the information we’re collecting.”

The group recently started using AI to assess hotspots detected by satellites and send real-time alerts to community forest patrols about potential wildfires in remote and environmentally sensitive parts of Cambodia.

Reuters interviewed 15 major environmental, conservation and development organizations about their AI use. All said they used the technology in some form and expressed concern about the environmental impact of the data centers powering it. The centers, filled with servers, can require vast amounts of electricity, along with water for cooling.

It’s a global dilemma for individuals, governments and industries balancing AI’s benefits with its enormous risks. The tradeoffs likely will grab attention at the U.N.’s COP31 climate conference this month, when host Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably.

U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres wants major AI companies to publicly disclose their systems’ environmental impacts.

Researchers at the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health estimate the global data-center footprint could more than double by 2030, reaching a size about twice that of Jakarta, the Indonesian megalopolis.

Paul Kokiro, a Kenyan bush and drone pilot at a Save the Elephants research camp, operates a surveillance drone during an elephant survey, at the Samburu National Reserve this month. | REUTERS

The International Energy Agency, meanwhile, estimates global data centers will consume about 945 terawatt-hours of electricity annually by 2030, producing the equivalent of more than 300 million metric tons of carbon dioxide. That’s double current consumption and about equal to Japan’s annual electricity use.

The agency also projects that global data center water consumption will increase from about 560 billion liters (147.9 billion gallons) in 2023 to about 1.2 trillion liters (317 billion gallons) annually by 2030.

Technology giants including Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet’s Google have reported rising emissions linked in part to data center expansion, raising questions about their ability to meet their own long-term climate goals.

Amazon said its artificial-intelligence products were among the most sustainable due to the company’s purchases of low-carbon energy and its efforts to use power and water efficiently.

Microsoft and Google didn’t respond to requests for comment.

Breakthroughs once thought impossible

Many of the organizations that spoke to Reuters believe AI’s benefits currently outweigh its costs because the technology is enabling work that was previously difficult, expensive or impossible.

Kenya’s Save the Elephants, a partner of the Wildlife Conservation Network, said it is using machine learning to improve population surveys and study elephant communication.

Frank Pope, the group’s chief executive, said an aerial survey of Kenya’s largest protected area last year generated roughly 200,000 images that took nine people nine months to review manually. AI models trained on Nvidia’s GeForce graphics platforms can now complete similar analyses in hours.

“The results have been eye-opening,” Pope said. “We found that human surveys were missing about a third of the elephants, roughly half of zebras and giraffes, and three-quarters of oryx populations.”

A monkey walks past obsolete elephant tracking collars at the Save the Elephants research center, at the Samburu National Reserve this month. | REUTERS

More accurate wildlife data can help secure financing for conservation, he said.

“Ultimately, these tools make nature measurable and therefore investable,” he said. “That’s a critical transformation, if we’re going to conserve biodiversity at scale.”

At the institute founded by the late conservation icon Jane Goodall, researchers are using AI to digitize decades of field notes about chimpanzee behavior in Tanzania’s Gombe National Park.

The project was once expected to take 13-15 years because the records were written by hand using the local Kiha language and scientific shorthand.

Thanks to a tool developed with Amazon Web Services, the notes can now be scanned, translated and structured in minutes, slashing the time needed to about two years, said Lilian Pintea, the Jane Goodall Institute’s vice president of conservation science.

During her lifetime, Pintea said, Goodall supported the use of AI to advance conservation science, provided people remained firmly in control of how it was used.

“AI technology should be seen as tools which are human-centered,” Pintea said.

Limiting the environmental impact

Some organizations are experimenting with ways to limit the environmental impact of their AI use.

The World Resources Institute (WRI), a research group that uses AI to accelerate its climate and environmental analyses, said it limits resource-intensive applications such as generating videos and images, while caching AI query results so identical searches don’t need to be reprocessed.

Paul Kokiro, a Kenyan licensed bush and drone pilot at the Save the Elephants research camp, flies a plane fitted with an automated oblique camera count system for aerial survey, at the Samburu National Reserve this month. | REUTERS

The U.S.-based Nature Conservancy has adopted a similar approach. It uses AI to analyze video captured on commercial fishing vessels for information on how many fish of different species they catch. But instead of uploading huge numbers of videos to centralized data centers, it has installed AI-powered digital cameras to process information aboard the vessels, reducing energy use and data-transfer requirements, said Vienna Saccomanno, a senior scientist at the organization.

“It takes a lot of engineering to make computation on the edge possible,” she said. “This was worth it to reduce both our carbon footprint and deliver these sustainability insights.”

Greenpeace International said it, too, uses some AI tools, mainly because software platforms it relies upon include AI features.

It’s imposing internal guidelines emphasizing transparency, human oversight and “intentional” AI use, the group said. But it would prefer to sidestep the technology due to its environmental impacts and is pushing back hard on the data center buildout.

“While other organizations are asking how to use AI responsibly, Greenpeace is asking whether it’s necessary to build all these massive data centers in the first place,” said Katrin Xueying Wu, a climate and energy campaigner with the organization.

Other groups now see AI as vital to effective environmental activism.

“It’s our job to save the planet. If we can do that more effectively and efficiently with the limited resources we’ve got by using AI, then we have to seriously engage in that possibility,” said Stuart Butchart, chief scientist at U.K.-based BirdLife International.

“If we don’t do it, then we’re sort of being derelict in our duty.”

World.title: Man arrested over operation of rogue cellular base station in Tokyo
World.content:
A Chinese man has been arrested on suspicion of illegally operating a mobile phone base station without a license in busy entertainment districts in central Tokyo, the Metropolitan Police Department said.

Yu Hai, a 31-year-old Chinese national living in Tokyo’s Kita Ward, is alleged to have installed radio equipment in a vehicle and operated an unlicensed base station in Tokyo’s Ginza district on Saturday, the police said.

He has denied the allegations against him, reportedly telling investigators, “I’ve never used any radio equipment before. I don’t know anything about it.”

World.title: Okinawa’s Koja calls for central government to explain ‘minimum’ military buildup
World.content:
Newly elected Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja has urged the central government to better explain the “minimum” defensive capabilities needed in the country’s most southerly prefecture as Japan focuses on its far-flung islands and tensions over the U.S. military presence there persist.

Speaking at a news conference Monday in Tokyo, Koja emphasized the need to balance the “Nansei shift” — a strategy seeking to deter adversaries by building up Japan’s defense capabilities in its southwestern region — with the wishes of Okinawa’s residents.

“I intend to firmly demand that the government explain exactly what constitutes the minimum necessary self-defense capabilities to maintain peace, and why particular military functions and facilities are required,” he said.

World.title: South Korea’s military ambitions get a reality check
World.content:
The deck is stacked against a significant shift in military control on the Korean Peninsula, yet that is exactly what South Korean President Lee Jae Myung is staking his leadership on. It’s the right idea, at the wrong time.

Seoul still relies on an American general to lead combined U.S.-South Korea military operations in wartime, one of the enduring legacies of the Korean War. Lee wants to put a South Korean in charge. Yet Seoul is having a difficult time with the second Trump administration — the two sides are divided over their trade agreement and Lee’s reluctance to get involved in the U.S. president’s war in Iran.

That acrimony is bleeding into all aspects of the relationship. Indeed, the U.S. Ambassador to South Korea, Michelle Steel, has described ties as being in a state of turbulence. So why is Lee pushing so hard now to speed up the timeline to take wartime operational control of the combined forces, when Washington has indicated 2029 is a possibility and the allies have yet to agree on a final date?

World.title: Woman narrowly escapes death as folding table falls from Hong Kong building
World.content:
A woman narrowly escaped death after a folding table fell from an industrial building in Hong Kong and landed beside her on Monday evening, leaving her with only a minor hand injury.

Police later arrested a man in connection with the incident, which occurred at about 6.15pm on Cheung Shun Street outside Maxim’s Centre in Cheung Sha Wan.

Video circulating online shows the 32-year-old woman walking along the pavement towards the rear of a parked car.

World.title: Tribunal wrong to clear ex-lawmaker Margaret Ng of misconduct, court told
World.content:
A disciplinary tribunal erred in its decision to clear barrister and former Hong Kong opposition lawmaker Margaret Ng Ngoi-yee of professional misconduct over her conviction for taking part in an unlawful assembly in 2019, a court was told on Monday.

The Hong Kong Bar Association, the professional body for the city’s barristers, sought a court ruling to revoke the decision, arguing that the panel had overlooked “the likelihood of Ng’s action bringing the legal profession into disrepute”.

Benjamin Yu Yuk-hoi SC told the High Court on Monday that the association’s council had applied for judicial review to seek a clarification of its code of conduct after the Barristers Disciplinary Tribunal found the complaint against Ng unsubstantiated.

World.title: China’s national development most acutely felt in Hong Kong and Macau, forum hears
World.content:
China’s global policies could offer an alternative to Western approaches to tackling international challenges, speakers at a forum in Macau have said, noting that the nation’s development and achievements are most acutely felt in that city and in Hong Kong.

At the second edition of the International Forum on Mutual Learning among Civilisations, which opened on Monday in Macau, speakers also said that lessons from history could inspire new approaches to modern problems.

“China’s global policy is quite opposite to what we have today in the world order in the West. There is, I would say, some inclination towards unipolarity,” Jasna Plevnik, president of the Croatian think tank, Geoeconomic Forum Croatia, told the South China Morning Post.

World.title: Hong Kong teams up with Monaco yacht club to develop Skytopia’s marina
World.content:
Hong Kong’s Airport Authority has signed an agreement with the Yacht Club de Monaco to explore an affiliation for its future marina along with other related services as part of its HK$100 billion (US$12.8 billion) Skytopia megadevelopment.

The authority, which manages Hong Kong International Airport, revealed on Monday that the collaboration with the Monaco-based yacht club marked a milestone for the Skytopia project.

“Its world-class expertise and international network will be beneficial to the development of our Yacht Bay project and the growth of Hong Kong’s yacht economy,” the authority said.

World.title: Britain must stop moving the goalposts for Hongkongers on BN(O) scheme
World.content:
The announcement of stricter rules for migrants wishing to settle in Britain has ended a lamentable period of anxiety and uncertainty for former Hong Kong residents forging a new life in the country.

When the plans were first proposed in May last year, Hongkongers living in the United Kingdom under a special visa scheme for British National (Overseas) passport holders feared there would be drastic changes to their pathway to citizenship.

World.title: Hong Kong’s landmark bill to fast-track Northern Metropolis nears passage
World.content:
A bill designed to streamline the development of Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis is a step closer to passage, with final discussions set to take place in the Legislative Council on Wednesday before it could be passed as early as this week.

Lawmaker Priscilla Leung Mei-fun said on Monday that the relevant bills committee held 12 meetings and scrutinised the legislation for about 30 hours, noting the measure was unprecedented.

“This marks the first time in Hong Kong’s history that dedicated legislation is enacted for a single area,” Leung said.

World.title: High drama as firefighters rescue stranded rider from Hong Kong revolving tower
World.content:
Firefighters used ropes and took about two hours to rescue a stranded rider after an observation tower at Hong Kong’s Ocean Park apparently malfunctioned in mid-air on Monday.

Another 40 people and a staff member who had been briefly stranded in the Ocean Park Tower about 70 metres above ground made it down on their own.

The theme park said the tower – part of the landmark tourist attraction in Hong Kong’s Southern district – experienced a fault signal at 2.21pm while carrying 42 people in its revolving deck.

World.title: Hong Kong lift contractor facing fraud probe over missing fire-safety frames
World.content:
A Hong Kong contractor is under criminal investigation for suspected fraud after authorities found it had failed to install fire-resistant door frames in about 90 per cent of the lifts it installed, with preliminary evidence also pointing to serious negligence and misconduct.

The Electrical and Mechanical Services Department (EMSD) said on Monday that Taizoom Elevator was suspected of fraud and making false statements.

The department reported the case to police on October 16, and a criminal investigation is under way. It is not believed to be an industry-wide problem.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019236/More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
World.title: More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019236/More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
World.content:
More Chinese regions are implementing autumn and spring breaks in compulsory education, expanding a decadelong national initiative. Some have also waived fees for students on break and rolled out support measures to help parents take leave at the same time as their children.

Spring and autumn holidays across all compulsory education schools have been rolled out provincewide in at least 15 provinces, as well as numerous cities in other provinces, such as the southern megacity of Shenzhen, domestic media reported last week. In China, compulsory education lasts nine years, encompassing primary and middle school. Breaks will occur in November and April for four to five days each.

The reform dates back to 2004, when Hangzhou, capital of the eastern province of Zhejiang, piloted the breaks. In 2013, the initiative expanded nationally when the State Council issued an announcement encouraging local governments to adopt it, and the rollout accelerated again in 2025 when central authorities urged more schools to implement the holidays.

Chu Zhaohui, a researcher at the China National Academy of Educational Sciences, told domestic media outlet Red Star News that the holidays actually boost learning.

“Learning isn’t confined to schools or taught only by teachers and parents,” Chu said, adding that the holidays give students space for self-exploration.

At the same time as introducing spring and autumn holiday policies, many cities have also added supporting measures so parents can sync their leave. In October, Longnan city in the northwestern Gansu province encouraged employers to implement paid leave and prioritize compensatory rest for employees with school-age children, aligning staff leave with school holidays.

Foshan, a city in the southern Guangdong province, also issued a proposal on Nov. 3 calling on employers to prioritize arranging leave for employees with children during the autumn holiday. The city’s five-day autumn break begins Nov. 11.

Many tourist spots are also waiving entrance fees for children during the upcoming fall break. In the eastern city of Wuxi, a theme park dropped entry fees for students 16 and under throughout November; 15 top tourism sites in Huangshan in the eastern Anhui province, a city known for its mountain of the same name, are now entry-free for children under 18; and the Dujiangyan scenic area in the southwestern Sichuan province waived fees for primary and middle school students between Nov. 12 and 16.

The breaks have significantly boosted travel demand, according to online travel booking platform Qunar. Data from Qunar revealed that in November, air ticket bookings for children 12 and under increased 1.6 times year on year, while parent bookings rose by 50%.

Wang Qiyan, director of the Leisure Economy Research Center at Renmin University, told Red Star News that spring and autumn breaks “enable off-peak travel, avoiding the packed scenic spots of winter and summer vacations.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Tourists take photos of St. Sophia Square during the autumn break in Harbin, Heilongjiang province, Nov. 4, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019228/A Bad Review, a Suicide, and a Debate Over Cyberbullying in China
World.title: A Bad Review, a Suicide, and a Debate Over Cyberbullying in China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019228/A Bad Review, a Suicide, and a Debate Over Cyberbullying in China
World.content:
On Oct. 6, 2026, a female customer posted complaints on multiple social media platforms about a fried skewer stall in Gao County, Yibin, in southwestern China’s Sichuan province. “Avoid XX Copper Pot Potatoes. The owner can’t take the heat,” she wrote. She had bought a 10-yuan ($1.40) fried food combo from the stall, run by a 33-year-old woman surnamed Hu, but was dissatisfied with the portion of potatoes. “She just refused to add potatoes afterward,” the customer added. Her location-tagged posts quickly spread, and negative comments about Hu and her stall flooded the comment sections.

Hu responded to the criticism, writing, “I stand behind my portions.” Three days later, on Oct. 9, she jumped into a river and died by suicide.

Hu had run the stall for more than four years, sleeping less than six hours a night. In her suicide note, she described the enormous pressures she faced in life. She had hoped to watch her child grow up, she wrote, but the video telling people to avoid her stall had been the straw that broke the camel’s back.

She also wrote: “These past two days I have experienced what I consider cyberbullying. One person complained about no potatoes in her order, and then the comments came flooding in about bad service and poor-tasting food.”

This was not the first tragedy of its kind. In August 2025, a 57-year-old obstetrician-gynecologist surnamed Shao in Zhoukou, central China’s Henan province, jumped to her death. According to her family, she had endured more than seven months of cyberbullying over a medical dispute. In 2023, after a primary school student in Wuhan, capital of the central Hubei province, was killed in a traffic accident on campus, his mother was subjected to online attacks and later jumped to her death. In cases like these, public opinion often attributes the tragedies to cyberbullying.

But in Hu’s case, labeling the entire incident “cyberbullying” and placing the blame on the customer who posted the negative review would exaggerate the power of a single act of expression.

The customer maintained that she was simply describing a genuine experience, with “no malice, incitement, or falsehood.” She did not insult or personally attack anyone, disclose private information, or call for coordinated attacks online or offline. Her criticism may have been harsh, subjective, or exaggerated, but based on the content of her posts alone, it is difficult to characterize it as cyberbullying.

Many negative comments about the stall owner appeared beneath the posts, but there is currently no evidence that they were all malicious. Public criticism can be harsh, but legal liability must rest on provable facts.

In July 2026, China released a draft Anti-Online Violence Law for public comment. It defines online violence as “concentrated or sustained” acts involving “insult and abuse, rumor-mongering and defamation, incitement of hatred,” and similar behavior. A negative review based on a genuine transaction cannot automatically be classified as cyberbullying because it has harmful consequences. Moreover, the draft has not yet become law.

A common misconception is that anything posted online will inevitably spread and attract attention. That is simply not true. People publish vast amounts of content every day, but only a tiny fraction attracts widespread attention.

Consider Dr. Shao’s case. Following an investigation, the platform disclosed that her account had received more than 10,900 comments, about 60 of which were suspected of containing attacks or other inappropriate content. The rest were classified as normal or neutral interactions. Although the platform’s findings should not be treated as a definitive record of every offensive interaction, they serve as a reminder that not every comment should be regarded as a malicious attack.

None of this excuses genuine cyberbullying. In 2018, a female doctor surnamed An in Deyang, Sichuan, became involved in a dispute with a boy at a swimming pool. The boy’s family posted edited surveillance footage online accompanied by inflammatory text. After enduring sustained online attacks, An died by suicide. In 2021, a court sentenced three defendants to prison for criminal insult.

The law is not powerless against cyberbullying. Precisely because it has the power to punish such behavior, however, we must distinguish criminal incitement and insults from harsh criticism.

Tragedies often result from a combination of factors. We cannot draw a direct causal line from a single negative review and the comments that followed to a person’s suicide. The negative review was one link in a chain of events, but it was neither the sole cause nor something that made the outcome inevitable.

Hu’s final message makes clear the immense pressures she faced in her personal life and as a small business owner. Her psychological state and the support available to her at the time also deserve attention.

The platform’s decision to promote the post to nearby users is just how online reviews work. Positive and negative reviews must be visible to help consumers distinguish good businesses from bad ones. But regulating them presents a dilemma.

Any screening system risks two types of errors: false positives, in which legitimate criticism is flagged as malicious, and false negatives, in which malicious comments go undetected. Tightening controls reduces false negatives but increases false positives, while relaxing them has the opposite effect. Platforms must therefore balance the costs of both.

For platforms such as the consumer review service Dianping and the short-video app Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, determining a post’s motives is difficult, and predicting its consequences even harder. Siding with businesses risks suppressing legitimate criticism, while siding with consumers risks allowing malicious attacks. There is no one-size-fits-all solution.

Anyone who has maintained a blog or public social media account knows how pervasive online negativity can be, with abusive comments and private messages a common occurrence. We cannot expect everyone to tolerate such abuse, but where should we draw the line in regulating it?

Cyberbullying typically involves a series of acts including verbal abuse, defamation, and insults. Such behavior may constitute a civil infringement and, in serious cases, give rise to criminal liability. But the definition of cyberbullying must not become so broad that it exaggerates the harm caused by ordinary expression.

The “clear and present danger” standard in U.S. legal history offers a useful reminder that speech should not be restricted merely because it causes discomfort. However, that standard arose in a specific legal context and cannot be directly applied as a general principle of Chinese law.

If we endlessly magnify the psychological harm that speech can cause and attribute tragic outcomes solely to what people say, the argument that “speech can be harmful” risks becoming a blanket justification for restricting expression.

If we blame every tragedy on the criticism that preceded it, consumers may hesitate to post negative reviews, and others may begin to self-censor. Free expression would suffer, potentially undermining market competition.

Such a focus on cyberbullying also overlooks two critical issues: the pressures facing small business owners and the need for better mental health support. Long hours, unstable incomes, and the stresses of running a business can make a single bad review feel overwhelming. China’s national mental health hotline, 12356, also has an important role in identifying and responding to people in crisis.

We must confront genuine cyberbullying without silencing legitimate criticism, while also addressing gaps in mental health care and support for small businesses. Blaming a single review may offer a convenient explanation for Hu’s death, but it brings us no closer to understanding the tragedy or preventing the next one.

Translator: Gabriel Kwan.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019225/China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
World.title: China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019225/China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
World.content:
As it expands its weather-warning systems across the Global South, China has handed over equipment for a customized version of MAZU — an AI-powered weather prediction tool created by the China Meteorological Administration — to Sri Lanka, one of eight countries where the platform has been deployed.

The device, described by domestic media as a rectangular black box roughly the size of a portable toolbox, was presented to Sri Lanka’s meteorological department on Nov. 1. It will form part of a system designed to warn of heavy rain, strong winds, and cyclones, and is expected to enter service by the end of the year.

Launched in July 2025, MAZU takes its name from a Chinese sea goddess revered as a protector of sailors. It combines AI forecasting models developed by Chinese research institutions with data from the country’s weather satellites.

Conventional weather forecasting relies on supercomputers to calculate how the atmosphere will change using equations based on physical laws. AI models, by contrast, learn from years of weather data.

“Chatbots familiar to the public learn patterns in language, while AI weather models learn how the atmosphere evolves,” Niu Zeyi, an assistant researcher at the Shanghai Typhoon Institute who led the development of a forecasting model used in MAZU, told Sixth Tone. “By training on years of meteorological data, these models can predict future weather conditions based on current variables such as wind, air pressure, temperature, and humidity.”

Once trained, AI models can produce forecasts faster and more cheaply than conventional methods. One model can generate a 24-hour global forecast in 1.4 seconds, about 10,000 times faster than traditional numerical methods. For forecasts covering 15 to 60 days, AI models can reduce computing costs to one-thousandth of those of conventional methods.

But most of the savings come from running routine forecasts, Niu said. Training models, building datasets, and maintaining systems still require investment — resources many countries in the Global South lack.

MAZU’s cloud-based services are being tested by 58 countries, according to domestic media, and China plans to deploy the system in 30 countries over the next five years.

In Pakistan, the system has reportedly incorporated local radar and satellite data to develop warnings for heavy rainfall and glacial lake outburst floods. In Djibouti, the model developed by Niu’s team helps provide tailored weather warnings for the East African country’s port.

Studies show AI models can be less accurate than conventional methods when predicting record-breaking extremes, for which there is little historical data. Local weather in complex terrain also remains difficult to forecast, and it is not always clear how AI models arrive at their predictions.

The models also need to be adapted to local conditions, Niu said. “Our approach is to work with local meteorological agencies to improve datasets, conduct independent evaluations, and make local adjustments.”

Even with AI, he added, “human forecasters must still combine observations, AI predictions, and their own judgment before authorities issue warnings.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: The weather warning system Mazu at the China Meteorological Administration booth during 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai, July 18, 2026. VCG）

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019218/China’s Traditional Colors Are Trending. But What Are We Missing?
World.title: China’s Traditional Colors Are Trending. But What Are We Missing?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019218/China’s Traditional Colors Are Trending. But What Are We Missing?
World.content:
Traditional Chinese colors have become a popular topic on Chinese social media, with posts sporting catchy headlines such as “Our Ancestors Had the Ultimate Eye for Beauty” and “Out-of-This-World Color Combinations in ‘Dream of the Red Chamber.’” Open one of these posts, and you’ll often find neatly arranged color swatches labeled with evocative traditional names such as tianqing, “celestial blue”; yuebai, “moon white”; qiuxiang, “autumn fragrance”; and yanzhi, “rouge.”

In my opinion, this enthusiasm is undoubtedly a good thing. Traditional colors deserve greater attention and should be made more accessible. Color swatches can also be useful for showcasing the colors of historical artifacts and help modern audiences connect with the past. But this kind of simplification is a double-edged sword. In making something rich and complex easier to understand, it can also reduce it to a crude, one-dimensional representation. What makes information easier to communicate can also obscure or distort its meaning.

In fact, color swatches have significant limitations when it comes to representing and explaining traditional colors. They can only scratch the surface of a much richer cultural history.

Modern color charts emerged from Western industrial and commercial systems designed to control production quality and reproduce specific colors. But this standardized, scientific approach often falls short when applied to traditional Chinese colors. Anyone who has visited an exhibition of antique clothing or textiles and tried to photograph it may have experienced this firsthand. What appears to the naked eye as a beautiful pine green might look mustard yellow on a smartphone screen. Or the various golds and yellows of an imperial dragon robe might lose their distinctiveness entirely. If even digital cameras equipped with sophisticated image-processing algorithms struggle to capture these colors, what chance does a simple color swatch have?

So why do modern industrial color charts fall short in representing traditional Chinese colors?

First, color swatches are designed to standardize colors within specific product categories, whereas traditional Chinese color names developed within particular craft traditions. As these traditions evolved, a color’s name could refer to subtly different hues in different periods.

Several factors contributed to these variations. In the age of traditional handicrafts, differences in materials and craftsmanship could produce markedly different hues. Local production conditions also gave products from different regions their own distinctive characteristics. Fashions changed over time, altering the shades associated with particular color names. Even on a single garment, colors could appear different depending on the lighting, viewing angle, or direction of the weave.

Traditional indigo dyeing offers a good example. Indigo must first be fermented in vats and chemically reduced before it can be used to dye fabric. A single dip produces a pale blue, and the color deepens after each subsequent immersion. As a result, even fabrics dyed in the same vat can emerge in countless different shades.

Second, modern industrial color standards demand precision, assigning each color a numerical value. Traditional color names, however, did not follow this quantitative model. Rather than corresponding to a single fixed value, they generally described a natural range of hues.

Take xinghuang, or “apricot yellow,” for example. The yellowish-red of a ripe apricot is not a precisely defined hue. Yet despite natural variations in its color, people can still recognize the familiar shade of a ripe apricot.

Finally, the meanings and appearances of colors have changed considerably throughout Chinese history. These changes reflected rulers’ preferences, interpretations of cultural doctrines, shifts in folk customs, the rise and decline of craft techniques, and the movement of goods through domestic and overseas trade.

Consider qing, a color term widely used in ancient China. Depending on the context, it could describe the blue of the sky, the green of plants, or even the black of someone’s hair or eyes. By the Ming (1368–1644) and Qing (1644–1911) dynasties, it still encompassed a broad range of hues. People wore qing-colored robes, but their exact shades varied. Although the “Da Ming Huidian,” or “Collected Statutes of the Ming Dynasty,” prescribed shiqing for officials’ outer robes, surviving examples range from reddish tones to bluish-green and darker, more somber shades. Meanwhile, the robe the emperor wore during rituals at the imperial tombs was yuanqing, a shade that appeared almost black.

Another example is zi, or “purple.” Examining the cloud and wave motifs on Qing imperial dragon robes reveals how the color evolved over successive reigns, from dark brownish shades early in the dynasty to mauve hues in the middle period and brighter purples in the late Qing.

Furthermore, in ancient China, color was not simply something to admire or enjoy. It also symbolized divine authority and helped define ritual conventions and social hierarchies, distinguishing the central government from local authorities and the nobility from ordinary people.

Ancient China developed a five-color system associated with concepts such as the five directions and five elements. Qing, chi (vermilion), yellow, white, and black were the five primary colors, while green, red, bi (jade), purple, and liuhuang (“flowing yellow”) were the five auxiliary colors. Successive rulers used these distinctions between primary and auxiliary colors to reinforce social hierarchies.

During the Qing dynasty, for example, the emperor’s ceremonial attire followed a four-color system from the middle of the dynasty onward. He wore tianqing, “celestial blue,” when performing sacrifices to Heaven; minghuang, “bright yellow,” for sacrifices to Earth; dahong, “deep red,” for sacrifices to the Sun; and yuebai, “moon white,” for sacrifices to the Moon.

The Qing imperial court also expanded the use of yellow in imperial dress, a practice dating back to the Sui (581–618) and Tang (618–907) dynasties. Strict rules determined who could wear particular shades. Minghuang, “bright yellow,” was reserved for the emperor, empress dowager, empress, and imperial noble consort. Xinghuang, “apricot yellow,” was restricted to the crown prince and crown princess, while jinhuang, “golden yellow,” was worn by princes, noble consorts, and consorts. Xiangse, “fragrant yellow,” was designated for imperial concubines and various ranks of princesses and princely consorts.

Clearly, color swatches alone cannot convey such rich cultural meanings and historical details. But the problem goes beyond how we reconstruct traditional colors. It also concerns how we understand history itself.

Modern industrial products are generally designed for mass consumption, often favoring simplicity and practicality. By contrast, many of the objects that have survived from ancient China belonged to emperors, empresses, and other powerful figures. The differences between their world and ours, in social context, cultural values, and everyday life, mean that interpreting these objects through a modern lens can easily lead to superficial conclusions or misunderstandings.

This brings us back to today’s enthusiasm for traditional colors on social media. China’s color traditions never formed a fixed, unchanging system, and preserving a tradition involves more than simply reproducing the past. It is a process of critically engaging with what came before, deciding what to discard, what to preserve, and what to adapt or develop further.

But meaningful preservation must begin with an understanding of the historical traditions themselves. That means looking beyond individual colors to examine the contexts in which they emerged, how their meanings and uses changed over time, and the cultural, social, and material relationships that shaped them.

Translator: David Ball; portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: Visuals from the Palace Museum, reedited by Fu Xiaofan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019224/China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
World.title: China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019224/China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
World.content:
Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang pledged to share China’s market with the rest of the world and promote balanced international economic development at the opening ceremony of the 2026 China International Import Expo (CIIE) on Thursday.

“Mutual benefit is at the heart of trade and economic cooperation,” Ding said in his opening address. “Open and connected markets are fundamental for such partnerships.”

Ding also called for deeper investment cooperation, greater collaboration in technological innovation, and stronger dialogue to remove trade barriers.

This year’s CIIE, the ninth annual event and the largest edition to date, welcomes a record 4,142 overseas companies from 162 countries, regions, and international organizations to Shanghai’s National Exhibition and Convention Center. The event’s total exhibition area is also its largest, exceeding 440,000 square meters.

The event, which runs Nov. 5 to 10, welcomed more than 300 Fortune Global 500 companies and global leading enterprises, with 2,000 companies participating for the first time. A record more than 480 products will either make their global, Asia, or China debut at the expo, including a laparoscopic surgery robot by Johnson & Johnson, a cochlear implant capable of 360-degree sound coverage by Swiss hearing care firm Advanced Bionics, and a 6G terminal prototype by U.S. tech company Qualcomm.

This year’s exhibition comprises six main sections covering technical equipment, consumer goods, food and agricultural products, automobiles and smart mobility, medical devices and health care, and trade in services. It also offers a dedicated “innovation incubation zone” for tech startups.

CIIE has also expanded efforts to support African countries, with free exhibition booth space for the “least developed” countries up 17% from last year’s exhibition. The expansion comes as China introduced zero tariffs on imports from all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations in May.

Launched in 2018, CIIE is the world’s first national-level exhibition dedicated to imports. The expo underlines China’s continued efforts to promote inclusive economic globalization and build an open world economy.

In the first nine months of 2026, China’s imports of foreign goods reached 16.7 trillion yuan ($2.5 trillion), up 22.3% year on year, the fastest growth since 2021, according to official data.

(Header image: A view of the China International Import Expo’s exhibition center in Shanghai, Nov. 5, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019220/Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
World.title: Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019220/Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
World.content:
Applications aimed at preventing impulse purchases have soared in popularity during this year’s Double Eleven, the world’s largest shopping festival. The apps involve users listing the items they want, along with their prices, then sharing them with friends and strangers who vote on whether they should buy them.

Dozens of such mini-programs have sprung up across major platforms including WeChat and Alipay following the August success of the WeChat mini-program “Still Want to Buy?” (Hai Mai Me in Chinese), domestic media reported last week. Related hashtags have garnered tens of millions of views on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, as of Thursday.

Domestic e-commerce giant Alibaba launched Double Eleven, also known as Singles’ Day, on Nov. 11, 2009, as a 24-hour shopping event. The festival has since grown to a monthlong event across all e-commerce platforms and begins around mid-October.

The trend comes as young Chinese consumers become increasingly money-conscious. According to a May report by Ireland-based consulting firm Accenture, 82% of the country’s Gen Z — more than 230 million people — have started saving money or cutting back on non-essential spending.

The rise in anti-impulse-buy apps dates back to the release of Still Want to Buy? in August. Created by a 29-year-old developer under the pseudonym Qiancheng, the app gained more than 75,000 daily active users within three days of its launch, and total registered users exceeded 500,000 as of mid-September. More than 85% of users are females under 24, Qiancheng told local media.

He said the tool came about after his girlfriend suggested using automated office purchase approval systems — which employees must go through to obtain authorization for work-related purchases — to govern shopping decisions. He added that he often personally feels regret after making impulse purchases.

“It’s difficult to make money nowadays, so I think it’s worth letting people we trust help us make better spending decisions,” Qiancheng said.

However, Still Want to Buy? was taken down on Oct. 31, reportedly due to targeted reporting from online trolls. Qiancheng told local media he is applying to have the mini-program relisted and is developing an independent app to expand the program’s function.

WeChat mini-program “Wait Up, Wallet” also offers similar features to Still Want to Buy?, but it allows users to seek advice from total strangers.

This October, Lin Yinjie, a 20-year-old college student from the eastern Fujian province, vibe-coded a similar app, the Alipay mini-program “Hold On a Sec.” The app lets users log items and prices and set a cooling-off period, during which friends help them decide whether to buy. So far, the program is mainly used by Lin and her friends and does not have a wide audience.

Lin told Sixth Tone that she used to place orders mindlessly while scrolling shopping apps and social media. “As a student on a tight budget, I know how easily the desire to buy things can quietly drain my wallet,” she said.

“A 9.9-yuan ($1.50) purchase seems insignificant, but before you know it, you’ve spent hundreds of yuan,” she said, adding that, “A lot of things I think I really want turn out to be things I no longer care about after a few days.”

Over the past week, Lin says her tool has helped her save over 80 yuan, which she used to buy a camera memory card instead. “It’s like trading ‘unnecessary spending’ for something I actually need,” she said.

Public reactions to the apps have been mixed. While many users report receiving practical advice through the mini-programs, others note an unfortunate side effect. “When I review other people’s requests, I end up wanting to buy the items myself,” one user noted on Douyin. “It’s turned into a product recommendation feed.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG and Weibo, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019222/Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
World.title: Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019222/Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
World.content:
For nearly 27 years, Starbucks coffeehouses in China have been a haven for non-paying patrons attracted by its comfortable seating, ample power outlets, air conditioning, and free restrooms.

This stemmed from the American company’s foundational brand concept of making its outlets “third places” — safe, accessible spaces between home and work to relax and connect with friends, whether you intend to spend or not.

Now, it seems, spending is mandatory.

In late October, Starbucks China introduced a nationwide purchase-required seating policy, pledging to be “clear in its rules but warm in its execution,” with staff encouraged to politely stop non-paying customers from hogging tables and chairs. At the same time, it unveiled plans to invest more than 300 million yuan ($45 million) in reshaping the in-store atmosphere.

As the company undergoes major corporate restructuring while continuing to expand, does it risk losing its “third place” image in China?

Stirred up

The first Starbucks on the Chinese mainland opened in Beijing’s World Trade Building in 1999. Today there are about 8,000 outlets across 1,100 counties in the mainland.

Li Kele regularly visits her local store in the southwestern Sichuan province. After walking in and sitting down on Oct. 21, taking a moment to browse various online platforms for discounts, Li was soon approached by a barista brandishing a menu and asking if she needed any help. “The store never used to push customers to place an order,” she says.

Starbucks outlets have been attracting non-paying patrons since the 1980s, and the company officially adopted a worldwide open-door policy in 2018.

However, concerns over disruptive behaviors, alongside the company’s desire to prioritize paying customers and staff’s experience, prompted the global headquarters to reverse the policy in January last year.

The change began at its North American stores, where a new code of conduct stated that Starbucks coffee shops, patios, restrooms, and other facilities were for employees and customers only.

Anecdotal evidence suggests baristas in China began nudging seated patrons to make purchases in early 2026.

One customer shares that in January they observed employees at a Starbucks branch in Beijing’s central Xidan shopping district walking around the store offering table service to people without drinks, which is not typically available, and promoting discount coupons. Sometimes they’d subtly point out that the store was crowded and seating was scarce.

On Oct. 19, social media users in several cities began posting about signs spotted at Starbucks stores that stated customers should “make a purchase before taking a seat.”

When a domestic media outlet contacted Starbucks China for a response that same day, a spokesperson denied any plan to introduce a purchase-required seating policy. But within 48 hours, the company made a complete U-turn, announcing that such a policy would take effect on Oct. 22.

The move has sparked much debate online. Yet in real terms, implementation has so far been limited to advisory measures, such as signage.

“The latest wording is that they (head office) encourage us to ask people to leave,” says Zhang Yi, a part-time Starbucks barista. “They want us front-line staff to persuade non-paying customers to give up their seats in whatever way we consider peaceful.”

However, because the practice isn’t tied to their performance review, employees might be reluctant to enforce the new rules, Zhang adds. “If I’m on shift, I won’t do it. I’ll just work the way I always have.”

In the grind

Starbucks built its “third place” branding concept based on the American sociologist Ray Oldenburg’s 1989 book, “The Great Good Place,” in which he describes the human need for communal, welcoming social environments separate from home (the “first place”) and work (the “second place”).

This positioning requires providing space for relaxed socializing. But when revenues don’t keep pace with increases in rent and operating costs, it becomes a potential pain point.

When Brian Niccol was appointed CEO of Starbucks in September 2024, same-store sales — a metric that measures revenue growth from established locations — were on the slide in the U.S. market.

To reverse the trend, he launched “Back to Starbucks,” a plan aimed at “rediscovering the power of third places” by improving the in-store experience, such as reintroducing old-school ceramic mugs and handwritten names on cups, as well as more comfortable seating. He then scrapped the 2018 open-door policy.

Investor data suggests the changes have already had an effect in North America, where same-store sales were up by 8.1% year on year in the third quarter of fiscal 2026 (Sept. 29, 2025, to Sept. 27, 2026) and same-store transactions grew by 4.5% over the same period.

In China, recent growth in same-store sales has been powered more by product innovation, deliveries, and price adjustments, according to Cathy R. Smith, Starbucks’ chief financial officer.

As online take-out orders increase and in-store spending declines, running a brick-and-mortar “third place” becomes more expensive. In this case, seat-hogging shifts from being a tolerable service issue to an operational problem.

Pressing issue

In April this year, Starbucks completed a $4 billion joint-venture transaction with Boyu Capital, a China-focused alternative asset management and private equity firm based in Hong Kong. The deal gives Boyu a 60% share in Starbucks’ China retail business and transitions all 8,000 coffeehouses into licensed operations.

The U.S. coffee giant says it expects the transaction proceeds, along with the value of its retained 40% stake and licensing agreement, to account for more than $13 billion over the next decade. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026, Starbucks’ international segment operating margin increased to 19.1%, up from 13.6% a year earlier.

However, while the deal benefits global headquarters, Starbucks China still faces pressure to expand. At a partner forum in April, CEO Molly Liu confirmed the company is already two-thirds of the way to its goal of opening stores in more than 1,500 counties over the next three years.

With this in mind, the purchase-required seating policy looks more like an efficiency drive, as the company attempts to cut costs.

This also comes amid a major restructuring of Starbucks China’s workforce. As all staff are now part of the joint venture, they can no longer hold Starbucks shares, which trade on New York’s Nasdaq exchange. This means the end of the Bean Stock program in China, which since 1991 has awarded full- and part-time employees shares after a certain tenure.

Liu said at April’s partner forum that benefits would continue through fiscal 2026, with a new long-term incentive plan to be introduced in the fourth quarter. As of Nov. 4, there had been no further announcements.

As social insurance contributions are mandatory only for permanent staff in China, barista Zhang believes the company prefers to hire part-time workers. Jiemian News reported in January that Starbucks China’s official recruitment channels were promoting vacancies in 269 areas, with full-time positions making up just over 20%.

Behind its new seating policy is a contradiction Starbucks China cannot easily escape: the “third place” concept justifies the brand’s premium, yet recent growth has come from deliveries and discounts, bringing sales without a customer ever sitting down.

The joint venture and its target to grow to “as many as 20,000 locations over time” sharpen that contradiction. Smaller markets and leaner per-store costs make it hard to build to the original standard.

Therefore, tightening seating rules, restructuring its workforce, and expansion look less like separate decisions than part of one cost logic.

(Due to privacy concerns, Li Kele and Zhang Yi are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Zhan Fangge.

A version of this article originally appeared in Baobian News. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

World.title: Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019216/Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.content:
A Chinese app designed to report hotels that allegedly have bedbugs and other pests has been updated and re-released following controversy over the validity of the claims. The app attracted more than 300,000 users at its peak, flagging over 600 hotels nationwide, according to its creator.

In a Sunday post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, the creator of the app, a WeChat mini-program called “Bedbug Map,” announced that he alone would now review bedbug reports — previously, evidence was approved if a majority of users verified it. He also clarified that users are required to upload photographic evidence of bedbugs. The next day, he also posted a review of nearly 300 rejected bedbug reports, explaining why each had been declined.

Released Sept. 16, the mini-program lets users report hotels with bedbugs, cockroaches, or other pests, resulting in a bug or question mark icon over the hotel’s location. Tapping it reveals the number of user reports.

Controversy arose after reports that multiple hotels were asked by customers for refunds after they reported having found bedbugs via the app after their stay. One hotel was allegedly asked to refund 3,000 yuan ($450) in room charges after a report citing “two bumps” on a guest’s body was posted on the map and approved by users. According to the report, the hotel later asked a third party to inspect the premises, but found no traces of bedbugs.

The creator, a 26-year-old manufacturing industry worker who asked to remain anonymous, told Sixth Tone that in the past few days he had personally reviewed more than 700 pieces of photo evidence submitted over the previous two months.

A Wednesday check by Sixth Tone revealed that 232 hotels are now marked on the mini-program’s map, down from the more than 600 reported before Monday. The mini-program currently lists 36 hotels as having successfully appealed reports after submitting third-party evidence.

The app has also been taken down twice, most recently in late October, by WeChat parent company Tencent, citing its restrictions on applications run by and registered to individuals.

The creator told Sixth Tone that Bedbug Map was created with the help of AI in under two weeks. He said he got the idea after searching online for bedbug information after he and his girlfriend developed bites following a move, discovering most bedbug posts involved hotels.

On the day of its release, the mini-program attracted over 100,000 users, according to the creator. Under his release announcement on Xiaohongshu, many commented asking him to expand the function to public transportation, which he then added to the app. However, the function was removed in subsequent updates.

“I guess the reason the app was well-received is that it addresses a key pain point for the average traveler: the lack of cleanliness and the resurgence of bedbugs.”

The mini-program previously allowed users to submit reports without photo evidence. However, after users raised concerns about the potential for people to maliciously target hotels without evidence, the program was updated in late September to allow users to upload photographic evidence. Photos can be either uploaded or taken directly via the mini-program — in the latter case, the app automatically adds a watermark showing the time and location.

“I’m simply the initiator,” he said. “The goal is to get everyone involved in managing the mini-program’s data and reviews.”

Hotels can also appeal bedbug reports — indicated on the map by blue semicircular icons above such locations — as well as upload disinfection records, business licenses, and photos of pest-control operations.

The creator said he even recruited volunteers at one point to inspect the hygiene of hotels that filed appeals. However, the function was soon taken down because of concerns about volunteers’ safety, among other issues.

He said that managing the mini-program alone has “brought pressure and criticism,” adding that he hopes the government will “provide professional guidance to improve (the app’s) credibility.”

In an interview with domestic media, Lin Feiran, a lawyer at Beijing King & Capital Law Firm, suggested the company bring in professionals to identify insects reported at different locations.

State media outlet CNR News wrote in a Monday commentary that “a map pieced together by internet users being used to fill the gap in hygiene information shows that formal (reporting) channels are lacking,” encouraging hotel booking platforms to display bedbug records publicly.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.title: Amnesia? Witness ‘evasive’ response draws ire of senator-judges
World.content:
FOR THE DEFENSE. Jaime Adalin takes the witness stand in Sara Duterte's trial on November 9, 2026.

Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo reminds Adalin he could be cited in contempt for lying under oath

The first witness presented by the defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte appeared to have forgotten two things: his participation in an alleged Chinese consulate-sponsored trip in 2025 and the possibility that the Senate impeachment court could cite him in contempt.

On Day 40 of the impeachment trial, Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin drew the ire of senator-judges over his seemingly evasive answers about an alleged all-expenses-paid trip to China in November 2025.

House private prosecutor Jay Tolosa first raised the question as he challenged Adalin’s credibility following his earlier evasive answers.

“You would also admit that sometime in November 2025, you were one of the LGU officials of Davao who went to China on an all-expenses-paid tour sponsored by the Chinese consulate?” Tolosa asked.

However, instead of answering categorically, Adalin laughed and brushed off the question, saying: “I don’t think that’s relevant.”

This stunned the Senate impeachment court and drew laughter from the crowd.

“You are funny there, Engineer Jimmy,” presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero told Adalin.

But while Escudero appeared amused, other senator-judges were less entertained.

Senator-judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto noted that the impeachment court could request Adalin’s travel records from the Bureau of Immigration if he continued to claim he could not remember the details of his trip.

Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo, meanwhile, reminded the witness that he could be cited in contempt for lying or making a mockery of the proceedings while under oath.

“Presiding Officer, the witness appears to be making a fool of us. Sir, may I remind you that you’re under oath. What you’re doing right now — making fun of the trial — that is prohibited. We can cite you in contempt,” Tulfo said.

Adalin eventually confirmed that he had traveled to China on a personal trip last year. But when asked about another trip to the country in November 2018, he again claimed he could no longer remember the details, prompting another rebuke from Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo.

“Do you want me to give you even the CCTV footage of your trip? November 12, 2018, PR356 China, you stayed there for two days,” Tulfo said.

“You traveled a lot…And I’m not criticizing you, but how much is your salary? How come you are always abroad?” he added.

Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros also pressed Adalin for details about his travels. The assessor, however, maintained that he could not recall the places he visited or which agency facilitated the trips.

“Sir, I’m sorry but this is no laughing matter. It is unbelievable that an engineer, a city assessor, who claims to be knowledgeable on the maps that the defense and prosecution presented, is unaware of the areas he visited in a large country,” Hontiveros said.

Adalin explained that he was not particularly keen on traveling, which was why he had forgotten the details of his trips.

But Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo pointed to a more serious reason for the prosecution’s questions: alleged inward remittances from China.

“You know, Mr. Adalin, we are asking about your travel to China because Calle88 — a company that Duterte’s husband, Atty. Manases Carpio, co-owns — allegedly sent inward remittances worth P319 million from China and Hong Kong to them,” Tulfo said.

“It’s not good to hear that…government officials, especially those in high positions, are receiving money from China, a country that we have a territorial dispute with,” he added.

By the end of the questioning, Adalin had managed to recall some details of his trips. Next time, senators are likely to remind him about proper decorum in an impeachment court. – Rappler.com

World.title: Davao assessor hit over ‘inconsistent’ testimony at Sara Duterte impeachment trial
World.content:
Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin has initially said Mans Carpio's Davao property matched the 'residential lot' declared in Vice President Sara Duterte's 2024 Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth

MANILA, Philippines – Senator-judge Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan on Monday, November 9, questioned the credibility of a Davao City assessor over what he described as “inconsistent” testimonies during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

On Day 40 of the trial, Pangilinan questioned the shifting answers of Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin, who initially said that a property bought by Duterte’s husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, in Davao matched the “residential lot” declared in the Vice President’s 2024 Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN). The 379-square-meter property was acquired under a transfer certificate of title (TCT) ending in 0775.

“When you were testifying earlier, you said that the two properties in the SALN and the property description in the deed of sale were one and the same…but after the photos were shown, you were not sure,” Pangilinan said.

“How can you say you were sure the properties matched if you did not recognize the property in the photos?” he added.

Duterte is being tried for Article II, which involves allegations of unexplained wealth. Part of the accusations in the impeachment article are the undeclared properties in Duterte’s 2024 and 2025 SALNs.

The prosecution had previously alleged that Duterte failed to declare two properties in Davao: a lot in Matina, Davao City, which Carpio purchased for P6 million in July 2024, and a property in the Island Garden City of Samal, acquired for P3 million in 2018.

The defense, however, maintained that the properties were properly declared in Duterte’s SALN, while the prosecution questioned whether the land title cited by the defense corresponds to the property listed in the Vice President’s SALN.

During the trial, Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero asked Adalin whether the P10-million property listed in Duterte’s 2024 SALN was the same as Carpio’s property covered by the TCT ending in 0775. Adalin initially answered in the affirmative, citing similarities in the figures appearing in the tax declarations.

However, when the prosecution presented photographs of a commercial building in the said residential lot, the assessor expressed uncertainty about its identification.

Adalin later explained that the photograph without the business signage matched the image submitted to his office by its appraisers. But he could not confirm whether the restaurant named “Prime Bistro,” as shown in other photos, was the same property, as the photographs in their records did not bear any signage.

“So, in other words, when you said you are sure the properties were the same, you are actually not sure? Because when the photos were shown, you said you are unsure, and now, after discussing with your staff, you changed your answer. Why are your answers shifting?” Pangilinan said.

“Just an observation that, clearly, there are inconsistencies in your testimony. Forgive me, Engineer, but you say one thing, and then you say another thing,” he added.

During questioning by Senator-judge Bam Aquino, Adalin also acknowledged that he had not checked all of Duterte’s properties in Barangay 74-A despite his earlier confirmation that the properties in the SALN and transfer certificate matched.

“I was unable to check all of her properties because the subpoena only specified the title ending 0775,” Adalin said, adding that his office could submit an official document detailing the couple’s properties in the area if required by the impeachment court.

He was also asked if he had determined how many properties Duterte owned in the barangay.

“I’m not sure, although if we’re required to submit an official document, we will produce, as required,” he added. – Rappler.com
