World.title: House pushes thousands more multi-purpose buildings. Are they really needed?
World.content:
House appropriations panel senior vice chairperson Albert Garcia says multi-purpose buildings can be used for Zumba, basketball games, and even as evacuation centers

How many multi-purpose buildings does the country need?

For members of the House of Representatives, apparently, thousands more.

In the House-approved version of the proposed 2027 national budget, lawmakers inserted an additional P42.7 billion for multi-purpose buildings.

That brings the allocation from the P41 billion proposed by the Marcos administration to P83.7 billion — more than double the proposal! The sum is enough to fund an estimated 5,765 buildings.

A lot, right?

For congressmen, not quite.

House appropriations committee senior vice chairperson Albert Garcia and other lawmakers defended the allocation, arguing that the country has tens of thousands of barangays that need such facilities.

“How many barangays do we have? 42,000 barangays. That’s a mere 10% (referring to the allocation for multi-purpose buildings) of the need of barangays across the nation,” Garcia said.

Lawmakers also claimed that requests from local government units for multi-purpose buildings continue to pour into their offices.

So, what exactly do barangays need all these buildings for?

Garcia said multi-purpose buildings can serve several purposes, from covered courts and daycare centers to classrooms and venues for community meetings.

“Alam ‘nyo po sa mga probinsiya at barangay na nasa labas ng Metro Manila, napakaimportante po nitong multi-purpose building,” Garcia said. (In provinces and barangays outside Metro Manila, multi-purpose buildings are very important.)

An analysis by People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) and BetterGovPH, however, showed that most of the allocation in the previous years for multi-purpose buildings were in Metro Manila.

He cited covered courts as an example, saying these can host Zumba sessions, barangay consultations, and basketball games for young people.

“Halimbawa, covered court. Diyan po nag-Zu-Zumba ’yung ating mga kababayan sa barangay na ’yun for healthy lifestyle. Diyan po nagme-meeting si kapitan para konsultahin ang kanyang mga ka-barangay. Diyan po nagba-basketball tuwing hapon ’yung ating mga kabataan para umiwas sa droga, para maging mas malusog kaysa puro gadgets na lang ginagawa ng ating mga kabataan,” he said.

(For example, a covered court. That’s where our constituents in the barangay hold Zumba sessions to promote a healthy lifestyle. It’s where the barangay captain holds meetings to consult with residents. It’s also where young people play basketball every afternoon to keep them away from drugs and encourage them to stay healthy, rather than spend all their time on gadgets.)

Play Video

But not everyone is convinced that the billions in additional funding are adequately justified.

PBC and BetterGovPH flagged the multi-purpose building insertions, saying publicly available supporting documents were lacking to establish the need for these projects.

Fuentebella, however, defended the insertions, insisting they went through the proper process.

“Lahat po nito nanggaling sa request nila. Hindi lang po sa kagustuhan ng mga kongresista. So it’s a bottom-up budgeting ang ginagawa natin,” Fuentebella said. (All of these came from requests made by the communities themselves, not simply from the congressmen’s own preferences. So what we are practicing is bottom-up budgeting.)

He said that there are documents to support these projects, but these have yet to be seen by the public.

This isn’t the first time Congress has substantially increased funding for these projects.

In 2026, lawmakers more than doubled the P29.7 billion allocation proposed in the National Expenditure Program, raising it to P79.9 billion.

Budget analysis of PBC and BetterGovPH also showed that the government has allocated P739.6 billion for 79,970 multi-purpose building projects from 2015 to 2026.

Perhaps, they want more multi-purpose buildings to put their names or initials? – Rappler.com

World.title: Ateneo coach Louie Alas slapped with 2-game ban
World.content:
The suspension of Ateneo head coach Louie Alas comes at a critical juncture as the fifth-running Blue Eagles chase a UAAP Final Four spot

MANILA, Philippines – Ateneo’s woes continue amid a crucial stretch in the Blue Eagles’ UAAP men’s basketball Final Four chase.

The UAAP suspended Ateneo head coach Louie Alas for two games “following the accumulation of two infractions” and his “unsportsmanlike conduct,” the league said in a statement on Monday, November 9.

Alas will serve his suspension on Wednesday, November 11, when the Blue Eagles battle the Adamson Falcons, and on Sunday, November 15, when they take on the UST Growling Tigers.

The penalty stemmed from two incidents involving Alas during a tense matchup last Saturday, November 7, where the Maroons outlasted the Blue Eagles, 82-74.

Right at the buzzer, Alas confronted the UP side before cooler heads stepped in to prevent the situation from escalating.

“With less than a second remaining, Alas entered the court, pointed at UP’s Jacob Bayla, and cursed at him following the latter’s dunk,” the league said in a statement. “He again pointed at and cursed at the UP player during the post-game handshake.”

The league said the Ateneo mentor also “engaged in an exchange with UP assistant coach Christian Luanzon despite attempts by UP coaches to pacify him.”

“The Commissioner’s Office determined that his actions escalated tensions between the two teams and risked a potential altercation.”

Prior to the end-game commotion, Alas entered the court at the 3:55 mark of the first quarter, complaining about a non-call.

Alas “remained on the playing court despite being warned by the nearest referee to return to the sideline,” the league said.

He was assessed a technical foul for unsportsmanlike behavior during the game.

The UAAP cited another Alas infraction during Ateneo’s loss to UST, 80-68, on October 17.

“At the 5:15 mark of the third quarter, he attempted to distract UST’s Amiel Acido as the latter attempted a corner three-pointer. After Acido converted the shot, Alas touched the back of the UST player,” the statement said.

“Although the incident was missed by the game officials, the Commissioner’s Office reviewed the play and imposed the appropriate disciplinary sanction under the UAAP House Rules and applicable FIBA regulations.”

Alas’ suspension comes at a crucial time as the Blue Eagles, running fifth with a 5-6 record, try to chase a Final Four spot with just three games left in the second round.

Ateneo can appeal the suspension.

Last October, Alas also served an automatic one-game suspension after accumulating three infractions. – Rappler.com

World.title: Lights go out at Russia’s Novaya Gazeta, after years of defiant reporting
World.content:
PRESS FREEDOM. Dmitry Muratov, former editor-in-chief of the Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta, holds a poster in support of jailed reporters outside the outlet's office as the newspaper shuts down, citing what it describes as a relentless campaign by the authorities, in Moscow, Russia, on November 9, 2026.

'We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has effectively ceased to function,' says Novaya Gazeta co-founder Dmitry Muratov, a co-winner of the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize

MOSCOW, Russia – Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta wound up its operations on Monday, November 9, and quit its central Moscow office, bowing to what it said was a campaign of state pressure that had made it impossible to carry on reporting.

Its co-founder Dmitry Muratov, addressing journalists who gathered to witness the newspaper’s closure, issued an impassioned plea for free speech and human rights in wartime Russia.

“Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today,” he said.

“We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has effectively ceased to function.”

The closure marks the end of one of Russia’s most influential independent news outlets.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was part of a “rotational process” in a fiercely competitive media environment.

Paper known for courage of reporters

The newspaper, renowned for fearless reporting that led to six of its journalists being murdered over the years, was founded by Muratov and the last Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, using money from Gorbachev’s 1990 Nobel Peace Prize.

Inspired by Gorbachev’s vision of “glasnost,” or openness, it became one of Russia’s most influential newspapers and defenders of democracy, with investigations into corruption and critical coverage of politics.

After President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale war with Ukraine in 2022 and Russia imposed tight censorship laws, the paper halted its print edition but continued to publish online, becoming a refuge for independent journalists who chose to remain in the country.

But it announced late last month that it would have to close after it was designated a “foreign agent” and ordered to vacate its offices, and banks stopped processing reader donations on which it relied for financial survival.

Muratov, a co-winner of the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize, said people needed to understand that it was the Kremlin that was to blame for waging the war and suppressing free speech.

“We cannot blame the citizens themselves for this — especially the wonderful, truly remarkable younger generation. I urge you to distinguish between the Russian authorities and the Russian people,” he said.

He called for a broader ceasefire in Ukraine following a six-day truce in one area brokered by US first lady Melania Trump in late October.

Muratov also urged the release of what he said were around 4,000 political prisoners in Russia.

The Kremlin defends the need for censorship laws, denies there are any political prisoners and says that Russia is taking necessary action at a time of war to prosecute people engaged in subversive activity.

It was unclear whether the newspaper would attempt to regroup and publish in another form. In a long article on its website, describing its final weeks, journalist Irina Vorobyova was quoted as saying its spirit would survive like a “good virus.”

“Not even a nuclear explosion could destroy it. It will continue in everyone who was part of it,” she said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Alex Eala records new career-high world No. 15, lands as Asia’s 2nd best
World.content:
Filipina tennis superstar Alex Eala trades places with Japan's Naomi Osaka as the new world No. 15 after a solid runner-up finish in her season-ending 2026 Hong Kong Open run

MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala continues to wade through uncharted waters in her blossoming tennis career as she notched yet another career-high world rank of No. 15 in the latest WTA rankings released on Monday, November 9.

With this newest rise on the women’s tennis leaderboards, the 21-year-old Eala has now traded places with Japanese star Naomi Osaka, who took Eala’s old No. 17 spot, while Romania’s Sorana Cirstea sits between them at No. 16.

Like her rise to No. 15, Eala’s switch with Osaka is a historic career feat in itself, as the Filipina sensation is now the second-highest-ranked Asian in the world, trailing only world No. 1 Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan.

Both Osaka and Eala have since ended their respective 2026 seasons, with the Japanese standout bowing out of the Toray Pan Pacific Open Round of 16 last November 1, and the Filipina falling to American Claire Liu in a one-sided Hong Kong Open final last November 8.

“This season, it hass changed my life. It has changed my life for the better,” Eala said at the Hong Kong Open awarding ceremony alongside Liu, who rose 33 spots from world No. 102 to 69 with her title win.

“I’m incredibly proud of the work we’ve put in this year, and we’re the only ones who truly know what it took to arrive to this point in our journey,” added Eala, whose ranking surged this year after a historic title run at the Washington Open, a WTA 500 event.

“Thank you so, so much. This is only the beginning. And this one, like all of them, is ours. Thank you, everyone.”

Joining Rybakina, Eala, and Osaka as Asia’s top five are top Chinese stars Qinwen Zheng at world No. 22 and Xinyu Wang at No. 38.

Completing the world’s top 5, meanwhile, are Rybakina, Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus, Mirra Andreeva of Russia, and familiar Eala rivals Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula of the United States at No. 4 and 5, respectively.

Eala soon heads back to the Philippines to further celebrate her career highs and 2026 season overall with a big homecoming event, “Alex Eala Live: Game. Set. Celebrate,” at the 55,000-seater Philippine Arena on December 8.

There, Eala will play Southeast Asia’s second-best tennis star, world No. 60 Janice Tjen of Indonesia, in a marquee exhibition. – Rappler.com

World.title: Senators urge Marcos to declare state of calamity in Super El Niño-hit areas
World.content:
EL NINO. A store attendant at Trabajo Market in Manila assists a customer purchasing a water container on October 6, 2026. According to the vendor, there has been a slight increase in customers buying buckets, water containers, and other vessels for water storage following reports on the effects of El Niño.

The Senate resolution notes that despite over 100 cities and towns declaring a state of calamity as of October 2026, only one in five farmers has received aid

CEBU, Philippines – Twenty senators on Monday, November 9, have called on President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to declare a state of calamity in areas affected or threatened by the Super El Niño, allowing access to funds to combat the weather phenomenon’s impact on the country.

Under Republic Act No. 10121, the declaration of a state of calamity mandates remedial measures such as the imposition of a price ceiling on basic necessities and commodities, monitoring and prevention of hoarding and profiteering activities, programming of funds for the repair and upgrading of public infrastructure, and the granting of no-interest loans to affected communities.

Upon the recommendation of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC), the senators, through Proposed Senate Resolution No. 765, urged the President to declare a state of calamity to address challenges being faced primarily by the agricultural sector.

Among those who signed the resolution were Senate President Win Gatchalian, Senate President Pro Tempore Tito Sotto, and senators Kiko Pangilinan, Migz Zubiri, Bam Aquino, Risa Hontiveros, JV Ejercito, Lito Lapid, Joel Villanueva, Erwin Tulfo, Raffy Tulfo, Ping Lacson, Chiz Escudero, Alan Peter Cayetano, Pia Cayetano, Imee Marcos, Robin Padilla, Bong Go, Camille Villar, and Mark Villar.

According to the Department of Agriculture, the country has reported P6.87 billion in agricultural losses across 249,028 hectares as of September 26 — nearly half of the recorded losses during the 2023-2024 El Niño.

“Planting season ngayon sa ating mga palayan at kailangan ng tubig. Kailangan mag-plant din tayo ng mga remedial measure tulad ng pag-impose ng price ceilings at laban sa overpricing, profiteering, at hoarding,” Pangilinan said.

(It’s planting season in our rice fields, and we need water. We also need to plant remedial measures, such as imposing price ceilings and policies against overpricing, profiteering, and hoarding)

On November 5, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) announced that a very strong El Niño was present in the tropical Pacific Ocean and is expected to persist until the first half of 2027.

According to PAGASA, the weather phenomenon will potentially reach its peak by the end of 2026, increasing the likelihood of rainfall deficits and, consequently, raising the odds of dry spells and drought in the country.

“Based on the latest drought assessment, five provinces experienced meteorological drought, 11 provinces were under dry spell, and 10 provinces experienced dry conditions in October 2026,” PAGASA Administrator Nathaniel Servando said in a statement.

The Senate resolution stated that while more than a hundred cities and municipalities have declared a state of calamity, the Department of Agriculture has managed to provide aid to only 2.53 million out of 11.12 million target beneficiaries. This means only one in five farmers are getting the help they need amid drought and dry conditions.

According to the senators, around P39 billion is available under the country’s disaster response fund. – Rappler.com

World.title: Marcos leads rollout of laptops for schoolteachers
World.content:
TOOL FOR MENTORS President Marcos and Education Secretary Sonny Angara lead the ceremonial turnover of new laptops to teachers at Dagupan City National High School on Monday. The President, accompanied by first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, Angara and Agrarian Reform Secretary Conrado Estrella III, later observed teachers test their latest classroom tool. —Presidential Communications Office

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos on Monday led the nationwide rollout of laptops for public school teachers, starting with a ceremonial turnover of 209 Apple MacBook Neo units in Dagupan City, Pangasinan.

The event, held at Dagupan City National High School, kicked off the distribution under the Department of Education’s Computerization Program. Of the 231,725 laptops distributed, 169,008 were MacBook Neo units and 62,171 were Acer Swift Air 14 laptops. An additional 3,646 MacBook Neo devices were allocated for administrative officers.

Dagupan City National High School received 72 MacBook Neo units, while nine other public elementary, integrated, and secondary schools in the city received a total of 137 units. The laptops are expected to benefit around 5,000 students and 312 school personnel.

Article continues after this 

READ: DepEd saves P1.4B in landmark procurement of laptops via open bidding

“The support for our teachers continues,” Marcos said in his remarks during that event. “Along with these laptops, we are also providing assistance and training to help you make the most of them in your teaching.”

Internet connection

The President also assured teachers that the laptops were procured “through proper processes in accordance with law.” Through public bidding, the government saved P1.4 billion in the laptop procurement compared with standard retail prices.

READ: DepEd: Over 172,000 teachers, staff to get Apple laptops

“With partners such as Apple and the National Educators Academy of the Philippines, we will help you use these tools in your classrooms so you can make the most out of them,” Marcos said.

Article continues after this 

He added that the government would ensure that schools have reliable internet connection so teachers can make full use of the laptops.

“Because when we provide our teachers with the tools they need for work, we are also ensuring that our children are learning better. We are giving our learners greater opportunities to compete with their peers around the world. And we are ensuring that our learners have a greater chance of winning in life,” he said. /cb

World.title: House to also delete undocumented infra items
World.content:
House plenary session —File photo by Grig C. Montegrande/Inquirer

MANILA, Philippines — The House of Representatives will join the Senate in striking out infrastructure budget line items lacking documentation, FPJ Panday Bayanihan Rep. Brian Poe said on Monday.

“We will not accept projects that do not have proper papers or proper coordinates because that is unfair to the constituents,” said Poe, assistant majority leader and vice chairman of the House Appropriations Committee.

Camarines Sur Rep. Arnie Fuentebella, also a vice chair of the House budget panel, affirmed Poe, saying “that is the stand of the leadership of the House.”

Article continues after this 

READ: Dy: House will soon launch transparency platform on its website

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said last week his chamber would remove about 295 infrastructure projects worth P8.8 billion from its version of the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for next year, citing lack of supporting documents for those projects.

Budget watchdogs had expressed concern over thousands of projects under the Department of Public Works and Highways that lack planning documents. —Kenneth Christiane Basilio

World.title: Nartatez: PNP getting tips in Dela Rosa manhunt
World.content:
PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. —Photo from Office of the Chief PNP/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police has received not less than 500 tips regarding its manhunt on Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said on Monday, adding that police are conducting operations in remote islands to locate him.

“These were properly validated; we went to the locations and conducted operations,” the PNP chief said. “And even islands that I haven’t heard of, our police went there and even islands and areas where you need to cross 11 rivers.”

READ: PNP welcomes Palace challenge, vows no special treatment for Dela Rosa

Article continues after this 

Nartatez expressed hope that Dela Rosa would be apprehended soon, saying they were praying for his arrest to happen in the near future.

READ: Palace to police chief: Get Dela Rosa despite PNP past

The International Criminal Court has a pending arrest warrant on dela Rosa over his role as PNP chief during the drug war of then President Rodrigo Duterte, who is detained by the Hague tribunal.

Sen. Panfilo Lacson, also a former PNP chief, had earlier advised authorities to observe operational secrecy in its pursuit of the fugitive senator. —Andrea Gregorio

World.title: Chinese-run fish cages blamed for displaced Pangasinan fisherfolk
World.content:
CROWDED Fish cages operated by Chinese aquaculture companies in the waters off Sual, Pangasinan, as seen in this photo taken on Oct. 26. Local fishermen claim the structures have encroached on their traditional fishing grounds, restricting their access to the area. —Photo courtesy of Nicasio Abata

SUAL, PANGASINAN, Philippines — As Pangasinan and Zambales fishermen lose their fishing grounds in the West Philippine Sea, marginal fisherfolk in this coastal town face a similar problem with the reported encroachment of Chinese fish cage operators in their traditional fishing grounds.

Local fishermen are demanding the removal of hundreds of fish cages they said have occupied Calpay Shoal in Barangay Cabalitian, where generations of residents have made their living.

They accused workers of the Chinese operators of driving them away from the waters where their families have fished for generations, forcing them to sail to nearby coastal towns instead.

Article continues after this 

READ: Carpio pushes new case vs China over fishing rights

The Cabalitian fishermen said the Chinese operators previously confined their operations to the Sual Mariculture Zone, where thousands of fish cages are located.

But allegedly because of water pollution in the mariculture zone, the operators began transferring their cages to Calpay Shoal in Cabittaogan Bay off Cabalitian Island, said Nicasio Abata, 80, leader of the Small Fisherfolk and Stakeholders of Cabalitian.

In an interview with the Inquirer on Nov. 7, Abata said 99 fish cage structures had been transferred from the mariculture zone before May this year, followed by another 33 cages shortly afterwards.

No permit?

“They have no permission from the barangay or the local government to transfer to Calpay Shoal, making their operations illegal,” Abata said.

Article continues after this 

According to the Sual Municipal Agriculture Office, it had not issued any permit or authorization for the placement of fish cages in the shoal.

“The unmitigated operations of these illegal structures have restricted the traditional fishing grounds of marginalized local fishermen, caused severe ecological degradation, and directly threaten the marine biodiversity of the sea,” the Cabalitian fishermen said in a petition submitted to various government agencies.

Article continues after this 

But the impact extends beyond the fishing community. At least 10 small resorts on Cabalitian Island are also affected by the fish cage operations, according to the fishermen.

The Sual municipal council recognized what it described as serious violations by the Chinese operators and conducted four separate legislative and fact-finding hearings to address the issue.

The municipal council directed the operators to dismantle the fish cages. Instead of complying, however, they constructed seven more illegal cages in the area, the fishermen said.

On Sept. 21, Municipal Administrator Michael John Millan issued a cease-and-desist order (CDO) against two Chinese companies.

The order stated that a field inspection confirmed the two firms were collectively operating 132 fish cage units outside the legally defined boundaries of the Sual Mariculture Zone.

The CDO prohibited the operators from restocking or starting new aquaculture production cycles at Calpay Shoal. It also directed them to immediately dismantle and remove the 33 cages and relocate the remaining 99 cages to their legally designated locations under their fishery privilege.

“Failure to dismantle the 33 structures will compel this Office to execute forcible demolition, permanent revocation of business permits and fishery privilege, and formal criminal prosecution against corporate officers under the full authority of the law,” the order said.

Despite the directive, the Chinese operators installed seven more cages in Calpay Shoal on Oct. 1 and another 12 on Nov. 6, Abata said.

Maricel Ambrocio, who represented the two companies, later signed a binding undertaking to remove all 33 fish cages from Calpay Shoal on or before Nov. 30, the final deadline set for clearing the area.

A municipal council committee report on Sept. 25 also recommended declaring Calpay Shoal an excluded zone reserved for traditional municipal fishing and vessel passage.

The fishermen said 284 residents signed their first petition against the fish cage structures on June 8.

According to the fishermen, their campaign was not directed against legitimate aquaculture operations within the designated mariculture zone, but against the occupation of traditional fishing grounds and the alleged operation of fish cages without the necessary permits.

They said they simply wanted their fishing grounds restored so they could continue earning a living from waters on which their communities had depended for generations.

Meanwhile, an aquaculture operator who has been operating inside the mariculture park said the number of Chinese nationals running fish cage businesses in the area had increased.

The operator also questioned the entry of a new player identified as “Thailander,” whom the operator claimed was also Chinese.

“They have been operating in Sual for decades but are not Filipinos of Chinese descent. They were not born here. They came from mainland China and came here only to take advantage of our resources,” the operator said. /cb

World.title: BARMM racing to pass 2027 regional budget
World.content:
Bangsamoro Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua —Bangsamoro gov’t photo

COTABATO CITY, BARMM, Philippines — Bangsamoro Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua directed all new Cabinet members and heads of offices on Monday to speed up their proposed budget allocations as the Bangsamoro Parliament laid down its priority legislative agenda for its first 100 days in office.

On top of the priorities is the passage of the proposed Bangsamoro Expenditure Program for Fiscal Year 2027 before the end of the year, otherwise, the region will have a reenacted budget in the coming year. Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao’s (BARMM’s) 2026 budget is P114 billion.

The BARMM Cabinet and Parliament have about 52 days before the year ends, including nonworking holidays, to pass the proposed budget.

Article continues after this 

READ: Macacua names new BARMM Cabinet members

Minister Ubaida Pacasem of the Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management clarified that ministries could modify their proposed programs and activities, provided these remained within their respective budget ceilings.

Cabinet members who recently assumed office requested sufficient time to review the proposals prepared by their predecessors, guided by the timeline for passing the new regional budget.

READ: Spending program, revenue code top agenda in first BARMM Cabinet meeting

Also included as a priority agenda within the first 100 days of the Macacua administration is creating a technical working group (TWG) to “right-size” the BARMM bureaucracy and establishing offices for senior advisers on parliamentary affairs and on religious and moral governance.

Article continues after this 

The agenda also includes creating two special offices to support transitioning Moro National Liberation Front combatants and the rehabilitation and development of their communities, creating a TWG to develop the legislation for the charter of the Bangsamoro Economic Zone Authority, and establishing a Bangsamoro State University System incorporating tertiary institutions transferred to the regional government.

Also on the priority list are convening the Council of Leaders and reactivating the Intergovernmental Relations Body to strengthen coordination between the Bangsamoro and national governments.

Article continues after this 

Integrity

During its first cabinet meeting, Macacua called on the newly appointed ministers and heads of offices to treat their positions as a responsibility to the Bangsamoro people, emphasizing integrity and accountability in carrying out the ruling coalition party’s development agenda.

“Our appointments are not merely positions of authority and privilege. They are, above all, an ‘amanah’, a sacred trust carried with the highest expectation of integrity, accountability, and genuine service to the Bangsamoro people,” Macacua said.

He noted that the next five years would be crucial for setting the direction of the first regular Bangsamoro government and strengthening the credibility of institutions built throughout the seven-year transition period that began in 2019.

World.title: Accountability, aid for Leyte fishers urged after submarine cable oil leak
World.content:
CLEANUP A Philippine Coast Guard officer removes oil residue along the shoreline of Barangay Tugas in Tabango, Leyte, on Monday, following a leak from an underwater transmission cable. —Photo from Philippine Coast Guard-Eastern Visayas

TACLOBAN CITY, LEYTE, Philippines — The Green Party of the Philippines Leyte chapter urged the National Grid Corp. of the Philippines (NGCP) to address the effects of the mineral oil leak off Tabango town, Leyte, and provide compensation to affected fishing communities.

The group said NGCP should take responsibility for the environmental damage and possible effects on the livelihoods of coastal residents, particularly fisherfolk.

“That is highly condemnable in the strongest possible terms. The NGCP should be penalized and must pay damages to the affected fisherfolk communities,” the group said in a statement on Monday.

Article continues after this 

READ: 250 kilos of oil waste recovered after NGCP cable leak in Leyte

According to the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG), it collected approximately 250 kilograms of oil-contaminated waste from the shoreline of Barangay Tugas in Tabango, as cleanup operations continue following an estimated 2,000-liter mineral oil leak.

The Marine Environmental Protection Unit-Western Leyte recovered another 50 kg of contaminated materials on Monday using absorbent pads along the affected shoreline near the NGCP Tabango Cable Terminal Station.

Disposal

In a statement, the PCG said the recovered materials were segregated, properly handled and placed in designated containers pending disposal in accordance with environmental regulations.

The leak was detected around 3 p.m. on Nov. 4 from Submarine Cable No. 7 of the Leyte-Cebu 230-kilovolt interconnection submarine transmission line, which connects Tabango, Leyte and Daanbantayan, Cebu.

Article continues after this 

READ: Visayas power woes may persist until 2028, DOE chief warns

According to NGCP, the leak was discovered about 5 meters offshore from its Cable Terminal Station in Barangay Tugas during low tide. The company estimated that around 2,000 liters of mineral oil had escaped into the coastal waters.

Article continues after this 

NGCP said it immediately deployed personnel to the affected area and installed containment and absorbent materials to prevent the oil from spreading. It also sought assistance from the PCG for containment and recovery operations.

The source of the leak was identified around 3 a.m. on Nov. 5, allowing response teams to concentrate containment measures on the affected section of the cable.

“NGCP is currently conducting an investigation to determine the cause of the oil leak,” it said in a statement when sought by the Inquirer for a reaction on the incident.

Coast guard personnel from Western Leyte, Ormoc and Villaba, together with the Marine Environmental Protection Unit-Eastern Visayas, also deployed containment booms and absorbent materials as part of the continuing response.

World.title: Legazpi City declared insurgency-free
World.content:
Officials of the Philippine Army and police officers, along with local government executives, release white doves during a ceremony marking Legazpi City’s declaration under Stable Internal Peace and Security status on Monday, Nov. 9. —Photo by Michael B. Jaucian

LEGAZPI CITY, ALBAY, Philippines — The Philippine Army has declared Legazpi City under Stable Internal Peace and Security (SIPS) status after recording no armed encounters or insurgent activities in the city over the past 12 months.

The declaration was made on Monday, Nov. 9 during a ceremony at the Legazpi City Convention Expo Hall A, recognizing the efforts of the local government, military, police, national government agencies and community stakeholders in maintaining peace and security.

Lt. Col. Cliff Chester L. de Ocampo, commander of the 31st Infantry (Charge) Battalion of the 9th Infantry Division, credited local officials and residents for their cooperation in achieving the milestone.

Article continues after this 

READ: 59 Bicol areas, entire Catanduanes declared insurgency-free – Army

“It is all about the cooperation of people and other stakeholders, plus the government agencies, in attaining a peaceful and secure community,” he said.

Councilor Charlton Lajara, chair of the city council’s committee on peace and order, said the declaration was based on the Army’s assessment showing no armed encounters or insurgent activities in the city over the past year.

Mayor Hisham Ismail said the improved security situation, particularly in the city’s southern communities, could help attract investors and encourage businesses to explore previously less-developed areas.

BGen. Ariel Reyes, acting commander of the 9th Infantry Division, said the declaration would give residents more opportunities to live peacefully, improve their livelihoods and pursue better economic prospects.

Article continues after this 

“An insurgency-free community could also boost investor confidence, encourage business establishments, generate jobs and accelerate development,” Reyes said.

He said sustaining peace would require community ownership and continued cooperation among residents, local officials and security forces.

Article continues after this 

Asked about the insurgency situation in the Bicol region, Reyes said it was nearing insurgency-free status.

“The remaining subregional communities of the New People’s Army (NPA) and communist rebels had been dismantled, weakening their organizational structure and capabilities,” he said. /cb

World.title: Bataan drug buy-bust operation uncovers alleged drug den; 7 arrested
World.content:
INQUIRER.net file photo

MARIVELES, BATAAN, Philippines — A police buy-bust operation that was supposed to target a suspected drug peddler led to the discovery of an alleged drug den inside a residential house along De Guzman Boulevard in Barangay Poblacion on Monday afternoon, Nov. 9.

Seven people, whose ages ranged from their mid-20s to 30s, were arrested, according to an initial police report sent to Police Col. Marites Salvadora, Bataan police director.

Mariveles police operatives, accompanied by barangay officials, were preparing to conduct the operation after receiving intelligence reports about the presence of a suspected drug peddler in the area.

Article continues after this 

READ: 5 arrested in Bataan drug bust

However, the police poseur-buyer reportedly spotted several men holding a suspected drug session inside the house, prompting the operatives to cordon off the property and arrest those inside.

READ: Shabu bust in Bataan nets 2 suspects

Residents welcomed the police operation, saying drug addiction had become a cause for concern in the community.

Sources also reportedly told police that Barangay Poblacion had become a known hideout for drug suspects and was later used as a drug den. /cb

World.title: Myanmar Foreign Debt Falls to $10.8b but Experts Warn of Collapse
World.content:
Despite World Bank data showing Myanmar’s foreign debt fell to US$ 10.8 billion in 2025, experts warn loan repayments by the internationally isolated regime are fuelling economic collapse.

Myanmar’s external debt dropped from $13.5 billion in 2021 to $10.8 billion in 2025, according to the latest figures released by the World Bank on November 5. The report said public and public-guaranteed loans account for 95 percent ($10.3 billion) of the total debt which comes under three categories: multilateral, bilateral, and private creditors.

The World Bank and International Monetary Fund are Myanmar’s primary multilateral lenders, owed $3.8 billion, with Japan and China its largest bilateral creditors (owed over $1.5 billion).

As Myanmar’s top international donor, Japan funds special economic zones and large-scale infrastructure including railways and power grids. Japan remains Myanmar’s biggest creditor despite cancelling over 300 billion yen ($3 billion) in debt to facilitate financial reintegration in 2013 and then suspending new loans after the 2021 coup.

Meanwhile, Chinese loans have financed key infrastructure, energy, pipelines, and Belt and Road projects across Myanmar. Regular regime payments halved Chinese debt from $3 billion to around 1.5 billion between 2021 and 2025.

However, analysts warn that the heavy burden of foreign currency repayments amid an international aid freeze and deepening economic crisis are fuelling kyat depreciation and severe shortages.

“Having to make loan repayments during an economic crisis and foreign currency shortage has driven the country into trouble,” said a local economist, who requested anonymity for safety reasons.

“Repayments may reduce the debt, but there is no money left for imports — and no international aid to cover the outflows.”

He added that as a developing nation, Myanmar is dependent on international funding such as concessional loans and development grants to fund large-scale infrastructure.

Post-coup economic mismanagement compounded by foreign sanctions and an exodus of foreign investors have plunged Myanmar into severe economic crisis. At the same time, escalating armed conflict around key economic projects has stalled their development.

Against this backdrop, the regime’s Ministry of Finance and Revenue recently stated that the soaring 2025–26 budget deficit was driven by a drop in funding from its closest allies, China, India, and Russia, as key projects hit security snags. Speaking to lawmakers, deputy minister Kyaw Htin acknowledged that the expected foreign funding failed to materialize.

With access to international loans limited, the rubber-stamp parliament in October approved short-term export credit from Belarus, sparking widespread criticism that the high-interest loan repayments will only deepen hardships for the Myanmar public.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Plans April Vote in 55 Constituencies Despite Continued Clashes
World.content:
Myanmar’s regime plans to hold elections in 55 constituencies across 37 townships on April 4, 2027, including 12 townships where it has regained at least partial control from resistance forces in recent years. Voting was not held in those 12 townships during the regime’s general election in December 2025 and January 2026, which was widely dismissed as a sham.

In an announcement Thursday, the regime said it would hold voting in 34 Lower House constituencies, using the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system; five Upper House constituencies; and 16 regional/state parliament constituencies across the country.

The townships include Tonzang and Falam in northern Chin State and Tigyaing, Banmauk and Indaw in Sagaing Region, all recaptured by the regime this year, as well as Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region, which it recaptured in 2025.

Also included on the regime’s list of townships scheduled to vote in April are Sagaing’s Kawlin, which the Myanmar military recaptured in 2024, and the Sagaing resistance strongholds of Pale, Yinmarbin, Shwebo and Taze.

A military analyst pointed out that the regime only controls the towns in Pale, Yinmarbin, Shwebo, Taze, Tigyaing, Banmauk and especially Indaw.

“The regime wants to show it is able to control the whole country, and that its administration is operating,” said Zin Yaw, a military defector who has monitored Myanmar’s conflicts since defecting after the coup.

The absence from the list of southern Chin State towns that the regime has been trying to retake since May 2026, as well as Arakan Army-controlled towns in Rakhine State, amounts to an admission by the regime that it hasn’t been able to restore its authority in these areas, he said.

The regime announced Lower House elections in Myeik, Tanintharyi Region; Nyaunglebin, Pauk Khaung and Padaung in Bago Region; Chauk and Minbu in Magwe Region; Pyin Oo Lwin, Meiktila, Natogyi, Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region; Kyaikmayaw in Mon State; Mayangone, Shwepyithar, Hlegu, Tamwe, Cocokyun and Hlaing Tharyar in Yangon Region; Kyaukme, Monghpyak, and Mong Pan in Shan State; Maubin in Ayeyarwady Region; and Zabuthiri, Dekkhinathiri and Ottarathiri in Naypyitaw.

The Upper House constituencies on the list are in Kachin State, Chin State, Magwe Region, Bago Region and Mandalay Region.

The list also includes state/regional parliament constituencies in Tonzang and Falam in Chin State; Tigyaing, Banmauk, Indaw, Kawlin, Pale, Yinmarbin, Taze and Shwebo in Sagaing Region; Zigon and Thegon in Bago Region; Natogyi, Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region; and Yegyi in Ayeyarwady Region.

The Myanmar military recently suffered heavy losses to resistance ambushes in Indaw Township. Clashes continue there and in upper Sagaing.

Despite the ongoing armed conflicts in many areas, political parties cooperating with the regime’s electoral process said they are making preparations for the vote.

Saw Than Myint, joint secretary of the Shan and Ethnic Democratic Party (SNDP), which secured 37 seats in the regime-backed general election, said the party plans to compete in the upcoming by-election but is still discussing details.

People’s Pioneer Party (PPP) chair Saw Han Aye said the party hopes to field candidates in at least one-third of the 55 constituencies, as required under the Political Parties Registration Law for parties competing at the national level.

He acknowledged that security concerns remain in some areas, adding that participation would ultimately depend on individual candidates’ willingness.

The PPP was founded by Thet Thet Khine, a former regime minister who was barred in October 2025 from running in the general election on grounds of violating rules on personal debts.

The Irrawaddy contacted People’s Party chair Ko Ko Gyi, a former 88 Generation student protest leader, about the party’s plans but received no response.

Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s regime organized the nationwide election in three phases in December 2025 and January 2026, with voting in 263 out of 330 townships. Civilian leaders, including Aung San Suu Kyi, remained imprisoned, while major opposition parties had been dissolved.

With only nine parties participating at the national level, the election was dominated by the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and allied parties, allowing the USDP to secure a majority of the seats.

Since installing himself as president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic campaign in an effort to gain legitimacy for his regime, visiting China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia and India, while his military forces continue targeting civilians in attacks and atrocities. The absence of elections in the 55 constituencies has underlined his regime’s lack of legitimacy, observers say.

World.title: Over 2m Myanmar Migrants in Thailand Reject Regime’s Identity Document
World.content:
Over 2 million Myanmar migrant workers in Thailand have participated in a poll calling on the parallel National Unity Government (NUG) to issue identity documents amid a mass boycott of the regime’s new Certificate of Identity (CI) process.

The poll also aims to demonstrate to the Thai government that they recognize the NUG as their legitimate government, not the military regime.

Thailand hosts an estimated 4 million Myanmar workers, both documented and undocumented. Migrant worker groups estimate that at least 600,000 are required to apply for CIs in this round. However, most are staying away from the regime’s newly opened Thai CI centers in protest against new tax and remittance rules that critics condemn as extortion. To apply, workers must prove they have remitted 25 percent of their wages through official regime channels and paid 2 percent annual income tax. The vast majority are refusing, fearing payment would help fund the regime’s war on civilians while lending it political legitimacy.

Meanwhile, Thai opposition lawmakers and labor rights groups have urged the government to review or scrap the centers, branding them a threat to national security and sovereignty.

The workers themselves made their overwhelming opposition clear in a weeklong online poll launched Sunday by the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT). Many appealed to Thai authorities to grant them work and residency permits without the CI document.

The poll result reflected resounding support among migrant workers for an alternative identification process managed by the NUG, Khin Soe of the MMWRCCT told The Irrawaddy.

“The regime CI process is a trap to extract foreign currency and information for military conscription,” he said. “The workers know this, so they don’t want to apply.”

He said the poll result would be sent to the NUG’s Labour Department to push for worker ID issuance, while a separate workers’ online petition would be delivered to the Thai government.

“The Thai government may argue it has to cooperate with the regime on the CI process to ensure national security, but we are appealing to them on humanitarian grounds. If they need an alternative authority to issue identity documents, this poll shows that millions of workers want the NUG to do it. As guests living under Thai law, we are not making demands, we are simply presenting these results as a respectful request,” Khine Soe said.

Launched on October 18, the campaign and petition contain four requests, including the right to stay and work legally without a CI, and has drawn support from Thai labour rights groups and politicians.

Among them is MP Anuson Tamajai, a prominent economist who urged the government to review or cancel the CI centers, arguing their unchecked operations compromise national security and sovereignty.

Highlighting migrant workers’ indispensable role in Thailand’s economy, he also called for an investigation into whether demanding remittance and tax payments in exchange for ID certificates violates Thai law.

The Thailand Migration Reform group recently warned that allowing Naypyitaw to control migrant registration “undermines Thai sovereignty and fuels corruption.” It urged Thai authorities to revert to the Pink Card system for migrant workers.

On Friday, Thai Labor Minister Julapun Amornvivat told media after a meeting of the Foreign Workers Management Policy Committee that CIs are required by migrants’ countries of origin for identity verification, but the process operates entirely within Thai territory.

He said his ministry will send a formal letter to its regime counterpart expressing opposition to the mandatory remittance policy, arguing it undermines migrant worker rights and fails to align with international standards.

Dismissing the backlash, the cash-strapped regime has doubled down on its push to skim foreign currency from low-paid overseas workers. Newly appointed Labor Minister Maung Myint has threatened workers with legal action and a ban on returning home if they don’t make tax and remittance payments.

However, the boycott shows no sign of weakening, with only a trickle of applicants reported at the five CI centres across Thailand since they opened on October 14.

World.title: China Wields Carrot and Stick at Beijing Meet, Regime Seeks Elections in Shan, and More
World.content:
We’ll always hold your hand, Beijing promises Myanmar regime

“China will always be a strategic partner that Myanmar can rely on,” Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Myanmar investment minister Aung Kyaw Hoe on the sidelines of the 11th Lancang–Mekong Cooperation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting on Tuesday.

The reassurance came as part of a carrot-and-stick package amid alarm in Beijing over recent meetings between U.S. and Myanmar officials that seemed to augur the start of re-engagement.

The U.S. has released an Integrated Country Strategy for its mission in Myanmar, which identifies goals for expanding Washington’s diplomatic, economic and humanitarian influence in the country. Besides singling out scam networks, it also sets goals for boosting American exports to the impoverished war-torn country and gain access to Myanmar’s “bountiful” rare earth resources—besides aiming to “counter China’s influence.”

Myanmar is China’s most important external source of rare earth minerals and a major global source of heavy rare earth elements, particularly dysprosium and terbium, which are essential for electric cars, wind turbines, advanced electronics and military technologies. But mines are concentrated in areas beyond the reach of the regime in Kachin and Shan states.

Online scam operations have become a major point of convergence and competition in the two superpowers’ approach toward Myanmar. During the meeting with Aung Kyaw Hoe, Wang urged his regime to prevent the “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, referring to the vast scam compounds that flourished there.

China grows impatient over stalled investment projects

But in the same meeting Wang applied plenty of stick, urging Myanmar’s regime to get a move on in realizing long-stalled projects that form part of the planned China–Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) that would provide Beijing with overland access to the Indian Ocean. Wang told Aung Kyaw Hoe the two sides must “coordinate development and security” so they can “steadily advance” key CMEC projects.

Wang’s message echoed remarks made by his President Xi Jinping during regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Beijing in June, when Xi also called for swift implementation of CMEC projects.

The corridor’s flagship schemes include the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port and special economic zone in Rakhine State and a planned railway linking Kyaukphyu with Yunnan via Mandalay and Muse. On China side, the railroad is already entering its final phase but on the Myanmar side fighting continues across many parts of the route.

Aung Kyaw Hoe promised the regime is doing all it can but, true to form, also used the occasion to beg for even more Chinese investment.

Border trade gates reopen as armed groups consolidate control

China has significantly eased restrictions on trade through several Myanmar border crossings controlled by Beijing-linked ethnic armed organizations, allowing fuel, medicines, construction materials and other previously banned goods to enter northern Shan and Kachin.

The move suggests China is adjusting its border policy to accommodate new realities on the ground, where it appears the military regime in Naypyitaw has permanently lost control. With Operation 1027, key border trade gates and routes in northern Shan fell into the hands of the ethnic Chinese Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), and its erstwhile partner in the Brotherhood Alliance, the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA).

Beijing initially closed the crossings to pressure them into making peace with the generals, but trade has long resumed and is now growing exponentially.

According to Chinese Customs at the Mengding crossing with MNDAA-controlled Chinshwehaw, the total value of trade there and at nearby Mangka eached 4.92 billion yuan in the first eight months of this year, up 49.3 percent on-year.

Customs figures also show increased trade through Namhkam crossing controlled by the Ta’ang National Liberation Army, as well as through the Kyin San Kyawt gate controlled jointly by the Brotherhood Alliance in Muse Township, which once accounted for some 70 percent of cross-border trade. The regime still controls a couple of crossings in Muse, where it bans the import of fuel from China.

In a move to prevent those groups from financing their armies through cargo taxation, the cash-strapped regime is now reduced to blocking routes south of Lashio, imposing a crackdown on what it calls “smuggled” goods—which in reality means roadside extortion.

Late last month, Min Aung Hlaing urged his ministers to intensify their crackdown on illegal trade and make sure that cross‑border commerce is conducted only through “legal” channels, i.e. those his regime controls. Myanmar’s consul general in Kunming met with the customs department director this week to discuss facilitating flows of “officially traded goods” between the neighbors and improving cooperation on customs procedures.

Naypyitaw seeks to roll out elections into Shan borderlands

Defence Minister Yar Pyae who also chairs the junta’s peace negotiation committee, this week visited areas held by China-linked ethnic armed groups with a view to rolling out the regime’s sham elections across their part of the country as well.

Yar Pyae went to Panghsang, the headquarters of United Wa State Army (UWSA), and Mongla, the fiefdom of the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA) near the Chinese border. The visit comes after Chinese Special Envoy to Myanmar Deng Xijun urged granting “high-level” autonomy to ethnic minorities.

Together with the MNDAA, they are widely regarded as being under heavy Chinese influence, with Chinese widely spoken and the yuan used as the major currency in their territories.

All three trace their origins to the 1989 mutiny that fractured the Communist Party of Burma. Most people in NDAA territory are ethnic Chinese with roots in Yunnan, but the Wa are a Mon‑Khmer-speaking people more closely related to the Palaung.

Both the UWSA and NDAA have long upheld ceasefires they signed with the military in 1989 in return for de-factor autonomy in their areas, sustained by cross‑border trade and Chinese investment.

In Mongla, Yar Pyae discussed holding the vote, which was omitted there when the regime orchestrated polls in the parts of Myanmar it controls in the winter of 2025-26 that led to military dictator Min Aung Hlaing declaring himself president. Naypyitaw is aiming for next April, regime media said. But none of the townships under the control of the UWSA or NDAA were included on the junta’s recently announced list of constituencies slated for catch-up and by-elections.

Historically, no national elections have been conducted either in Mongla or Panghsang, although voting has taken place in some townships of the constitutionally defined Wa Self-Administered Division where government administration was present. Formally, the UWSA is stuck at a stage of demanding official statehood, and the NDAA is demanding official autonomous status.

World.title: Arakan Army Faces Second Front at Bangladesh Border
World.content:
Amid intensified fighting as the Arakan Army (AA) closes in on the Arakan (Rakhine State) capital of Sittwe, a second front is heating up along the border with Bangladesh, where regime-aligned Rohingya armed groups are escalating conflict.

These attacks are not isolated border incidents. They reflect a history of cooperation between Myanmar’s military and Muslim armed organizations during the 2024 battles for Buthidaung and Maungdaw. For Bangladesh, they raise difficult questions about its security interests and the prospects of repatriating the hundreds of thousands of Rohingya refugees now within its borders. For the AA, they raise the question whether it can maintain stability across its home state.

A major concern is that armed networks established during the military regime’s territorial retreat are continuing to exert pressure on the AA while the main body of its forces confronts the regime elsewhere.

From cooperation to proxy warfare

During the 2024 Arakan offensive, the military suffered major territorial losses. Facing the AA’s advance, it cast around for additional manpower and local allies, and alighted on armed organizations that, ironically, were associated with a population it had systematically persecuted. One of them was the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA).

The International Crisis Group has documented the regime’s ammunition supplies to ARSA, along with recruitment arrangements that transferred Rohingya refugees to military facilities for training.

ARSA and another armed group, the Rohingya Solidarity Organization (RSO), received training, weapons and tactical support during the fighting while maintaining contacts with regime personnel after the AA captured Maungdaw in December 2024, according to the Transnational Institute.

Here was the military that was responsible for the 2017 atrocities that drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya into Bangladesh, brazenly cooperating with Rohingya armed organizations against the AA.

For the junta, however, the strategic advantages outweighed any qualms it might have had. Armed groups operating along the state’s northern frontier could challenge AA positions even after its own conventional military bases had fallen, and thereby divert precious resources from the AA’s other battlefronts.

As a bonus for a regime that has long sustained itself by divide-and-rule tactics, it risked deepening mistrust between the state’s Arakanese and Muslim communities.

Maungdaw remains a strategic front

Thus when the AA eventually captured Maungdaw, it transformed the military balance along the Bangladesh border but could not fully eliminate the armed groups operating through remote terrain and cross-border networks.

In September last year, ARSA fighters attacked an AA border security position near Inn Chaung village in northern Maungdaw. AA forces subsequently retook the position, while the attackers reportedly fled to Bangladesh.

Further clashes followed, and by late October this year, residents reported that ARSA was renewing recruitment, armed movements and attacks against AA outposts in northern and southern Maungdaw.

“ARSA activities have resurged in both northern and southern Maungdaw Township,” one resident told my news organization, Development Media Group.

With the AA confronting regime forces around Sittwe, repeated ARSA attacks could now force it to divert much-needed troops, intelligence resources and supplies to the border.

This would benefit Myanmar’s military even without direct command of these operations.

There is an important caveat. ARSA, RSO and a third militia active at the border, the Arakan Rohingya Army (ARA) have distinct leadership structures and interests. Their historical cooperation with the military regime does not mean that every recent attack was centrally coordinated.

Bangladesh’s border dilemma

A further complication lies in Bangladeshi involvement in these skirmishes. The AA accuses certain officers of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) of providing the Rohingya armed groups with logistical assistance, ammunition and intelligence, and allowing them to operate near border security positions.

The International Crisis Group, too, has documented the complicated relationships between these groups and elements of Bangladesh’s security establishment.

The allegations require credible investigation, but any such shenanigans must also be distinguished from official Bangladeshi government policy. Publicly, the BGB has denied supporting ARSA or the RSO.

Bangladesh faces legitimate challenges involving border security, with more than 1 million Rohingya refugees and the prospect of their eventual repatriation creating a massive headache for Dhaka.

But it will eventually have to confront the reality that the territory from which the refugees fled is now controlled by the AA, and that fundamentally changes the political realities.

Some Bangladeshi security personnel may still regard these avowedly Muslim armed organizations as potential leverage over the AA. But helping them with their cross-border attacks would now in fact undermine border stability and make peaceful repatriation more difficult.

In other words, Bangladesh’s security interests would be better served by stopping ARSA and co. from exploiting refugee communities, and instead maintaining effective communication with the AA authorities controlling the opposite side of the border.

Beyond armed groups and military control

The motivations behind Rohingya armed mobilization long predate any cooperation with Myanmar’s military.

Decades of discrimination, statelessness, displacement and uncertainty have created grievances that armed organizations can exploit. Refugees facing declining humanitarian assistance and limited opportunities are particularly vulnerable to recruitment and intimidation. But that cannot justify attacks on civilians, abductions or forced recruitment.

Nor should ARSA, RSO and ARA be treated as representative of Muslim communities as a whole. The Arakanese, Muslim and other communities in Maungdaw face threats from armed violence, disrupted livelihoods and insecurity. Abuses by all armed participants, including the AA, require impartial investigation and accountability.

The AA’s territorial gains have brought responsibilities extending beyond military security. Effective governance means it must protect civilians regardless of ethnicity or religion, address grievances and prevent communal tensions from escalating.

The Maungdaw conflict demonstrates that territorial control does not necessarily end a war.

Myanmar’s military has lost most of its positions in Arakan, yet its airpower, remaining military strongholds and historical relationships with armed groups continue to complicate the AA’s security calculations.

Preventing further escalation requires credible investigation of alleged weapons supplies and cross-border assistance, effective border management, protection of refugees from coercive recruitment, and sustained engagement between Bangladesh and the AA.

It also requires meaningful dialogue with Muslim civilian representatives and equal protection for all communities.

Unless the networks and grievances sustaining violence are addressed, no lasting peace can come to Arakan.

Aung Marm Oo is the editor-in-chief and executive director of Development Media Group, a news agency based in Arakan. He faces charges under Myanmar’s Unlawful Associations Act and has been in hiding since May 2019.

World.title: Hurry Up With Our Investment Projects, China tells Myanmar Regime
World.content:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has renewed Beijing’s call for the Myanmar regime to “steadily advance” key projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), which is designed to give Beijing direct access to Indian Ocean.

Wang made the remarks during a meeting on Tuesday with Myanmar Investment and Foreign Economic Relations Minister Aung Kyaw Hoe, who is in Beijing for the 11th Lancang–Mekong Cooperation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.

A clearly exasperated Wang stressed the need for the two sides to “coordinate” development and security, as many parts of Myanmar are plagued by civil war, making it hard for the China-backed projects to proceed.

In turn, Wang promised Chinese support for the rebranded regime’s efforts to achieve international recognition. “China will always be a strategic partner that Myanmar can rely on,” he said.

The remarks come as the U.S. shows signs of re-engaging with Naypyitaw in search of business.

Wang also called for stronger efforts to combat scams and online gambling. He urged Myanmar to prevent the “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, referring to online scam operations that flourished along the Thai-Myanmar border.

He urged Naypyitaw to do more to ensure the safety of Chinese nationals, organizations and projects operating in the country.

Aung Kyaw Hoe, for his part, promised that his regime does want to accelerate the CMEC projects and step up cooperation with China and regional countries in combating online scam operations. He duly thanked his hosts for supporting Myanmar in international forums, according to a statement from the Chinese Embassy.

When Myanmar’s putschist leader Min Aung Hlaing last visited Beijing in June after declaring himself president, Chinese President Xi Jinping also urged him to speed up the CMEC projects, a key component of Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

He too urged the regime to provide stronger security guarantees for Chinese personnel and investments in Myanmar, many of which are in areas now controlled by the resistance or ethnic armed organizations over which Beijing holds no sway.

The planned corridor includes several flagship projects, notably the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port in Rakhine State and a railway linking Kyaukphyu through Mandalay and Muse with China’s Yunnan Province.

The Kyaukphyu Special Economic Zone and deep-sea port project is particularly important for Beijing because it would provide China with direct access to the Indian Ocean while supporting economic development in Yunnan and other southwestern Chinese provinces.

But other than pay lip-service to the plans and hold out its hand for more investment, the Myanmar regime has done little to advance these projects, instead losing itself in dreams of reviving the long-mothballed Myitsone Dam Project in quite a different part of the country.

In its frustration, China has now reopened border crossings with areas controlled by ethnic armed organizations in northern Shan State to allow lucrative trade to resume, whether the regime likes it or not.

A China analyst told The Irrawaddy that Beijing “knows very well that Min Aung Hlaing’s stubbornness is holding everything up. The fighting is still going on, the peace talks haven’t delivered any results, there’s been no progress in northern Shan State, and the border crossings are still not operating normally.”

For the CMEC projects to move forward, Min Aung Hlaing “has to engage in talks with the ethnic armed groups first,” she added. “In that sense, I think China was quite deliberately sending that message.”

World.title: Kyat Slump Disrupts Thai Border Trade as Import Costs Rise
World.content:
The rapid depreciation of Myanmar’s currency has disrupted border trade with Thailand, prompting some traders and money changers along the border to suspend transactions as they struggle to cope with volatile exchange rates and mounting import costs.

The currency weakened to around 680 baht per 100,000 kyats this week, down from more than 700 baht in recent weeks. The currency also fell against the U.S. dollar, with the market exchange rate rising from just above 4,700 kyats per dollar at the end of October to more than 4,900 on Wednesday. The rate was just around 4,400 kyats in early October.

The latest slump is fueling concerns over another wave of inflation in a country heavily reliant on imports from Thailand. Myanmar imports a wide range of goods from its neighbor, including electrical appliances, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and foodstuffs, making fluctuations in the baht exchange rate significant for consumers.

Market insiders attributed the kyat’s latest decline to the regime’s plan to borrow 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to finance a budget shortfall for fiscal year 2026-27, which ends on March 31. The regime has already sold treasury bonds worth trillions of kyats, leading to speculation that it will simply print banknotes to cover the deficit.

They also pointed to Myanmar’s continued inclusion on the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) blacklist, delays in export licensing and policy inconsistencies between ministries as factors undermining confidence in the market.

The swift depreciation of the kyat has left traders struggling to price goods and manage working capital.

“A gradual rise doesn’t create much difficulty. The problem is when rates surge rapidly,” a trader in Myawaddy told The Irrawaddy.

“If exchange rates rise further, we will need more capital to restock. Some traders have temporarily stopped trading and making payments, and are waiting to see where the market moves.”

The uncertainty has spread beyond traders. Some major money changers in Myawaddy and across the border in Thailand suspended transactions on Wednesday, opting to wait for the next day’s opening rates before resuming business, according to border exchange operators.

The volatility is not confined to the Thai border. Traders in Muse, on Shan State’s border with China, are facing similar difficulties as the kyat continues to weaken against the yuan, market sources said.

Traders warn that prolonged instability in foreign exchange markets could further squeeze trade. Importers say their profits are shrinking, but are reluctant to increase prices for fear that demand may decline further.

A trader in Myawaddy said transport costs remain a major contributor to rising prices, with expenses along trade routes increasing because of checkpoints and demands for unofficial payments.

“Price increases are caused more by transport costs than exchange rates,” he said. “Costs at checkpoints rise sharply whenever authorities announce crackdowns or tighter controls.”

Exporters also say the weaker kyat is raising shipping costs because freight charges, container fees and port services are paid in U.S. dollars. At the same time, they complain that mandatory foreign-exchange conversion rules prevent them from fully benefiting from higher market exchange rates.

Under existing regulations, exporters must convert 35 percent of their export earnings at the Central Bank’s official rate, creating a significant gap between official and market rates. The Central Bank’s official reference rate remains 2,100 kyats per dollar, while its market trading rate is about 3,660 kyats per dollar. The market rate was around 4,900 kyats on Thursday. Before the coup, the kyat traded at roughly 1,300-1,400 per U.S. dollar.

An exporter from Mon State explained that the depreciation of the kyat has sharply increased the capital required to buy export commodities such as corn and onions.

“Previously, we could buy a container of goods for 10 million kyats from local producers. Now it can require more than 15 million kyats,” he said.

Traders say prices of Thai imports, particularly electrical goods, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and food items, are already climbing as a result of the stronger baht and rising transportation costs.

World.title: Thai Foreign Minister to Visit Myanmar Ahead of ASEAN Summit
World.content:
BANGKOK—Thailand’s foreign minister said he will visit Myanmar on November 12, days before a regional summit where Bangkok will be pressing to normalize ties with the war-torn country.

Sihasak Phuangketkeow’s trip also comes during raised tensions along the countries’ shared border, where Bangkok said clashes between Myanmar’s military and ethnic rebels caused property damage and injured a Thai civilian in Thailand on Thursday.

His visit, announced late Tuesday, is scheduled shortly before a November 16-18 summit of leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Manila.

Myanmar’s leaders have not been invited to high-level ASEAN meetings since former general Min Aung Hlaing led a 2021 military coup that ousted democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war.

Sihasak told reporters in Beijing his government wants to “hear Myanmar’s latest position” ahead of the summit.

“De-escalation by all parties will help create a conducive atmosphere for essential dialogue and the peace process,” he said.

“If there is progress on these fronts, it will be a positive factor for ASEAN to consider at the leaders summit, as we decide how to move forward on the situation in Myanmar, including Myanmar’s participation in ASEAN meetings,” he added.

Sihasak, who last visited Myanmar in April, said he would meet his counterpart, Tin Maung Swe, on November 12, and a meeting with Min Aung Hlaing was “in the works”.

In July, Bangkok hosted a meeting between Tin Maung Swe and foreign ministers of several ASEAN member states, the first such gathering since the 2021 coup.

The following month Min Aung Hlaing met with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul in Bangkok, with the two nations’ military chiefs holding talks two weeks after.

Min Aung Hlaing took over as civilian president in April following elections widely dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Since then he has been given a red-carpet welcome across the region, in India, China and several ASEAN nations.

Myanmar is expected to send a senior civil servant to the Manila summit.

Thailand has stepped up security on its western frontier following last week’s cross-border fire.

On Wednesday, Myanmar’s military blamed “terrorist insurgents”—the term it commonly uses to refer to ethnic-minority armed groups and pro-democracy forces—for wounding a Thai national, according to a statement in state media.

World.title: Kazakh Athletes Win Gold in Aerial Hoop Competition in Italy
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s athletes Gauhar Zhanaliyeva and Bakhyt Kadyrova won first place in the duet aerial hoop discipline at an international pole and aerial sports competition held in Turin, Italy, on Nov. 6-8.

The competition brought together athletes from several countries. Representing Kazakhstan in the aerial hoop discipline, Zhanaliyeva and Kadyrova competed in both duet and solo categories.

“Thanks to our physical preparation, artistry, choreography and stage presentation, we managed to take first place,” Zhanaliyeva told The Astana Times.

The competition marked their first international event. They are now preparing for their next competition, scheduled to take place in Bishkek, the Kyrgyz Republic, in December.

World.title: Astana Hub Marks Eight Years With $6.7 Billion in Ecosystem Revenue
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s international technology cluster, Astana Hub, is marking its eighth anniversary, with ecosystem participants generating $6.7 billion in total revenue, $2.4 billion in IT services exports, and attracting more than $2 billion in startup investment since 2019.

Today, the ecosystem brings together 2,700 companies, including 560 with foreign participation, positioning Astana Hub as a key center for technology entrepreneurship, investment, and innovation in Central Eurasia, Astana Hub reported on Nov. 6.

“Today, Astana Hub is a fully fledged technology ecosystem bringing together 2,700 companies, including 560 with foreign participation. It provides an environment where ideas become products, startups grow into international businesses, and talented people find opportunities to fulfill their potential,” said Astana Hub CEO Magzhan Madiyev.

He noted that the ecosystem’s achievements reflect sustained efforts to develop entrepreneurship, technology and human capital, adding that its greatest accomplishments are measured not only by economic performance but also by the people, companies and technologies shaping Kazakhstan’s digital economy.

Expanding regional and international presence

Astana Hub’s network now includes 20 regional IT hubs, which serve as centers for IT education, startup development and local technology communities. Since their launch, they have hosted more than 5,200 events, attracting 80,000 participants and showcasing 700 startups.

Kazakhstan’s technology profile has also been strengthened through major international events, including the Digital Qazaqstan forum in Shymkent, AI & Digital Bridge 2026 in Astana and the first GITEX AI Kazakhstan.

Another milestone was HackAlem AI, which brought together 2,415 participants and set a Guinness World Record with the participation of NVIDIA and OpenAI.

Astana Hub is also expanding its international presence through innovation hubs in the United States, the United Arab Emirates, China, Malaysia and the United Kingdom. Its international programs help Kazakhstan startups access foreign markets, investment and expertise.

Developing AI and technology talent

Education and workforce development remain central to the ecosystem. TUMO Astana currently serves 2,430 teenagers aged 12 to 18, offering training in 11 digital and creative disciplines, including programming, robotics, game development and generative AI.

The Tech Orda program has trained 11,410 people through 133 IT schools, with 90% of graduates reportedly employed. Meanwhile, Tomorrow School, Kazakhstan’s first peer-to-peer artificial intelligence school, has expanded to 14 cities and currently has 481 students. More than 80 participants have secured IT positions before completing the program.

Another initiative, ML School Kazakhstan, launched with academic support from the Yandex School of Data Analysis, received 822 applications for its first intake, with 32 participants enrolled in the two-year program.

The ecosystem also supports early-stage entrepreneurs through incubation and acceleration programs. Startup Garage has supported more than 1,400 projects, while Silkway Accelerator has graduated 83 startups. The AI’preneurs program has produced 125 graduates and 51 startup projects, generating more than $618,000 in combined sales and attracting $400,000 in investment.

Supporting startups and investment

Astana Hub Ventures provides investment support to technology companies, with a portfolio covering more than 90 startups. Its 2026 portfolio includes Higgsfield, Mirai Tech, Perceptis, PanDev Metrics, Luwo, Admyra, Resti and Scano.
