World.title: Breaking: Todd Russell, Beaconsfield mine disaster survivor, dies
World.content:
Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor Todd Russell has died at the age of 54 after a medical illness, his family has confirmed.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff posted this morning: "Vale Todd Russell. Thoughts this morning are with Todd's loved ones and everyone who had the absolute pleasure of knowing him."

Russell was one of two Tasmanian miners thrown into the world spotlight after becoming trapped by a rockfall on Anzac Day 2006.

He and co-worker Brant Webb were presumed dead after the body of a third miner, Larry Knight, was found amongst the rubble, nearly a kilometre underground.

But the pair were discovered alive, trapped in the basket of the vehicle they had been working in — a space about the size of a dinner table.

"We had how many tonnes of rock suspended above us like a jigsaw puzzle and we only needed one rock to move for it to come crushing in, killing Brant and myself," Russell told ABC podcast I Was Actually There in 2024.

Initially, Russell could only move his forearms and his head: "Everything else was completely buried," he told the ABC.

" You can imagine the bone bruising from the rocks that landed on top of us. "

The pair survived on a single muesli bar and groundwater that seeped through the nearby rocks for the five days it took before rescuers, who had been blasting a new tunnel to reach them, made contact.

As Australia's TV news crews joined the growing scrum around the Beaconsfield mine tower in April 2006, work went on underground to save Russell and Webb.

Australia and the world were captivated, and then on May 9, the pair emerged not only to cheers, but to their lives forever changed.

Loading...

"It was just a constant barrage of media frenzy for days on end," Russell told the podcast.

"Like reporters hanging over your fence when you're trying to have a cup of tea and a bit of toast for breakfast.

"It was constant, not only for the first few days, but probably for the first 18 months.

Todd Russell and Brant Webb emerge from the Beaconsfield mine shaft after two weeks underground. (ABC News)

"I hated it because you went to work as a normal person, and you come out of there with your identity lost. And people felt that they knew you because they'd been watching you for 14 days."

There was a book about the mine collapse within months of the pair's rescue.

The following year, rock band The Foo Fighters released a song called 'Ballad of the Beaconsfield Miners'.

Todd Russell and Brant Webb pictured during an interview about their ordeal. (Channel Nine: Channel Nine)

A telemovie, Beaconsfield, was released to mark the sixth anniversary of the pair's rescue.

Behind all of this was a man struggling with mental ill health, exacerbated by the loss of his parents in the years after his rescue.

Todd Russell speaks to the media as he leaves the Launceston Magistrates Court on July 24, 2008, during the inquest into the mine disaster. (Dale Cumming: AAP)

He told the podcast he came home one day to find his wife and kids packed and in the car, ready to leave him.

The disaster that 'shocked' a town and brought worldwide attention Twenty years later, the Beaconsfield mine rescue continues to defy belief.

"There was only one person that couldn't see the direction that I was heading, and that was myself," he said.

Russell sought professional help to deal with his experience inside the collapsed mine — and the aftermath of the event.

He told the podcast that in 2024 he had been working on rebuilding his relationships and that he had become a proud grandfather.

Todd Russell waves as he arrives at Launceston Hospital, after being rescued. (Reuters)

Russell did not venture into a mining career until he was in his late 20s.

Above ground, he was a keen footballer and hunter, and later, he became part of the Beaconsfield Fire Brigade, retiring as its chief in 2026.

But publicly, he was best known because of the famous mine rescue.

Todd Russell served as a firefighter for his local region of northern Tasmania. (Facebook: Todd Russell)

In 2022, he told sports podcast The Friday Frothy he saw himself in two ways:

"There's Popeye, who's a big tough man. But there's Tweety Bird. Behind the scenes, a lot of people don't see when I go and sit and cry.

"I put on a tough exterior when I'm out in public and stuff, and they think, 'Oh, he's going alright,' but they don't realise I'm hurt.

" I still can't understand why I was spared that night and why I'm still here. "

Todd Russell was a keen hunter. (Facebook: Todd Russell)

"Obviously I was kept here for a reason — whether it's to go and speak at safety conventions and talk to people about how life is much better than it can be with the help of professionals.

" I get up every morning and thank my lucky stars I get to see another day. "

Todd Russell (centre), pictured in early November 2026. (Facebook: Michael Ferguson)

On November 3, Russell took to social media to announce that "years of pain, uncertainty, appointments, treatments, setbacks, and endless battles plus the emotional exhaustion of having to pick myself up time and time again, have left me with nothing left to give".

"The time has come, medically and physically, where there are no further options on either front for me & there is no more fight left in me.

"I will leave hospital tomorrow after 8 and a half months for the last time to see out my days in my own home surrounded by my wife, kids, loved ones and friends.

"A massive thank you to the incredible staff at the Launceston General Hospital; their overwhelming support, care and kindness have helped to soften the daily grind of what has been an incredibly difficult journey."

Todd Russell is survived by his wife and children.

World.title: Police officer wore explicit patch on uniform during teen's arrest
World.content:
A WA Police officer displayed an obscene phrase on his uniform while arresting a teenager, body-worn camera footage obtained by the ABC has revealed, as he allegedly offered the boy bail in exchange for information.

WARNING: This story contains material which might be offensive to some readers.

The phrase "FOLD C**TS" was emblazoned on a patch worn by Constable Lachlan Costello while he was detaining a 16-year-old on suspicion of burglary in the Mid West WA city of Geraldton in September 2024.

Police say the phrase is a "common" term and the constable is "well-regarded by local youth".

Colloquially, "folding" can refer to hitting someone with enough force to make them collapse.

"Folding" can also refer to a controversial restraint used by youth detention officers in WA, which was banned in 2022 following a Four Corners investigation.

Camera switched off

Body-worn camera footage, obtained from police via a Freedom of Information (FOI) request, shows Constable Costello handcuffing the teenager and seating him inside a car to question him.

About 90 seconds later, the officer turns off his camera.

The 16-year-old later pleaded guilty to possession of unlawfully obtained property. (Supplied)

Video from a different officer's body-worn camera shows Constable Costello later gesturing for his colleague to follow him around the corner to talk.

Still wearing the patch with the explicit language on his chest, Constable Costello tells the other officer: "He [the teenager] doesn't know anything."

But four seconds of the audio from the video released by WA Police has been muted.

In that missing audio, which is uncensored in a version seen by Aboriginal Legal Service WA (ALSWA) lawyers, the ABC understands Constable Costello admits offering the 16-year-old bail in exchange for information.

"I told [the teenager] if you tell us everything, we'll get you off bail. Off camera, obviously," Constable Costello says in the uncensored recording, according to the ALSWA.

The officer then appears to notice his colleague's bodycam recording, saying, "Oh your f**king …" before momentarily raising his hand to obscure the camera.

Constable Lachlan Costello covers his colleague's body-worn camera after he realises it is recording. (Supplied)

ALSWA director Peter Collins said there was "no good reason" for WA Police to censor the audio of Constable Costello's admission.

"Police should never be offering an inducement of being given bail in order to extract admissions from somebody," he said.

Peter Collins says the officer's patch is "one of the worst" things he has seen from police aside from physical violence. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

The arrested 16-year-old had $10,000 cash and cannabis in a bag, and later pleaded guilty to possession of unlawfully obtained property.

WA Police said its internal affairs unit investigated Constable Costello, who was "served a managerial notice" for wearing the patch, offering bail, questioning the teenager without notifying a responsible adult and breaching body-worn camera use policy.

Mr Collins said there should be no place for such conduct in the police force.

"Who knows what that managerial intervention actually constituted? I suspect it was a slap over the wrist, and nothing more," he said.

'Worst I've seen'

Mr Collins said the fact Constable Costello wore the explicit patch while making an arrest, and in the presence of other colleagues, was "despicable".

"It shows a callous disregard for the responsibilities entrusted in him as a sworn police officer," he said.

" Aside from cases where police have used actual force unlawfully … this is right up there as the worst thing I've ever seen. "

The explicit label was clearly visible on Constable Lachlan Costello's chest. (Supplied)

A similar explicit phrase was written on a wrist strap worn by rugby league player Kane Evans during a 2021 game. The NRL fined him $5,000.

Officer 'well-regarded'

Police said Constable Costello was actively engaged with the young local community through sport where the term was "common".

"He remains well regarded by local youth. While this context was considered, it does not excuse the conduct," a WA Police spokesperson said.

" On this occasion, the officer exercised poor judgement and was appropriately sanctioned and educated. "

Mr Collins said any officers who were aware of the patch were complicit in the behaviour.

"He's there with his colleagues who would have seen it, and presumably senior officers at the police station at which he works would have also seen it," Mr Collins said.

Constable Lachlan Costello and the four other officers who attended the incident in September 2024. (Supplied)

WA Police said it was an "isolated incident".

"The patch was identified by a supervisor and the matter was addressed at the time," a spokesperson said.

"It was subsequently confirmed the patch had been removed before the officer attended his next incident."

Camera obstruction 'not a one-off'

Mr Collins said while the patch was "unprecedented", officers turning off or blocking their body-worn cameras occurred frequently.

He said other officers at the scene of the September 2024 arrest also appeared to intentionally obscure their cameras.

"There's no proper basis for any of this behaviour by the police on this occasion, and it's not a one-off," Mr Collins said.

WA Police said the "deliberate obstruction or inappropriate use of body-worn cameras" was not an accepted practice.

"Where concerns regarding the use of body-worn cameras are identified, they are investigated and dealt with appropriately," a spokesperson said.

World.title: Leaked documents reveal confidential Woodside deal with traditional owners
World.content:
Traditional owners say Woodside's proposed $50 billion expansion into the Browse Basin cannot go ahead while a confidential mining agreement over its most valuable asset remains "unfit for purpose".

They have broken their silence in a push to modernise the 1998 land access deal that ushered in the North West Shelf joint venture, more than 1,530 kilometres north of Perth.

The agreement for Australia's biggest oil and gas project was written more than a decade after scores of sacred Indigenous sites, some of which were thought to date back 50,000 years, had been demolished by its construction.

The agreement covers Woodside's Karratha Gas Plant, which processes 14 per cent of WA domestic gas. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

Speaking publicly for the first time, senior present and former members of Ngarluma-Yindjibarndi Foundation Limited (NYFL) decried the document's signing and claimed it pressured elders who could not read or write

"Ngurra (country) is the main thing for our people: to have our country, not to be destroyed, not to be touched or damaged," elder and NYFL director Ricky Smith said.

" They should be paying for it because it's our country. "

The construction of the gas plant predates the agreement by more than a decade. (Supplied: Ken Mulvaney)

Woodside is seeking to shore up gas production at the facilities by tapping the Browse Basin off the Kimberley coast and pumping the resource to its Karratha Gas Plant via a 900km pipeline.

The ABC understands NYFL tabled a new agreement at a meeting with Woodside executives last November, calling for $30 million a year on the assumption currently approved gas fields will deplete within the next 10.

Woodside countered the $300 million package in May with an offer of $20 million cash for the same period, on top of the terms agreed upon in 1998.

The company would also transfer NYFL 20 homes over 10 years and $400,000 annually to manage the properties.

Ricky Smith says Woodside needs to negotiate a new agreement to ensure the community becomes stronger. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

NYFL chief executive Sean Paul Stephens said the organisation had formally asked government not to approve Woodside's bid for Browse while talks were at an impasse.

Woodside said it was "proud" of its long-standing relationship with NYFL but acknowledged the negotiations.

"The North West Shelf Project recognises that expectations and standards for agreement making with Aboriginal communities have evolved significantly since 1998 and is working with NYFL to modernise the arrangements," a spokesperson said.

Confidential terms

The near-200-page agreement followed a native claim lodged by the Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi people for the Pilbara region's Burrup Peninsula in the early 1990s.

The two language groups are among five with cultural ties to the peninsula, a landscape scarred by colonial violence and traditionally known as Murujuga.

By NYFL's calculation, the $500,000 compensation alone equates to about $50 to $100 per cultural site affected. (ABC News: Chris Lewis)

The deal, viewed by the ABC, included a lump sum of $500,000 "as compensation for deprivation of any possession of land or waters".

These funds were used to establish NYFL and released the gas joint venturers of liability for damaging the area's dense collection of Aboriginal rock art.

The meaning behind Murujuga's petroglyphs Ahead of UNESCO releasing its final assessment of the area's world-heritage potential, the Burrup's traditional owners tell the stories behind the landmark rock art.

NYFL estimates 1,700 engravings were moved and thousands more destroyed to build the North West Shelf's onshore processing facilities.

By its calculation, the $500,000 compensation alone equates to about $50 to $100 per cultural site affected.

The agreement also set out strict confidentiality and no-challenge clauses that former NYFL chairperson Clinton Walker says have stifled people from standing up for country.

"We were forced with gag clauses … we couldn't speak up for what we wanted," Mr Walker said.

Clinton Walker says elders did not understand the 1998 deal. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

Another $2.5 million was put aside by the deal for the Roebourne Cultural Centre, along with "goodwill" annual donations of $1.25 million to NYFL, partly indexed to inflation.

In 2019, Woodside said it updated some conditions after NYFL declared insolvency, increasing its community investment across a complex suite of programs.

NYFL correspondence obtained by the ABC said Woodside currently provided the foundation about $1.7 million each year, unlike the value-based royalties paid by other Pilbara mining companies.

In October, Woodside posted a year-to-date operating revenue of $17 billion.

NYFL estimates 1,700 petroglyphs were removed and more demolished. (Supplied: Ken Mulvaney)

A 2023 study by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development found certain streets of Karratha and Roebourne, two towns close to the gas project, were among the most disadvantaged in Australia.

Mr Stephens says traditional owners bore the greatest costs of WA's resource boom and gained little material benefit.

"It is being locked out of the engine room that people describe the Pilbara to be," he said.

"The life expectancy for First Nations men in the Pilbara is almost 30 years less than a non-Indigenous person like myself, and that tells us that the system is broken."

Elders allegedly pressured

In 2003, the WA government brokered the Burrup and Maitland Industrial Estates Agreement (BMIEA) for the land around the Karratha Gas Plant and not covered by the NYFL deal, extinguishing native title rights to clear the way for further industrial development.

A few months later, the Federal Court ruled Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi native title did not extend to the Burrup Peninsula.

The layout of agreements on Murujuga. (ABC News)

It leaves NYFL's path to a new agreement unclear, with no legal right to the compensation provisions that have led other groups to win payouts for economic and spiritual loss.

Mr Walker, who was a teenager in 1998, said Woodside was eager to pre-empt the native title decision, and some elders did not understand what they were signing.

"They didn't really know a lot of English. They couldn't read," Mr Walker said.

A Woodside spokesperson said the agreement was fairly understood under the future act stipulations of the Native Title Act 1993, and all signatories received independent professional advice.

Several of the elders signed with the letter "X" because, NYFL says, they could not write their names. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

NYFL opposes Browse

Ahead of a Commonwealth decision to extend the North West Shelf for 40 years, NYFL wrote to successive state and federal environment ministers in the hopes of securing support for a new deal.

It never received a response.

Minister knew of rock art fears before granting Woodside extension The federal environment minister was advised pollution from Woodside's Karratha Gas Plant may be causing irreversible changes to ancient rock art, before granting the company a 40-year extension with strict conditions.

When federal Environment Minister Murray Watt approved the extension in 2025, he did so with 48 conditions aimed at protecting the surviving Murujuga rock art, which received a UNESCO World Heritage listing shortly after.

He said he weighed these heritage risks against the project's social and economic benefits, but did not mandate a modern agreement with NYFL.

Woodside is now awaiting permission to breach Australia's largest undeveloped gas reserve in the Kimberley's Browse Basin.

The project is expected to cost upwards of $50 billion to develop and, according to Deloitte modelling, generate more than $141 billion in gross domestic product over a 31-year span.

NYFL says Browse must not be approved with the 1998 agreement unresolved.

Mr Smith said it was about ensuring a legacy for the generations to come.

"Make a good agreement with each other to benefit and help our family to get strong," he said.

World.title: Thousands choose festive favourite as 2026 Australian Insect of the Year
World.content:
The gold Christmas beetle is the newly crowned 2026 ABC Australian Insect of the Year.

The golden-jacketed summer visitor from northern Queensland won over more than 39.3 per cent of online voters in the annual campaign run across the ABC News website.

The gold Christmas beetle was chosen by 17,454 voters in the ABC's online poll. (Supplied: Alan Henderson, Minibeast Wildlife)

A grand total of 44,472 people voted for the third ABC Australian Insect of the Year, with 17,454 nominating the gold Christmas beetle (Anoplognathus aureus) among a field of six finalists.

The poll proved a beetle quinella, with the cute-as-a-button tortoise-shelled ladybird (Harmonia testudinaria) snaring just under a quarter of the vote (11,069 votes, 24.9 per cent).

Just under a quarter of respondents voted for the tortoise-shelled ladybird. (Supplied: Peter Rowland, PRPW)

The mysterious Otway glow-worm (Arachnocampa otwayensis) was selected by 10.9 per cent of respondents (4,830 votes) to sneak onto the podium, just ahead of this year's plucky underdog, the stalk-eyed signal fly (Achias australis) with 10.1 per cent (4,508 votes).

The Otway glow-worm earned 10.9 per cent of votes. (Supplied by Karl Magnacca, iNaturalist Australia)

Two spectacular butterflies: the Mallee bronze azure butterfly (Ogyris subterrestris) and orchard swallowtail butterfly (Papilio aegeus) secured 8 per cent (3,574) and 6.8 per cent (3,037) of the vote respectively.

The unusual stalk-eyed signal fly captured just over 10 per cent of votes. (Supplied: Kai Squires, iNaturalist Australia)

This year's Australian Insect of the Year campaign received nominations from the CSIRO (Dr Keith Bayless), Australian Entomological Society (Dr Mark Schutze), Zoos Victoria (Jessie Sinclair), Gardening Australia magazine (AB Bishop) and nature author-photographer Peter Rowland.

However, it was Invertebrates Australia founder and director Kate Umbers who nominated the gold Christmas beetle as a finalist.

Kate Umbers selected the gold Christmas beetle as a finalist. (Supplied: Invertebrates Australia)

Dr Umbers says it is a timely victory as scientists try to unravel why there are fewer Christmas beetles seen than a few decades ago.

"We know that at least some of the Christmas beetle species are in trouble from a conservation point of view," Dr Umbers said.

" Some [Christmas beetle] species haven't been seen in decades. "

"This result tells us people do love them, they care about what's happening to them, and that gives us hope we can bring them back from the decline we suspect they're currently in.

"Our memories from childhood have the power to drive conservation today.

"Being named [Australian Insect of the Year] gives me hope those childhood Christmas beetle memories will continue for many generations to come."

The critically endangered Mallee bronze azure butterfly polled about 8 per cent of the overall vote. (Supplied: Indra Bone, iNaturalist Australia)

Lost beetles

The announcement of the 2026 Australian Insect of the Year coincides with several conservation programs, including Australian Pollinator Week (November 7-15) co-ordinated by the Wheen Bee Foundation, and Bugs in my Backyard week (November 16-22), a national citizen science campaign run by Invertebrates Australia and the Invasive Species Council.

The orchard swallowtail butterfly, a common garden visitor, attracted 6.8 per cent of votes. (Supplied: Peter Rowland, PRPW)

Invertebrates Australia also conducts a conservation program dedicated to Australia's 35 Christmas beetle species.

"We're asking people to record any Christmas beetles they see around them all summer," Dr Umbers said.

"We are getting a fantastic data set now after five years of the Christmas beetle count.

"We're really starting to understand the patterns coming through for Christmas beetles, including some which hadn't been seen for 20 or 30 years.

"Researchers can jump in and see if it's one of those Christmas beetles that haven't been seen in a long time."

The duck-billed Christmas beetle (Anoplognathus montanus), one of 35 or 36 Christmas beetle species. (Supplied: Peter Rowland, PRPW)

Invertebrates Australia invites Australians to upload Christmas beetle sightings and photographs to the iNaturalist Australia website, an online network which can be accessed by scientists.

"It's really exciting we are getting such a rich data set," Dr Umbers said.

"This one allows us to do all kinds of important things like assess their conservation status and get conservation actions in place for the Christmas beetles that need it the most."

The ABC's Australian Insect of the Year was launched in 2024 to promote Australian native invertebrate conservation.

That first online poll received 13,593 votes across six finalists, with the blue-banded bee (Amegilla cingulata) winning with more than 50 per cent of the vote.

Last year 23,915 Australians voted in the second online campaign, with the graphic flutterer dragonfly (Rhyothemis graphiptera) taking out the award with just under 26 per cent of the total vote.

Past Insect of the Year winners, the blue-banded bee (2024) and graphic flutterer dragonfly (2025). (Supplied: Peter Rowland, PRPW)

Veteran entomologist Ken Walker, who nominated last year's champion, said the response this year showed many Australians were beginning to appreciate the vital role insects played in our ecosystem.

"I feel people are beginning to see invertebrates as so much more than just 'creepy crawlies'," Dr Walker said.

Ken Walker is hopeful attitudes are changing towards insects and other invertebrates. (Supplied: Museums Victoria)

"There is an innate fondness for cute, furry and cuddly.

"Insects were not seen that way in the past, and that may now be changing."

Dr Walker said as views towards insects changed, it opened up the possibility for deeper conversation.

"That's the big thing; once you get past that, you can start to talk about conservation," he said.

World.title: Oscar Piastri spilts with manager Mark Webber
World.content:
McLaren Formula 1 driver Oscar Piastri and fellow Australians Mark and Ann Webber say they have ended their management agreement.

Nine-time Grand Prix winner Webber began working with Piastri in 2019 and was instrumental in Piastri joining McLaren in 2023 to replace compatriot Daniel Ricciardo, rather than staying at Alpine.

Renault-owned Alpine had wanted to promote Piastri to a race seat after double world champion Fernando Alonso announced he was leaving for Aston Martin, but the Australian rejected the offer.

Norris suffers champagne mishap in Brazil Lando Norris was near perfect to claim victory in Brazil.

"We are proud to have played a pivotal role in the formative years of Oscar's career and to have placed him in F1 so that he could compete at the front so early in," Webber said in a statement on Monday.

"Following our reduced trackside involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close.

"This will allow Oscar to build on his achievements under a new management structure and for us to embark on our new ventures."

Piastri, who won back-to-back titles in Formula 3 and Formula 2 in 2020 and 2021, thanked the pair for support and recognised their guidance had been invaluable.

The Australian has not won a race this season, after looking like he might win the championship last year before being overhauled by teammate Lando Norris and ending up third. He finished sixth in Brazil on Sunday.

The winner of nine grands prix has not been on the podium for 16 races and is seventh in this year's standings.

Reuters

World.title: Share price tumbles as Nvidia investigates CEO and 'foreign intelligence'
World.content:
Shares of Nvidia have tumbled more than 5 per cent after the computer chip maker opened an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort".

Nvidia's announcement of the investigation followed Mr Huang's acknowledgement that he had been intimate with a business executive who, according to The New York Times, US intelligence determined was gathering information for China.

China's Foreign Ministry dismissed the spying allegations as a smear campaign against Beijing.

Nvidia chips power many of the data centres and computing systems used to train and run AI models.

Its advanced processors have also been a focus of US export restrictions aimed at limiting China's access to cutting-edge semiconductor technology.

There's a small chance Mr Huang is removed or steps down as CEO, wrote Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., saying Mr Huang is "not replaceable".

"On the heels of last week's blue tidal wave, [in the midterms elections] this will also increase momentum for more regulatory scrutiny in the Beltway, especially around China and chip restrictions, at a time the AI arms race is heating up into its next gear between the US and China," Ives wrote.

Still, Mr Ives said there is a risk, as Mr Huang could be removed as CEO depending on the board's investigation and that it will remain an overhang on shares near term.

Shares of Nvidia and other major AI companies have sold off steadily since early October on growing fears of a bubble in the sector.

Nvidia has fallen 23 per cent in the past 30 days, including Monday's sell-off, local time in New York.

Nvidia's stock slid $US10.48 to $US176.16. Shares hit an all-time high last month.

AP

World.title: Live: Wall Street roars despite Nvidia spy slump, ASX set to rise
World.content:
NEXTDC boss Craig Scroggie is in a world of pain.

A community dispute has disrupted a big build, causing the share price to crater. That low price enticed a rival to buy almost 10% of the stock.

He told a conference late yesterday winning community support had become the company's top priority.

NEXTDC had previously said it would stop work on all projects without customer contracts following a big setback on a facility in the inner-west of Melbourne.

"The last couple of weeks [I] certainly didn't expect to be in the position we're in today having to deal with some delays," NEXTDC's chief executive, Craig Scroggie, told the UBS Australasia conference.

"That's unfortunately probably reflective of the global environment in relation to the engagement, social licence, people's feelings about artificial intelligence and data centres being the physical embodiment of that."

Scroggie said the M3 delay meant the top priority was to win community backing for that project and "anything that didn't have a customer contract and a customer commitment that we absolutely have to deliver on is now no longer a priority".

The company previously announced it would pause projects where it didn't have a customer signed up to take on the "compute" created by it.

He did not say how many projects would be paused. The company had 11 centres in development or in the planning stages, according to its 2026 annual report.

"That work can't restart until we clearly communicate that we've solved this problem, that we've earned the trust of everybody that's been supporting us, and then we will get back to work."

NEXTDC's rivals Goodman Group and its New York-listed partner, Digital Realty bought a 9.9% stake in the company last week following the share price plunge.

"When you have a challenge like we've had in the last couple of weeks, it's not really any surprise to me that people … look at that and say, now might be the time," Scroggie said.

Goodman and Digital Realty said they had no plans at the moment to launch a takeover offer, but reserved the right to do so. They said they would "look forward to a potential collaboration with the NEXTDC board and management on the ways and forms in which the parties may help to address the challenges facing the company".

Following their share raid, NEXTDC's share price recovered the ground lost from the earnings writedown.

The company has its annual general meeting in 10 days.

- with Reuters

World.title: Popovic refuses to blacklist Socceroos who pull out of Jordan friendly
World.content:
Australia coach Tony Popovic insists Socceroos players who are reluctant to play Jordan due to security concerns will not be blacklisted from the national team set-up if they elect to withdraw from his squad.

The Socceroos, currently in camp in Doha, face Qatar in a friendly on Saturday, before they are expected to make the trip to Amman to take on Jordan next Wednesday.

Players have privately questioned the value of the friendlies due to the postponement of January's Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia to December 2027, and because of the security risk posed by travelling to Jordan.

Socceroos wary of Jordan friendly due to security threats The Socceroos have named an under-strength squad for upcoming friendlies against Qatar and Jordan, with Football Australia to monitor security in Jordanian capital Amman.

"If players are available for selection moving forward in any camps, any decisions made [in November] will not affect their possibility or availability for selection," Popovic said.

While usually rated one of the safer countries in the Middle East, Jordan has been the subject of heightened security concerns after a stabbing in Amman and an attack on an orthodox church in the country's south.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) advises Australians to reconsider their need to travel to Jordan "due to the unpredictable security situation" and the "threat of terrorism".

"The plan is to play the games, unless something else changes," Popovic said. "The safety and the wellbeing of the players and staff is of paramount importance."

Indonesia cancelled a friendly in Jordan this month, while the players' union, Professional Footballers Australia, said the Socceroos players had "overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated".

Alex Robertson has withdrawn from the friendly against Jordan for personal reasons. (Getty Images: Steve Christo)

The Socceroos coach revealed on Monday that Cardiff midfielder Alex Robertson had withdrawn from selection due to personal reasons — not related to security concerns — while Nashville's Patrick Yazbek had pulled out with an undisclosed injury.

Jackson Irvine has been left out after becoming a father for the first time, while back-up goalkeeper Paul Izzo remains in Denmark as he awaits the arrival of his first child.

Mat Ryan has been left out of the national team set-up for the second successive international window, leaving questions over the veteran goalkeeper's long-term Socceroos future.

"I think with [Ryan] and some of the other players, the focus just shifted with the Asian Cup changing. I'd like to see some other goalkeepers," Popovic said.

Popovic has left out Mat Ryan (pictured) for the second consecutive international window. (Getty Images: Jay Barratt)

"With 12 months of planning coming up I wanted to give some boys a chance; we haven't seen Joe Gauci or Tom Glover for a while.

"We [Ryan and I] have had discussions and he understands the decision."

Meanwhile, Popovic is taking a relaxed approach to his contract situation.

His deal was signed to expire at the conclusion of the Asian Cup but the delay by 11 months has thrown his commitment up in the air.

At the same time, reports in England have named Popovic as a potential contender to take charge of Premier League side Crystal Palace.

The Palace role would be a major step up for a coach who hasn't managed in a top-five league.

"I think both parties are comfortable with the situation," Popovic said of his Socceroos contract. "We've got no issues with how this is progressing."

AAP

World.title: NRL officially clears Parramatta star Addo-Carr to resume career
World.content:
Breaking SportNRLNRL 2026 NRL officially clears Parramatta star Addo-Carr to resume career Adrian Proszenko Updated November 10, 2026 — 8:17am ,first published November 6, 2026 — 5:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The NRL has officially cleared Josh Addo-Carr to resume his NRL career, a move that ensures he will be part of Parramatta’s side for their season-opening clash in Las Vegas. The Eels resolved at a board meeting on Friday to retain Addo-Carr after he produced a false-positive result for cocaine at a random police roadside test. However, the last impediment to a return was getting the green light from the NRL’s integrity unit, which was investigating the circumstances of the incident. Loading That came on Tuesday morning, ensuring one of the game’s cult heroes can resume his career. “We are obviously very happy with the outcome,” said Addo-Carr’s high-profile lawyer Elias Tabchouri.



“This has been a difficult process to navigate. We are very thankful to both the Parramatta Eels and the NRL for the way they have approached this matter. “We are very relieved for Josh and his family and are looking forward to him having a stellar year for the Eels.” Addo-Carr will now be able to participate in pre-season training and add to his tally of 234 first-grade games. Josh Addo-Carr is set to resume his career with Parramatta. Getty Images While “The Foxx” will get the chance to fulfil the final year of his $450,000 contract, the 31-year-old has paid a price as a result of the incident. It has cost him, an incumbent Australian representative, the chance to be considered for Kangaroos selection for the World Cup.



Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2026 Addo-Carr reveals financial cost of false-positive drugs test There was also a financial cost after a raft of existing or prospective sponsors – including JAC Motors, P&O Cruises, Rexona, Nike, DoorDash, Red Bull, Weighplate and television series Rivals: Sport vs. Sport – cut ties after his initial roadside drugs test. The value of those endorsements is estimated to be worth close to $400,000, a figure almost as high as his playing contract. Addo-Carr spent about a month in rehab after the incident. The former Storm star was sacked after providing a positive roadside test while employed at Canterbury in a separate incident two years ago. Last week, Addo-Carr – who arrived at his Monday meeting with the board clutching a religious book specifically aimed at prison inmates – said he was hopeful of continuing his NRL career. “I have always been committed to the Parramatta Eels and nothing has changed,” Addo-Carr said in a statement provided to this masthead on Tuesday.



“I turned up today with a book that has changed my life and this is a chance to put into practice what I’ve learnt. I feel like I’ve still got so much to give this club and community. “I appreciate the Eels giving me an opportunity to provide my version of events and I hope I get another chance to pull on the blue and gold.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

Washington: Republican congressman Thomas Massie filed a resolution to impeach Pete Hegseth, arguing the defence secretary abused the power of his office by waging war against Iran without congressional approval and in the absence of an imminent threat. Massie, who has split from President Donald Trump and the administration on several key issues, read out the impeachment resolution in the House of Representatives on Monday afternoon (US time). Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, filed an impeachment resolution against Pete Hegseth. Bloomberg Over eight articles of impeachment, Massie accused Hegseth of violating multiple sections of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, ignoring laws that minimise civilian casualties, conducting extrajudicial killings of people on boats alleged to be carrying drugs, suppressing free speech and kidnapping a foreign leader. Hegseth, speaking earlier on Monday, defended his record as having made the world a better and safer place, and dismissed criticism as “politically motivated”. He said he was not worried about gathering enough votes to defeat the impeachment resolution.



The defence secretary was also backed by President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who both called the attempt to impeach him “unfair”. Speaking in the House, Massie alleged Hegseth had breached the War Powers Resolution because he “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation [Iran]” without authorisation by Congress. Pete Hegseth in the Philippines last month, where he also met with Defence Minister Richard Marles. Getty Images Hegseth continued to break the law by ignoring a congressional resolution directing the president to remove US forces from hostilities with Iran, Massie said. Massie also accused Hegseth of ignoring laws that minimise civilian casualties, citing the death or injury of more than 200 civilians at the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran on the first day of the war.



Hegseth directed the Defence Department in a manner that “foreseeably dismantled the safeguards necessary to distinguish civilian objects from military objectives”, he said. Massie put on public record details of the incident, for which the Pentagon has not admitted responsibility. The school was hit by three BGM-109 Tomahwak cruise missiles fired from US Navy warships, he said. They struck between 10.23am and 10.45am on a Saturday morning, while students were at the school. Loading “Secretary Hegseth thereby effected the murder of civilians and abused the trust of the men and women under his command by requiring them to conduct military operations within a targeting and legal-review system that he had deliberately degraded,” Massie told the House. In other articles of impeachment, the Republican congressman accused Hegseth of the extrajudicial killings of 243 alleged drug traffickers on small boats in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean.



By killing people who were merely suspected of criminal conduct – and without establishing a lawful basis for treating them as military targets – Hegseth “arrogated to himself and the Executive Branch the roles of judge, jury and executioner, and asserted a unilateral power to determine who may live and who may die”, Massie said. He also accused Hegseth of suppressing free speech by attempting to intimidate Democratic senator Mark Kelly over criticism, kidnapping a sovereign foreign leader by the abduction of Venezuela’s then president Nicolás Maduro, and executing an unlawful war in Yemen through Operation Rough Rider in March 2025. President Donald Trump has stuck by Pete Hegseth despite conjecture that the defence secretary could be dumped from cabinet. AP Massie told the House that Hegseth acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law, and had demonstrated that he would remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office. Republicans still control both chambers of Congress until January. The resolution could pass the House if a small number of Republicans join Democrats in voting to impeach Hegseth, though he would then have to be convicted in the Senate to be removed from office.



Massie – who is retiring from Congress – had widely telegraphed his intention to reintroduce a resolution to impeach Hegseth following last week’s midterm elections. Related Article Analysis

US politics ‘Fog of war’ might excuse an admiral, but it won’t let Hegseth off the hook Hegseth has scheduled a news conference about the impeachment for Tuesday morning (US time), but defended his record when he briefly spoke to reporters while travelling on Monday. “We’re not worried about that,” he said of the impeachment proceedings. “There’s a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements - but their disagreements are with success. “Getting our European partners to step up is historic. Getting these countries in central and South America to come together into a counter-cartel coalition and put the cartels on the run is historic.



“The things that we’ve accomplished in [operations] Midnight Hammer and Absolute Resolve and Southern Spear and Epic Fury are things that will change the face of the globe for a generation. “We are very proud of the president’s America First agenda, of our ‘peace through strength’ posture. We know the world is a better and safer place as a result. So if we want to litigate that, the success of those things, I’m happy to do it all day long.” Hegseth said people who took issue with what the US did in those military operations were “taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished”. Trump said during an interview on CBS’s 60 Minutes on Sunday that he had confidence in Hegseth, and it was “very unfair” to try to impeach him. “We had two wars, we won both. We won Venezuela, we won Iran,” Trump said. “How do you impeach a guy – we had two wars, we won them both, let’s impeach him.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas is leading the states in demanding the federal government invest more in aged care.

Malinauskas, a Labor Party star, said federal funding was not resulting in the 10,000 aged care beds needed to meet demand every year. He said federal governments had known for decades that an ageing population was going to see a surge in demand for aged care services in the middle of this decade.

“The freight train has now arrived at the station, and the country is not ready for it,” he told Radio National.

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas. Peter Rae

“To be fair to the federal government, they know how acute the problem is, but it’s about having the will to invest the funds that need to be prioritised in order to see a change.”

State health ministers wrote to their federal counterpart, Mark Butler, and Aged Care Minister Sam Rae on Friday to say it was unacceptable for so many older Australians to be living in hospital because they could not get into aged care.

“We’ve seen the number of beds in South Australia go from 89 aged care beds per 1,000 people in South Australia down to 62, so that is a massive reduction at a time when we’ve got an ageing of the population, and now we’re seeing our hospitals paying the price,” Malinauskas said.

World.title: Trump’s close ties to Nvidia billionaire under scrutiny amid ‘Chinese spy’ probe
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesTechnology & democracy Trump’s close ties to Nvidia billionaire under scrutiny amid ‘Chinese spy’ probe Courtney Rozen November 10, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. US President Donald Trump’s close relationship with embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang came under renewed scrutiny, after the company said its board was investigating whether the tech executive has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang is one of Trump’s closest allies in Silicon Valley, and the relationship between the two dates to at least 2025. Over the past two years, he has repeatedly voiced support for the administration’s agenda and become a regular presence in Washington as Nvidia sought to sell advanced chips to the Chinese market. US President Donald Trump with Huang in 2025. Bloomberg Advanced chips are the backbone of the US AI boom and government officials have previously tried to restrict China’s access to them through export controls to stifle its AI capabilities. Nvidia’s board launched its probe after a New York Times report said Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom US intelligence officials believe passed information to the Chinese government. Nvidia shares hit a seven-month low on Wall Street on Monday, wiping hundreds of billions of dollars off the value of the company.



Related Article Updated

Technology & democracy ‘I was unfaithful to my wife’: Nvidia boss admits to affair with suspected Chinese spy As one of Silicon Valley’s biggest celebrities during the AI boom, Huang’s confession plunges Nvidia into a crisis that threatens to reverberate through the broader industry. After advocating for years to sell more of Nvidia’s AI processors to China, the world’s largest market for chips, his links to the country will come under greater scrutiny than ever before. “This tech competition is really happening at the level of private companies, which are headed by CEOs,” former US intelligence analyst Elly Rostoum told Bloomberg TV. “This seems quite frankly quite careless.” A direct line Huang has a direct line to the president. A Reuters reporter saw Huang’s full name pop up on Trump’s phone in December 2025.



Huang flew with Trump to China on Air Force One in May, the first visit by a US president to China in nearly a decade. Huang attended a high-profile state dinner in September for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House. The company committed $US25 million ($36.2 million) for Trump’s planned White House ballroom, according to media reports. Nvidia shares sank on Wall Street on Monday after the probe was announced. AP The New York Times reported that Trump was briefed on Huang’s relationship with the woman and that she was giving information to the Chinese government, and chose not to act on the information. Neither the White House nor Nvidia’s communications team immediately responded to a Reuters request for comment on their relationship. China denied it engaged in an attempt to ensnare the Nvidia CEO, saying the spying allegations were unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing.



In a routine news briefing, a Chinese spokesperson rejected claims it used the woman as a spy. “The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday. As one of Silicon Valley’s biggest celebrities during the AI boom, Huang’s confession plunges Nvidia into a crisis that threatens to reverberate through the broader industry. Huang’s relationship with Trump has coincided with several favourable policy developments for the company. In April 2025, the administration backed off plans to restrict exports of certain Nvidia AI chips to China after Huang attended a dinner at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club in Florida. In December 2025, Trump said the US would allow Nvidia to export its H200 processors, its second-best AI chips, to China and collect a 25 per cent fee on such sales.



Related Article Opinion

AI Wall Street’s $4.7 trillion meltdown may have a silver lining Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Trump has lavished Huang with praise, awarding him the nation’s highest honour for scientific achievement in October. The same day Trump gave Huang the award, the president disclosed buying up to $US1.6 million and selling up to $US1 million in Nvidia stock during the summer. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told Reuters at the time that third-party financial institutions independently manage the president’s portfolio. Trump told reporters he had not spoken to Huang about the allegations, calling Huang an “honourable guy.” “I hope everything’s fine,” he said about Huang. “He’s done such an incredible job.”

World.content:

Paris: Iranian hackers have been blamed for causing chaos in European supermarkets by gaining online access to refrigerators and sending their temperatures soaring, destroying food at hundreds of stores. French Foreign Minister ⁠Jean-Noël Barrot named Iran as the country behind the hack and called for European sanctions against Tehran, amid broader concerns about Iranian cyberattacks and terrorism. Freezers are emptied and goods loaded into shopping carts to be thrown away in Sjöbo, Sweden, early this month. AP The declaration came at a Paris meeting of US, European and other G7 foreign ministers, who are preparing to debate ways to end the war in the Middle East, in their first meeting since American voters turned against US President Donald Trump and his Republican allies in last week’s midterm elections. French retailers said last month that the attacks on October 11 and 12 changed the controls on refrigerator systems to increase their temperatures to as much as 50 degrees during the night, when the stores were closed.



The attack led to fires in some locations and melted equipment in others, while destroying food at about 700 supermarkets including major chains such as Intermarche, Carrefour and Monoprix. A separate attack on November 2 raised refrigerator temperatures at dozens of grocery stores in countries including Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg, while targeting at least one IKEA store. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, right, welcomes US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to a G7 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting at the French Foreign and European Affairs Ministry in Paris on Monday. Christophe Petit Tesson/Pool EPA French blood banks were also hit by the most recent hack at three locations, forcing staff to move the donated blood to avoid losing the supplies. The French foreign minister said he wanted sanctions applied against Iran given the gravity of the October attacks.



“I can confirm that this attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he said. “This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression. The family photograph at the start of the G7 summit in Paris. From left, EU Vice-President for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas; German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul; British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband; US Secretary of State Marco Rubio; French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Barrot; Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand; Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani; and Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi. Brendan Smialowski/POOL AFP via AP “It is the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on French soil, and it represents a major threat to our national interests and the security of the French people. That is why it will not go unanswered. “We will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack.”



The European Union’s special representative for foreign affairs, Kaja Kallas, said foreign ministers could consider the issue at a meeting next week. Related Article Updated

Antisemitism Ambassador expelled, terror law changes: Iran’s brazen antisemitic attacks on Australian soil “Our response should be strong,” said Kallas, a former prime minister of Estonia, speaking to reporters at the G7 meeting in Paris. The focus on Iran follows action in Australia last year to identify and name the Iranian government as the organiser of two attacks on Australia soil, setting fire to the Lewis Continental Kitchen in Sydney on October 20 and the Adass Israel Synagogue in Melbourne on December 6. Spy agency ASIO believes Iran also directed other attacks on Australia.



The Australian government expelled the Iranian ambassador and three other diplomats, suspended operations at the Australian embassy in Tehran and moved to list the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a terrorist organisation. While the European Union already lists the IRGC as a terrorist organisation, many countries there, including France, have maintained diplomatic ties with the regime during the Middle East war. Destroyed refrigerated goods being thrown away at an ICA Baronen store in Stockholm. Fredrik Sandberg/TT/TT News Agency via AP At least some of the refrigerator units affected on Monday of last week used temperature control systems from Danish firm Danfoss, according to Reuters. The same company’s systems were also targeted in the French ​attack last month, and the company said it was working with customers on fixing the problems. The attack on the French blood banks on November 2 changed temperatures at three sites, but did not lead to the loss of any donated blood. French security agencies are not naming Iran as being behind these incidents.



“Even if the modus operandi is similar, nothing at this stage allows us to confirm that it is the same attacker,” said Vincent Strubel, the director general of the National Cybersecurity Agency of France. World.title: Early childhood education centres are growing. Some experts are worried
World.content:
NationalVictoriaChildcare Early childhood education centres are growing. Some experts are worried Nicole Precel and Bridie Smith November 10, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Childcare centres are becoming mega facilities to attract more enrolments, with developers passing the risk of their big builds onto families, research has found. Melbourne’s rising land and construction costs increasingly determine childcare centres’ location and size, rather than where the need is highest, according to the report by national advocacy group The Front Project. Etta Curry and her children Nancy 5, Colver, 18 months and family dog Olive. Eddie Jim The increasing size of early learning centres was due to developers needing to reach a certain level of enrolments to get a return on investment. “But bigger is not necessarily better when it comes to high-quality provision,” said The Front Project chief executive Dr Caroline Croser-Barlow.



“Developers are making perfectly legitimate considerations, but it has a direct impact on children.” Researchers found the business model, akin to a food chain of lenders, developers and landlords, was designed to benefit investors. Each takes a cut along the way. While not unique to the early childhood education industry, Croser-Barlow said the sector was unusual because families couldn’t easily switch services and governments tended to lift subsidies when fees started to hurt household budgets. A Productivity Commission report released in June showed the Child Care Subsidy accounted for about $20 billion a year in government spending nationally. “There is no downward pressure, and one of the things that has led to is oversupply in particular areas,” she said.



“It doesn’t sound like a problem, but problems arise later if it leads to dropping enrolments and cost-cutting because the sorts of costs that are cut are usually staffing costs and those are the most important in terms of quality.” Related Article Education Childcare upheaval stokes family pressure, but experts say there’s a solution After wages, property is the second-largest cost in early childhood education and care, accounting for about 15 per cent of operational costs, the report found. More than 200 childcare centres nationally have closed in the past year. Reservoir mum Etta Curry says she had to find a new centre for her children when their small not-for-profit, Merrilands Uniting Early Learning, was pushed out of the market after four private centres opened nearby.



Curry said the “complete oversupply” of centres had created hundreds of extra childcare places in Reservoir’s north-west, despite Darebin City Council identifying only 123 were needed by 2041. She said the extra places could mean existing centres would operate at reduced capacity, meaning lower margins and more staff sharing between sites. “If we allow these not-for-profits to close, it will be even harder to unscramble the egg,” she said. “A market system does not have children’s best interest at heart. I think the government should do all they can to fund these small not-for-profits from shutting down.” Croser-Barlow said that while landlords were protected by contracts which required tenants to cover losses accrued by a terminated lease, childhood education providers bore a large share of the risk. And families also paid a price.



“[The model] is not optimised for supporting a continuity of service for families,” she said. Researchers reviewed around 20,600 property transaction records dating back to the 1940s, and matched them against the national register of services. They also spoke to 50 developers, landlords, fund managers, providers, regulators and advisers. They found 68 per cent of investors were self-managed super funds, ‘mum-and-dad’ investors, and high-net-worth private investors. Early Childhood Australia chief executive officer Samantha Page said the report provided more evidence for the benefits of moving away from a market-driven early learning sector.



“We have been concerned for several years now that new services are getting too big,” Page said. “Particularly when operated by inexperienced providers who do not understand the impact of group size and learning environments on educators and their capacity to provide both active supervision of children and intentional teaching through play-based pedagogy.” Related Article Childcare Why some educators think Labor’s $14 billion kinder promise won’t work A communiqué released following a joint meeting of Australian education ministers last week agreed one of the functions of a proposed national Early Education and Care Commission would be to provide government with insights on “supply and demand, market shape and workforce development” in the early childhood education sector. Minister for Early Childhood Education Jess Walsh said a key role of the commission would be helping to plan and coordinate the system across the country, including locating services where they were needed.



“We will consider the findings of The Front Project’s report alongside other evidence as we continue work towards a universal early education and care system,” she said. Walsh also said the government’s Service Delivery Prices project would help them better understand the finances of delivering quality early learning, and their $1 billion Building Early Education fund was supporting new and expanded services in areas of need. Croser-Barlow said the announcement was both pleasing and disappointing. “It’s way more progress than we’ve had for a decade or so, but it still seems to be stuck in the slow lane when, for families, this is a really urgent issue,” she said.

World.title: Not a Test rugby player: Former England star torches Suaalii after Twickenham rout
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Not a Test rugby player: Former England star torches Suaalii after Twickenham rout Iain Payten November 10, 2026 — 5:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Former England winger Chris Ashton has questioned why Rugby Australia “keep signing rugby league players”, saying the Wallabies’ highest-paid star Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii is not a Test-standard rugby player and wouldn’t get a start in the English side. Ashton teed off on Suaalii and the Wallabies after their dismal 45-22 defeat against England at Twickenham on Monday morning (AEDT), and he wasn’t alone, with numerous other ex-England players and pundits also piling into the “toothless” and “woeful” Wallabies. Loading Ashton, who played rugby league for Wigan and England before switching to union and representing England 44 times, was scathing of the Wallabies’ listless effort at Twickenham. Speaking on the BBC Rugby Union Weekly podcast, Ashton said the Wallabies were hugely disappointing. “I think the biggest tell in games of this level is how much energy and effort that players are putting in, and Australia were operating at about 20 per cent,” Ashton said. “It was almost a carbon copy of last season (a 25-7 England win). I just can’t get my head around it. We keep trying to find positives for Australia, and that they’re moving in the right direction, but I ain’t seeing it.



“And they keep signing rugby league players. This Suaalii gamble, [I] dread to think how much he gets paid, he doesn’t look like a ... international rugby union player to me.” Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii of Australia is tackled by Henry Slade and Tommy Freeman. Getty Images Ashton said Suaalii’s best game as a rugby player was his Test debut at Twickenham in 2024, but since then, he hasn’t been impressed. “If he was English, he wouldn’t be playing for England. He just won’t be there,” Ashton said. “But yet he’s here, he’s running around every week for Australia. “And they’ve got two or three more coming, rugby league lads that they want to get for the World Cup. I’ve no idea where Australia are heading, and what direction they’re going in. And they’ve got a World Cup coming up in less than a year.”



Suaalii was shifted to the wing for Monday morning’s clash and had success in aerial contests, but didn’t see much ball in attack, with only eight carries. Ashton said it took him three years to acclimatise to rugby, and said during BBC commentary for the match it looked like Suaalii didn’t know what he was doing in rugby. Chris Ashton scoring a try against the Wallabies in London in 2010. AP “When I’m watching him, I’m watching him ruck, he looks like me when I didn’t know, and I didn’t have a clue what was going on,” Ashton said post-game. “He doesn’t know how to ruck, he doesn’t know where to hit the ruck. They (Australia) are in all sorts, and they’re trying to force him into this team, and they’ve signed more rugby league lads.” Rugby Australia has signed two NRL players – Zac Lomax and Angus Crichton – in the last year. When it was raised on the BBC podcast that Australia and England would likely play each other in the rugby World Cup quarter-finals next year, Ashton said: “We’re into a semi if that’s the case.” Writing in the Daily Mail, former England halfback Ben Youngs was a little kinder to Suaalii but said the fact backrower Henry Pollock was allowed to play wing without being tested showed how badly the Wallabies played.



“He [Pollock] was laughing after the game about how easy it was and that’s a damning indictment of Australia. If England were playing against New Zealand, France or South Africa, they would ruthlessly try to target him off strike moves and contestable kicks,” Youngs wrote. Henry Pollock doing his signature pulse check after scoring a second try. Getty Images “Australia did none of that. They gave him an armchair ride. That’s rugby IQ 101. Where’s your nous? Where’s your match understanding? They could have Mark Nawaqanitawase and Joseph Suaalii as all-star wingers at the World Cup but if that was their standard of half-backs, then they are going nowhere. “For all of England’s brilliance, I still can’t get over how poor Australia were. They were toothless.” Writing in The Guardian, rugby correspondent Gerard Meagher said of the “woeful” Wallabies: “There was none of the counterattacking swagger that they are capable of and little of the ball‑carrying thrust that some of their heavyweights can produce – at least not until the game was well and truly up.”



Surprisingly, however, England hooker Jamie George leapt to the Wallabies defence, saying their performance was nullified by a strong England showing, and that Australia can still have a decent tour. Related Article Tight Five

Wallabies The Wallabies are in freefall, and it’s difficult to see how things improve “I thought they played well today. I genuinely thought that they were pretty good across the whole,” George said. “You know, there was a lot of tough contests out there. I think we’ve got to give ourselves a little bit of credit here. A lot of teams when you win convincingly, you talk about the opposition maybe not showing up. “I think maybe the key here is to focus on how we were able to not let them play their game because they’re a very, very good team, and I think they’ll show that throughout this autumn.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

Breaking SportNRLNRL 2026 NRL officially clears Parramatta star Addo-Carr to resume career Adrian Proszenko Updated November 10, 2026 — 8:17am ,first published November 6, 2026 — 5:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The NRL has officially cleared Josh Addo-Carr to resume his NRL career, a move that ensures he will be part of Parramatta’s side for their season-opening clash in Las Vegas. The Eels resolved at a board meeting on Friday to retain Addo-Carr after he produced a false-positive result for cocaine at a random police roadside test. However, the last impediment to a return was getting the green light from the NRL’s integrity unit, which was investigating the circumstances of the incident. Loading That came on Tuesday morning, ensuring one of the game’s cult heroes can resume his career. “We are obviously very happy with the outcome,” said Addo-Carr’s high-profile lawyer Elias Tabchouri.



“This has been a difficult process to navigate. We are very thankful to both the Parramatta Eels and the NRL for the way they have approached this matter. “We are very relieved for Josh and his family and are looking forward to him having a stellar year for the Eels.” Addo-Carr will now be able to participate in pre-season training and add to his tally of 234 first-grade games. Josh Addo-Carr is set to resume his career with Parramatta. Getty Images While “The Foxx” will get the chance to fulfil the final year of his $450,000 contract, the 31-year-old has paid a price as a result of the incident. It has cost him, an incumbent Australian representative, the chance to be considered for Kangaroos selection for the World Cup.



Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2026 Addo-Carr reveals financial cost of false-positive drugs test There was also a financial cost after a raft of existing or prospective sponsors – including JAC Motors, P&O Cruises, Rexona, Nike, DoorDash, Red Bull, Weighplate and television series Rivals: Sport vs. Sport – cut ties after his initial roadside drugs test. The value of those endorsements is estimated to be worth close to $400,000, a figure almost as high as his playing contract. Addo-Carr spent about a month in rehab after the incident. The former Storm star was sacked after providing a positive roadside test while employed at Canterbury in a separate incident two years ago. Last week, Addo-Carr – who arrived at his Monday meeting with the board clutching a religious book specifically aimed at prison inmates – said he was hopeful of continuing his NRL career. “I have always been committed to the Parramatta Eels and nothing has changed,” Addo-Carr said in a statement provided to this masthead on Tuesday.



“I turned up today with a book that has changed my life and this is a chance to put into practice what I’ve learnt. I feel like I’ve still got so much to give this club and community. “I appreciate the Eels giving me an opportunity to provide my version of events and I hope I get another chance to pull on the blue and gold.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: ‘Judge, jury and executioner’: Republican congressman files resolution to impeach Hegseth
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaUS politics ‘Judge, jury and executioner’: Republican congressman files resolution to impeach Hegseth Michael Koziol Updated November 10, 2026 — 8:07am ,first published 6:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Washington: Republican congressman Thomas Massie filed a resolution to impeach Pete Hegseth, arguing the defence secretary abused the power of his office by waging war against Iran without congressional approval and in the absence of an imminent threat. Massie, who has split from President Donald Trump and the administration on several key issues, read out the impeachment resolution in the House of Representatives on Monday afternoon (US time). Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, filed an impeachment resolution against Pete Hegseth. Bloomberg Over eight articles of impeachment, Massie accused Hegseth of violating multiple sections of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, ignoring laws that minimise civilian casualties, conducting extrajudicial killings of people on boats alleged to be carrying drugs, suppressing free speech and kidnapping a foreign leader. Hegseth, speaking earlier on Monday, defended his record as having made the world a better and safer place, and dismissed criticism as “politically motivated”. He said he was not worried about gathering enough votes to defeat the impeachment resolution.



The defence secretary was also backed by President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who both called the attempt to impeach him “unfair”. Speaking in the House, Massie alleged Hegseth had breached the War Powers Resolution because he “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation [Iran]” without authorisation by Congress. Pete Hegseth in the Philippines last month, where he also met with Defence Minister Richard Marles. Getty Images Hegseth continued to break the law by ignoring a congressional resolution directing the president to remove US forces from hostilities with Iran, Massie said. Massie also accused Hegseth of ignoring laws that minimise civilian casualties, citing the death or injury of more than 200 civilians at the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran on the first day of the war.



Hegseth directed the Defence Department in a manner that “foreseeably dismantled the safeguards necessary to distinguish civilian objects from military objectives”, he said. Massie put on public record details of the incident, for which the Pentagon has not admitted responsibility. The school was hit by three BGM-109 Tomahwak cruise missiles fired from US Navy warships, he said. They struck between 10.23am and 10.45am on a Saturday morning, while students were at the school. Loading “Secretary Hegseth thereby effected the murder of civilians and abused the trust of the men and women under his command by requiring them to conduct military operations within a targeting and legal-review system that he had deliberately degraded,” Massie told the House. In other articles of impeachment, the Republican congressman accused Hegseth of the extrajudicial killings of 243 alleged drug traffickers on small boats in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean.



By killing people who were merely suspected of criminal conduct – and without establishing a lawful basis for treating them as military targets – Hegseth “arrogated to himself and the Executive Branch the roles of judge, jury and executioner, and asserted a unilateral power to determine who may live and who may die”, Massie said. He also accused Hegseth of suppressing free speech by attempting to intimidate Democratic senator Mark Kelly over criticism, kidnapping a sovereign foreign leader by the abduction of Venezuela’s then president Nicolás Maduro, and executing an unlawful war in Yemen through Operation Rough Rider in March 2025. President Donald Trump has stuck by Pete Hegseth despite conjecture that the defence secretary could be dumped from cabinet. AP Massie told the House that Hegseth acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law, and had demonstrated that he would remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office. Republicans still control both chambers of Congress until January. The resolution could pass the House if a small number of Republicans join Democrats in voting to impeach Hegseth, though he would then have to be convicted in the Senate to be removed from office.



Massie – who is retiring from Congress – had widely telegraphed his intention to reintroduce a resolution to impeach Hegseth following last week’s midterm elections. Related Article Analysis

US politics ‘Fog of war’ might excuse an admiral, but it won’t let Hegseth off the hook Hegseth has scheduled a news conference about the impeachment for Tuesday morning (US time), but defended his record when he briefly spoke to reporters while travelling on Monday. “We’re not worried about that,” he said of the impeachment proceedings. “There’s a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements - but their disagreements are with success. “Getting our European partners to step up is historic. Getting these countries in central and South America to come together into a counter-cartel coalition and put the cartels on the run is historic.



“The things that we’ve accomplished in [operations] Midnight Hammer and Absolute Resolve and Southern Spear and Epic Fury are things that will change the face of the globe for a generation. “We are very proud of the president’s America First agenda, of our ‘peace through strength’ posture. We know the world is a better and safer place as a result. So if we want to litigate that, the success of those things, I’m happy to do it all day long.” Hegseth said people who took issue with what the US did in those military operations were “taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished”. Trump said during an interview on CBS’s 60 Minutes on Sunday that he had confidence in Hegseth, and it was “very unfair” to try to impeach him. “We had two wars, we won both. We won Venezuela, we won Iran,” Trump said. “How do you impeach a guy – we had two wars, we won them both, let’s impeach him.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘For one night, it was like we were all back living our childhood dreams’
World.content:
Sponsored CultureMusicMelbourne Park ‘For one night, it was like we were all back living our childhood dreams’ Sponsored by Melbourne Park Jaymie Hooper November 10, 2026 — 7:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
