For Emily Leveque, 37, Hilary Duff’s sold-out concert at Rod Laver Arena last month was a chance to revisit the music she grew up with. Joined by her sister, Laura, and surrounded by thousands of fellow fans wearing glitter and sparkling costumes, Leveque knew it was going to be an unforgettable night. Sisters Emily (left) and Lauren making memories to last a lifetime at the Hilary Duff concert. The connection was there before Duff took the stage. “The concert hadn’t started yet, but the arena was playing music from the early 2000s,” Leveque recalls. “It really took us back, and at one point everyone was singing along to Since U Been Gone by Kelly Clarkson. It made the teenager in me come alive.” As soon as the house lights dipped and Duff’s silhouette appeared, Leveque, along with the rest of the crowd, leaped to her feet. “We were belting out tunes all night,” she says. “Making those memories with my sister will be something I hold onto for a long time.”



The sisters’ experience says as much about who is in the crowd as who is on stage. Across Melbourne Park’s six venues, audiences span generations, musical tastes and cultural backgrounds, each bringing their own connection to the events they come to see. A calendar shaped by its audiences “Four million people come through Melbourne Park each year for a blockbuster calendar of more than 500 events,” says chief executive officer John Harnden. “From global entertainment megastars, sport, family events, business events and, of course, the Australian Open, we pride ourselves on having something to suit every taste.” That range of events is driven by an understanding who wants to see them. Harnden credits the precinct’s broad range of partners for its varied calendar of events. “Over the past few years, we have deliberately broadened the range of hirers we work with, which has allowed us to expand our audience demographics,” he explains. “Last year, 67 per cent of our hirers were returning partners, while 33 per cent of our content came through new or emerging hirers,” he adds. “That combination helps to keep the calendar consistent, the offering fresh and audiences coming back.”



A place for more communities Four million people visit Melbourne Park each year for a blockbuster calendar of more than 500 events. For music fans, that can mean hearing the songs they grew up with or seeing an artist who shares their language or cultural background. Melbourne Park has responded to demand for a wider range of international acts by building relationships with promoters who can bring them to Australia. That growth has been particularly pronounced in Asian Pop. Where a decade ago, Asian performers accounted for zero per cent of events held at Melbourne Park, last year they represented 15 per cent of all acts. “We’ve recently seen some incredible emerging artists hit our stages,” Harnden adds. “Karan Aujla played two nights at Rod Laver Arena, MAMAMOO performed at John Cain Arena and Elissa performed at Margaret Court Arena.” An audience beyond Melbourne



The diversity of the calendar attracts visitors from across the state and country, with one in four guests who attend a headline event at Rod Laver Arena travelling from interstate or overseas. “Fans are prepared to travel to see the acts that matter to them,” Harnden says. “Thirty per cent of our K-pop audiences travel from elsewhere in Victoria or interstate, while for country music, 70 per cent come from outside Melbourne.” “The event gives people a reason to travel, but those visitors also pack the city’s restaurants and bars, and stay in hotels,” Harnden says. “That drives important economic benefits for the state and reinforces the important contribution live events make to the visitor economy.” United through sound Karan Aujla played two sold out shows at Rod Laver Arena in August.



No matter where you’ve travelled from or which artist you came to see, the true power of Melbourne Park is its ability to bring people together. “When we last measured it, nine in 10 people came to Melbourne Park with at least one other person,” Harnden says. “That’s a reminder of how much the occasion matters, as well as the performance. For communities with a strong connection to an artist or a particular kind of music, seeing that artist here in Melbourne can mean a great deal.” It certainly did for Leveque, who says that seeing Hilary Duff alongside her sister and almost 15,000 fans is an experience she’ll never forget. “Those songs hold so many memories for my sister and I,” she says. “Most of the crowd grew up listening to this music, and for one night, it was like we were all back living our childhood dreams.”



The evening concluded with an explosion of confetti and balloons, but even as the crowds dispersed from the stadium, the energy remained high. “After the show ended, people were still singing and dancing as we walked back to our car on Flinders Lane,” Leveque says. “It was a very wholesome experience and I’m so glad I got to be a part of it. It felt like everyone was just out for a good time.” Find out what’s on at melbournepark.com.au

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas is leading the states in demanding the federal government invest more in aged care.

Malinauskas, a Labor Party star, said federal funding was not resulting in the 10,000 aged care beds needed to meet demand every year. He said federal governments had known for decades that an ageing population was going to see a surge in demand for aged care services in the middle of this decade.

“The freight train has now arrived at the station, and the country is not ready for it,” he told Radio National.

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas. Peter Rae

“To be fair to the federal government, they know how acute the problem is, but it’s about having the will to invest the funds that need to be prioritised in order to see a change.”

State health ministers wrote to their federal counterpart, Mark Butler, and Aged Care Minister Sam Rae on Friday to say it was unacceptable for so many older Australians to be living in hospital because they could not get into aged care.

“We’ve seen the number of beds in South Australia go from 89 aged care beds per 1,000 people in South Australia down to 62, so that is a massive reduction at a time when we’ve got an ageing of the population, and now we’re seeing our hospitals paying the price,” Malinauskas said.

World.title: Trump’s close ties to Nvidia billionaire under scrutiny amid ‘Chinese spy’ probe
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesTechnology & democracy Trump’s close ties to Nvidia billionaire under scrutiny amid ‘Chinese spy’ probe Courtney Rozen November 10, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. US President Donald Trump’s close relationship with embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang came under renewed scrutiny, after the company said its board was investigating whether the tech executive has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang is one of Trump’s closest allies in Silicon Valley, and the relationship between the two dates to at least 2025. Over the past two years, he has repeatedly voiced support for the administration’s agenda and become a regular presence in Washington as Nvidia sought to sell advanced chips to the Chinese market. US President Donald Trump with Huang in 2025. Bloomberg Advanced chips are the backbone of the US AI boom and government officials have previously tried to restrict China’s access to them through export controls to stifle its AI capabilities. Nvidia’s board launched its probe after a New York Times report said Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom US intelligence officials believe passed information to the Chinese government. Nvidia shares hit a seven-month low on Wall Street on Monday, wiping hundreds of billions of dollars off the value of the company.



Related Article Updated

Technology & democracy ‘I was unfaithful to my wife’: Nvidia boss admits to affair with suspected Chinese spy As one of Silicon Valley’s biggest celebrities during the AI boom, Huang’s confession plunges Nvidia into a crisis that threatens to reverberate through the broader industry. After advocating for years to sell more of Nvidia’s AI processors to China, the world’s largest market for chips, his links to the country will come under greater scrutiny than ever before. “This tech competition is really happening at the level of private companies, which are headed by CEOs,” former US intelligence analyst Elly Rostoum told Bloomberg TV. “This seems quite frankly quite careless.” A direct line Huang has a direct line to the president. A Reuters reporter saw Huang’s full name pop up on Trump’s phone in December 2025.



Huang flew with Trump to China on Air Force One in May, the first visit by a US president to China in nearly a decade. Huang attended a high-profile state dinner in September for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House. The company committed $US25 million ($36.2 million) for Trump’s planned White House ballroom, according to media reports. Nvidia shares sank on Wall Street on Monday after the probe was announced. AP The New York Times reported that Trump was briefed on Huang’s relationship with the woman and that she was giving information to the Chinese government, and chose not to act on the information. Neither the White House nor Nvidia’s communications team immediately responded to a Reuters request for comment on their relationship. China denied it engaged in an attempt to ensnare the Nvidia CEO, saying the spying allegations were unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing.



In a routine news briefing, a Chinese spokesperson rejected claims it used the woman as a spy. “The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday. As one of Silicon Valley’s biggest celebrities during the AI boom, Huang’s confession plunges Nvidia into a crisis that threatens to reverberate through the broader industry. Huang’s relationship with Trump has coincided with several favourable policy developments for the company. In April 2025, the administration backed off plans to restrict exports of certain Nvidia AI chips to China after Huang attended a dinner at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club in Florida. In December 2025, Trump said the US would allow Nvidia to export its H200 processors, its second-best AI chips, to China and collect a 25 per cent fee on such sales.



Related Article Opinion

AI Wall Street’s $4.7 trillion meltdown may have a silver lining Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Trump has lavished Huang with praise, awarding him the nation’s highest honour for scientific achievement in October. The same day Trump gave Huang the award, the president disclosed buying up to $US1.6 million and selling up to $US1 million in Nvidia stock during the summer. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told Reuters at the time that third-party financial institutions independently manage the president’s portfolio. Trump told reporters he had not spoken to Huang about the allegations, calling Huang an “honourable guy.” “I hope everything’s fine,” he said about Huang. “He’s done such an incredible job.”

World.content:
WorldEuropeCyber warfare Iran blamed for ‘sabotage’ attacks on hundreds of European fridges David Crowe November 10, 2026 — 5:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Paris: Iranian hackers have been blamed for causing chaos in European supermarkets by gaining online access to refrigerators and sending their temperatures soaring, destroying food at hundreds of stores. French Foreign Minister ⁠Jean-Noël Barrot named Iran as the country behind the hack and called for European sanctions against Tehran, amid broader concerns about Iranian cyberattacks and terrorism. Freezers are emptied and goods loaded into shopping carts to be thrown away in Sjöbo, Sweden, early this month. AP The declaration came at a Paris meeting of US, European and other G7 foreign ministers, who are preparing to debate ways to end the war in the Middle East, in their first meeting since American voters turned against US President Donald Trump and his Republican allies in last week’s midterm elections. French retailers said last month that the attacks on October 11 and 12 changed the controls on refrigerator systems to increase their temperatures to as much as 50 degrees during the night, when the stores were closed.



The attack led to fires in some locations and melted equipment in others, while destroying food at about 700 supermarkets including major chains such as Intermarche, Carrefour and Monoprix. A separate attack on November 2 raised refrigerator temperatures at dozens of grocery stores in countries including Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg, while targeting at least one IKEA store. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, right, welcomes US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to a G7 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting at the French Foreign and European Affairs Ministry in Paris on Monday. Christophe Petit Tesson/Pool EPA French blood banks were also hit by the most recent hack at three locations, forcing staff to move the donated blood to avoid losing the supplies. The French foreign minister said he wanted sanctions applied against Iran given the gravity of the October attacks.



“I can confirm that this attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he said. “This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression. The family photograph at the start of the G7 summit in Paris. From left, EU Vice-President for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas; German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul; British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband; US Secretary of State Marco Rubio; French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Barrot; Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand; Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani; and Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi. Brendan Smialowski/POOL AFP via AP “It is the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on French soil, and it represents a major threat to our national interests and the security of the French people. That is why it will not go unanswered. “We will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack.”



The European Union’s special representative for foreign affairs, Kaja Kallas, said foreign ministers could consider the issue at a meeting next week. Related Article Updated

Antisemitism Ambassador expelled, terror law changes: Iran’s brazen antisemitic attacks on Australian soil “Our response should be strong,” said Kallas, a former prime minister of Estonia, speaking to reporters at the G7 meeting in Paris. The focus on Iran follows action in Australia last year to identify and name the Iranian government as the organiser of two attacks on Australia soil, setting fire to the Lewis Continental Kitchen in Sydney on October 20 and the Adass Israel Synagogue in Melbourne on December 6. Spy agency ASIO believes Iran also directed other attacks on Australia.



The Australian government expelled the Iranian ambassador and three other diplomats, suspended operations at the Australian embassy in Tehran and moved to list the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a terrorist organisation. While the European Union already lists the IRGC as a terrorist organisation, many countries there, including France, have maintained diplomatic ties with the regime during the Middle East war. Destroyed refrigerated goods being thrown away at an ICA Baronen store in Stockholm. Fredrik Sandberg/TT/TT News Agency via AP At least some of the refrigerator units affected on Monday of last week used temperature control systems from Danish firm Danfoss, according to Reuters. The same company’s systems were also targeted in the French ​attack last month, and the company said it was working with customers on fixing the problems. The attack on the French blood banks on November 2 changed temperatures at three sites, but did not lead to the loss of any donated blood. French security agencies are not naming Iran as being behind these incidents.



“Even if the modus operandi is similar, nothing at this stage allows us to confirm that it is the same attacker,” said Vincent Strubel, the director general of the National Cybersecurity Agency of France. World.title: Early childhood education centres are growing. Some experts are worried
World.content:
NationalVictoriaChildcare Early childhood education centres are growing. Some experts are worried Nicole Precel and Bridie Smith November 10, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Childcare centres are becoming mega facilities to attract more enrolments, with developers passing the risk of their big builds onto families, research has found. Melbourne’s rising land and construction costs increasingly determine childcare centres’ location and size, rather than where the need is highest, according to the report by national advocacy group The Front Project. Etta Curry and her children Nancy 5, Colver, 18 months and family dog Olive. Eddie Jim The increasing size of early learning centres was due to developers needing to reach a certain level of enrolments to get a return on investment. “But bigger is not necessarily better when it comes to high-quality provision,” said The Front Project chief executive Dr Caroline Croser-Barlow.



“Developers are making perfectly legitimate considerations, but it has a direct impact on children.” Researchers found the business model, akin to a food chain of lenders, developers and landlords, was designed to benefit investors. Each takes a cut along the way. While not unique to the early childhood education industry, Croser-Barlow said the sector was unusual because families couldn’t easily switch services and governments tended to lift subsidies when fees started to hurt household budgets. A Productivity Commission report released in June showed the Child Care Subsidy accounted for about $20 billion a year in government spending nationally. “There is no downward pressure, and one of the things that has led to is oversupply in particular areas,” she said.



“It doesn’t sound like a problem, but problems arise later if it leads to dropping enrolments and cost-cutting because the sorts of costs that are cut are usually staffing costs and those are the most important in terms of quality.” Related Article Education Childcare upheaval stokes family pressure, but experts say there’s a solution After wages, property is the second-largest cost in early childhood education and care, accounting for about 15 per cent of operational costs, the report found. More than 200 childcare centres nationally have closed in the past year. Reservoir mum Etta Curry says she had to find a new centre for her children when their small not-for-profit, Merrilands Uniting Early Learning, was pushed out of the market after four private centres opened nearby.



Curry said the “complete oversupply” of centres had created hundreds of extra childcare places in Reservoir’s north-west, despite Darebin City Council identifying only 123 were needed by 2041. She said the extra places could mean existing centres would operate at reduced capacity, meaning lower margins and more staff sharing between sites. “If we allow these not-for-profits to close, it will be even harder to unscramble the egg,” she said. “A market system does not have children’s best interest at heart. I think the government should do all they can to fund these small not-for-profits from shutting down.” Croser-Barlow said that while landlords were protected by contracts which required tenants to cover losses accrued by a terminated lease, childhood education providers bore a large share of the risk. And families also paid a price.



“[The model] is not optimised for supporting a continuity of service for families,” she said. Researchers reviewed around 20,600 property transaction records dating back to the 1940s, and matched them against the national register of services. They also spoke to 50 developers, landlords, fund managers, providers, regulators and advisers. They found 68 per cent of investors were self-managed super funds, ‘mum-and-dad’ investors, and high-net-worth private investors. Early Childhood Australia chief executive officer Samantha Page said the report provided more evidence for the benefits of moving away from a market-driven early learning sector.



“We have been concerned for several years now that new services are getting too big,” Page said. “Particularly when operated by inexperienced providers who do not understand the impact of group size and learning environments on educators and their capacity to provide both active supervision of children and intentional teaching through play-based pedagogy.” Related Article Childcare Why some educators think Labor’s $14 billion kinder promise won’t work A communiqué released following a joint meeting of Australian education ministers last week agreed one of the functions of a proposed national Early Education and Care Commission would be to provide government with insights on “supply and demand, market shape and workforce development” in the early childhood education sector. Minister for Early Childhood Education Jess Walsh said a key role of the commission would be helping to plan and coordinate the system across the country, including locating services where they were needed.



“We will consider the findings of The Front Project’s report alongside other evidence as we continue work towards a universal early education and care system,” she said. Walsh also said the government’s Service Delivery Prices project would help them better understand the finances of delivering quality early learning, and their $1 billion Building Early Education fund was supporting new and expanded services in areas of need. Croser-Barlow said the announcement was both pleasing and disappointing. “It’s way more progress than we’ve had for a decade or so, but it still seems to be stuck in the slow lane when, for families, this is a really urgent issue,” she said.

World.title: RNZ blowout = big cuts + big hit to reputation
World.content:
RNZ's been overspending for months after "almost incomprehensible" financial errors. Significant and swift cuts to jobs and costs will follow, just as RNZ's management and governance changes in 2027. Mediawatch looks at how it happened - and what happens next.

Book of revelations

The state-owned broadcaster's top brass kept a tight lid on the alarming details until the annual financial results and latest annual report were published on Monday.

On Page 38 - under the heading 'Explanations of Significant Variances Against Budget' -

RNZ reported a planned $0.5 million loss was actually an $11.8m deficit.

Significant variance indeed. About $1 for every $6 of revenue.

The budget included $2m for land sales "incorrectly accounted as revenue". Personnel expenses were $3.2m over budget, including $1.4m for previous redundancies.

Operating expenses increased by $6.4m, including the move of RNZ's Auckland operation to TVNZ's HQ down Hobson Street costing $1.85m more than planned.

Decommissioning transmission towers to sell RNZ's Henderson sites cost $1m more - and making good its Titahi Bay site north of Wellington a further $1.7m.

Some costs that should have been apparent as they accrued were apparently not flagged until October when the deadline for finalising RNZ's accounts approached.

A passage in RNZ's latest annual report summarising a budget blowout prompting heavy cuts to spending and staff. RNZ Mediawatch

Uh-oh and empty chairs

The first serious sign of trouble came early in October when Hilary Parker suddenly resigned without explanation as RNZ's chief financial officer. She left the job the same day, just weeks before the accounts deadline - also not normal.

That prompted an emergency RNZ board meeting on a Sunday and RNZ board member Richard Dellabarca - a chartered accountant - was subbed in as CFO as the deadline loomed.

RNZ's recently-appointed board chair Brent Impey said at the time there was "nothing untoward" - and certainly nothing criminal - to report.

Former RNZ chief financial officer Hilary Parker. LinkedIn

But anxiety amped up when Impey agreed to be questioned on RNZ's Checkpoint on 8 October, then bailed out with 45 minutes to go.

RNZ deputy political editor Craig McCulloch had taken notes when he spoke to Impey earlier.

"He said (Parker) left of her own accord. He did not elaborate on the reasons because it was an employment matter," McCulloch told Checkpoint, also pointing out the media minister at the time, Paul Goldsmith, had been informed.

"A lot of moving parts here - and many more questions," McCulloch concluded.

Into the light

Some of the questions were finally put to RNZ's chair on Monday, when Impey did appear on Checkpoint.

Impey - only appointed chair in July, but also a board member before that - told Lisa Owen it was "almost incomprehensible" RNZ did not know its true financial position for so long.

Impey said an independent review - to begin soon and conclude quickly - would establish just how RNZ ended up setting budgets, policy and plans on the basis of financial information that were so poor.

"We will definitely be looking to have this completed by the early part of next year. It can't go on," he told Checkpoint.

Goldsmith said that while the deficit and subsequent job cuts were an "operational matter for RNZ to speak to", the government expects "clear steps to be taken to improve the situation".

Those steps are clear now.

Brent Impey, Chair of the Radio New Zealand Board of Governors RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Carrying the can

Impey told Checkpoint it was an "organisational failure" and responsibility lay at several levels. He cited senior management, and the RNZ board and its Audit and Risk Committee.

RNZ's CEO Paul Thompson also said he took responsibility.

"I am gutted this has occurred after more than a decade of leadership of RNZ," he wrote in a statement.

On Checkpoint Owen noted the just-published annual report also listed him as eligible for a bonus.

"I'm not prepared to get into what the board is or isn't going to do around a particular individual. All I will say is that the correct word that you used there was eligible," Brent Impey responded.

Owen also asked if non-disclosure agreements were in play.

"Yes. That's why there are employment issues that relate to individuals and it would be quite inappropriate to talk about those."

RNZ's CEO Paul Thompson. RNZ / Jeff McEwan

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408150007112

Owen spoke to Thompson as he arrived at the Auckland building on Tuesday morning and asked how he could not have known that the company was in such financial trouble.

"We were relying on incorrect information and I don't really have much more to say," Thompson said.

"I've taken responsibility which I know I need to do as chief executive. I've got a job to do to move the organisation forward and ... [RNZ board chair Brent Impey] gave you those interviews yesterday."

Owen asked if Thompson would leave the organisation now, given jobs would be lost.

"Look Lisa, the situation around the jobs is about our underlying funding position. It has gone down by ... $6 million a year. We thought we were addressing that. We weren't. So the changes to the jobs at RNZ are about adjusting to our funding that's been set by the government."

Jobs on the line

But while Impey insisted it was "not appropriate at this point to single out individuals", RNZ's managers will have to do exactly that to urgently "right-size" - in Impey's words - RNZ by March 2027.

"In August, we said staffing would need to reduce by approximately 25 to 30 roles by 30 June 2027," said RNZs annual report.

"We now expect a larger reduction on an earlier timetable"

Forty more redundancies will be added to 18 roles axed in response to funding cuts in the last Budget, reducing RNZ staff to 289 by March 2027.

"Every level and every department" will be in scope for losses, said Thompson.

By March 2027, the 'right-sized' RNZ will also have a new CEO, operating under a recently-appointed chair and board reporting to a new minister, yet to be appointed by a Government we may not have until next year.

RNZ services at risk?

Former TV3 news chief Mark Jennings knows about making news in a 'permanent state of efficiency' over three decades at the mostly debt-strapped broadcaster.

Asked what planned cuts could do to RNZ's output and morale, he replied: "Bad things to both".

"Obviously a decent chunk has to probably come out of news ... at a time when the whole media is contracting and lots of people have looked to RNZ as a sort of safety net."

"I think morale has been built up at RNZ. So it's disappointing to think about what the impact is going to be," Jennings told Checkpoint.

Jennings seized on Impey's comment about "cultural issues within the organisation that need to be looked at".

"Is it that people don't speak up when something's wrong?" he asked.

"This could potentially give some politicians ammunition around RNZ's future. The management here has certainly not done RNZ's reputation - and its place in our landscape - much good at all," said Jennings, now co-editor of Newsroom.

Former TV3 news chief Mark Jennings. RNZ / Dru Faulkner

Reputational damage

RNZ's reputation also took a hit in 2023 over 'pro-Russia editing.' That also prompted an independent external review and greater oversight of online news publishing.

A plan to replace RNZ Concert on FM with a youth-based network in 2020 was reversed after a backlash from the network's fans.

The current accounting controversy is very different, but a common thread is an apparent lack of top-level oversight and board members failing to spot the risks to RNZ's reputation.

RNZ wouldn't be the only public institution accused of "organisational failures" lately.

The Listener's Danyl McLachlan pointed to the 'accountability sink' concept of British economist Dan Davies whereby the connection "between a decision, its consequences and a person who has the authority is broken."

Think Wellington City Council and Moa Point, Tauranga City Council and the Mount Maunganui landslide and concealed IT failures at MBIE.

All of these were more costly than RNZ's blowout.

But it's also damaging for a public broadcaster which assures listeners every hour that you can trust it.

Earlier this year, the Minister of Media and Communications Paul Goldsmith urged RNZ to strengthen public trust in RNZ in his formal letter of expectations.

RNZ assured him it was committed to this and was also considering his suggestion RNZ adopt 'a cost-per-audience' measure in future.

If so, it will need to be better at knowing the actual costs.

Minister of Media and Communications Paul Goldsmith. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Former minister says get a grip

While the current minister - had little to add on Monday, a former minister in Labour-led governments was more outspoken.

"You can't allow this to carry on. You might not let the people who are directly involved at the time solve it because it does seem to beggar belief that they allowed it to get to this position," Steve Maharey, the minister of broadcasting from 2002 to 2007told RNZ's Nights.

"It's very hard to understand how any public organisation would get itself into a position ... where you're dismissing one out of six of your staff.

"It happens because people just haven't paid attention. I've been given governance calls in big organisations like ACC and small organisations in local government. These kinds of things are just bread and butter ... very routine things.

"It is not a big organisation. People who are doing the financial controlling in RNZ day-to-day should be escalating these issues through to the board ... and there are people who are going to be held accountable for it."

The bulk of RNZ's public funding - just over $62m in the past financial year - comes via broadcasting funding agency NZ On Air.

"If you've got a funder, it would be following its money and you would suspect that it hasn't been doing that," Maharey told RNZ's Nights.

NZ On Air earlier told RNZ News it was only informed of Hilary Parker's resignation six days after she left RNZ in October.

Steve Maharey, the minister of broadcasting from 2002 to 2007. supplied / CBB

RNZ's state-owned. Should the state help it?

Maharey got the job of minister of broadcasting in 2002, shortly after RNZ received a special one-off payment from his Labour-led government after overspending imperilled its news operations.

But that's not an option RNZ's board is pursuing this time.

"We don't need money now," Impey told Checkpoint on Monday.

He said $51m was "due to come in" from selling of land with transmitter sites in Henderson to NZTA for roading.

"We're going to be sitting down with Treasury and working out how much of that RNZ can retain."

RNZ's just-published - and hastily-rewritten - annual report includes its response to the Minister of Media and Communications' letter of expectations in April.

"New Zealand's media sector is navigating its most disruptive period in its history," it states.

"The consequences are already visible: ongoing job losses, bureau closures, reduced investigative capacity, and the emergence of news deserts in regional New Zealand. The journalism workforce is approximately 25 percent of what it was fifteen years ago.

"RNZ now reaches more than 80 percent of New Zealanders monthly - extraordinary growth achieved with a modest Crown investment. The Board is deeply conscious of its obligation to deploy that investment with rigour and accountability," it adds.

World.title: Minister says taxpayers, staff and audience victims of RNZ budget blowout
World.content:
Audio player for " E tu says RNZ staff shouldn't bear cost of financial errors " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics/2487361%2Fminister-says-taxpayers-staff-and-audience-victims-of-rnz-budget-blowout

E tu says RNZ staff shouldn't bear cost of financial errors Morning Report Download MP3 8m

The Associate Finance Minister says news that RNZ has recorded an almost $12 million deficit for the year to June 2026 is a shock.

David Seymour - who is also a shareholding Minister of RNZ - said it seems there's been an "illusion of calm" maintained by poor financial reporting.

The public broadcaster on Monday revealed an $11.8m loss, more than 25 times the $470,000 RNZ had expected to lose over the year to June.

CEO Paul Thompson, who is departing at the end of the year, took responsibility for the result.

He said internal reports gave an inaccurate picture of the finances, meaning the scale of the loss only became clear in October.

Nick Monro

RNZ's former chief financial officer Hilary Parker resigned unexpectedly in early October. The board said it would commission an independent review into what went wrong.

Speaking to Morning Report, Seymour said the victims of this deception are taxpayers, and RNZ employees and audience.

Audio player for " David Seymour responds to RNZs financial result " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics/2487361%2Fminister-says-taxpayers-staff-and-audience-victims-of-rnz-budget-blowout

David Seymour responds to RNZs financial result Morning Report Download MP3 10m

"That is very sad for many people who work in the organisation," he said.

"A lot of good people work there, and they're being shielded from a reality and then abruptly exposed to it."

He acknowledges it was a strange situation given there is a caretaker government in place, and the Broadcasting Minister was not returning to parliament.

Seymour said that businesses must work within the revenue they're able to earn, which requires managing costs sustainably, "that simply hasn't been done."

He said normally the resolution in this case would be that "people need to go." But the Chief Financial Officer's departure was what initially revealed the problem, he said, the CEO's already announced his departure and the Chair has recently been replaced.

"So, all of the things that a government would look to do in a circumstance like this, are already happening."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408150007112

Checkpoint's Lisa Owen spoke to RNZ CEO Paul Thompson as he arrived at the Auckland building on Tuesday morning and asked how he could not have known that the company was in such financial trouble.

"We were relying on incorrect information and I don't really have much more to say," Thompson said.

"I've taken responsibility which I know I need to do as chief executive. I've got a job to do to move the organisation forward and ... [RNZ board chair Brent Impey] gave you those interviews yesterday."

Owen asked if Thompson would leave the organisation now, given jobs would be lost.

"Look Lisa, the situation around the jobs is about our underlying funding position. It has gone down by ... $6 million a year. We thought we were addressing that. We weren't. So the changes to the jobs at RNZ are about adjusting to our funding that's been set by the government."

Asked whether the CEO should leave earlier, Seymour acknowledged he'd been a critic of Thompson for a long time, "if the board was to make a decision, they certainly should."

But he pointed to the current caretaker government as a complicating factor as well. He said with Paul Goldsmith - the Broadcasting Minister - not returning to Parliament, other ministers may have to take a role in it over the next few days and weeks.

"Suffice it to say that we do find ourselves in a strange sort of interregnum where, nonetheless, these matters must be dealt with to the extent they can be by a caretaker government and then properly by a newly installed government."

Seymour wouldn't rule out the ACT seeking ministerial oversight of public broadcasters in a new government it was part of.

He wouldn't specify if RNZ needed to make more cuts because making a judgement on what the appropriate level of funding was required an understanding of what services will be available for that level of funding.

"As it turns out, there was a loose joint in the steering mechanism of accounting that has prevented us from knowing that. So, I think without having the information required, because it has been so spectacularly mis-provided, it would be difficult to answer that question at the moment."

Seymour acknowledged RNZ was a Crown entity that had emergency broadcasting requirements and its own content production, and was largely funded by New Zealand on Air for that reason.

"But I generally take a sceptical view about the role of government as an owner and management of commercial enterprises, and not to be churlish, but I think this episode we're discussing this morning is a very good reminder to anybody who thinks that government or public sector management is always good or better. This is the kind of thing that can and does happen when people are largely spending other people's money."

Job cuts 'detrimental to the service'

E tū director Amy Hansen agreed with Seymour that there had been victims but said the situation was part of a much bigger issue around investment in the media industry.

RNZ / Nate McKinnon

"This is where I disagree with Seymour... the funding that has gone into such an important public infrastructure like broadcasting, it's been underinvested in years.

"While there has been mismanagement, it has also been not enough money in the first place to be able to deliver the great work that you do."

She told Morning Report the news had come as a " shock and disappointment".

"I think walking into the studio this morning, it has been a sombre environment to walk into."

She said there had been little opportunity for employees to process what was happening.

She said of the 58 jobs that need to be cut, 18 had already gone through the voluntary redundancy process.

Hansen pointed out that through a busy election time, the workforce had already been running short.

"People have been working really, really hard with less, and so to hear that further cuts are on the way, it's just going to be detrimental to the service."

She said it was too soon to be making decisions around staffing with the country still under a caretaker government and former broadcasting minister Paul Goldsmith yet to be replaced.

Hansen urged a slowing down in immediate decision-making until a new broadcasting minister was in place.

World.title: Explainer: What are physician associates, and how might they change health care?
World.content:
"Physician associate" is now a registered profession in New Zealand, after gaining popularity as a career in the US and UK. Groups such as the Resident Doctors' Association have voiced concern about its introduction, saying money would be better spent on doctors and nurses.

But what does a physician associate actually do? And how can they help a health system in crisis? Health correspondent Kate Green reports.

Explainer - Working in urgent care, you never know what's going to walk through the door.

Andie Cook has been working as a physician associate in New Zealand for the past decade, and is currently based at an urgent care centre in Hawke's Bay.

Coughs, colds, chest pains and respiratory illnesses are common, she says, as are injuries - especially fractures - and abdominal pain.

But it is not just urgent care where you can find a physician associate. They work in all areas of health, from general practice to hospitals.

As of 1 October, the role is now officially recognised and regulated as a profession in New Zealand.

Formerly known as physician assistants, and more colloquially as PAs, these healthcare workers are more common overseas, particularly in places like the US, UK and Canada.

Despite currently lacking the ability to legally prescribe medication in New Zealand, they see patients, form diagnoses and treatment plans, and then if medication is needed they review the case with a supervising doctor, who can prescribe.

Overseas, PAs do have the ability to prescribe, and Cook hopes that will be the next step for the profession in New Zealand.

When the news of the role's regulation was announced, Health Minister Simeon Brown said it demonstrated the Government's commitment to patient safety and providing high quality care. Many hope creating more pathways for people to work in healthcare will increase the number of appointments available for patients.

It also provides the approximately 50 PAs already working in New Zealand some comfort. Until that point, Cook explains, there had been no authority in place to back PAs in complaints or wrongful dismissals, and nothing to stop people claiming to be PAs without adequate training or qualifications.

"It means safety, not just for the patient, but for us as a profession."

What training do PAs have?

Cook has a bachelor's degree, and spent eight years in the US military as a medic before going on to train as a physician associate at the University of Utah.

"My master's degree took 27 months of training of full-time study - book work [and] didactic [work] for half, and medical rotations the other half."

Next came the national board certifying examination, a five-hour test students must pass to be able to practice, followed by a six-year stint as a PA in the Air National Guard as an officer before moving to New Zealand.

The job is aligned with the medical model followed by doctors, Cook says - diagnosticians, rather than nurses - and the training is"very nitty-gritty, condensed, know what you need to know to get the job done, but not knowing it at that higher level that doctors know".

"Even though we are not a doctor, we can still see a wide breadth and depth of patients to help open and ease the pressures on the doctor."

Physician assistants are generally paid less than doctors. Cook says one advantage for clinics is being able to add another clinician to the team at a lower cost than employing another doctor.

Physician associates receive specialised training. (File photo) Supplied/ Waikato Hospital

What qualifications do PAs need to be registered?

The Medical Council offers four pathways to registration - the first three, by holding an accredited PA qualification already in Canada, the United States or the United Kingdom.

The fourth is for PAs already practising in NZ.

Medical Council chairman Dr Kenneth Clark says to register, someone must have three years of clinical practice experience within the past five years, working at least half-time, "in the same or a similar area of clinical practice to their proposed New Zealand position".

"The New Zealand experiential pathway also requires at least 24 months of practice in New Zealand immediately before applying."

The council assesses each application, including the applicant's qualifications, work history, references and fitness to practise. Physician associates initially enter a provisional scope of practice, with council approval required for their position, primary supervisor and supervision plan.

"Physician associates must continue to work under a doctor's supervision throughout their practice. Their primary supervisor must be a vocationally registered doctor. They may only work in settings where onsite supervision is available and must not be rostered to practise solo."

How did PAs get jobs in NZ before the profession was regulated?

Whether or not a GP practice chooses to employ a physician associate is at its own discretion.

Cook says she wanted to move to New Zealand, but knew it might be harder to find a job here - until one day she spotted a post on social media about an NZ-based clinic which employed a PA off the back of a trial, some years before.

"And they had such good success with her that they were reaching out to find another PA."

What concerns does the sector have?

Some groups are worried about the potential for confusion among patients about whether they are seeing a doctor, or someone with a different qualification.

Clark says clear identification is an essential part of patient safety and informed consent.

"[The Medical Council's] standards require physician associates to identify their profession clearly and tell patients they are not medical doctors. They must explain their role in a way patients can understand, including how it differs from other health practitioners' roles."

Video player removed for printing https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uCjs7QFMpYA

Cook says as a PA, she is used to explaining her role and her scope of practice. Role confusion is nothing new, and it isn't limited to PAs.

"Public education is key to fix this."

The Royal Australasian College of Physicians (RACP) is one group concerned about PAs becoming more common.

"We have concerns about safety, cultural competency when working with Māori patients, and precious resources being diverted away from existing training programs and the supervision of the next generation of doctors," wrote its president, Dr Hamish McCay, in April last year when the prospect of regulating the profession was first raised.

Proponents of the role say regulation will hopefully lead to the creation of local training courses - but for now, the only physician associates working here have been trained overseas.

RACP Māori health committee chair Dr Matt Wheeler says health workers without local qualifications will lack cultural awareness, particularly when it comes to Māori health, and he is concerned this will increase health inequity between Māori and non-Māori.

Other groups, such as the Resident Doctors Association, have called it a cost-cutting exercise, and many have questioned whether doctors have time to supervise other staff on top of their own workloads.

But Cook says: "Once you make that relationship with your supervising doctors, you'll find that most every doctor that you interview who has worked with a PA says it is not a burden whatsoever."

For patients, she says the important thing is freeing up appointments.

World.title: 'They hate us': Outgoing National MP says party has gone 'too far to the right'
World.content:
Outgoing MP for Banks Peninsula Vanessa Weenink is worried National will be pulled "too far to the right" as she reveals many of her constituents told her they hated National in the lead up to the election.

The former National MP called herself a "squishy centrist" and said she would "worry for the party that they don't have enough squishy centrists or you know woke liberals like Chris Bishop".

"The risk is that the party might be pulled too far to the right.

"The risk is that they'll feel like they really have to consolidate with their base."

Heading into Parliament for her final caucus, she told media she was "gutted" to lose her seat.

But she said people in her electorate were telling her that they hated National.

"Oh look, a lot of people in that electorate were telling me literally that they hate us. Like they really got to that point.

"There were people there telling us they literally hate us, and then other people would tell us that 'look, you guys have lost your way. You used to be, you know, much more reasonable, and you're listening far too much to those other people in your coalition'."

Asked if she agreed with those comments, Weenink said "I wouldn't publicly agree with them, and I wouldn't necessarily disagree with everything they said either."

She said it was her opinion National got pulled too far to the right by its coalition partners. But she maintained Christopher Luxon was the right person to lead the party and that he was a strong enough leader to stop the pull to the right.

Asked why National's party vote was so low, she said "New Zealand is getting quite fed up with with what seems to be a bit of bickering and fighting, and they just actually want to get on with the real issues."

Asked if National was to blame for some of that bickering, she said "oh yeah, absolutely."

"There'll be a bit of a review and a navel gazing after all of this."

She wouldn't say if National had been too negative during the campaign.

She also revealed that Opportunity approached her to stand as a candidate in Banks Peninsula for that party, which she said was "ridiculous."

She said an Opportunity candidate in that race would have helped split the vote and potentially led to her victory, acknowledging that wasn't a resounding endorsement but said "it's not a resounding success anywhere is it?"

"It's a very divided, close electorate where there's only 2% difference in the party vote between National and Labour."

She also said her constituents understood MMP, and voted for a Labour candidate to limit the overhang.

Mark Mitchell Nathan Mckinnon

'They haven't rejected us' - Mitchell

Senior National MP Mark Mitchell says New Zealanders haven't rejected the National Party after it received only 29 percent of the vote.

"They haven't rejected us because we're back in Parliament as the biggest party after what was a very difficult period of governance over those three years.

"Every party would have liked to have had a bigger percentage of the party vote, but I think the reality of it is, Kiwis have returned us as the biggest party with the most seats."

Mitchell maintained leader Luxon also had New Zealanders support, and the support of the National caucus and the Cabinet.

He absolutely didn't need to resign, Mitchell said.

Mitchell wouldn't say if National's campaign had been negative, but said it was a "funny campaign" because there was the strategic voting campaign, and "we had lots of things that sort of made the whole campaign a bit untidy."

Asked about the Deputy Leader role up for grabs, Mitchell said the party wasn't discussing that, instead it was focusing on farewelling a number of its MPs - including outgoing finance minister Nicola Willis.

Asked who would replace her, Mitchell said that was a decision for the Prime Minister. He would not speculate on David Seymour taking the role, despite National constantly referring to the Green party co-leader's desire for the job throughout the campaign and the ACT leader now also suggesting he could take on the role.

"When we form the new government, if we're lucky enough to have that mandate post 27th, you'll see who the new finance minister is."

Mitchell rejected outright the suggestion National would have done better under a Mitchell, Erica Stanford leadership ticket, "I think Christopher Luxon was without a doubt the right person to lead us into the election."

National Party leader Christopher Luxon on Election night MICHAEL BRADLEY / AFP

Asked if National would have done better with Bishop as campaign chair, rather than Simeon Brown, Mitchell wouldn't speculate.

"Simeon Brown was our campaign chair. He's done a very good job for us, along with our entire campaign team. For me, this campaign's been a difficult one. There's been all sorts of issues that have sort of come up, like the tactical voting and things like that.

"But overall, I'm very pleased with the result because we're the biggest party we return with the most MPs, and we're in a very strong position."

Asked if National could have done better than 29 percent, Mitchell said "we campaigned as hard as we could on the part vote."

"That is what the voters gave us, we just have to respect that."

Asked if it would be considered an appropriate win given the overhang, Mitchell said "it's MMP."

Mitchell rejected the notion that Luxon had lied about working with Opportunity, saying he was very clear during the campaign. Mitchell said it was the right thing to do to rule them out earlier.

"The voters decide. They decide what the makeup is," adding that right now National didn't need Opportunity to make up the government.

"Under MMP, we have to wait and see what the people of New Zealand deliver to us. We don't have any choice on that. Our choice was we didn't want to work with Opportunity, and we'd rather not have Opportunity in Parliament.

"We had the campaign, and the people have spoken, and what they've said is that Opportunity is going to Parliament."

Mitchell referred to Luxon saying after the election he was going to "do politics differently," and he's going to work with other parties, and "we should do that, and we should identify whether it's things of common interest."

World.title: 'A lot to answer for': Chris Bishop slams vote-splitting campaigns as he farewells Parliament
World.content:
Audio player for " Chris Bishop prepares to leave Parliament after 12 years " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2486133%2Fa-lot-to-answer-for-chris-bishop-slams-vote-splitting-campaigns-as-he-farewells-parliament

Chris Bishop prepares to leave Parliament after 12 years Morning Report Download MP3 10m

Outgoing senior National MP Chris Bishop says the overhang campaign run by the Māori Party, billionaire Harry Mowbray and others was bad for democracy.

Bishop lost his Hutt South seat by fewer than 900 votes, and National failed to win any list seats.

Bishop told Morning Report there needs to be a reassessment of the electoral system in the wake of the overhang, which he described as "gaming the system."

He says the campaign was confusing and became a distraction from the real issues.

"I think the Māori Party have got a lot to answer for with their campaign, and I think Harry and his crew have as well."

"Most importantly, I think it was terribly confusing for voters," Bishop said.

Meanwhile, Te Pāti Māori co-leaders Rawiri Waititi and Debbie Ngarewa-Packer have criticised Labour for not endorsing their party's overhang strategy, saying if Chris Hipkins had been more supportive then he would already be Prime Minister.

As it stands, Te Pāti Māori has an overhang of five seats, though incoming Te Tai Tokerau MP Aperahama Edwards will be waiting for the special votes to see if he has fully beaten the Green's Hūhana Lyndon.

Edwards currently leads by 436 votes.

Ngarewa-Packer said the party was confident.

"We've experienced this in the past, and we know how the specials go. And I think Tai Tokerau has made a really wise decision"

Waititi added Edwards would need to lose "two to one" in the specials.

"So when you look at those numbers, it'll be quite difficult to pull that back. That's assuming he finds nothing, and I don't think that's the case."

Waititi said Te Pāti Māori was "the only party" that was absolutely committed to making this a one-term government.

"If the other parties had come on with the strategy, I don't think we would be in this situation now where we we're having to wait for the 27th of November. In actual fact, even if the other two Māori seats, Te Tai Tonga and Ikaroa-Rāwhiti, had gone with the strategy, and if Chris Hipkins had focused on getting rid of these fellas and not on the Māori seats and us, he would have woken up on Sunday morning being the Prime Minister. And the numbers are telling you that."

Labour's Willie Jackson says Te Pāti Māori "obviously" holds some responsibility for opening the overhang conversation, but there was some "principle" with regards to what they were talking about.

"The other side, in my view, is you got the big end of town trying to totally manipulate."

Jackson said those engineering the overhang strategy on the right would have looked at Te Pāti Māori's strategy as giving them an excuse.

He said the billionaires would have "looked at it that way I'm sure."

"But you got to have a look at all the money that's been put in. And I think that we do have to have a look at MMP. I think the reality is obviously there's areas that have to be looked at. I mean, this overhang's a bit ridiculous."

Jackson said there was a difference though in MPs espousing the strategy compared to outsiders doing so.

He said Te Pāti Māori were considering Māori workers and women who have been attacked consistently over the last three years, "so they have been along with us at the coalface."

"That's quite different from millionaires and billionaires who are who are looking to just maintain their interests and also looking to change our society as we know it. So I think there are big difference."

Departing MPs a 'blow to caucus' - Upston

Arriving at Parliament on Tuesday morning, senior National MP Louise Upston says losing her colleagues is "the nature of politics" but still a blow.

"It's not just a blow to caucus. They have made an extraordinary contribution."

Audio player for " Jo Moir on the arrivals and departures at parliament " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2486133%2Fa-lot-to-answer-for-chris-bishop-slams-vote-splitting-campaigns-as-he-farewells-parliament

Jo Moir on the arrivals and departures at parliament Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Upston said today was about welcoming the new MPs, as well as farewelling those who were leaving.

"In the weeks ahead, once we've got final results, we can focus on other things."

Upston would not say who should take over the finance role from Nicola Willis, acknowledging that while there would be "interest and speculation" it was something for after the special votes had landed.

Incoming Kāpiti MP Tim Costley said it would have been "amazing" to have colleagues like Chris Bishop return, saying they still had so much to offer.

"They have been fantastic. Clearly, they can hold their heads up high, but they'll be gutted."

Costley, who looks to have retained the newly redrawn electorate, said he expected emotions at this morning's caucus meeting to be mixed.

"It's going to be pretty tough to say goodbye to some great friends, great MPs, great ministers, people that have served their community and the country really well," he said.

Election night 'soul-destroying' - Bishop

In a post on Facebook on Monday night, Bishop described Saturday night as "soul-destroying" and said that although there are still Special Votes to be counted, it's unlikely they will change the decision in Hutt South.

"I've rung Ginny Andersen to concede the election and congratulated her on winning Hutt South.

"After 12 years as a list and electorate MP in Hutt South, I'm out of Parliament. Feels surreal, but that's democracy and the voters are never wrong.

"I'm very proud of the local campaign we ran. National's party vote in Hutt South was less than 25 percent but on current numbers I'm less than 1000 behind - with a personal vote of 43 percent. We knocked on more doors than we've ever knocked on, delivered over 100,000 leaflets, held a dozen street corner meetings and community BBQs, and had over 300 signs up around the electorate, just to name a few things. A massive thank you to my amazing campaign team and all of the volunteers who turned up time after time to support me and support National.

"There are people who have helped me in now FIVE election campaigns who've been there right from the start. Thank you.

"I tried to run a positive and upbeat campaign. There's too much negativity out there, too much polarisation and there's too many great things happening in the Hutt. I think Lower Hutt is a better city than it was 12 years ago when I first became an MP and I hope people agree I've had a small role in making that happen.

"I've had many very nice messages from across the political spectrum since Saturday night - thank you to everyone who has rung, texted, called or emailed. It really means a lot. I won't pretend politics is easy - it isn't - so it's nice to hear that people appreciate your efforts.

"Both my two electorate offices in central Hutt and Wainuiomata will be closing in late/November and early December. Hutt South has been very well served by excellent constituency staff for me during the last twelve years and I feel for them - they're out of jobs too. A big shout-out in particular to Dawn McKinley who has worked in my Wainuiomata office for over ten years now. She's a legend.

World.title: Why additional MPs may cost millions
World.content:
Audio player for " What will cost me more, cooling my house down or heating it up? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2459965%2Fwhy-additional-mps-may-cost-millions

What will cost me more, cooling my house down or heating it up? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

An overhang resulting in additional MPs could end up costing about $5 million more in the first year.

On the preliminary results, the typical 120-seat Parliament is expected to increase by 11 MPs, with both National and Te Pāti Māori winning more electorate seats than their party vote entitles them to.

National has an extra seven "overhang" MPs, while Te Pāti Māori has an extra four.

Audio player for " How much will overhang MPs cost taxpayers? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2459965%2Fwhy-additional-mps-may-cost-millions

How much will overhang MPs cost taxpayers? Checkpoint Download MP3 2m

Victoria University associate professor in public management and policy Barbara Allen pointed to the new Speaker's Determination for 2026 which gives members of parliament who are not ministers a staff allocation of $215,818 in their first year in parliament, and a non-staff allocation of $62,145.

They also receive a salary of about $180,000 a year, a basic expense allowance of $19,300, IT hardware funding of $10,400 and $13,682 once per term in staff IT costs.

That adds up to a total of about $500,000 per member of parliament in the first year.

With 11 extra MPs, that adds at least another $5.5 million.

"That's based on an additional non-ministerial list MP. That doesn't include other allowances they might get," Allen said.

In addition, parties receive funding according to the number of members in their caucus.

"There's $26,500 per caucus member. That seems to be an extra amount that's not directly related to the MP themselves."



People who win an electorate seat get $322,325 in staff costs if they are not a minister - those in "large" constituencies get $428,833.

Offices would need to be found for the additional MPs.

She said overall the cost of the additional members of parliament would still be small in the scheme of the overall cost of government.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said data showed the average cost per member of parliament had dropped almost $750,000 in 2012, in 2025 dollars, to less than $700,000.

He said the bulk of that cost related to the wider business of running parliament rather than directly to the MPs themselves.

"The bigger issue is the erosion of trust, we have record low trust in government, in politics. This kind of stuff makes it worse."

Geoff Plimmer, associate dean of research in the school of business and government at Victoria University agreed the additional cost was a drop in the bucket.

"It's trivial when the government spends billions and billions every year. We need to pay our MPs reasonably well to get quality people. This is the democratic process at work. There are other discussions to be had about whether we need to look at the design of MMP but those are for down the line."

He said it could be moot whether another 10 seats could be added to Parliament's relatively small debating chamber.

"They're often not all always there. Maybe they can hot desk in parliament and experience what life is like for many public servants and others."

World.title: The young Kiwis heading to the world's biggest climate change gathering
World.content:
Pacific communities must be at the forefront of global climate change action, three young Kiwi activists heading to the world's annual climate summit say.

Ataria MacDonald, Aigagalefili Fepulea'i-Tapua'i and Aditi Tiwari - all in their twenties - are among an estimated 80,000 people heading to COP31, which kicked off in Antalya, Türkiye overnight.

This year's conference is taking place against a backdrop of global political upheaval, including ongoing disruption to fossil fuel supply chains.

That has sharpened many countries' focus on electrifying their economies, and the transition to clean energy is a priority on this year's 'action agenda' - the practical discussions that sit alongside the formal negotiations.

New Zealand's delegation is heading over at an unusual moment, with a caretaker government in place following Saturday's inconclusive election.

Caretaker climate minister Simon Watts will attend from 15 to 18 November, and RNZ understands that Labour's Deborah Russell and the Green's Francisco Hernandez will also go.

MacDonald, Fepulea'i-Tapua'i and Tiwari are not part of New Zealand's official delegation, but will attend as 'civil society' delegates, who represent communities, NGOs and other organisations all pushing for climate action.

MacDonald (Ngāti Manuhiri), 26, the aquaculture project manager for her iwi, is one of three iwi rangatahi attending the conference alongside chief executive Nicola Rata-MacDonald.

Ngāti Manuhiri's rohe reaches from Takapuna to Mangawhai, and includes the islands of the Hauraki Gulf (Tīkapa Moana).

"One of the biggest issues I think we're facing across Tāmaki and Hauraki Gulf is the sedimentation that's happening," she said.

Ataria MacDonald, the aquaculture project manager for Ngāti Manuhiri, will head to COP31 with two other rangatahi from her iwi as well as its CEO. Supplied

Ataria MacDonald, the aquaculture project manager for Ngāti Manuhiri, will head to COP31 with two other rangatahi from her iwi as well as its chief executive.

While sedimentation itself is not directly caused by climate change, it is made worse by increasing storms and extreme rainfall events, which increase bank and coastal erosion.

Mahurangi Harbour, in particular, has been badly affected by sediment run-off.

That had not only affected the iwi's cultural practices, but hurt the wider community, MacDonald said.

"We have oyster farmers in that area that are no longer able to rely on that as their livelihoods and create a living from there."

The invasive Caulerpa seaweed posed another existential threat to the health of the Gulf, and the risk of further pest species arriving was rising as New Zealand's ocean waters warm.

"There are a lot of issues that are happening in our climate that aren't actually caused by ourselves as a [Pacific] region, but we're left dealing with the consequences."

Caulerpa washed up on the beach on Aotea/Great Barrier Island. Invasive marine species may increasingly gain a foothold as the ocean around New Zealand warms. Sid Ware / Ministry for Primary Industries

With tens of thousands of people going to COP, and hundreds of different events, MacDonald said she would be "trying to find something micro in such a macro conference".

"What we have established is an indigenous network online with groups, mobs from Australia, the Pacific region, and we are all collectively attending COP31 to connect as indigenous people," she said.

"It's almost using a global context to actually connect at a regional level."

The Pacific was originally set to play a significant role in this year's COP, with Australia bidding to host the conference in partnership with island states.

However, a late bid from Türkiye resulted in this year's unusual co-hosting arrangement and a shift from Adelaide to Antalya.

Australia has still pledged to represent the interests of the Pacific, but MacDonald said there would have been a much stronger attendance from Pacific island states if the conference was in Adelaide.

"We all were really banking on the idea that it would be closer to home."

A pre-conference event was held in Fiji and Tuvalu in October, but many countries opted to skip it.

New Zealand was among the 50-odd nations that did attend, and Simon Watts signed the country up to the event's concluding Taku Palasoa declaration.

Climate minister Simon Watts will head to COP31 next week in a caretaker role ahead of the final election result. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Aigagalefili Fepulea'i-Tapua'i, 23, will head to Türkiye firmly grounded in the Pacific.

She set up youth climate group 4 Tha Kulture while she was still in high school at Aorere College in Māngere, and is currently executive director of the Aotearoa Climate Action Network.

"The Pacific is not just a nice to have," she said.

"We are there to represent people who are living through the everyday impacts [of climate change]. And it's very easy for that to get lost when people are going through the motions of COP."

It was also easy for New Zealand to forget its place in the Pacific.

"We have this idea that we are part of the Anglosphere, where actually, when it comes to the climate context … what happens in the Pacific happens to us too, eventually," Fepulea'i-Tapua'i said.

"So it's really important that we support and stand in solidarity with the Pacific."

Fepulea'i-Tapua'i said Watts "spoke very ambitiously" about keeping the 1.5°C Paris Agreement target within sight while he was in the islands.

"I would love to see the New Zealand government carry that through to COP31. It needs to be more than words."

She and other advocates from the Pacific would push hard for stable, meaningful climate finance, she said.

"We are there to represent those who are unjustly living through the worst impacts of climate change."

Aigagalefili Fepulea’i-Tapua’i sets a rat trap as part of her work with the South Auckland-based Beautification Trust. Supplied

Aigagalefili Fepulea'i-Tapua'i sets a rat trap as part of her work with the South Auckland-based Beautification Trust.

Currently, climate financing was typically treated as a form of charity or aid - which did not recognise either the dignity of Pacific peoples or match the scale of the challenge they faced.

"We're not victims - we are resilient people."

The challenge was to support that "without it becoming an expectation that resilience is an endless resource", Fepulea'i-Tapua'i said.

"Families can't afford to constantly have to recover - whether that's flooding or other natural disasters that come in future."

Like Ataria MacDonald, she was expecting the conference to be "quite chaotic".

"Things develop so fast that you have to be really, really responsive. But I think that it's exciting. I think that any opportunity we have to speak truth to the experiences of the people that we represent is exciting."

For Porirua climate advocate Aditi Tiwari, 26, that experience is so close to home it's almost lapping at the door.

"Just a kilometre away from my house is the Pāuatahanui Inlet.

"We see how the community suffers from every single flood or every single season of rising sea levels," she said.

"How are we going to combat that?"

Floodwaters surrounded houses in Pāuatahanui after flash flooding in Wellington in April this year. Supplied

Already this year, she has been part of a community effort to plant 10,000 natives along the inlet to help reduce shoreline erosion.

It's that grassroots voice that Tiwari hopes to take to COP31 as a delegate for the Global Shapers Community, a network set up by the World Economic Forum.

However, she's travelling there solo, paying her way to Türkiye through crowdfunding, community raffles and support from friends and whānau in Porirua.

One of her grounding experiences as a teenager arriving in New Zealand in 2014 was learning about the concept of mana whenua and connecting that back to similar ideas in India, where she was born.

"It goes beyond beach cleanups or tree planting - it's the feeling and the sense of belonging that you belong to the land," she said.

"And what does that mean? What is your shared responsibility as someone who lives and breathes here? So I think that was my first connection to climate."

Aditi Tiwari was part of community efforts to plant 10,000 native seedlings along the Pāuatahanui Inlet shoreline earlier this year. Supplied

One of her jobs while she is in Antalya is to deliver the joint statement from rangatahi who went to Aotearoa's Youth COP, held in Auckland in September.

"I consider myself very privileged to be able to go," she said.

Young people had "incredible ideas" to contribute but often did not get a seat at the table.

"I've been told time and time again in the last two months that, at least we have you, who is going to represent us and take all our cool whakaro and all our knowledge, not just to the international stage, but also bring that back home and be able to share that."

COP31 will run until 20 November, with a 'cover decision' - a high-level political statement agreed on by all members - expected in the final days.

This year's cover decision could include official acknowledgement that the world will exceed the 1.5°C target and will need to pursue an 'overshoot' scenario, where both the temperature peak and the length of time the world spends above 1.5°C are limited as much as possible.

A UN report published in September said that would require deep cuts to emissions, as well as removing carbon already in the atmosphere.

A path away from fossil fuels will also form part of this year's discussions, after last year's host, Brazil, put together a draft voluntary 'road map'.

Last year, New Zealand opted not to join a push from about 80 countries to include developing such a 'road map' on the formal agenda.

World.title: 'Nail in the coffin': Wellington's Penthouse Cinema could face closure if council rates change
World.content:
Audio player for " Wellington businesses fear impact of proposed rates change " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2480531%2Fnail-in-the-coffin-wellington-s-penthouse-cinema-could-face-closure-if-council-rates-change

Wellington businesses fear impact of proposed rates change Morning Report Download MP3 4m

A family-run cinema in Wellington says potential council rating changes could be the "nail in the coffin" for the movie theatre, if it was forced to pay an extra $77,000 per year in rates.

And a hospitality business owner is alarmed that paying an extra $100,000 in rates could also force him to shut the doors in a struggling inner-city.

Wellington City Council is consulting on a possible shift to the way it calculates rates - from a capital value to land value based rating system with feedback sought by 15 November.

The council had put out a calculator tool for people to figure out their rates under the potential new system, but hadn't included the impact of a separate proposal to reduce commercial rates - a business owner says that'd caused shock in the community due to the apparent size of the increases.

Capital value rating calculates the bill based on the value of someone's land and buildings, whereas land-based value assesses just the value of the land. The move was underpinned by a drive among some councillors to incentivise growth, and target land-banking in the city.

Penthouse Cinema in Brooklyn. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Penthouse Brooklyn Cinema general manager Fergus Kisby-Macleod said rates for the cinema and adjoining carpark could increase by over $77,000 under a land value system - according to the council's calculator.

"I couldn't believe it, I thought it was fake," Kisby-Macleod said.

The cinema and cafe were 1729 square metres, and the carpark was 435 square metres, Kisby-Macleod said. He said the cinema and carpark were both on a relatively big piece of land, not far from the centre city.

He said the possible increase could be the "final nail in the coffin" for the business, forcing it to close - or lead to an increase in ticket prices or shortening of opening hours.

"We've never really wanted to change operating hours because we're trying to be a community venue and stay open seven days a week, but with these bottom line costs going up - just to open the doors in the morning before you've even started - to get another setback it makes it very hard to justify certain costs of opening for the day."

Trinity Group owner Jeremy Smith. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Kisby-Macleod said the movie theatre had been family-run for 51 years, with his grandfather opening it in 1975. He said the business tried to keep ticket prices lower than other cinemas for the community, but this would have to change if the rating estimates eventuated.

Jeremy Smith, director of Trinity Group hospitality company, said his bar Lulu on Courtenay Place - which was 1080 square metres, could face an increase of $102,000 in rates under a shift to a land-value system according to the calculator, from $68,000 to $170,000 per year.
