"We definitely are not going to revitalise [Courtenay Place] ... if people can't pay their bills they're going to shut the doors ... we just recently had Dakota's shut their doors, I know there's quite a few others hanging on by their fingernails."

Lulu on Courtenay Place. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

The council was considering reducing commercial rates from 3.7 times residential rates to 3 times residential rates over a number of years. This hadn't been included in the council's calculator tool.

Smith, who was also on the board of Hospitality NZ, said if the council was considering lowering commercial rates, it should have "absolutely" factored that into the calculator for the change - but he expected many residents wouldn't want an increase to their rates so businesses could lower theirs.

He said the calculator showed high-rise office buildings, like the Majestic Centre - which could have over $700,000 in savings, and the Deloitte high-rise, which could have over $1 million in savings - had large decreases in rates under the system, compared to smaller businesses.

"Whereas the smaller property owners, and the tenants in the buildings are going to be heavily penalised," Smith said.

A staff member makes a coffee at The Arborist. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Greens councillor for Wharangi/Onslow-Western ward, Rebecca Matthews, who'd been pushing for the change for six years, said the council wanted to hear from people about their concerns.

"Productive businesses, don't have nearly as much to be concerned about as unproductive major commercial land-holdings where nothing has happened."

Matthews said land-value based rates was about driving affordable housing development in the inner-city.

"Other cities, for example throughout Australia, have land value rates and have more thriving hospitality sectors than we currently have in Wellington. It's not like in Wellington we don't have an issue now with empty shops and businesses that are not active, so this is an attempt to revitalise the city."

Councillor Rebecca Matthews. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Mayor Andrew Little said the council was consulting because it wanted to hear people's views on an issue that'd been hanging around the city for some years.

Work Auckland Council did some years ago showed roughly 60 percent of property owners would have a reduction, 40 percent would have an increase, Little said, but the extent of increases and decreases wasn't clear.

"It would be good to hear from anybody affected by it, good or bad, so that we get a picture of what the impact could be, so that we then know what to do next."

Little did not state his preference on either system saying he wanted a rating system that was "fair", and did not create disincentives for the development the city needed.

He said the proposal to decrease the commercial differential for businesses was quite a separate proposal the council was looking at, with different views around the council table.

World.title: Oscar Piastri splits with manager Mark Webber
World.content:
McLaren Formula 1 driver Oscar Piastri and fellow Australians Mark and Ann Webber say they have ended their management agreement.

Nine-time Grand Prix winner Webber began working with Piastri in 2019 and was instrumental in Piastri joining McLaren in 2023 to replace compatriot Daniel Ricciardo, rather than staying at Alpine.

Renault-owned Alpine had wanted to promote Piastri to a race seat after double world champion Fernando Alonso announced he was leaving for Aston Martin, but the Australian rejected the offer.

Norris suffers champagne mishap in Brazil Lando Norris was near perfect to claim victory in Brazil.

"We are proud to have played a pivotal role in the formative years of Oscar's career and to have placed him in F1 so that he could compete at the front so early in," Webber said in a statement on Monday.

"Following our reduced trackside involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close.

"This will allow Oscar to build on his achievements under a new management structure and for us to embark on our new ventures."

Piastri, who won back-to-back titles in Formula 3 and Formula 2 in 2020 and 2021, thanked the pair for support and recognised their guidance had been invaluable.

The Australian has not won a race this season, after looking like he might win the championship last year before being overhauled by teammate Lando Norris and ending up third. He finished sixth in Brazil on Sunday.

The winner of nine grands prix has not been on the podium for 16 races and is seventh in this year's standings.

Reuters

World.title: Sandpapergate continues to wound Australia eight years on
World.content:
It's possible to forget now, obscured by the fog of the past eight years, just how extreme the national fury was in the wake of Cape Town, 2018.

This was a sporting scandal that broke containment lines. From your barista to your bus driver to the prime minister, everyone had something to say.

Sandpapergate touched something sensitive in the national psyche. It busted precisely the wrong myth, bruised just the wrong bit of our collective ego.

Khawaja's explosive Sandpapergate claim Usman Khawaja claims all staff and players knew that the Australian team was using sandpaper to tamper with the ball during the 2018 tour of South Africa.

And not even after Cameron Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner were tarred and feathered in the town square did the interest subside. Outrage was diluted by time into regret and curiosity, but there was a permanence to the damage done.

This next chapter was inevitable and in the end it was Usman Khawaja who put his hand up and first told his story, one now corroborated by his good mate Warner. The floodgates may well now open, and civil war could be at hand.

Khawaja's version, which has trickled out gradually over the course of four days, is only barely revelatory. The notion knowledge of the sandpaper plot went beyond the banned trio is not new, stands to reason and has been hinted at consistently almost from day one.

Bancroft himself back in 2021 insinuated with only a degree of subtlety that the great conspiracy extended beyond he, Smith and Warner. It was Bancroft's comments that prompted the indignant statement from the bowlers, which Khawaja claims further enraged Warner.

Given what Khawaja and Warner have now shared publicly, you can only imagine the atmosphere inside that dressing room. Fractured relationships may have been held together by shared on-field goals, but once that field is no longer shared, all bets are off.

The wider reaction has been curious. Some have pointed blame at Khawaja, which is unsurprising and something he likely expected.

It seems that by in going first he is seeking to clear the runway for Warner to eventually tell his tale in greater, potentially more scathing detail. Whether Khawaja has done this out of pure friendship, a form of penance or a little of both is something only he will know, but arguing he is simply trying to make a buck from a book is an oversimplification.

Darren Lehmann rejected Usman Khawaja's claims, but said ball tampering had been widespread in international cricket. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Darren Lehmann, meanwhile, the coach at the time and the only other person to suffer any significant repercussions, rejected some of Khawaja's assertions but offered up the fact that ball tampering had been "going on for 150 years" by "everyone in the world".

The substance of Khawaja's claims have not sparked any great backlash or rebuttal, but the timing, source and medium of them have drawn ire. And from all of that combined, much can be gleamed.

The greatest sin committed by the Australian cricket team in Cape Town in 2018 — or at least the sin that cost them the most — was taking the Australian public for fools.

Lehmann was, of course, correct when he said that ball tampering had been around forever and that basically everybody did it. Performed with the correct amount of tact it could be passed off as one of the game's "dark arts", and even those who did get caught generally only received fines or very minor suspensions.

As you could sense in Lehmann's tone, this was not as much of a taboo inside Australian cricket, even down to the dog-eat-dog ranks of grade cricket, as it was to the uninitiated who, quite justifiably, simply saw cheating as cheating and not part of some wider unspoken code.

In any case, before Cape Town most Australians were comforted by the belief that they were above such a thing. That Test match permanently shattered illusions. Mints and fingernails are one thing, but something as blatant and guileless as sandpaper? Not only were we ball tamperers, we were incredibly bad at it too.

Then came the first cover-up. Not the one Khawaja has allegedly lifted the lid on, but the instinctive, reflexive lie that came from Cricket Australia and the players on the day, when it was claimed that the contraband in Bancroft's pocket was a piece of sticky tape covered with "granules" from the pitch.

As ever, the cover-up was worse than the crime. The cavalier hubris of the whole affair, from conception to execution to deception, stung our sense of Australian exceptionalism and prompted an exceptional punishment.

Steve Smith breaks down speaking to media at Sydney International Airport upon return from South Africa. (AAP: Brendan Esposito)

Eight years on and with a perpetual war of words seemingly pending, it's hard to see how many lessons have been learned. "Ball tampering is bad" may be the extent of them.

Trying to wring the truth out of this mess may forever prove impossible, arguably by design. Khawaja said he was stunned that at no point during the investigation was he questioned or approached in any way. Indeed, if your goal is to ascertain what everybody knew, it does seem counterproductive not to simply ask everybody what they knew.

We have received hints at the truth, raised eyebrows and winking "no comments". Even Khawaja's recollections are in the main broad enough to avoid direct accusation, and therefore responsibility.

If everyone is ball tampering, then is anyone really ball tampering? If everyone knew about it, then who do you actually blame for it? At this point we're left with Joe Pesci in JFK, screaming at us about mysteries wrapped in riddles inside enigmas. "Even the ball tamperers don't know who did it! Don't you get it?"

And all the while Australians, who have always cared less for a case of whodunnit and more about the irreparable breach of trust, are still being played for fools.

Usman Khawaja (far right) says David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft were the victims of the saga. (Getty Images: Nick Potts/PA Images)

Khawaja says Bancroft, Smith and Warner are the greatest victims and his point is valid. They suffered unprecedented consequences for not entirely unprecedented acts. If they did indeed carry the can for their equally implicated teammates then they have right to feel beyond aggrieved.

But the sense of loss felt by Australians was what justified those consequences at the time and what is fuelling the emotion of today. Rightly or wrongly, some element of our national identity will always be attached to our men's Test cricket team and the wounds that remain stem from a feeling of betrayal.

Nothing we have learned this week helps to mend those wounds. Yet more cover-ups, more accusations, more denials, more quasi-confessions. The water is only muddier, the deeds of the past worth less, and the worst, surely, still yet to come.

World.title: Focus on Sheffield Shield as Test selection comes to the crunch
World.content:
Potential Australia Test players will start their auditions this Wednesday when a full round of Sheffield Shield matches begin.

Two more Shield rounds follow before the first Test against New Zealand begins in Perth on December 9.

It is likely the squad for the first few Tests will be named some time after this week's matches and before the following round of matches in late November.

The Test squad will assemble in Perth on December 3, and with the bowling unit relatively settled, the interest lies in who gets selected in Australia's spluttering batting line-up.

Australia confirmed Marnus Labuschagne would not be considered for Test selection this summer against New Zealand. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

The next one or two Sheffield Shield rounds could answer some of the questions that were posed when Australia gave up a one-nil lead in South Africa to eventually lose the final two Tests, the series and the number one Test ranking.

The most pressing issue is the name of the number three batter following Marnus Labuschagne's disappointing tour of South Africa.

Since returning to the national side at the beginning of last year's Ashes series, the Queenslander has made just 426 runs in 10 Tests at an average of 23.66.

Labuschagne's return of zero and four during the third Test in Cape Town was the final straw for most commentators, and Australia's chairman of selectors, George Bailey, confirmed he would not be considered for the four-Test series against New Zealand this summer.

Cooper Connolly is the incumbent number seven in the Australian Test side. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone, file photo)

Labuschagne's ousting could mean Western Australia's Cooper Connolly retains his spot in the side, having got the gig at Cape Town when Steve Smith sat out because of his neck injury.

Connolly has been selected to play for Australia in the three one-day internationals against England, with the first on Friday, and so will not be playing in the Shield this week.

Western Australia's next Shield match against Tasmania in Perth, which starts on November 23, will give him some red-ball match practice if he is named in the squad.

If not Connolly, who else could come into the Test side?

Jack Clayton of the Queensland Bulls is scoring a mountain of runs and putting his name forward as a possible Test batter. (Getty Images: Mark Brake)

Apart from Shield enthusiasts, not many people would have heard of 27-year-old Queenslander Jack Clayton, but he is the hot player this season and one who has been endorsed for Test selection by his former state teammate, Usman Khawaja.

The number four has scored 303 runs in three Shield matches this year at an average of 75.75 and moreover has scored runs in every game with a recent 104 and two 50s.

He has another opportunity to push his claim when Queensland takes on Tasmania in Brisbane this week.

Oliver Davies of New South Wales is leading the Sheffield Shield run-scorers list after three matches. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Aggressive New South Wales opener Oliver Davies is at the top of the Shield batting charts with 332 runs at 66.40

However, 253 of those runs came in one innings in the first Shield match of the season and since then the 26-year-old has posted just one other significant score of 52.

His opening partner, discarded Test batter Sam Konstas, continues to push his name forward, with 229 runs at 76.33, including a century, a 50 and a one-day ton.

Sam Konstas of the NSW Blues is hoping to revive his Test career. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The pair will be part of the NSW side to play South Australia this week at Cricket Central in Sydney's Silverwater.

Victorian youngsters Campbell Kellaway and Oliver Peake are often talked up, and while neither have set the Shield alight this season, they have another chance against WA come Wednesday.

Oliver Peake of Victoria is one of the young Victorian batters tipped for higher honours. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Of the older campaigners, 33-year-old former Test players NSW's Kurtis Patterson and Western Australia's Cameron Bancroft are both in the runs, but will their ages work against them?

The jury is still out on NSW's 34-year-old Nic Maddinson, who was surprisingly called up for two Tests in South Africa after missing all of last season's Sheffield Shield while recovering from testicular cancer treatment.

Nic Maddinson was a surprise recall for the first two Tests against South Africa, but was dropped for the decider. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

And what of the batting order and most pressingly the number three position after Labuschagne's axing?

Moving Steve Smith up to three seems the obvious solution and the one most pundits are calling for.

His average of 65.22 from 30 innings at first drop is better than at any other spot in the line-up, but he has only batted there once since 2017, scoring 17 against England in Perth last year.

Steve Smith has returned to his home in New York while he recovers from a neck injury. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Then there is the issue of his dodgy neck joint that flared up in South Africa, which he is now resting at his New York home.

Smith is expected to return for NSW's match against Queensland on November 22 at the SCG.

Cameron Green is another option for first drop.

Like his fellow Western Australian, Connolly, Green will miss this week's round of matches as part of the Australian squad for the one-day series.

The big watch on Green is his bowling fitness following an abdominal injury prior to the South African Tests.

Cameron Green returned to the Australian side for the third Test against South Africa as a batter only after suffering an abdominal injury. (AP: Halden Krog)

He returned in Cape Town as a batter only and continues to build up his bowling loads in training.

He could bowl in the one-dayers, otherwise his only opportunity to prove his match fitness will be the Shield match against Tasmania.

If Green can bowl, it is hard to see Tasmania's Beau Webster returning to number seven.

Webster was dropped for the third Test at Cape Town after taking just one wicket in his previous four Tests and scoring 81 runs at 13.50.

Western Australia's Josh Inglis would seem to be a lock to stay in the team after his first innings century at Cape Town batting at five.

Matthew Renshaw starred for Australia during the series against South Africa. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

Queenslander Matthew Renshaw's solid return to the opening position at Cape Town helps Inglis's cause.

Both Inglis and Renshaw are in the one-day squad but will get another shot at four-day cricket the following week.

Sheffield Shield matches are so often the forgotten cricket fixtures of the summer, but right now they are of crucial importance.

Sheffield Shield matches Wednesday, November 11:

New South Wales v South Australia, Sydney

Victoria v Western Australia, Melbourne

Queensland v Tasmania, Brisbane

World.title: Fagan's understudy Bruce named Brisbane's new senior coach
World.content:
Brisbane has chosen Cameron Bruce to be its new head coach after the departure of three-time premiership winner Chris Fagan.

The 47-year-old, who served as an assistant under Fagan for the last five seasons, beat out a strong collection of candidates including Nathan Buckley and Adam Simpson.

Bruce wins the Brisbane role having acquired more than a decade of AFL assistant coaching experience at three different clubs.

His coaching career began with Hawthorn, where he was an assistant under Alastair Clarkson for five seasons between 2013 and 2017, a period which yielded the club three premierships.

Bruce served as an assistant under Fagan for all three of Brisbane's premierships over the last three seasons. (James Wiltshire/AFL Photos via Getty Images)

Bruce then joined Carlton as an assistant under Brendon Bolton before departing at the end of 2021 following an extensive review into the underperforming club.

Bruce enjoyed a 13-year career as a player, making a combined 234 appearances for Melbourne and Hawthorn. He was a member of Melbourne's 2000 grand final side and was also a best and fairest winner for the Demons in 2008.

Fagan has joined Carlton as the club's new director of coaching after his exit from Brisbane following a decorated, decade-long stint.

Bruce is expected to be formally named Brisbane's senior coach on Tuesday.

World.title: Warner says Khawaja's ball-tampering claim '100 per cent accurate'
World.content:
David Warner has backed Usman Khawaja's claims on the 2018 ball tampering scandal, saying the statements in his book, Sabr, are "100 per cent accurate".

Warner, who was Australia's vice-captain at the time, was suspended from domestic and international cricket as a result of the scandal and was also permanently barred from leadership positions.

Speaking for the first time in eight years on the saga, Warner emphatically backed Khawaja, his childhood friend.

"Uzzie, I throw my full support behind you. I thank you for everything you've done," he said in an Instagram statement.

Loading Instagram content

"It's 100 per cent accurate, what you've said.

"Now everyone knows the truth, it's out there. People wanted to know it, you've come out and said it, and now people are saying, 'Why eight years on?' talking about selling a book.

"This is Usman's story. This is what Usman believes. Uzzie wrote down every single thing from that day on. Uzzie, thank you."

Warner slammed Cricket Australia's investigation into the incident in the wake of the 2018 tour of South Africa. Khawaja was not interviewed as a part of the probe.

David Warner was suspended from all international and domestic cricket for 12 months following Cricket Australia's investigation into the incident. (AAP Image/Ben Rushton)

"Now, this whole interview process was rushed and botched," he said.

"Uzzie was sitting next to Cameron Bancroft [in the dressing room]. Uzzie was not interviewed. How that is a thorough investigation? It baffles me.

"We're not here to point fingers and we're not opening old wounds.

"It's about accountability, transparency ensuring that the truth is properly examined, and perhaps it's time people stop scrutinising the person asking for accountability, and asking those responsible for the investigation to provide it.

"There [were] a lot of statements and inaccuracies over the last eight years that were out in the media by people and there were a lot of people who stayed silent."

Khawaja says he has thrown nobody 'under the bus' Usman Khawaja has revealed Steve Smith talked him out of going public with claims of widespread knowledge around ball-tampering during the 2018 saga.

Warner said his delayed response to Khawaja's claims being made public was down to explaining his involvement in the scandal to his daughters.

"The last couple of days, I've been talking to my daughters and that is why it's taken me a couple of days to get this out, because I've had to tell them exactly what had happened, especially my 12-year-old Ivy," he said.

"[She] wanted to know why we were holding her, why there were so many cameras and why we were all crying on TV.

"That was a hard thing to do, but one thing I did say is, 'Girls, tell the truth because lies will eventually get out.' It is a very tough time.

"This is for everyone in Australia. It has been the question that everyone is asking. Uzzie, you've said it how it is, it is 100 per cent accurate.

"It has been a tough time for my family, Steven [Smith] and Cameron [Bancroft] no doubt, but this is what needed to come out."

Warner is the first of the banned trio to speak publicly in the wake of Khawaja's comments being made public.

World.title: Greene's ex-teammate says he abandoned Giants with Cats move
World.content:
One of former GWS captain Toby Greene's ex-teammates has likened his move to Geelong as an abandonment.

The Giants' greatest player in their 15-year history, Greene left for the Cats in search of more family support for his young clan in his home state Victoria.

It was a sucker punch for the Giants, who had already parted ways with veteran forwards Jesse Hogan (Collingwood) and Jake Stringer (St Kilda).

The Giants' list overhaul did not end there, with star defender Lachie Whitfield (Carlton) and Kieren Briggs (Richmond) also leaving.

Toby Greene wasn't the only Giant to depart this summer, with veteran duo Jesse Hogan (left) and Jake Stringer (right) also joining rival clubs. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

Young GWS defender Joe Fonti didn't waste time sugarcoating when asked about Greene's trade to the Cats.

"It's obviously hard when your captain abandons your side," Fonti said on Monday.

"I know Toby's a great, great fella, and he would have had his reasons.

"I suppose that sort of justifies it for him, so I can respect that.

"But it's not easy when your captain abandons you.

"It does sting a little bit, but yeah, onto bigger and better things, I guess."

The Giants at least received a vote of confidence in their mission from midfielder Tom Green.

Due to come off contract at the end of next season, vice-captain Green knocked back big money from Tasmania and instead added two more years to his deal at GWS.

The 25-year-old, who missed all of last season with an ACL tear, has long been touted as Greene's replacement as captain.

Last year's vice-captain, Connor Idun, has been touted as a potential captain of the Giants. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Brendon Thorne)

Star defender Connor Idun is also a ready-made leader for the Giants after serving as a vice-captain last season with Green.

"It's definitely really special that that's something that he's done and committed to the club," Fonti said of Green.

"He's one of our best leaders, really well-spoken and a great role model.

"To have him potentially step into that captaincy role would be really special.

"We've got a bunch of good leaders, so it could be anyone, but he's definitely one of them."

Joe Fonti (left) says GWS's young brass of players are ready to step up in the absence of the departed veterans. (AAP/Darren England)

The Giants have lost 1,088 games of experience during the trade period, but Fonti says the young group is ready to rise to the challenge.

Fonti, who has played 44 games across three seasons, will be looking to take up Whitfield's spot in defence.

"That's really cool and exciting that we've sort of got a young core coming through," Fonti said.

"A lot of what's coming from the media at the moment is that we're young and we potentially might struggle this year.

"But I don't see it in that way whatsoever. We play our best when our backs are against the wall."

AAP

World.title: Leniu handed two-match ban after making money gesture to referees
World.content:
Parramatta's marquee off-season recruit Spencer Leniu is poised to miss the first two games of the 2027 campaign — including the Eels' trip to Las Vegas — after being sin-binned in Samoa's World Cup semifinal loss to Australia.

Leniu was sin-binned by referee Adam Gee for dissent late in the first half of Sunday's 44-12 loss to the Kangaroos in Sydney.

The prop made a money gesture with his hand as he walked towards the tunnel, a sign that many interpreted as the Samoan forward questioning the integrity and impartiality of match officials.

Against Samoa, Australia's old power conquered the new world Rugby league's Davids have gotten much bigger in recent times but Australia's win over Samoa in the World Cup semifinal was a reminder of Goliath's power.

Leniu was handed a grade three contrary conduct charge on Monday.

The 26-year-old, who will join Parramatta after winning the 2026 premiership with Sydney Roosters, will miss the club's opening two games of the season, which includes their trip to the US to face Gold Coast.

In the unlikely event he contests the charge, Leniu would incur an additional one-game ban if he were to lose his appeal.

The prop's outburst came during a frustrating night for Samoa, from which Samoan halves Ronald Volkman and Jarome Luai have avoided suspension for dangerous contact.

Samoa were on the wrong end of a 9-4 penalty count and coach Ben Gardiner suggested Gee had handed the Kangaroos several "home-ground calls".

"It was a real home-ground advantage for Australia," Gardiner said.

"They had the music pumping in the background and we had a lot of Samoan fans here to support us, which was brilliant.

"But they got the home-ground calls, got a really good start and then it was just too hard for us to chase back from there."

AAP

World.title: Luckless Test hopeful Morris continues horror injury run at party
World.content:
Test hopeful Lance Morris is again under an injury cloud after hurting his hand at a social event following Western Australia's one-day clash against England on Saturday.

It is understood Morris was at a party when he cut his non-bowling left hand.

Morris is set to consult a hand specialist today to determine the extent of the injury, and a timeline on his return to playing.

It comes just over a year after Morris had spinal fracture surgery he hoped would save his cricket career, after struggling to string games together in recent years.

Morris (centre) picked up three wickets in Western Australia's tour match against England at the weekend. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

There were encouraging signs in Saturday's outing as Morris finished with figures of 3–29 off 10 overs, claiming the wickets of England superstar Joe Root, as well as Tom Banton and Gus Atkinson.

Morris was called into Australia's Test squad in late 2022 after an impressive start to the Sheffield Shield season, with some considering it a matter of time until he made his Test debut.

However, since then he has managed just three one-day internationals, six Shield matches and 22 Big Bash games, due to a wretched injury run.

Ahead of last season Morris underwent stabilisation surgery, a process that involves bolts and wire being put into his lower back.

Labuschagne axed from Aussie squad for New Zealand Tests Australia's chairman of selectors confirms the omission of Marnus Labuschagne after an extended lean run of form at the Test level.

Just last week he told ABC Sport's Tom Wildie he hoped to bowl faster than ever after the procedure, hopeful it would not affect his pace and strength.

"That [a loss of pace] was a huge question for me leading into the surgery because I knew that was the asset that made me potentially selectable for red-ball cricket," he said last week.

"I had to look around at other guys that have had the surgery, the likes of Jofra [Archer], Jasprit Bumrah, the guys that have returned to Test cricket at the same speed if not better.

"I've got one eye on the speed gun at all times to see where things are at, but I'm pretty happy with where it's at."

With regular fast bowlers Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Captain Pat Cummins all well into their 30s, Australia is expected to soon be looking for other pace bowling options in the Test arena, with Morris long considered a likely contender for a spot in the XI.

Tech.title: Apple’s $50 Intelligence Usage Packs extend access to some AI features
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

After publishing a support article in early September outlining usage limits for some Apple Intelligence features, the company has updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for a one-time purchase price of $49.99, as spotted by 9to5Mac. It has a built-in AI assistant to do things like “start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.”

These Intelligence Usage Packs, as Apple calls them, will allow users to continue accessing certain Apple Intelligence features that have usage limits because they rely on cloud-based AI models from OpenAI or Google Gemini. The Usage Packs can only be used by the Apple Account that purchased them (Family Sharing isn’t supported) and, as Apple explains on its website, any unused additional usage will roll over from month to month, but will expire 12 months after it was purchased.

For Logic Pro, Apple says the usage limit is “impacted by the complexity of conversations you have with the assistant.” Users finding themselves running out of access can find the option to buy an Intelligence Usage Pack in the Intelligence Features > Show Usage section of the app’s main menu. Currently, only Logic Pro has the option to buy more usage, but it’s expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers that are getting access to Apple’s AI chatbot.

Tech.title: Anthropic launches new Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2 models
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Anthropic is announcing two new models today: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, which it says are designed to take on “daunting” technical challenges. The company claims the new models show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, and can generate outputs faster than the 5.1 versions of the Fable and Mythos models.

Claude Fable 5.2 is good at challenging software engineering problems, Anthropic says, and can orchestrate agent teams and tackle long-running projects. The new model has also solved some complex scientific problems, including two open theoretical physics problems.

During prerelease testing, the two models have “helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours,” Anthropic says.

Claude Fable 5.2 is launching today. As for Claude Mythos 5.2, only vetted organizations will have access to start. The new 5.2 models follow the release of Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 in September.

The price of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate has fluctuated between $20 and $30 per month over the last year, but you can get three months of the top plan for around $19 per month. At Newegg, using the coupon code BNWF2656 at checkout knocks $11 off the usual cost of a three-month subscription. That brings the price down to just $57.99 for three months. In addition to full access to over 500 games on both Xbox consoles and Windows PC machines, the upgraded Ultimate plan includes EA Play and Ubisoft Plus Classics, which have their own libraries and benefits, and Fortnite Crew for full access to the Fortnite battles passes. On Xbox, Ultimate enables online multiplayer, as well.

Previously a straightforward proposition, the service has undergone a variety of changes over the last year that has made it slightly less appealing. Xbox Game Pass Ultimate was previously $29.99 per month, but earlier this year Microsoft removed the Call of Duty games from the library, and in the process dropped the price to $22.99.

More recently, Microsoft added hourly limits to cloud gaming. All Game Pass plan subscribers previously enjoyed an unlimited amount of cloud gaming on their computer or mobile device, but now plans scale the number of included hours, with the Ultimate plan including 15 hours per month. That news came just weeks before announcing pay-as-you-go plans for non-Game Pass subscribers.

Once built, it’s a sizable set, standing 13.5 inches tall and 15.5 inches deep, and the Pikachu has posable ears and limbs. This seems like a fantastic gift, either to yourself or to another Pokémon fan you care about.

Tech.title: Instagram’s Effect Builder makes new filters from AI prompts
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After expanding its Edits app to macOS last week, Instagram’s next move is launching this Effect Builder that generates custom filters for your Stories posts with AI. Available now for US residents who are over 18, it has a prompt box for describing your filter idea to the chatbot, with an option to attach style reference images.

Then you can upload your own photos to preview the AI-generating effects, and ask for changes in follow-up prompts. There’s also an option to allow Instagram’s AI to rewrite your prompt, which turned my one-line test prompt “Make a filter that turns photos into comic book pages” into several AI-generated paragraphs of detailed style requests on everything from color palette to lighting. The filter Effect Builder generated as a result still looked nearly identical to its output for my original one-liner.

Previous Next

1 / 2 Instagram’s AI rewrote my prompt into lengthy, detailed instructions. Screenshot: The Verge / Instagram

You can submit your filters to Instagram directly from Effect Builder, but effects have to pass a safety review before they’ll be available to other users. Instagram says after an effect is approved, it “shows up in Instagram Stories for anyone to use, and whenever someone uses your effect we’ll link back to your profile so that it’s easy for others to find your work.”

Tech.title: James Gunn is out as DC movie leader
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Soon, James Gunn and Peter Safran will no longer head up Skydance’s DC Studios. After taking the helm of DC Studios as co-CEOs in 2022, Gunn and Safran are being replaced by former Marvel SVP of Production and Development Jeremy Latcham, Deadline reports.

However, Gunn and Safran will “continue to produce on various DC projects” and are still working on the Superman followup Man of Tomorrow, Deadline says. Gunn also posted on Instagram that he and Safran have “just been engaged on another DC project which I’m writing.” In his Instagram post, Gunn said that his time at DC Studios has been “trying, to say the least. I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that).”

The change in leadership follows the recent closure of the megamerger between Paramount and Warner Bros., which resulted in the combined Skydance company that’s led by CEO David Ellison. Latcham takes over DC Studios on December 1st and will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, the co-chairs of Skydance Motion Picture Group.

Tech.title: The future of AI hinges on… Jensen Huang’s sex life?
Tech.content:
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.

I would prefer that these people’s sex lives were none of my business but I guess we have to talk about Jensen Huang and the National Security Incident. Who could have guessed that the guy who was out here signing titties might not have great judgment about how to behave around women?

Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — is a former TV reporter. That was before she became “an executive” at Megaspeed, which bought $4.8 billion of hard-to-get Nvidia chips, starting around the time she was being photographed with Jensen in a Taipei bar in 2024. “To many in the industry, the well-funded push by Megaspeed into A.I. appeared to come out of nowhere,” The New York Times wrote, tactfully. Our girl Alice is also an alleged honeypot who was recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security. (China is denying all this, btw.)

You know shit is going good when your corporate spokesperson has to tell the Times that of course your company does not disclose classified information to your customers

What is Megaspeed? Well. The company has ties to the Chinese military and builds data centers in “Southeast Asia” (it has offices in Singapore and Indonesia) to sell compute to Alibaba. The chips it is using to do that are banned from being imported to China. Incidentally, Nvidia has been lobbying very intensely to get rid of import controls on its chips so it can sell them in China.

This is all public knowledge in part because Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly “oversaw” a memo detailing Alice’s recruitment and relationship with Jensen, and then someone leaked it. (Powerful memo game, Marco, getting credit for one you didn’t even write!) Rubio passed his little note around in May, ahead of a trip to China taken by President Donald Trump. Jensen initially didn’t make the list of invitees on the trip — at least, not until Trump saw media coverage of the perceived snub. Trump and Jensen? They’re close. Which makes it even more interesting that Trump was personally briefed on the findings and did nothing, according to the Times.

You know shit is going good when your corporate spokesperson has to tell the Times that of course your company does not disclose classified information to your customers. John Rizzo, the spokesman, also told the Times that Nvidia’s customers don’t ask Nvidia to lobby for changes to the chip restriction. Bit of a hat on a hat, John. First of all, they don’t have to — Nvidia’s financial incentives do it for them. Second, imagine this is a regular company. The business model of Megaspeed is that the chips are restricted, and that Megaspeed gets ahold of them. Megaspeed has no incentive to upend this situation! Unless, you know, it’s acting against its financial interest because it’s a front for Chinese spies… in which case, that statement is going to be embarrassing.

Speaking of embarrassing, Rizzo told the Times “that Mr. Huang’s interactions with Ms. Huang were ‘not unusual’ and consistent with the kinds of meetings he has with any of Nvidia’s many customers.” Oh, okay. Who else was Jensen fucking?

Nvidia has an extraordinary structure

Because two days after that statement, Jensen sent the most incredible email addressed “To my colleagues at Nvidia” in which he admitted he had been “unfaithful.” Then, he wrote, “To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.” Are… your wife and family on the Nvidia employee email list?

Well, yes! His son is a director of product management; his daughter is a senior marketing director. He even gave a job to his son-in-law!

Also, Nvidia has an extraordinary structure. Jensen has 60 direct reports. Leave aside that there is no possible way to manage that many people well. I would like to direct your attention to something else entirely: If he is in trouble, there is no part of the company that is untouched. The usual problems attain, of course — he was in a position to have gotten any information she might have requested! He could have left company laptops available for infiltration! But because of the structure, he also could have issued commands to his many direct reports that benefited the CCP. Neat! I sure hope someone who knows a lot about cybersecurity is going through Nvidia with a fine-toothed comb.

Is he in trouble? Well, Nvidia is opening an investigation into Jensen, who is also its largest individual shareholder. (At least there’s no dual-class stock!) Nvidia shares are, as of this writing, down almost five percent, which seems like an underreaction.

I don’t know where Jensen’s actual wife, Lori, is in all this

Perhaps more consequentially, the Democratic Party just swept back into power and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) seems mad. Also, the voters hate the data centers that house Nvidia chips, and I notice a lot of ambitious politicians thinking about the next presidential elections. For instance, there’s Rubio’s name attached to the memo. I also notice Trump’s popularity is at an all-time nadir. Besides any Democrats positioning themselves for a run, a Republican looking to create some daylight between himself and Trump could easily do so by going to town on Jensen, who is Trump’s buddy. I do not think Rubio is the only ambition monster to worry about.

I don’t know where Jensen’s actual wife, Lori, is in all this. They got married in 1985. She gave up her job as a microchip designer to raise their kids. I would be very surprised if there is a prenup. I would be somewhat surprised if there was a postnup. Jensen doesn’t own as much of Nvidia as Jeff Bezos did of Amazon when he cheated on and divorced his wife, but it’s something to keep an eye on, if Lori decides she’s out.

We’ve talked once or twice about Nvidia’s central role in the AI ecosystem — and specifically, that it is heavily involved in financing AI neoclouds. It has investments in SpaceX, CoreWeave (where it was, as of the time of the IPO, the company’s second-biggest customer), and OpenAI, among others. Jensen has been promoting “compute as an asset class.”

Nvidia is, effectively, the central bank of AI

One of the reasons I have been uncertain about when and how the AI bubble will pop is that it seems to me that Nvidia can bail out any or all of these companies anytime it needs to, just like it did for CoreWeave when its IPO was threatened. Neoclouds exist because Nvidia wanted to create competition for its chips, so its biggest customers — Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Oracle — couldn’t exert too much pricing pressure. Certainly I am not the only person who has noticed that Nvidia is, effectively, the central bank of AI. If Nvidia is in a particularly bad way, it kind of seems like, at minimum, the neoclouds get fucked too. Oddly, CoreWeave is up about 6 percent as of this writing; the stock market moves in mysterious ways.

So Jensen can’t go down, as there’s no one who can replace him, and Nvidia can’t go down, as nothing can replace it. The AI industry better hope there isn’t some further revelation coming that would make one of these things unavoidable, such as the investigation finding proof that Alice directly accessed Nvidia’s systems while Jensen was showering or something. Might also be bad if, say, a US Commerce Department inquiry into Megaspeed was halted after Nvidia intervened. Didn’t we just hear somewhere that Jensen had been influencing the Trump administration’s policy on export controls?

Anyway, as of this note, Jensen isn’t planning to step down as CEO. Might as well settle in for the most fun we’ll have until we find out that Musk did IVF with a family member of Chinese President Xi Jinping.
